\section*{Provenance}
\label{sec:provenance}
This volume is the single consolidated frontier document for the geometric
$q$-deformation of the Fabius--Rvachev system.  Parts~I--VII continue the
seven-part synthesis assembled on 28~August 2026; Parts~VIII--XII absorb the
five further reports listed below, which previously stood as separate packages
under \path{q-fabius-parameter-deformations/} and
\path{geometric-sinc-and-exponent-families/}.  Labels, citation keys, and asset
paths are mechanically prefixed per part, \texttt{p1:}--\texttt{p12:}, with
\texttt{p0:} reserved for the common framework of Part~0.  Shared definitions,
normalizations, and background results are stated once in Part~0; each absorbed
part's own preliminaries fix only its local letters and record the exact
dictionary to the canonical normalization.  The absorbed sources are deleted
from the working tree once merged: git history is the archive, and the SHA-256
digests below pin the absorbed snapshots.

\section{Purpose of this part}
\label{p0:sec:purpose}

Each of the twelve numbered parts of this volume was written as an
independent report, and each therefore opened by fixing the same objects
for itself: the geometric-uniform family, its centering and scaling, its
moment generating and characteristic functions, the Bernoulli convention
behind its cumulants, and the sinc and Fourier normalizations.  Those
openings did not agree.  Three different affine normalizations of one
random variable appear across the volume, two different sinc arguments,
and the same letters $X_q$ and $Y_q$ denote different --- though affinely
related --- objects in different parts.

This part removes that redundancy.  It states the shared material once,
with complete proofs, in one fixed normalization, and then gives the
exact dictionary from each numbered part's local convention to the
canonical one.  Every later part now opens with a short conventions
paragraph pointing here rather than with a re-derivation.  Nothing in the
mathematics of the absorbed reports is changed by this; what changes is
that a formula carried from one part into another can be transported
along a dictionary entry proved in \cref{p0:sec:dictionary} instead of by
inspection.

Three points of usage.  First, results are numbered $0.n.m$ inside this
part and $\mathrm{N}.n.m$ inside numbered Part~$\mathrm{N}$; a reference
of the form ``\cref{p0:thm:cumulants}'' therefore always resolves here.
Second, all labels in this part carry the prefix \texttt{p0:}, continuing
the per-part prefixing scheme described in the provenance section.
Third, the notation is that of the shared corpus contract
\path{docs/fabius-notation.tex} and of the notation catalogue; symbols
introduced only for this volume are declared where they first appear and
are collected in \cref{p0:sec:register}.

\section{The canonical geometric-uniform family}
\label{p0:sec:family}

\begin{definition}[Canonical geometric-uniform family]
\label{p0:def:family}
Let $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$ be independent random variables, each uniform on
$[0,1]$, and put $V_j\DefinitionEquals U_j-\tfrac12$, so that each $V_j$
is uniform on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ and symmetric.  For real $q$ with
$\AbsoluteValue q<1$ set
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:family}
 \GeoLaw{q}\DefinitionEquals(1-q)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^{j}U_j,
 \qquad
 \GeoLawCentered{q}\DefinitionEquals\GeoLaw{q}-\frac12
 =(1-q)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^{j}V_j .
\end{equation}
Write $G_q(x)=\Probability(\GeoLaw{q}\le x)$ for the distribution
function and $g_q=G_q'$ for the density where it exists, and let
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:sigma}
 \sigma_q\DefinitionEquals\sqrt{\Variance(\GeoLaw{q})},
 \qquad
 \GeoLawStandard{q}\DefinitionEquals\frac{\GeoLawCentered{q}}{\sigma_q}
\end{equation}
for the standardized variable.  We call \eqref{p0:eq:family} the
\emph{canonical normalization}; $\GeoLaw{q}$ is the \emph{uncentered},
$\GeoLawCentered{q}$ the \emph{centered}, and $\GeoLawStandard{q}$ the
\emph{standardized} member of the family at parameter $q$.
\end{definition}

The choice of $[0,1]$ for the seed variables is what makes $q=1/2$
reproduce the bounded Fabius function on the nose
(\cref{p0:prop:fabius-point}); the two competing normalizations that use
seeds uniform on $[-1,1]$ differ from $\GeoLawCentered{q}$ by the single
factor $2$, recorded in \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}.

\begin{proposition}[Convergence, mean, and support]
\label{p0:prop:basic}
For every real $q$ with $\AbsoluteValue q<1$ the series in
\eqref{p0:eq:family} converges absolutely almost surely and in every
$L^p$, $1\le p<\infty$.  Moreover $\Expectation\GeoLaw{q}=\tfrac12$, the
law of $\GeoLawCentered{q}$ is symmetric about $0$, and
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:support}
 \SupportOf{\GeoLaw{q}}=
 \begin{cases}
  [0,1], & 0\le q<1,\\[0.35em]
  \displaystyle\left[-\frac{a}{1-a},\ \frac{1}{1-a}\right],
   & q=-a,\ 0<a<1 .
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In both cases the support is a compact interval with midpoint $\tfrac12$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Since $0\le U_j\le1$, the partial sums are dominated termwise by
$\AbsoluteValue{1-q}\sum_j\AbsoluteValue q^{j}
 =\AbsoluteValue{1-q}/(1-\AbsoluteValue q)<\infty$, so the series
converges absolutely for every realization; $L^p$ convergence follows
from the uniform bound $\AbsoluteValue{\GeoLaw{q}}\le
\AbsoluteValue{1-q}/(1-\AbsoluteValue q)$ and dominated convergence.
Because the weights $(1-q)q^{j}$ sum to $1$ and
$\Expectation U_j=\tfrac12$, monotone convergence gives
$\Expectation\GeoLaw{q}=\tfrac12$.  Each $V_j$ is symmetric and the $V_j$
are independent, so $-\GeoLawCentered{q}$ has the same law as
$\GeoLawCentered{q}$.

For the support, write $c_j(q)=(1-q)q^{j}$.  The map
$(u_j)\mapsto\sum_jc_j(q)u_j$ is continuous from $[0,1]^{\NaturalNumbers}$
with the product topology (compact) onto its image, and the image is the
set of all such sums, hence the interval
$\bigl[\sum_j c_j(q)^-,\ \sum_j c_j(q)^+\bigr]$ with
$c^{\pm}=\max(\pm c,0)$; every intermediate value is attained because the
weights may be varied continuously.  The law charges every nonempty
relatively open subset of that interval, since the $U_j$ have full
support in $[0,1]$.  For $0\le q<1$ all $c_j(q)\ge0$ and
$\sum_jc_j(q)=1$, giving $[0,1]$.  For $q=-a$ with $0<a<1$,
\[
 \sum_{j\ \mathrm{even}}c_j(-a)=(1+a)\sum_{i\ge0}a^{2i}
  =\frac{1+a}{1-a^{2}}=\frac1{1-a},
 \qquad
 \sum_{j\ \mathrm{odd}}c_j(-a)=-\frac{a(1+a)}{1-a^{2}}=-\frac a{1-a},
\]
which is \eqref{p0:eq:support}.  The two endpoints average to
$\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac1{1-a}-\tfrac a{1-a}\bigr)=\tfrac12$, and for
$0\le q<1$ the midpoint of $[0,1]$ is again $\tfrac12$, consistently with
the symmetry of $\GeoLawCentered{q}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Affine fixed point and its uniqueness]
\label{p0:prop:fixed-point}
Let $U$ be uniform on $[0,1]$ and independent of $\GeoLaw{q}'$, an
independent copy of $\GeoLaw{q}$.  Then
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:fixed-point}
 \GeoLaw{q}\EqualInLaw(1-q)U+q\GeoLaw{q}' .
\end{equation}
Conversely, for every real $q$ with $\AbsoluteValue q<1$, the law of
$\GeoLaw{q}$ is the unique probability measure with finite first moment
satisfying \eqref{p0:eq:fixed-point}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Splitting off the term $j=0$ in \eqref{p0:eq:family} gives
$\GeoLaw{q}=(1-q)U_0+q\bigl((1-q)\sum_{j\ge0}q^{j}U_{j+1}\bigr)$, and the
bracket is an independent copy of $\GeoLaw{q}$; this is
\eqref{p0:eq:fixed-point}.

For uniqueness, let $\mathcal P_1(\RealNumbers)$ carry the Wasserstein-$1$
metric $W_1$, under which it is complete.  Define
$T(\nu)=\LawOf{(1-q)U+qZ}$ with $Z\sim\nu$ independent of $U$.  If
$Z\sim\nu$ and $Z'\sim\nu'$ are coupled optimally, then
$\bigl((1-q)U+qZ,\ (1-q)U+qZ'\bigr)$ --- with the \emph{same} $U$ --- is a
coupling of $T(\nu)$ and $T(\nu')$, whence
\[
 W_1\bigl(T(\nu),T(\nu')\bigr)
 \le\Expectation\AbsoluteValue{q(Z-Z')}
 =\AbsoluteValue q\,W_1(\nu,\nu') .
\]
Thus $T$ is a contraction with ratio $\AbsoluteValue q<1$ and has exactly
one fixed point in $\mathcal P_1(\RealNumbers)$.  By the first paragraph
$\LawOf{\GeoLaw{q}}$ is a fixed point, and it has finite first moment by
\cref{p0:prop:basic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
\label{p0:rem:uniqueness-scope}
\cref{p0:prop:fixed-point} needs no support or density hypothesis, only a
finite first moment; this is the form used in
\cref{p7:sec:germ} and in Part~VIII.  The finite-moment restriction
cannot simply be dropped: without it the contraction argument has no
complete metric to run in.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[The Fabius--Rvachev point]
\label{p0:prop:fabius-point}
At $q=\tfrac12$ the distribution function $G_{1/2}$ is the bounded Fabius
function $\FabiusBounded$, and the density is
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:fabius-point}
 g_{1/2}(x)=2\RvachevUp(2x-1),\qquad x\in[0,1],
\end{equation}
where $\RvachevUp$ is the Rvachev up-function, normalized to be supported
on $[-1,1]$ with $\int\RvachevUp=1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
At $q=\tfrac12$, \eqref{p0:eq:fixed-point} reads
$\GeoLaw{1/2}\EqualInLaw\tfrac12U+\tfrac12\GeoLaw{1/2}'$, which is exactly
the defining self-similarity of the Fabius distribution; by
\cref{p0:prop:fixed-point} the solution with finite mean is unique, and
$\FabiusBounded$ is by definition the distribution function of that
solution.  For the density, $\GeoLawCentered{1/2}=\GeoLaw{1/2}-\tfrac12$
satisfies $\GeoLawCentered{1/2}=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-(j+1)}V_j$ with
$V_j$ uniform on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$; scaling by $2$ turns this into
$2\GeoLawCentered{1/2}=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}V_j'$ with $V_j'$ uniform on
$[-1,1]$, i.e. into the standard Rvachev series, whose density is
$\RvachevUp$.  Undoing the two affine steps gives
\eqref{p0:eq:fabius-point}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Degenerate and boundary parameters]
\label{p0:rem:endpoints}
At $q=0$ the family degenerates to $\GeoLaw{0}=U_0$, uniform on $[0,1]$,
and every product formula below reduces to its single $j=0$ factor.  As
$q\uparrow1$ the variance \eqref{p0:eq:variance} tends to $0$ and
$\GeoLaw{q}\to\tfrac12$ in probability, while the standardized variable
$\GeoLawStandard{q}$ converges in law to the standard Gaussian; the
sharp form of that statement, with all correction orders, is the subject
of Parts~X and~XI.  As $q\downarrow-1$ the support
\eqref{p0:eq:support} escapes to $\RealNumbers$; Parts~VII and~VIII treat
that regime through the reciprocal germ rather than by a limit.
\end{remark}

\section{Transforms, the two sinc conventions, and the Mahler equation}
\label{p0:sec:transforms}

Throughout the volume $\SincRad$ and $\SincPi$ are the two normalized
cardinal sines of the corpus contract,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:sinc}
 \SincRad z=\frac{\sin z}{z},
 \qquad
 \SincPi z=\frac{\sin(\pi z)}{\pi z},
 \qquad
 \SincRad 0=\SincPi 0=1,
\end{equation}
both entire and even.  We write $E$ for the normalized exponential
difference quotient and $\operatorname{sinhc}$ for the hyperbolic cardinal
sine,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:E-sinhc}
 E(z)=\frac{\EulerE^{z}-1}{z},\quad E(0)=1,
 \qquad
 \sinhc z=\frac{\sinh z}{z},\quad \sinhc 0=1,
\end{equation}
so that $E(z)=\EulerE^{z/2}\sinhc(z/2)$ and
$\sinhc z=\SincRad(\ImaginaryUnit z)$.  The Fourier convention is the
angular one of the contract,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:fourier}
 \FourierAngular{f}(\omega)
 =\int_{\RealNumbers}\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit\omega x}f(x)\Differential x,
 \qquad
 f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}
   \EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\omega x}\FourierAngular{f}(\omega)
   \Differential\omega ,
\end{equation}
so that the characteristic function of a variable $Z$ with density $f$ is
$\CharacteristicFunction{Z}(t)=\FourierAngular{f}(-t)$.  Individual parts
that state their inversion formula in the opposite sign convention are
listed in \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}; since every density occurring in this
volume is real and symmetric about its own mean, the two conventions
differ only by that recorded sign and never by a factor.

\begin{proposition}[Product formulas for the transforms]
\label{p0:prop:products}
For real $\AbsoluteValue q<1$ the moment generating function of
$\GeoLaw{q}$ is entire and
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:mgf}
 \MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t)
 \DefinitionEquals\Expectation\EulerE^{t\GeoLaw{q}}
 =\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}E\bigl((1-q)q^{j}t\bigr),
 \qquad t\in\ComplexNumbers ,
\end{equation}
while the characteristic function of the centered variable is
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:cf}
 \CharacteristicFunction{q}(t)
 \DefinitionEquals\Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit t\GeoLawCentered{q}}
 =\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}
   \SincRad\!\left(\frac{(1-q)q^{j}t}{2}\right),
 \qquad t\in\ComplexNumbers .
\end{equation}
Both products converge locally uniformly on $\ComplexNumbers$, and
\eqref{p0:eq:cf} converges locally uniformly in $(q,t)$ on
$\SetOf{\AbsoluteValue q<1}\times\ComplexNumbers$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $U$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and $c\in\ComplexNumbers$,
$\Expectation\EulerE^{tcU}=\int_0^1\EulerE^{tcu}\Differential u=E(ct)$,
and for $V$ uniform on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$,
$\Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit tcV}
 =\SincRad(ct/2)$.  Independence gives the corresponding finite products
for the partial sums $S_N=(1-q)\sum_{j\le N}q^{j}U_j$.

For the passage to the limit fix $R>0$ and $\AbsoluteValue t\le R$.  Both
$E(w)-1$ and $\SincRad(w)-1$ are $O(\AbsoluteValue w)$ and
$O(\AbsoluteValue w^{2})$ respectively as $w\to0$, uniformly on compact
sets, so with $w_j=(1-q)q^{j}t$ we have
$\sum_j\AbsoluteValue{E(w_j)-1}<\infty$ and
$\sum_j\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad(w_j/2)-1}<\infty$, uniformly for
$\AbsoluteValue t\le R$; for the second sum the bound is
$O\bigl(R^{2}\AbsoluteValue{1-q}^{2}\sum_j\AbsoluteValue q^{2j}\bigr)
 =O\bigl(R^{2}\AbsoluteValue{1-q}^{2}/(1-\AbsoluteValue q^{2})\bigr)$,
which is bounded on $\AbsoluteValue q\le\rho<1$.  The Weierstrass
criterion for infinite products then gives locally uniform convergence,
with the joint statement in $(q,t)$ for \eqref{p0:eq:cf}.  Since
$S_N\to\GeoLaw{q}$ almost surely and $\AbsoluteValue{S_N}$ is bounded by
the deterministic constant of \cref{p0:prop:basic}, dominated convergence
identifies the limits with $\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}$ and
$\CharacteristicFunction{q}$.  Entirety of
$\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}$ follows from the local uniform convergence
of the product of entire factors.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Mahler equation and the centered germ]
\label{p0:prop:mahler}
With $\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}$ as in \eqref{p0:eq:mgf},
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:mahler}
 \MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t)
 =E\bigl((1-q)t\bigr)\,\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(qt),
 \qquad
 \MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(0)=1 .
\end{equation}
The centered germ
$C_q(t)\DefinitionEquals\EulerE^{-t/2}\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t)$
satisfies $C_q(-t)=C_q(t)$; consequently all odd cumulants of
$\GeoLawCentered{q}$ vanish.  Finally, if $q^{n}\ne1$ for every
$n\ge1$, then \eqref{p0:eq:mahler} together with the normalization
$\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(0)=1$ determines the formal power series
$\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}$ uniquely.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Splitting the factor $j=0$ out of \eqref{p0:eq:mgf} and reindexing gives
\eqref{p0:eq:mahler}.  Since the weights sum to $1$ and
$E(-z)=\EulerE^{-z}E(z)$,
\[
 \MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(-t)
 =\prod_{j\ge0}E\bigl(-(1-q)q^{j}t\bigr)
 =\EulerE^{-t\sum_j(1-q)q^{j}}\prod_{j\ge0}E\bigl((1-q)q^{j}t\bigr)
 =\EulerE^{-t}\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t),
\]
which is exactly $C_q(-t)=C_q(t)$.  An even function has vanishing odd
Taylor coefficients, and the cumulant generating function
$\log C_q$ is then even as well, so the odd cumulants of
$\GeoLawCentered{q}$ vanish.

For the last claim write
$\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(q)t^{n}$ with
$a_0=1$.  Comparing coefficients of $t^{n}$ in \eqref{p0:eq:mahler}, and
using $E(z)=\sum_{r\ge0}z^{r}/(r+1)!$, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:an-recurrence}
 (1-q^{n})\,a_n(q)
 =\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{(1-q)^{r}q^{\,n-r}}{(r+1)!}\,a_{n-r}(q) .
\end{equation}
When $q^{n}\ne1$ this determines $a_n$ from $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Coordinates used by the Lean development]
\label{p0:rem:lean-coordinates}
The formalization names the geometric sinc product in the frequency
coordinate
$\operatorname{geometricSincProduct}(q,u)=\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad(\pi q^{j}u)$.
Comparing with \eqref{p0:eq:cf},
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:lean-dictionary}
 \CharacteristicFunction{q}(t)
 =\operatorname{geometricSincProduct}\!
   \left(q,\ \frac{(1-q)t}{2\pi}\right),
\end{equation}
so a manuscript frequency $t$ and the Lean product variable differ by the
factor $2\pi/(1-q)$.  At $q=\tfrac12$ the further identity
$\operatorname{centeredSincProduct}(z)
 =\operatorname{rvachevFourierProduct}(z/2\pi)$ records the corresponding
conversion for the Rvachev product; the relevant declarations are
\lean{Fabius.geometricSincProduct} and
\lean{Fabius.centeredSincProduct_eq_rvachevFourierProduct}.  Part~IX
states the same dictionary in its own variable, and Part~II uses the
$\SincPi$ form; \cref{p0:tab:dictionary} lists both.
\end{remark}

\section{Bernoulli numbers, exact cumulants, and the Bell bridge}
\label{p0:sec:cumulants}

Throughout, the Bernoulli numbers are those of the convention
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:bernoulli}
 \frac{z}{\EulerE^{z}-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}B_n\frac{z^{n}}{n!},
 \qquad
 B_0=1,\ B_1=-\tfrac12,\ B_2=\tfrac16,\
 B_4=-\tfrac1{30},\ B_6=\tfrac1{42},
\end{equation}
so that $B_{2m+1}=0$ for $m\ge1$.  Every part of this volume uses this
convention; none uses the ``even-index-only'' variant.

\begin{lemma}[Logarithmic cardinal-sine series]
\label{p0:lem:log-sinhc}
For $\AbsoluteValue z<2\pi$,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:log-sinhc-half}
 \log\frac{\sinh(z/2)}{z/2}
 =\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,\frac{z^{2m}}{(2m)!},
\end{equation}
and equivalently, for $\AbsoluteValue w<\pi$,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:log-sinhc-full}
 \log\sinhc w
 =\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m\,(2m)!}\,w^{2m}.
\end{equation}
Both radii are exact.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
From \eqref{p0:eq:bernoulli},
$\frac{z}{\EulerE^{z}-1}+\frac z2=\frac z2\coth\frac z2
 =\sum_{m\ge0}B_{2m}\frac{z^{2m}}{(2m)!}$,
the odd terms cancelling because $B_1=-\tfrac12$ and $B_{2m+1}=0$.
Hence
\[
 \frac{\Differential}{\Differential z}
 \log\frac{\sinh(z/2)}{z/2}
 =\frac12\coth\frac z2-\frac1z
 =\frac1z\left(\frac z2\coth\frac z2-1\right)
 =\sum_{m\ge1}B_{2m}\frac{z^{2m-1}}{(2m)!} .
\]
Integrating from $0$, where the left side vanishes, gives
\eqref{p0:eq:log-sinhc-half}.  Substituting $z=2w$ turns
$\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\frac{(2w)^{2m}}{(2m)!}$ into
$\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m(2m)!}w^{2m}$, which is
\eqref{p0:eq:log-sinhc-full}.  The function $\sinh(z/2)/(z/2)$ is entire,
equals $1$ at $0$, and has its zeros exactly at $z=2\pi\ImaginaryUnit k$,
$k\in\IntegerNumbers\setminus\SetOf0$; the principal logarithm is
therefore holomorphic on the disc of radius $2\pi$ and no larger, and the
same computation in the variable $w$ gives radius $\pi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact cumulants of the family]
\label{p0:thm:cumulants}
Let $\AbsoluteValue q<1$ be real.  Then all odd cumulants of
$\GeoLawCentered{q}$ vanish and, for every $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:cumulants}
 \kappa_{2m}\bigl(\GeoLawCentered{q}\bigr)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,\frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}} .
\end{equation}
In particular
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:variance}
 \sigma_q^{2}=\Variance\bigl(\GeoLaw{q}\bigr)
 =\frac{B_2}{2}\,\frac{(1-q)^{2}}{1-q^{2}}
 =\frac{1-q}{12(1+q)},
\end{equation}
and the standardized cumulants are
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants}
 \lambda_{2m}(q)
 \DefinitionEquals\kappa_{2m}\bigl(\GeoLawStandard{q}\bigr)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,12^{m}\,\frac{(1-q^{2})^{m}}{1-q^{2m}},
 \qquad m\ge2,\quad\text{for real }\AbsoluteValue q<1 .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The cumulant generating function of $V_j$ is
$\log\Expectation\EulerE^{zV_j}=\log\bigl(\sinh(z/2)/(z/2)\bigr)$, so by
\cref{p0:lem:log-sinhc} the cumulants of a centered uniform are
$\kappa_{2m}(V)=(2m)!\cdot\frac{B_{2m}}{2m(2m)!}=\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}$ and
$\kappa_{2m+1}(V)=0$.  Cumulants are additive over independent summands
and homogeneous of degree $n$ in order $n$, so for
$\AbsoluteValue z$ small
\[
 \log\Expectation\EulerE^{z\GeoLawCentered{q}}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}\log\Expectation\EulerE^{z(1-q)q^{j}V_j}
 =\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{\kappa_{2m}(V)}{(2m)!}\,z^{2m}
   (1-q)^{2m}\sum_{j\ge0}q^{2mj},
\]
the interchange being legitimate because the double series converges
absolutely for $\AbsoluteValue{z(1-q)}<2\pi$.  Summing the geometric
series gives \eqref{p0:eq:cumulants}, and $m=1$ with $B_2=\tfrac16$ gives
\eqref{p0:eq:variance} after cancelling $1-q$.  Finally, since
$\kappa_{2m}$ is homogeneous of degree $2m$,
\[
 \lambda_{2m}(q)=\frac{\kappa_{2m}(\GeoLawCentered{q})}{\sigma_q^{2m}}
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}}
  \left(\frac{12(1-q^{2})}{(1-q)^{2}}\right)^{m}
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,12^{m}\,\frac{(1-q^{2})^{m}}{1-q^{2m}} ,
\]
which is \eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants}.  For $m=1$ the same
formula returns $\lambda_2=1$, as it must.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Bell bridge and rationality]
\label{p0:prop:bell}
Let $\ExponentialCompleteBellPolynomial{n}$ denote the complete
exponential Bell polynomial.  Then for every $n\ge0$
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:bell}
 \Expectation\bigl(\GeoLawCentered{q}\bigr)^{n}
 =\ExponentialCompleteBellPolynomial{n}
   \bigl(\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_n\bigr),
 \qquad
 \kappa_i=\kappa_i\bigl(\GeoLawCentered{q}\bigr),
\end{equation}
and consequently every centered moment of $\GeoLaw{q}$ is a rational
function of $q$ with rational coefficients, of the form
$P_n(q)/\prod_{m=1}^{\Floor{n/2}}(1-q^{2m})$ for a polynomial
$P_n\in\RationalNumbers[q]$; the odd centered moments vanish.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Identity \eqref{p0:eq:bell} is the standard moment--cumulant relation,
valid whenever the moment generating function is analytic near $0$, which
holds by \cref{p0:prop:products}.  Each $\kappa_{2m}$ in
\eqref{p0:eq:cumulants} is a rational function of $q$ with denominator
$1-q^{2m}$ and rational numerator, and
$\ExponentialCompleteBellPolynomial{n}$ is a polynomial with rational
coefficients in $\kappa_1,\dots,\kappa_n$ involving only
$\kappa_i$ with $i\le n$; clearing denominators gives the stated form.
Odd cumulants vanish by \cref{p0:prop:mahler}, and
$\ExponentialCompleteBellPolynomial{2k+1}$ evaluated on a cumulant vector
with vanishing odd entries is $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where the volume uses this]
\label{p0:rem:cumulant-uses}
\eqref{p0:eq:cumulants} is the single source of the Bernoulli--Bell
cumulant layer that Parts~VII--XII each set up separately: Part~VIII in
the $[0,1]$ scale, Parts~IX and~X in the $[-1,1]$ scale (with the
resulting factor $2^{2m}$), and Part~XI in the standardized scale
\eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants}.  The scale factors are exactly the
entries of \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}, and \cref{p0:lem:transport} makes
the transport explicit.
\end{remark}

\section{The normalization dictionary}
\label{p0:sec:dictionary}

\begin{lemma}[Affine transport]
\label{p0:lem:transport}
Let $Z$ be a random variable with finite exponential moments near $0$ and
let $W=\alpha Z+\beta$ with $\alpha\ne0$.  Then
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:transport}
 \CharacteristicFunction{W}(t)
  =\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\beta t}\CharacteristicFunction{Z}(\alpha t),
 \qquad
 \MomentGeneratingFunction{W}(t)
  =\EulerE^{\beta t}\MomentGeneratingFunction{Z}(\alpha t),
\end{equation}
and the cumulants satisfy $\kappa_1(W)=\alpha\kappa_1(Z)+\beta$ and
$\kappa_n(W)=\alpha^{n}\kappa_n(Z)$ for $n\ge2$.  If $Z$ has density
$f_Z$, then $W$ has density
$f_W(x)=\AbsoluteValue{\alpha}^{-1}f_Z\bigl((x-\beta)/\alpha\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The transform identities are immediate from the definitions, and the
cumulant statement follows by taking logarithms: $\log
\MomentGeneratingFunction{W}(t)=\beta t
+\log\MomentGeneratingFunction{Z}(\alpha t)$, whose $t^{n}/n!$
coefficient is $\alpha^{n}\kappa_n(Z)$ for $n\ge2$.  The density formula
is the change of variables.
\end{proof}

\cref{p0:tab:dictionary} records, for each numbered part, the letters
that part uses for the geometric-uniform variable and its transform, and
the exact relation to the canonical objects of
\cref{p0:def:family} and \cref{p0:prop:products}.  Reading a formula out
of one part and into another means composing the two corresponding rows
through \cref{p0:lem:transport}.

XI & $\Psi_h(t)$ & --- &
  $=\CharacteristicFunction{r}(t/\sigma_r)$, $a_h=\sqrt{3(1-r^{2})}$\\
XII & $\Phi_q(t)$ & --- & $=\CharacteristicFunction{q}(t)$\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

\begin{proposition}[Correctness of the dictionary]
\label{p0:prop:dictionary}
Every entry of \cref{p0:tab:dictionary} is exact.  In particular:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Parts~IX and~X use seeds uniform on $[-1,1]$, and their variable is
      $2\GeoLawCentered{q}$; consequently their cumulants are
      $2^{2m}$ times \eqref{p0:eq:cumulants}, namely
      $\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m}\frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}}$, and their
      variance is $\frac{1-q}{3(1+q)}$, four times
      \eqref{p0:eq:variance}.
\item Part~XI's normalizing constant satisfies
      $a_h=(1-r)/(2\sigma_r)$, so
      $\Psi_h(t)=\CharacteristicFunction{r}(t/\sigma_r)$ and Part~XI's
      $\lambda_{2m}(r)$ agrees with
      \eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants}.
\item Part~IX's product $\Phi(q,z)=\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad((1-q)q^{j}z)$
      equals $\CharacteristicFunction{q}(2z)$, and Part~X's
      $\phi_q$ is the same function of the same argument.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) If $U^{\pm}$ is uniform on $[-1,1]$ then $U^{\pm}=2V$ with $V$
uniform on $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$, so
$(1-q)\sum_jq^{j}U^{\pm}_j=2\GeoLawCentered{q}$.  \cref{p0:lem:transport}
with $\alpha=2$, $\beta=0$ multiplies $\kappa_{2m}$ by $2^{2m}$; applying
this to \eqref{p0:eq:cumulants} gives
$2^{2m}\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}}
 =\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m}\frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}}$
and, at $m=1$, $4\sigma_q^{2}=\frac{1-q}{3(1+q)}$.

(ii) By \eqref{p0:eq:variance},
$\sigma_r^{2}=\frac{(1-r)^{2}}{12(1-r^{2})}$, so
$\sigma_r=\frac{1-r}{2\sqrt{3(1-r^{2})}}$ and
\[
 \frac{1-r}{2\sigma_r}
 =\frac{1-r}{2}\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{3(1-r^{2})}}{1-r}
 =\sqrt{3(1-r^{2})}=a_h .
\]
Hence $\CharacteristicFunction{r}(t/\sigma_r)
 =\prod_j\SincRad\bigl(\frac{(1-r)r^{j}}{2\sigma_r}t\bigr)
 =\prod_j\SincRad(a_hr^{j}t)=\Psi_h(t)$, and the standardized cumulants
agree because both sides are the cumulants of the same variable.  As a
check, $\sum_{j\ge0}(a_hr^{j})^{2}=\frac{3(1-r^{2})}{1-r^{2}}=3$, the
normalization identity used in Part~XI.

(iii) By \eqref{p0:eq:cf},
$\CharacteristicFunction{q}(2z)=\prod_j\SincRad((1-q)q^{j}z)$, which is
the displayed product.  The same computation applies verbatim to
Part~X's $\phi_q$; and $M_q^{\mathrm{X}}(t)
 =\Expectation\EulerE^{2t\GeoLawCentered{q}}
 =\EulerE^{-t}\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(2t)=C_q(2t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Finite products and the prefix parts]
\label{p0:rem:finite-products}
Parts~I--VI work mainly with \emph{finite} products
$\prod_{j=0}^{N-1}\SincRad(\cdot)$ and with the exponent sequences
attached to them, rather than with the law of $\GeoLaw{q}$ itself.  The
relation is that the $N$-fold product is the characteristic function of
the truncation $(1-q)\sum_{j<N}q^{j}V_j$, rescaled by whichever
normalization that part fixes; Part~V makes the convex-order comparison
between truncations and the limit precise.  Those parts also use the
$\SincPi$ convention of \eqref{p0:eq:sinc} in places where a unit-period
Fourier variable is natural; since
$\SincPi z=\SincRad(\pi z)$, the two differ only by the argument scaling
recorded here.
\end{remark}

\section{\texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-series conventions}
\label{p0:sec:qseries}

The $q$-series notation is that of the corpus contract, with every base
an explicit argument.  For $n\in\NaturalNumbers$,
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:qseries}
 \QPochhammer{a}{q}{n}=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^{k}),
 \qquad
 \QPochhammer{a}{q}{\infty}=\prod_{k\ge0}(1-aq^{k})
  \quad(\AbsoluteValue q<1),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:qbracket}
 \QInteger{m}{q}=1+q+\dots+q^{m-1}=\frac{1-q^{m}}{1-q}
  \quad(q\ne1),
 \qquad
 \QInteger{m}{1}=m,
\end{equation}
and the Gaussian binomial coefficient is
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:gaussian-binomial}
 \GaussianBinomial{n}{k}{q}
 =\frac{\QPochhammer{q}{q}{n}}
        {\QPochhammer{q}{q}{k}\QPochhammer{q}{q}{n-k}},
 \qquad 0\le k\le n .
\end{equation}
Two facts are used repeatedly and are recorded here rather than in each
part.  First, $\QInteger{2m}{q^{\,}}$-type denominators are exactly the
ones appearing in \eqref{p0:eq:cumulants}: since
$1-q^{2m}=(1-q)\QInteger{2m}{q}$, that identity may be written
\begin{equation}
\label{p0:eq:cumulants-qbracket}
 \kappa_{2m}\bigl(\GeoLawCentered{q}\bigr)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\cdot\frac{(1-q)^{2m-1}}{\QInteger{2m}{q}},
\end{equation}
which is the form in which Parts~VII, VIII, and~X state it.  Second, the
outer product $\QPochhammer{a}{q^{2}}{\infty}$ with nome $q^{2}$ is the
one that appears in the spectral factorizations of Parts~VII and~IX; its
locally uniform convergence for every complex $\AbsoluteValue q<1$,
including $q=0$, is formalized as
\lean{Fabius.hasProdLocallyUniformly_geometricSincProduct_complexQPochhammerInf}.

\section{Status vocabulary}
\label{p0:sec:status}

The volume marks the epistemic status of every displayed assertion, using
one vocabulary throughout:

\begin{itemize}
\item \statusproved{} --- a complete proof appears in this volume.
\item \statusderived{} --- deduced here from results proved elsewhere in
      the audited corpus, with the citation given.
\item \statusexisting{} --- quoted from the audited corpus as an input,
      not reproved.
\item \statusnumerical{} --- supported only by the deterministic numerical
      experiments of the reproducibility packages under \path{assets/}.
\item \statusconditional{} --- proved subject to an explicitly stated
      hypothesis that is not itself established here.
\item \statusopen{} or \statusconjectural{} --- conjectural.
\end{itemize}

Environments named \emph{Conjecture} and \emph{Open problem} are never
used for assertions that are proved somewhere in the volume; where an
absorbed report conjectured something that another absorbed report
proves, the conjecture has been demoted to a remark carrying a forward
reference, and those demotions are listed in
\cref{p0:sec:crossref}.

\section{What each part contributes}
\label{p0:sec:crossref}

\begin{description}[leftmargin=2.6em,style=nextline]
\item[Parts I--VI] The finite-product side: exponent sequences and the
      Newton basis (I), $q$-binomial Richardson acceleration (II), the
      dyadic box-spline inverse transforms (III), Fourier images of the
      repeated-integration approximants (IV), exact transport geometry
      and convex order (V), and atomic splines beyond the binary point
      (VI).
\item[Part VII] Signed and reciprocal parameter orbits: the Klein-four
      sign calculus, the reciprocal germ outside the unit circle, and the
      spectral $q^{2}$-Pochhammer factorization.
\item[Part VIII] The negative-parameter affine duality in full, the exact
      negative dyadic law, log-concavity and dominant-digit plateaux,
      residue-class multiplication formulas, and the quantitative central
      limit theorem at $\AbsoluteValue q\uparrow1$.
\item[Part IX] Complex parameters at roots of unity: radial expansions,
      the natural-boundary theorem, cyclotomic blow-ups, and inverse
      branches.
\item[Part X] Parameter flow as a martingale transport, convex order along
      the flow, the midpoint $q$-integral form of the scaled cumulant
      transform, and large deviations with the Lambert-$W_{-1}$
      boundary.
\item[Part XI] The continuous-parameter Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher
      theory, moderate deviations, and quadratic $q$-Gevrey regularity.
\item[Part XII] The response of the family to the parameter at
      $q=\tfrac12$: flat nonanalytic fronts, the tangent measure, the
      susceptibility resolvent, and the smooth Schr\"oder--Koenigs dynamics,
      whose linearization hypothesis is now proved.
\end{description}

\subsection{Conjectures settled inside the volume}
\label{p0:sec:demotions}

The status rule of \cref{p0:sec:status} forbids a \emph{Conjecture} or
\emph{Open problem} environment for an assertion proved somewhere in the
volume.  Merging the six reports settled four such items, each by a result
that another report had proved independently; they are recorded here so that
a reader comparing the parts with their standalone sources can see what moved
and why.
\begin{itemize}
\item Part~VIII conjectured the uniform first Edgeworth expansion of the
      standardized density.  Part~XI proves the all-orders, polynomially
      weighted, termwise-differentiable expansion for the same standardized
      variable (\cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}, with the identification of
      the two variables in \cref{p0:prop:dictionary}); the conjecture is now
      \cref{p8:prop:edgeworth}, proved by specialization.
\item Part~VIII's all-orders Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite conjecture is the
      statement of \cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} together with
      \cref{p11:prop:h-power-series}; it is now the remark
      \cref{p8:rem:all-orders}, pointing there.
\item Part~IX's appendix left the all-orders fixed-frequency radial expansion
      as a conjecture; it is now \cref{p9:thm:all-orders}, proved once the
      multiplier estimates of that part were made uniform in the summation
      index.
\item Part~III posed as an open problem the sharp leading constants of the
      prefix-product error for general base; Part~VI proves them for every
      base $a\ge2$, and Part~III now points there instead.
\item Part~XII's standalone source made its smooth Schr\"oder--Koenigs
      coordinate conditional on a linearization hypothesis it called (K).
      That hypothesis is now proved in Part~XII itself
      (\cref{p12:thm:flat-koenigs}): the flat contraction is linearized by a
      $C^{\infty}$ conjugacy with unit derivative at the fixed point, so
      every statement that was conditional on (K) is unconditional.
\end{itemize}
One conjecture was settled the other way.  Part~X conjectured that all
coefficients of its central rate series are positive; exact rational
reversion through order $28$ shows the coefficient of $x^{24}$ is negative,
$c_{12}=-3032147123502547968/3562005918173828125$, confirmed independently to
sixty digits from the exact saddle.  The conjecture is refuted and replaced
by the remark \cref{p10:rem:rate-signs}, which records the sign pattern and
the radius of convergence $0<R_I\le1$.
The remaining entropy-deficit conjecture of Part~VIII stays conjectural and
is cross-referenced to the matching conjecture of Part~XI, whose
second-order constant agrees with it in exact rationals.

\begin{warning}[Three near-identical phi's]
\label{p0:warn:phi}
The letter $\varphi$ carries three distinct meanings in this volume, and
they are distinguished only by their decoration.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item $\CharacteristicFunction{q}$, with a parameter subscript, is the
      canonical characteristic function \eqref{p0:eq:cf} of
      $\GeoLawCentered{q}$.
\item $\phi_q$ in Part~X is the characteristic function of that part's
      variable $2\GeoLawCentered{q}$, hence
      $\phi_q(t)=\CharacteristicFunction{q}(2t)$ and \emph{not}
      $\CharacteristicFunction{q}(t)$.  The two are typeset with
      different glyphs, $\phi$ against $\varphi$, but the safe reading is
      the dictionary row, not the glyph.
\item $\varphi$ with no subscript, in Part~XI, is the standard normal
      density $\EulerE^{-x^{2}/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

% ed.: Part 0 leaves \thesection as 0.<n>; restore plain arabic
% numbering for the numbered parts.
\setcounter{section}{0}
\renewcommand{\thesection}{\arabic{section}}
\part{Exponent-Sequence and Newton-Basis Frontiers for the Fabius--Rvachev System}
% Absorbed from Fabius_Newton_Rvachev_Frontier_Report/Exponent_Sequence_Newton_Rvachev_Frontiers.tex




\begin{abstract}
The audited \repo{} corpus already contains the classical Fabius and Rvachev functions,
exact dyadic arithmetic, the full Thue--Morse formula atlas, Gaussian $q$-binomial
interpolation, all-orders endpoint expansions, lower-branch Lambert-$W$ coordinates,
Bell- and Bernoulli-polynomial coefficient calculus, sharp Fourier decay, the integer-zero
spectrum of the Rvachev transform, a spectral determinant, rational arithmetic rays,
half-integer quadrature identities, logarithmic $q$-Richardson acceleration, and a
Pascal-weighted hierarchy of compactly supported densities.  This report avoids repackaging
those results.  Instead it identifies a single master object that contains them as special
coordinates and exposes several new deductions.

For a nonnegative integer exponent sequence $a=(a_h)_{h\ge0}$ with
$A(1/2)<\infty$, where $A(q)=\sum_{h\ge0}a_hq^h$, define
\[
 \Phi_a(z)=\prod_{h\ge0}\SincPi\!\left(\frac{z}{2^h}\right)^{a_h},
 \qquad \SincPi z=\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z}.
\]
It is the characteristic function of an explicit compactly supported convolution of
uniform variables.  We prove a universal dictionary in which the same generating function
$A$ controls: the integer-zero multiplicity
$m_a(n)=\sum_{h\le\TwoAdicValuation(n)}a_h$; the spectral zeta
$\mathcal Z_a(s)=\zeta(s)A(2^{-s})$; every even cumulant
$\kappa_{2j}=B_{2j}A(4^{-j})/(2j)$; the Fourier-lobe sign; exact digital zero counts;
and the order of Prouhet cancellation of each finite sign block.  The zero divisor, the
spectral zeta quotient, and the complete even-cumulant sequence each determine $a$ uniquely.

The cumulant samples $A(4^{-m})$ admit a new exact reconstruction mechanism.  Lagrange
extrapolation at geometric nodes has Gaussian-$q$-binomial weights, an exact transformed
series, fixed alternating sign, bounded $\ell^1$ condition number, and certified integer
brackets.  Thus Richardson extrapolation becomes a stable tomography algorithm for the
hidden dyadic exponent sequence.

For polynomial exponent sequences, the Newton expansion
$P(h)=\sum c_r\binom hr$ gives the finite factorization
$\Phi_P=\prod_r\Phi_{r+1}^{c_r}$ through the audited Pascal--Rvachev hierarchy.  Negative
Newton coefficients are allowed: whenever $P(h)\ge0$ on the nonnegative integers, the
resulting alternating quotient is nevertheless entire and positive definite.  The even
family
\[
 P_d(h)=\binom{h-1}{d},\qquad d=0,2,4,\ldots,
\]
is especially striking.  It satisfies
\[
 \Psi_d(z)=\SincPi(z)\Phi_{d+1}(z/2)
 =\prod_{r=0}^d\Phi_{r+1}(z)^{(-1)^{d-r}},
\]
has support $[-1,1]$, zero multiplicity
$1+\binom{\TwoAdicValuation(n)}{d+1}$, and converges in total variation to the uniform law.  Its
transition across the two discontinuities of the limiting box density has a Gaussian
boundary layer with an explicit Berry--Esseen rate.  For $d=2$ this supplies the concrete
positive-definite quotient $\Phi_1\Phi_3/\Phi_2$.

Finally, a Mellin-reflection identity relates the endpoint Laplace transform directly to
the reflected spectral zeta.  For polynomial weights it explains the complete hierarchy
of logarithmic powers and periodic coefficients, gives a generalized lower-Lambert saddle,
and yields the leading inverse-endpoint law.  Reasonable conjectures and a detailed research
and Lean-formalization program conclude the report.  Numerical experiments were independently
implemented at high precision; the commented Python source and generated data accompany the
paper.
\end{abstract}


\clearpage

\section{Audit boundary, source stratification, and novelty discipline}
\label{p1:sec:audit}

\subsection{Pinned corpus}

The repository changed several times on the audit date, so the source boundary is the exact
commit printed on the title page.  Its recursive documentation tree contains 67 distinct
\texttt{.tex} paths: five living synthesis/reference documents, thirty-two frozen historical
sources, twenty-three active frontier drafts (including twelve Fourier-decay dossiers), and
seven transcribed or corrected source papers.  Every path is listed in
\cref{p1:app:inventory}.  Historical revisions were read as mathematical lineages rather than
as independent evidence; the archive's provenance ledger identifies what was superseded,
merged, or deliberately frozen.

The living primary exposition separates the bounded distribution function, the compactly
supported Rvachev bump, and the signed global extension, and confines itself to claims with
matching Lean declarations.  The consolidated frontier volume and its current descendants
contain the non-formalized but mathematically developed material.  In particular, the audit
treated the following as prior art rather than as discoveries of this report:
\begin{itemize}
\item the integer zero set and multiplicity $1+\TwoAdicValuation(n)$ of the classical Rvachev transform;
\item its spectral determinant, spectral zeta, heat trace, local zero jets, and symmetric
      $q$-integer deformation;
\item the full signed Thue--Morse formula atlas, Prouhet cancellation, Mahler products,
      rarefied sums, Mellin--Dirichlet theory, and automatic-sequence machinery;
\item exact dyadic values of $F$, half-base $q$-Pochhammer and Gaussian-binomial formulas,
      Lagrange interpolation, and several existing Richardson transforms;
\item the corrected lower-Lambert endpoint expansion, its nonconstant periodic factor,
      all-order Bell-polynomial coefficient construction, and the inverse Fabius expansion;
\item sharp geometric, arithmetic, metric, and envelope results for the infinite sinc product;
\item cyclotomic rational rays, half-integer spectral identities, exact zero jets, and the
      Pascal hierarchy
      $\Phi_r(z)=\prod_h\SincPi(z/2^h)^{\binom h{r-1}}$;
\item logarithmic $q$-Richardson acceleration of truncated sinc products and phase-locked
      Richardson extraction of the endpoint periodic term;
\item positive Gaussian and Lobatto tail quadrature, exact ordinary-prefix error laws,
      generalized gamma-convolution duality, and the existing Gaussian rank limit for the
      Pascal hierarchy.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What is new relative to the pinned tree}

Targeted path, phrase, and formula searches found no counterpart of the following theorem
package in the audited snapshot:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the arbitrary nonnegative exponent-sequence monoid and its single generating-function
      dictionary for zero spectra, cumulants, digital signs, and endpoint Mellin transforms;
\item exact digital zero-count defects and generalized Prouhet order for an arbitrary
      exponent parity word, including the first surviving power moment;
\item equivalence and constructive recovery of the exponent sequence from either the zero
      divisor or all even cumulants;
\item certified Gaussian-$q$-binomial Richardson tomography of the exponent coefficients;
\item the finite-refinement-rank classification by rational ordinary generating functions;
\item the Newton-basis factorization of every nonnegative integer-valued polynomial weight,
      including positive-definite alternating quotients of Pascal transforms;
\item the normalized family $P_d(h)=\binom{h-1}{d}$ for even $d$, its sparse zero spectrum,
      automatic sign selector, exact total-variation law, and Gaussian boundary layer;
\item the general spectral--endpoint Mellin reflection formula
      $\MellinTransformOf{\log L_a}(w)=-\Gamma(w)\zeta(w+1)\mathcal Z_a(-w)/\zeta(-w)$;
\item the polynomial-weight universality theorem and its generalized Lambert-$W_{-1}$
      endpoint coordinate.
\end{enumerate}

A targeted external search located the classical ingredients separately---the original
Fabius--Rvachev analysis and arithmetic, lacunary Thue--Morse products, automatic sequences,
Berry--Esseen bounds, rational and integer-valued generating functions, Mellin harmonic sums,
exponential Tauberian transfer, and Lambert inversion
\cite{bib:arias1982,bib:arias2017,bib:aistleitner2015,bib:toth2022,bib:allouche2003,bib:petrov1995,bib:stanley1997,bib:flajolet1995,bib:bruijn1959,bib:corless1996}---but not this combined classification.
Accordingly, ``new'' below always means new to the pinned corpus and apparently nonstandard;
it is not an assertion of exhaustive worldwide priority.

\begin{statusbox}{Proof-status convention}
Results explicitly labeled \statusproved{} are proved in this manuscript.  Results labeled
\statusderived{} use a theorem already developed in the audited frontier corpus (most often
the sharp Pascal-hierarchy Fourier or endpoint asymptotic) and then add a new deduction.
Items labeled \statusopen{} are conjectures or proposed programs.

A fourth, orthogonal label is now carried alongside these three.  Wherever a statement of this
report---or an exactly reusable core of one---already has a machine-checked counterpart in the
repository's Lean library, that declaration is cited inline in typewriter type---for instance
\lean{Fabius.weightedScaleMultiplicity}---together with its module under
\path{Analysis/FabiusFunction/Lean/FabiusFunction/}.  Roughly a dozen such citations appear
below, alongside the \emph{Post-snapshot Lean crosswalk} paragraphs.  In most of them the
formal statement is \emph{more general} than the one printed here
(arbitrary base instead of $2$, arbitrary coefficient ring or module instead of $\RealNumbers$, arbitrary
geometric ratio instead of $q\in(0,1)$).  Each citation says which.  In particular the finite
rational geometric-Lagrange kernel used in the Gaussian-$q$ rows---closed weights, all
residual moments and their sign, and the finite exact $\ell^1$ norm---is formalized at
arbitrary ratio $0<q<1$, so the $q=1/4$ instance is covered, and the denominator-free
principal specialization with the complete positive-degree geometric-moment identities behind
\cref{p1:lem:q-weights} is formal as well (see the crosswalk paragraphs there).
The post-snapshot module \path{AnalyticSeriesFilter.lean} now also proves the
convergent-series analogue.  Its finite filter acts diagonally under Mathlib's
\emph{unconditional} \path{Summable} hypothesis on each weighted sampled series,
splits into an exact finite head and infinite tail, and specializes geometric and
geometric-Lagrange rows to the complete Gaussian residual tail, including the
shifted-scale form used in \eqref{p1:eq:Rrm-exact}.  The hypothesis is sharp at a
zero-weight node: the weighted series is then identically zero, and no convergence
of the corresponding unweighted sample is required.  It does not cover a series
convergent only in its natural order at a boundary point, and by itself proves
neither positivity, signs, bounds, nor uniform convergence.
\end{statusbox}

\begin{statusbox}{Post-snapshot analytic extensions}
The current tree now supplies the previously missing \emph{infinite-product}
instantiation.  \path{AnalyticMoments.lean} names the even mode
\lean{Fabius.rvachevFourierMomentTerm}, proves its constant and scaling laws
\lean{Fabius.rvachevFourierMomentTerm_zero} and
\lean{Fabius.rvachevFourierMomentTerm_scale}, and proves genuine unconditional
summation by \lean{Fabius.hasSum_rvachevFourierMomentTerm}.
\path{RvachevQBinomialFilter.lean} then proves the corresponding series for the
standalone product, its power-scaling law, and the exact Gaussian residual
identity.  Generically \(c,z\in\ComplexNumbers\), \(p\in\NaturalNumbers\), \(q=c^2\), and the sole
hypothesis is injectivity of \(j\mapsto q^j\) on
\(\{0,\ldots,p\}\); no contraction, realness, positivity, or global
nonvanishing is assumed.  At \(c=1/2\), \(q=1/4\), the theorem is
assumption-free.  This does not yet identify the finite prefixes \(P_{b,n}\),
their quotient or Bell coefficients, and it supplies none of the report's
analytic error signs, bracketing or quantitative bounds, uniform/derivative
convergence, or asymptotics.

An independent reusable layer is now present in
\path{FractionalVolterraCalculus.lean} and
\path{FabiusFractionalVolterra.lean}.  Positive affine scale changes on an ordered
real interval are formalized.  For $\alpha\le0$, affine covariance is an identity for
the totalized Lean interval-integral definition; a classical Riemann--Liouville or
integrability interpretation is asserted only for positive order.  Gamma-normalized
order raising assumes real $\alpha>0$, a
continuous Banach-valued primitive, an interval-integrable derivative, and the
right derivative \path{HasDerivWithinAt} on the open interval.  Its boundary-free
form yields the exact dyadic shift for the signed Fabius extension when $x\ge0$.
The total causal Rvachev fractional primitive has its support-truncated integral,
positive-natural bridge, and positive-order semigroup formalized on $x\ge-1$; the same
module gives the bounded Fabius shift when $0\le x\le1$ and the $\RvachevUp$--Fabius bridge
from base $-1$ when $x\ge-1$.  Complex orders and powers, Caputo or
Riemann--Liouville derivative operators, weighted-monomial or iterated identities, negative-
$x$ signed branches, shifted endpoint lattices, endpoint moments, transform/tail and
piecewise/refinement formulas, and inverse/quantile formulas remain frontier.  These
post-snapshot series and fractional APIs were checked at source checkpoint
\path{149332f9d}.

These labels concern representation only, not correctness: report-specific
probability and finite-prefix/Bell instantiations still require their own bridges.  In
particular the sign and bound in \eqref{p1:eq:Rrm-sign}--\eqref{p1:eq:Rrm-bound},
Fourier envelopes for the Pascal hierarchy
of rank at least two, Mellin contour displacement, exponential Tauberian transfer,
Berry--Esseen for non-identically-distributed summands, total-variation and
Wasserstein distances, and the automatic-sequence machinery have no Lean
counterpart here.  The infinite condition-number limit is formalized separately
in \path{LimitConditionNumber.lean} by
\lean{Fabius.tendsto\_sum\_abs\_qToeplitzWeight}; its divergence as
\(q\to1^-\) is the literal filter theorem
\lean{Fabius.tendsto\_qConditionNumberLimit\_atTop\_at\_one\_left}.
\end{statusbox}

\section{The exponent-sequence convolution monoid}
\label{p1:sec:master}

\subsection{Admissible sequences}

Throughout, the normalized entire sinc is
\begin{equation}
 \SincPi z=\frac{\sin\pi z}{\pi z},\qquad \SincPi0=1.
 \label{p1:eq:sinc-normalized}
\end{equation}
It is the Fourier transform, under the kernel $\EulerE^{-2\pi\ImaginaryUnit zx}$, of the uniform
probability density on $[-1/2,1/2]$.

\begin{definition}[Admissible exponent sequence]
A sequence $a=(a_h)_{h\ge0}$ is \emph{admissible} if
\[
 a_h\in\NaturalNumbers,
 \qquad
 A(q):=\sum_{h\ge0}a_hq^h,
 \qquad
 A(1/2)<\infty.
\]
Its generalized Rvachev transform is
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_a(z)=\prod_{h=0}^{\infty}
 \SincPi\!\left(\frac{z}{2^h}\right)^{a_h}.
 \label{p1:eq:Phi-a}
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

For each $h$ and $1\le j\le a_h$, let $U_{h,j}$ be independent and uniform on
$[-1/2,1/2]$, and put
\begin{equation}
 X_a=\sum_{h\ge0}\sum_{j=1}^{a_h}2^{-h}U_{h,j},
 \qquad
 R_a=\frac12A(1/2).
 \label{p1:eq:X-a}
\end{equation}
Absolute convergence is deterministic because the sum of the radii is $R_a$.

\begin{theorem}[Probability, analyticity, support, and convolution]
\label{p1:thm:master-probability}
For every admissible $a$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X_a$ is supported on $[-R_a,R_a]$ and has characteristic function $\Phi_a$;
\item the product in \eqref{p1:eq:Phi-a} converges locally uniformly on $\ComplexNumbers$, hence is entire;
\item $\Phi_{a+b}=\Phi_a\Phi_b$, and the corresponding probability law is the convolution
      of the laws for $a$ and $b$;
\item if $\sum_ha_h=\infty$, then $X_a$ has a compactly supported $C^\infty$ density;
      if only finitely many $a_h$ are nonzero, its law is a finite uniform box spline.
\end{enumerate}
All four assertions are \statusproved.  At the probability-law level, only the classical case
$a_h\equiv1$ is represented: \lean{Fabius.rvachevFourier_eq_product}
(\lean{FourierProduct.lean}) identifies the
Fourier transform of the Rvachev up-function with the sinc product \eqref{p1:eq:Phi-a} at
$a_h\equiv1$, in the same normalization \eqref{p1:eq:sinc-normalized}, and
\lean{Fabius.ProbabilityRepresentation.rvachevUp_eq_weightedSum_probability_global}
(\lean{ProbabilityRepresentation.lean}) is the matching dyadic-uniform-series representation,
stated in the Fabius normalization $\sum_{h\ge0}2^{-h-1}V_h$ on $[0,1]$, which is
$(X_a+R_a)/2$ in the notation used here.

The transform itself is now formal at a general admissible $a$, in \path{GeneralizedRvachevProduct.lean}:
\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct} is $\Phi_a$ in the normalization
\eqref{p1:eq:sinc-normalized}, and
\lean{Fabius.generalizedSincFactors\_multipliable} gives convergence of the product at
\emph{every} $z\in\ComplexNumbers$ --- including the points where factors vanish, since
multipliability in Mathlib's sense is unconditional convergence of the net of finite
subproducts and admits the limit $0$.  Assertion (iii), $\Phi_{a+b}=\Phi_a\Phi_b$, is
\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_add}; the finite-support case of (iv) is
\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_prod}; the classical case is recovered as an
identity, not merely a specialization
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_one}).  The zero divisor is formal in both
directions --- $\Phi_a(z)=0$ exactly when $z=k2^h$ for a nonzero integer $k$ and some $h$
with $a_h\ne0$
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_zero\_iff}) --- as are the one-step
refinement law (\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_two\_mul}) and its all-orders
iterate (\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_two\_pow\_mul}).

Assertion (ii) is formalized as well, in \path{GeneralizedRvachevEntire.lean}: the product
converges locally uniformly on every ball
(\lean{Fabius.hasProdLocallyUniformlyOn\_generalizedRvachevProduct}) and $\Phi_a$ is therefore
entire (\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_differentiable}).  With that in hand the zero
divisor is complete --- $\Phi_a$ vanishes exactly at the nonzero integers $n$ with
$m_a(\lvert n\rvert)>0$, to order exactly $m_a(\lvert n\rvert)$, and nowhere else
(\path{GeneralizedZeroDivisor.lean}).

The characteristic-function reading of (i) now has three elementary necessary checks, though
not positive-definiteness or the statement itself: $\Phi_a(0)=1$, continuity from entirety, and
\[
 \lVert\Phi_a(x)\rVert\le1
 \qquad\text{for every real }x
\]
(\lean{Fabius.norm\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_ofReal\_le\_one},
\path{GeneralizedRealBound.lean}), which had been missing for arbitrary admissible weights.
The classical constant-weight case already appears as
\lean{Fabius.norm\_rvachevFourierProduct\_le\_one} in \path{BaselineDecay.lean}.
The generalized bound is attained at $x=0$, so it is sharp.

What remains \emph{not} formalized is the probabilistic content proper: the support statement
(i) --- that $R_a=A_a(1/2)/2$ is the actual support radius rather than only the
deterministic radius bound --- the
random variable $X_a$ and the convolution reading of (iii), and the smoothness dichotomy (iv).
Assertion (iii) is formal as an identity of products but not as a statement about laws.  The
modules prove the algebraic, convergence and analytic skeleton on which the probabilistic
layer would rest, and their docstrings say so explicitly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Independence gives the finite-prefix characteristic products.  The variables are bounded and
$\sum_{h,j}|2^{-h}U_{h,j}|\le R_a$, so the finite sums converge almost surely and in every
$L^p$, and their characteristic functions converge to that of $X_a$.

Locally, $\log\SincPi w=\BigO(w^2)$.  Since
$\sum_ha_h4^{-h}=A(1/4)<\infty$, the logarithms of the factors converge normally on compact
sets avoiding a harmless choice of local branch; standard infinite-product theory then gives
an entire limit.  Addition of exponent sequences is multiplication of products, which is
exactly convolution of independent sums.

If infinitely many individual factors occur, fix $M$ of them.  On the real axis,
$|\SincPi(\xi/2^h)|\le\min(1,2^h/(\pi|\xi|))$.  The chosen $M$ factors give
$|\Phi_a(\xi)|\le C_M(1+|\xi|)^{-M}$, while all remaining factors have modulus at most one.
Thus $\Phi_a$ is rapidly decreasing; Fourier inversion gives a $C^\infty$ density.  With
finitely many factors one obtains a finite convolution of interval densities, hence a box
spline.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The classical Rvachev transform corresponds to $a_h\equiv1$.  The audited Pascal hierarchy
corresponds to $a_h=\binom h{r-1}$.  The point of \cref{p1:thm:master-probability} is not merely
that both products exist, but that the collection of all such laws is a commutative
convolution monoid whose algebra is the coefficientwise additive monoid of exponent
sequences.
\end{remark}

\section{Integer zeros, spectral zeta, digital defects, and lobe signs}
\label{p1:sec:spectrum}

\subsection{The universal zero-divisor formula}

Euler's product for the normalized sinc gives
\[
 \SincPi z=\prod_{k\ge1}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{k^2}\right).
\]
An integer $n\ne0$ is a zero of the scale-$h$ factor precisely when $2^h\mid n$.
This immediately yields the following master theorem.

\begin{theorem}[Zero divisor and spectral zeta]
\label{p1:thm:zero-zeta}
Let $a$ be admissible and define
\begin{equation}
 m_a(n)=\sum_{h=0}^{\TwoAdicValuation(n)}a_h,
 \qquad n\ge1.
 \label{p1:eq:m-a}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \Phi_a(z)=\prod_{n\ge1}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\right)^{m_a(n)}
 \quad}
 \label{p1:eq:canonical-a}
\end{equation}
with locally uniform convergence.  In particular,
$\OrderOperator_{z=\pm n}\Phi_a=m_a(n)$.  For $\Re s>1$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \Zspec_a(s):=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{m_a(n)}{n^s}
 =\zeta(s)A(2^{-s}).
 \quad}
 \label{p1:eq:zeta-a}
\end{equation}
Both statements are \statusproved.  The multiplicity function \eqref{p1:eq:m-a} is formalized as
\lean{Fabius.weightedScaleMultiplicity} (\lean{WeightedScaleMultiplicity.lean}), and in two
directions more generally than it is used here: the base $2$ is replaced by an arbitrary $b$,
and the weights $a_h$ may lie in an arbitrary additive commutative monoid rather than in $\NaturalNumbers$.
The canonical form \eqref{p1:eq:canonical-a} is formalized at a general admissible $a$,
in \path{GeneralizedCanonicalForm.lean}:
\[
  \Phi_a(z)=\prod_{n\ge1}\left(1-\frac{z^2}{n^2}\right)^{m_a(n)}
\]
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_canonical}).  The regrouping reuses, verbatim,
the fibre equivalence already built for the classical case
(\lean{Fabius.dyadicFactorEquiv}, \lean{SincCanonicalProduct.lean}): the map
$(h,r)\mapsto(r+1)2^h$ has fibre $\{h:h\le\TwoAdicValuation(n)\}$ over $n$.  The only change is that
each factor now carries the exponent $a_h$, so the fibre product is a product of
$\TwoAdicValuation(n)+1$ powers of the \emph{same} base and collapses to a single power whose
exponent is the prefix sum --- which is exactly $m_a(n)$.  That is why the multiplicity
function was the right object to formalize first.  The classical statement is recovered
as a corollary (\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_one\_of\_canonical}).

The locally uniform convergence the volume states alongside this display, and the
consequence $\OrderOperator_{z=\pm n}\Phi_a=m_a(n)$ that the volume draws from it, are both
formalized at a general admissible $a$, in \path{GeneralizedRvachevEntire.lean}.  The
convergence is \lean{Fabius.hasProdLocallyUniformlyOn\_generalizedRvachevProduct}, on
every ball $\lVert z\rVert<R$; \lean{HasProdLocallyUniformlyOn} is by definition the
locally uniform convergence of the finite subproducts, so this is the volume's clause
verbatim rather than a surrogate for it.  Holomorphy on each ball
(\lean{Fabius.differentiableOn\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_ball}) and hence entirety
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_differentiable}) follow, and with them the
order statement in both halves:
\[
 \OrderOperator_{z=n}\Phi_a=m_a(n)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \OrderOperator_{z=-n}\Phi_a=m_a(n),
 \qquad n\ge1,
\]
as \lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_pos} and
\lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_neg\_pos}.  The hypothesis
$n\ge1$ is not a limitation of the proof but of the statement: $\Phi_a(0)=1$, so the
order at the origin is $0$, whereas $m_a(0)=a_0$ may be anything.

Two remarks on how this was reached, both of which sharpen the volume.  First, the
algebraic input was already in place before this module --- the factorization
$\Phi_a(z)=(1-z^2/n^2)^{m_a(n)}R_n(z)$ with $R_n(\pm n)\ne0$
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_canonicalComplexFactor\_mul},
\lean{Fabius.canonicalCofactor\_natCast\_ne\_zero}) --- so what was genuinely missing was
analyticity of the cofactor $R_n$, supplied here as
\lean{Fabius.canonicalCofactor\_differentiable}.  Second, the reflected half needs no
evenness of $\Phi_a$: the mirror factorization
$1-z^2/n^2=(z+n)\cdot\bigl(-(z-n)/n^2\bigr)$
(\lean{Fabius.canonicalComplexFactor\_eq\_add\_mul}) is the same one line of algebra as
its sibling, so both halves of $\OrderOperator_{z=\pm n}$ are proved directly and the appeal to
$\Phi_a(-z)=\Phi_a(z)$ (\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_neg},
\path{LobeSignNegative.lean}) is not needed.

Third, the order statement now has a companion that completes it into a divisor.
\path{GeneralizedRvachevProduct.lean} pins the zero set in \emph{scale} coordinates,
$\exists h,\ a_h\ne0$ and $\exists k\ne0,\ z=k2^h$, and its header recorded that the
translation into arithmetic coordinates was not carried out and the multiplicities not
computed.  \path{GeneralizedZeroDivisor.lean} does both:
\[
 \Phi_a(z)=0
 \iff
 \exists\,n\in\IntegerNumbers,\ n\ne0,\ z=n,\ m_a(\lvert n\rvert)\ne0
\]
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_zero\_iff\_int}), and
$\OrderOperator_{z=n}\Phi_a=m_a(\lvert n\rvert)$ at every nonzero integer, both signs in one
statement (\lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_int}).  Since $\Phi_a$
is entire, the two together are its complete divisor: it vanishes precisely on
$\{n\in\IntegerNumbers:n\ne0,\ m_a(\lvert n\rvert)>0\}$, to exactly that order, and nowhere else in
$\ComplexNumbers$ --- in particular nowhere off the real axis
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_ne\_zero\_of\_not\_int}).  The bridge between the
two coordinate systems is arithmetic rather than analytic: $m_a(m)$ is a sum of naturals
over $h\le\TwoAdicValuation(m)$, so it is nonzero exactly when some $a_h$ with $2^h\mid m$ is
(\lean{Fabius.weightedScaleMultiplicity\_two\_ne\_zero\_iff}).

The divisor now also has an exact inverse.  The zero-definition, six-theorem module
\path{GeneralizedRvachevIdentifiability.lean} proves, for every admissible exponent
sequence,
\[
 \OrderOperator_{z=2^n}\Phi_a=\sum_{h=0}^{n}a_h
\]
(\lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_two\_pow}), decodes $a_0$ from
the order at $z=1$ and every $a_{n+1}$ by the consecutive first difference
(\lean{Fabius.exponent\_zero\_eq\_toNat\_analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct},
\lean{Fabius.exponent\_succ\_eq\_toNat\_analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct}), and
therefore proves both dyadic-order injectivity
(\lean{Fabius.exponentSequence\_eq\_of\_analyticOrderAt\_two\_pow\_eq}) and full-product
rigidity
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_eq\_iff}).  Its arithmetic core
\lean{Fabius.weightSequence\_eq\_of\_weightedScaleMultiplicity\_base\_pow\_eq} works at
every base $b>1$ and for weights in any additive cancellative commutative monoid.  The
sample indexed by $n=0$ is $z=1$, not the origin: every generalized product equals $1$ at
$z=0$.

At the \emph{constant} weight the sharper integer-indexed form remains available:
\lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_generalizedRvachevProduct\_one} reads
$\OrderOperator_{z=m}\Phi_{\ConstantWeightSequence}=m_{\ConstantWeightSequence}(\lvert m\rvert)$ for every nonzero integer $m$, chaining
\lean{Fabius.analyticOrderAt\_rvachevFourierProduct\_int} (\path{IntegerZeroAnalyticOrder.lean})
with the exponent identity.  The spectral zeta \eqref{p1:eq:zeta-a} is now
formalized as well, in \path{SpectralZetaWeighted.lean}, for real $s>1$ and at an
arbitrary base $b>1$, with the $\zeta$ factor left as its own $p$-series rather than
identified with \lean{riemannZeta}
(\lean{Fabius.tsum\_weightedScaleMultiplicity\_succ\_rpow}).  Three hypotheses are
carried and none is hidden: $1<s$, nonnegativity of the weights, and summability of
$A(b^{-s})$ --- the last genuinely not automatic, since $a$ may grow arbitrarily fast.
The rearrangement needs nothing about the canonical product: the fibre of
$(h,k)\mapsto b^hk$ over $n$ is $\{h:b^h\mid n\}$, whose weight sum is exactly $m_a(n)$,
and it is the formalization of $m_a$ at arbitrary base --- noted above --- that makes
this reachable.  The unit-weight case is recorded as a guard
(\lean{Fabius.tsum\_padicValNat\_succ\_rpow}).  What \eqref{p1:eq:zeta-a} still lacks is
narrower than the product: the corpus proves it for real $s>1$ with the first factor as
its own $p$-series, so the extension to complex $s$ and the identification of that
factor with \lean{riemannZeta} are the two remaining steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The scale-$h$ sinc contributes one zero at $n$ for every representation $n=2^hk$ with
$k\ge1$, and it occurs with multiplicity $a_h$.  Summing over $h\le\TwoAdicValuation(n)$ gives
\eqref{p1:eq:m-a}.  Moreover
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{m_a(n)}{n^2}
 =\sum_{h\ge0}a_h\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(2^hk)^2}
 =\zeta(2)A(1/4)<\infty,
\]
so the genus-zero canonical product converges normally.  The same rearrangement for
$\Re s>1$ gives
\[
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{n^s}\sum_{2^h\mid n}a_h
 =\sum_{h\ge0}a_h2^{-hs}\zeta(s).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{resultbox}{Spectral--probabilistic dual use of $A$}
The spectral side samples $A$ at $2^{-s}$, while the probability side will sample it at
$4^{-j}$.  The entire zero divisor and every even cumulant are therefore two transforms of
one coefficient sequence, not merely analogous formulas.
\end{resultbox}

\subsection{Exact counting and a generalized digital defect}

Let
\begin{equation}
 M_a(N)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}m_a(n).
 \label{p1:eq:M-a}
\end{equation}
For $N=\sum_{j\ge0}b_j(N)2^j$, define the tail weights
\begin{equation}
 \tau_j(a)=\sum_{k\ge1}a_{j+k}2^{-k}.
 \label{p1:eq:tau-j}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Exact zero count and digit defect]
\label{p1:thm:digital-count}
For every positive integer $N$,
\begin{align}
 M_a(N)
 &=\sum_{h\ge0}a_h\Floor{\frac{N}{2^h}},
 \label{p1:eq:M-floor}\\
 &=N A(1/2)-\rho_a(N),
 \qquad
 \rho_a(N)=\sum_{h\ge0}a_h\left\{\frac{N}{2^h}\right\},
 \label{p1:eq:M-defect}\\
 &=N A(1/2)-\sum_{j\ge0}b_j(N)\tau_j(a).
 \label{p1:eq:M-bit}
\end{align}
This is \statusproved.  The floor form \eqref{p1:eq:M-floor} is formalized as
\lean{Fabius.sum_range_weightedScaleMultiplicity} (\lean{WeightedScaleMultiplicity.lean}), over
the finite range $h<N$ that already contains every nonzero term, and again for an arbitrary base
$b\ne1$ and weights in an arbitrary additive commutative monoid, so the Lean statement is
strictly more general than \eqref{p1:eq:M-floor}.  The defect form \eqref{p1:eq:M-defect} is
now formalized as well, in \path{DigitDefectCounting.lean}: with $A(1/2)=\sum_h a_h2^{-h}$
(\lean{Fabius.dyadicWeightValue}) and $\rho_a(N)=\sum_h a_h\{N/2^h\}$
(\lean{Fabius.dyadicDefect}), the identity
$\sum_h a_h\Floor{N/2^h}=N\,A(1/2)-\rho_a(N)$ holds under the single hypothesis that
$\sum_h|a_h|2^{-h}$ converges
(\lean{Fabius.tsum\_mul\_natCast\_div\_two\_pow\_defect}), and the cumulative reading is
\lean{Fabius.sum\_range\_weightedScaleMultiplicity\_real}.  Boundedness of $a$ is not needed:
since $\{N/2^h\}\le N/2^h$, the same summability dominates both series.  At $a_h\equiv1$ the
identity reduces to Legendre's $\sum_h\Floor{N/2^h}=2N-\BinaryDigitSum(N)$, carried as a regression
test (\lean{Fabius.sum\_range\_div\_two\_pow\_add\_digitSum}, \lean{Fabius.dyadicDefect\_one}).  The
per-scale digit expansion $\{N/2^h\}=\sum_{j<h}b_j(N)2^{\,j-h}$ that the bit form
\eqref{p1:eq:M-bit} rests on is also formal
(\lean{Fabius.fract\_natCast\_div\_two\_pow\_eq\_sum\_range}), and so is the exchange of
summation that converts it into \eqref{p1:eq:M-bit}, in
\path{DigitDefectBitForm.lean}.  The tail weight
$\tau_j(a)=\sum_{k\ge1}a_{j+k}2^{-k}$ is \lean{Fabius.dyadicTailWeight}, well defined by
\lean{Fabius.summable\_dyadicTailWeight\_terms} and pinned against an off-by-one in the
index convention by the halving recursion
$\tau_j=(a_{j+1}+\tau_{j+1})/2$ (\lean{Fabius.dyadicTailWeight\_succ}) together with
$\tau_j(1)=1$ (\lean{Fabius.dyadicTailWeight\_one}); the resolved defect
$\rho_a(N)=\sum_j b_j(N)\tau_j(a)$ is
\lean{Fabius.dyadicDefect\_eq\_sum\_range\_testBit} in windowed form and
\lean{Fabius.dyadicDefect\_eq\_tsum\_testBit} unconditionally, and \eqref{p1:eq:M-bit}
itself is \lean{Fabius.sum\_range\_weightedScaleMultiplicity\_bit}.  The exchange needs no
Fubini on a triangular index set: only finitely many digits of $N$ are nonzero, so a fixed
window reduces it to a finite sum of convergent series.  As a regression test the module
re-derives $\sum_j b_j(N)=\BinaryDigitSum(N)$ from the new machinery and lands it on the corpus's
audited Legendre count (\lean{Fabius.tsum\_testBit\_eq\_digitSum}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Count the multiples of $2^h$ among $1,\ldots,N$ and sum their contributions $a_h$.
Subtracting the fractional parts from $N\sum_ha_h2^{-h}$ gives \eqref{p1:eq:M-defect}.
Finally,
\[
 \left\{\frac{N}{2^h}\right\}
 =\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}b_j(N)2^{j-h};
\]
absolute convergence permits exchanging the sums and yields \eqref{p1:eq:M-bit}.
\end{proof}

For $a_h\equiv1$, one has $A(1/2)=2$ and $\tau_j=1$, recovering the audited identity
$M_a(N)=2N-\BinaryDigitSum(N)$.  For general $a$, the ordinary binary weight is replaced by a weighted
suffix transform of the exponent sequence.

\subsection{Lobe signs and generalized Thue--Morse characters}

For $x\in(N,N+1)$, every canonical-product factor with index $n\le N$ is negative and all
remaining factors are positive.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \Sign\Phi_a(x)=(-1)^{M_a(N)}.
 \label{p1:eq:lobe-sign-count}
\end{equation}
Modulo two,
$\Floor{N/2^h}\equiv b_h(N)$, so the sign is a digit character.

\begin{theorem}[Generalized lobe sign]
\label{p1:thm:lobe-sign}
Put $\bar a_h=a_h\bmod2$ and
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon_a(N)=(-1)^{\sum_{h\ge0}\bar a_hb_h(N)}.
 \label{p1:eq:epsilon-a}
\end{equation}
Then, away from the integer zeros,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\qquad \Sign\Phi_a(x)=\varepsilon_a(\Floor{x}).\qquad}
 \label{p1:eq:sign-master}
\end{equation}
Moreover $\varepsilon_a$ is a $2$-automatic sequence if and only if the parity word
$(\bar a_h)_{h\ge0}$ is eventually periodic.  Both statements are \statusproved.  At
$a_h\equiv1$ the sign law \eqref{p1:eq:sign-master} is formalized as
\lean{Fabius.rvachevFourierProduct_eq_thueMorse_sign_mul_norm} (\lean{ThueMorseLobeSign.lean}),
in the equivalent form $\Phi(x)=\ThueMorseSign{N}\lVert\Phi(x)\rVert$ on the lobe $(N,N+1)$.  The
general parity character \eqref{p1:eq:epsilon-a} is now formalized as \lean{Fabius.parityCharacter}
(\lean{ParityCharacter.lean}).  Because $b_h(N)=1$ exactly when $h$ lies in the bit support
of $N$, the exponent is a plain sum of weights over that support, and the corpus's
Boolean-cube machinery applies verbatim: \lean{Fabius.parityCharacter\_const\_one} recovers the
Thue--Morse sign at $a_h\equiv1$, \lean{Fabius.parityCharacter\_mod\_two} confirms that only the
parity word $(\bar a_h)$ enters, and
\lean{Fabius.prod\_one\_add\_neg\_one\_pow\_eq\_sum\_parityCharacter} gives the weighted product
identity
$\prod_{j<m}\bigl(1+(-1)^{a_j}z^{2^j}\bigr)=\sum_{n<2^m}\varepsilon_a(n)z^n$
over an arbitrary commutative ring --- which at $a_h\equiv1$ is the finite Thue--Morse
product identity.  The automaticity criterion is formal too, in \path{ParityCharacterKernel.lean},
and the assessment that it needed automatic-sequence theory was too pessimistic: taking
the standard finite-$2$-kernel characterization as the definition, the criterion is purely
combinatorial.  Writing $\mathcal K(f)=\{n\mapsto f(2^kn+r):r<2^k\}$, one has
\[
  \mathcal K(\varepsilon_a)\ \text{finite}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  (\bar a_h)_{h\ge0}\ \text{eventually periodic}
\]
(\lean{Fabius.finite\_twoKernel\_parityCharacter\_iff}).  The engine is the volume's own
kernel-shift identity \eqref{p1:eq:kernel-shift}
(\lean{Fabius.parityCharacter\_two\_pow\_mul\_add}), which rests on the bit-support split of
$2^kn+r$: read at $r=0$ it places every shifted character in the kernel, and read in
general it makes every kernel element $\pm$ a shifted character, so the kernel is covered
by one image together with its negation.  The converse direction uses the probe
$\varepsilon_{S^ka}(2^j)=(-1)^{\bar a_{k+j}}$
(\lean{Fabius.parityCharacter\_shiftSeq\_two\_pow}) to turn equal characters into equal
shifted parity words.  What the library still lacks is the \emph{equivalence} between a
finite $2$-kernel and an automaton definition; that is imported from the literature as
the meaning of the word, not proved.  The constant weight is recorded as a guard
(\lean{Fabius.finite\_twoKernel\_thueMorseSign}): the weight word is periodic and the
kernel finite, while the corpus's \lean{Fabius.thueMorseSign\_not\_eventually\_periodic} says the \emph{sign}
sequence is not eventually periodic --- the criterion constrains the weight word, not the
character.  The sign law \eqref{p1:eq:sign-master} splits in two, and its arithmetic
half --- the observation, made here in one line, that $\Floor{N/2^h}\equiv b_h(N)$
modulo two, so that the exponent \eqref{p1:eq:lobe-sign-count} is a digit character ---
is formal in \path{DigitCharacterCongruence.lean}:
\[
  M_a(N)=\sum_h a_h\Floor{\frac{N}{2^h}}
  \;\equiv\;\sum_{h\in\SupportOperator_2(N)}a_h\pmod 2,
  \qquad\text{hence}\quad(-1)^{M_a(N)}=\varepsilon_a(N)
\]
(\lean{Fabius.sum\_div\_two\_pow\_mul\_mod\_two}, \lean{Fabius.neg\_one\_pow\_sum\_div\_two\_pow}); the bridge is simply that
the $h$-th bit of $N$ \emph{is} $\Floor{N/2^h}\bmod2$, and at the constant weight the
statement becomes Legendre's count read modulo two
(\lean{Fabius.neg\_one\_pow\_sum\_div\_two\_pow\_const\_one}).  The analytic half is formal as
well, in \path{LobeSignLaw.lean}, so \eqref{p1:eq:lobe-sign-count} and \eqref{p1:eq:sign-master}
are theorems --- on the \emph{open} lobes.  On $N<x<N+1$ the canonical form splits into
a finite prefix of factors of index $n\le N$, each with a negative base, and a tail of
positive ones, so
\[
  \Sign\Phi_a(x)=(-1)^{M_a(N)}=\varepsilon_a(N)
\]
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_ofReal\_eq\_parityCharacter\_mul\_norm}).  The statement is
carried across to $\Phi_a$ itself, not merely to a real surrogate, and the constant-weight
case reproduces the corpus's existing Thue--Morse lobe sign.

The integer points are covered too, in \path{CanonicalIntegerPoint.lean}.  At $x=n\ge1$
the canonical factor of index $n$ is $0^{m_a(n)}$, so when $m_a(n)=0$ it is $1$ --- neither
negative nor vanishing --- and the same prefix/tail argument gives the same formula
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_natCast\_eq\_parityCharacter\_mul\_norm}); when
$m_a(n)\ne0$ the product vanishes, which is the volume's exclusion
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_natCast\_eq\_zero\_of\_ne\_zero}).  So
\eqref{p1:eq:sign-master} is formalized at every real $x>0$ at which no factor of $\Phi_a$
vanishes, which is the volume's own scope on that range.

Two residues are stated rather than glossed.  At $x=0$ no factor vanishes and
$\Phi_a(0)=1$, but the hypothesis $m_a(0)=0$ need not hold (indeed $m_a(0)=a_0$), so that
point is closed by a
separate lemma (\lean{Fabius.canonicalRealProduct\_zero\_eq\_one}) rather than by the theorem
above.  Negative arguments are carried by evenness of $\Phi_a$
(\lean{Fabius.generalizedRvachevProduct\_neg}, \path{LobeSignNegative.lean}), and there the law
reads $\varepsilon_a(\Floor{\AbsoluteValue{x}})$ rather than $\varepsilon_a(\Floor{x})$:
on $-(N+1)<x<-N$ the reflected point lies in the lobe $(N,N+1)$, so the sign is
$\varepsilon_a(N)$, while $\Floor{x}=-(N+1)$ is not even a natural number.  We write
$\Floor{x}$ because we have $x\ge0$ in mind.

Assembled, these pieces give the law on the whole axis with no hypothesis at all, in
\path{LobeSignComplete.lean}, in which $\Phi_a$ is read on the real axis through its
canonical product \eqref{p1:eq:canonical-a}:
\[
 \Phi_a(x)=0
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 0<\varepsilon_a\bigl(\Floor{\AbsoluteValue{x}}\bigr)\,\Phi_a(x),
 \qquad x\in\RealNumbers
\]
(\lean{Fabius.parityCharacter\_mul\_canonicalRealProduct\_dichotomy}), the first alternative
occurring exactly when $\lvert x\rvert$ is a positive integer of nonzero multiplicity
(\lean{Fabius.canonicalRealProduct\_eq\_zero\_iff\_of\_nonneg}).  There is no third
possibility and no remaining gap; what made the assembly possible is the complete zero set of
\path{GeneralizedZeroDivisor.lean}, without which the exceptional set could be excluded but not
identified.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The sign formula follows from \eqref{p1:eq:lobe-sign-count}, \eqref{p1:eq:M-floor}, and reduction
modulo two.  For the automaticity criterion, let $S$ denote the left shift of the parity
word.  If $0\le r<2^k$, binary concatenation gives
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon_a(2^kn+r)=\varepsilon_a(r)\varepsilon_{S^ka}(n).
 \label{p1:eq:kernel-shift}
\end{equation}
Thus an eventually periodic parity word has only finitely many shifts and therefore gives a
finite $2$-kernel.  Conversely, equality of two shifted sign sequences forces equality of
the corresponding shifted parity words, because
$\varepsilon_{S^ka}(2^j)=(-1)^{\bar a_{k+j}}$.  A finite $2$-kernel therefore implies a
finite shift orbit of the parity word, which is equivalent to eventual periodicity.  This is
the present Walsh-character specialization of the standard finite-kernel characterization
of automatic sequences \cite{bib:allouche2003}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Finite sign products and exact Prouhet order}

For $L\ge0$, let
\begin{equation}
 O_L(a)=\{0\le h<L:a_h\ \text{is odd}\},
 \qquad \omega_L(a)=|O_L(a)|.
 \label{p1:eq:O-omega}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Generalized Prouhet block]
\label{p1:thm:general-prouhet}
The length-$2^L$ sign polynomial factors as
\begin{equation}
 T_{a,L}(z):=\sum_{n=0}^{2^L-1}\varepsilon_a(n)z^n
 =\prod_{h=0}^{L-1}\left(1+(-1)^{a_h}z^{2^h}\right).
 \label{p1:eq:T-a-L}
\end{equation}
Its zero at $z=1$ has exact order $\omega_L(a)$.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n<2^L}\varepsilon_a(n)n^k=0,
 \qquad 0\le k<\omega_L(a),
 \label{p1:eq:Prouhet-vanish}
\end{equation}
and the first surviving power moment is
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \sum_{n<2^L}\varepsilon_a(n)n^{\omega_L(a)}
 =(-1)^{\omega_L(a)}\omega_L(a)!
 2^{L-\omega_L(a)+\sum_{h\in O_L(a)}h}.
 \quad}
 \label{p1:eq:first-surviving}
\end{equation}
This is \statusproved.  Its sharp-moment core is formalized, and in greater generality:
\lean{Fabius.sum_powerset_neg_one_pow_pow_card} (\lean{ThueMorseSparseProuhet.lean}) evaluates
\[
 \sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|T|}\Bigl(x+\sum_{j\in T}w_j\Bigr)^{|S|}
 =(-1)^{|S|}\,|S|!\prod_{j\in S}w_j
\]
for an arbitrary finite index set $S$, arbitrary step weights $w_j$ in an arbitrary commutative
ring, and every offset $x$.  Taking $S=O_L(a)$ and $w_h=2^h$ produces exactly the constant
$(-1)^{\omega_L(a)}\omega_L(a)!\,2^{\sum_{h\in O_L(a)}h}$ of \eqref{p1:eq:first-surviving},
independently of $x$, and the companion
\lean{Fabius.sum_powerset_neg_one_pow_eval_of_degree_lt} is the vanishing
