\part{Negative Parameters, Reciprocal Bases, and the Gaussian Boundary}



\begin{abstract}
The current \texttt{ProveIt/Analysis/FabiusFunction/docs} corpus develops the Fabius and
Rvachev functions from probability, functional equations, exact dyadic arithmetic,
$q$-calculus, infinite sinc products, Thue--Morse cancellation, Legendre expansions,
Lambert--$W$ endpoint asymptotics, and formalized analysis.  When this report was
written, its integrated frontier volume explicitly left open, for the
geometric-uniform family, the density
interpretation at negative parameters, centered affine transport, log-concavity and
central plateaux, explicit Bernoulli cumulants and Bell moments in the generic
parameter, and Gaussian-limit statements.

This report gives paper-level solutions or substantial advances for those gaps.  For
\(0<r<1\), if
\[
 X_q=(1-q)\sum_{n\ge0}q^nU_n,
 \qquad U_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1),
\]
then the central identity is
\[
 X_{-r}-\frac12\ \doteqL\
 \frac{1+r}{1-r}\left(X_r-\frac12\right).
\]
It gives the exact negative-parameter CDF, quantile, support, smooth density, entropy
scaling, sinc product, and all derivative transports.  It also diagnoses a sign issue
that was deliberately left uninterpreted in the repository: the previously selected
total function at \(q<0\) is the \emph{negative} of the Radon--Nikodym density.  At
\(q=-1/2\) one obtains
\[
 F_{-1/2}(x)=F\!\left(\frac{x+1}{3}\right),\qquad
 g_{-1/2}(x)=\frac23\RvachevUp\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{3}\right),\qquad
 Q_{-1/2}(u)=3F^{-1}(u)-1,
\]
which transports the complete Lambert--\(W_{-1}\), Legendre, and Thue--Morse derivative
structures to the support \([-1,2]\).

A second exact duality concerns normalized finite geometric sums: reversal of the
digits proves invariance under \(q\mapsto q^{-1}\).  Consequently the bases
\(2,-2,4,-4\), and all real \(\lvert q\rvert>1\), have canonical weak limits given by
the reciprocal-base laws.  A residue-class decomposition yields a multiplication
formula for the laws and their infinite sinc products.  The same framework proves
log-concavity for every real \(\lvert q\rvert<1\), exact central plateaux when
\(\lvert q\rvert<1/2\), and a Gaussian boundary as \(\lvert q\rvert\uparrow1\).  The
latter comes with an explicit Berry--Esseen bound, closed standardized Bernoulli
cumulants, Bell-polynomial moment corrections, and a quartic characteristic-function
expansion.  Reproducible numerical experiments accompany the proofs.

All claims of novelty in this report mean \emph{novel relative to the inspected
repository corpus}; no claim of global publication priority is made.
\end{abstract}

\section{Scope, corpus audit, and novelty boundary}

\subsection{The inspected corpus}

The review used the current integrated exposition
\texttt{Fabius\_Function\_and\_Rvachev\_Up.tex}, the mathematical glossary, the
non-elementarity article, the Lean walkthrough, the consolidated
\texttt{semi-formalized-research-frontiers.tex}, the archive index and its historical
families, and the TeX sources stored under \texttt{papers}.  The archive is important
for priority control: many early notes are frozen historical stages, while the two large
integrated sources are the canonical current synthesis.  The principal public entry
points are \cite{bib:repo2026c,bib:repo2026d,bib:repog,bib:repoh,bib:repoi}.

The repository's own frontier box is unusually specific.  It records that the law
\(\mu_q\) is absolutely continuous for every \(\lvert q\rvert<1\), but that the chosen
function called \(f_q\) has only been identified with the Radon--Nikodym density for
\(0<q<1\).  It separately lists centered affine transport, log-concavity, strictness,
central plateaux, explicit Bernoulli cumulants, Bell moments, and Gaussian limits as
unpromoted research layers \cite{bib:repo2026d}.  These declarations make it possible
to state a sharp non-duplication target.

\subsection{What is taken as established}

The absorbed report imported seven foundational layers from the repository
with a single blanket citation.  In the merged volume six of them are proved,
and each is now cited by its in-volume number; only the last remains a corpus
input.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item existence and almost-sure convergence of the weighted uniform series:
      \cref{p0:prop:basic};
\item the affine independent-copy equation and uniqueness of its
      probability-law fixed point for every real \(\lvert q\rvert<1\),
      including negative \(q\): \cref{p0:prop:fixed-point} among laws with a

\item exact support for the geometric law: \eqref{p0:eq:support};
\item the density formula for \(0<q<1\): \cref{p8:thm:all-sign-density},

\section{Geometric-uniform preliminaries}

\subsection{The law, its centered form, and its transform}

Let \((U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) random variables.  For
real \(q\) with \(\lvert q\rvert<1\), define
\begin{equation}
 X_q=(1-q)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}q^nU_n.                 \label{p8:eq:Xq-def}
\end{equation}
The series converges absolutely almost surely.  Put
\begin{equation}
 V_n=U_n-\frac12,
 \qquad
 Y_q=X_q-\frac12=(1-q)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}q^nV_n.     \label{p8:eq:Yq-def}
\end{equation}
The centering follows from \((1-q)\sum_{n\ge0}q^n=1\).  Every \(V_n\) is symmetric,
which is the source of the negative-parameter duality.  Note the
normalization shift across the part boundary recorded in
\cref{p0:tab:dictionary}: Part~VII's \(Y_q\) is this part's \emph{uncentered}
\(X_q\), and this part's \(Y_q\) is its centering.

Write
\[
 F_q(x)=\Probability(X_q\le x),
 \qquad
 \psi_q(t)=\Expectation \EulerE^{itY_q},
 \qquad
 \SincRad z=\begin{cases}\sin z/z,&z\ne0,\\1,&z=0.\end{cases}
\]
Independence gives the centered infinite sinc product
\(\psi_q(t)=\prod_{n\ge0}\SincRad\bigl((1-q)q^nt/2\bigr)\), which is
\eqref{p0:eq:cf}; \eqref{p7:eq:psi-sinc} records it together with the
functional equation \(\psi_q(t)=\SincRad\bigl(\tfrac{(1-q)t}2\bigr)\psi_q(qt)\)
and the zero list.  The signs of the individual arguments disappear because
\(\SincRad\) is even, but the
factor \(1-q\) remains and will encode the affine stretch between \(q=r\) and \(q=-r\).

\subsection{The affine fixed point}

If \(X_q'\) is an independent copy of \(X_q\), then splitting off the first digit yields
\begin{equation}
 X_q\ \doteqL\ (1-q)U_0+qX_q'.                       \label{p8:eq:affine-fixed-point}
\end{equation}
\Cref{p0:prop:fixed-point} proves that this equation characterizes the law
uniquely among probability measures with a finite first moment, for every real
\(\lvert q\rvert<1\) and without any support or density assumption.  The
moment hypothesis, which that contraction argument needs for its complete
metric, is not needed for the conclusion.

\begin{lemma}[Uniqueness among all probability laws]\label{p8:lem:fixed-point-all-laws}
Let \(\lvert q\rvert<1\) be real and let \(\nu\) be any probability measure on
\(\RealNumbers\) such that \(Z\sim\nu\) satisfies \(Z\doteqL(1-q)U+qZ'\) with \(U\)
uniform on \((0,1)\), \(Z'\sim\nu\), and \(U,Z'\) independent.  Then \(\nu\) is
the law of \(X_q\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Iterating the equation \(N\) times gives, for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
 Z\ \doteqL\ S_N+q^NZ_N,
 \qquad
 S_N=(1-q)\sum_{n<N}q^nU_n,
\]
with \(Z_N\sim\nu\) independent of \((U_n)_{n<N}\).  For every
\(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 \Probability\bigl(\AbsoluteValue{q^NZ_N}>\varepsilon\bigr)
 =\nu\bigl(\SetOf{z:\AbsoluteValue z>\varepsilon\AbsoluteValue q^{-N}}\bigr)
 \longrightarrow0
 \qquad(N\to\infty),
\]
because \(\nu\) is a finite measure: no moment is used.
Since \(S_N\) converges almost surely to a variable with the law of \(X_q\)
(\cref{p0:prop:basic}), the sum \(S_N+q^NZ_N\) converges in probability to
that variable, hence in law to the law of \(X_q\); as its law is \(\nu\) for
every \(N\), \(\nu\) is that limit.
\end{proof}

In the positive range, \(X_r\) is supported on \([0,1]\).  At \(r=1/2\),
\begin{equation}
 F_{1/2}=F,
 \qquad
 g_{1/2}(x)=2\RvachevUp(2x-1),                                \label{p8:eq:half-bridge}
\end{equation}
where \(F\) is the bounded Fabius function and \(\RvachevUp\) is the Rvachev up-function.

\subsection{$q$-brackets, Bernoulli cumulants, and Bell polynomials}

For an integer \(m\ge1\), set
\begin{equation}
 [m]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1}=\frac{1-q^m}{1-q}             \label{p8:eq:q-bracket}
\end{equation}
when \(q\ne1\), with the continuous value \([m]_1=m\).  We use the Bernoulli convention
\(B_2=1/6\), \(B_4=-1/30\), \(B_6=1/42\).  A centered uniform
\(V\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-1/2,1/2)\) has \(\cump_{2m}(V)=B_{2m}/2m\) and
\(\cump_{2m+1}(V)=0\); this and the resulting cumulants of \(X_q\) are
\cref{p0:thm:cumulants}.
The complete exponential Bell polynomial \(\mathcal B_n\) converts cumulants to moments:
\begin{equation}
 \Expectation Z^n=\mathcal B_n\bigl(\cump_1(Z),\ldots,\cump_n(Z)\bigr). \label{p8:eq:bell-moment}
\end{equation}

\section{Negative parameters: an exact affine duality}

\subsection{The coupling, and the notation it fixes}

The affine sign conjugacy, with its digitwise coupling, is
\cref{p7:thm:sign-conjugacy}: for \(0<r<1\),
\begin{equation}
 X_{-r}-\frac12\ \doteqL\ c_r\left(X_r-\frac12\right),
 \qquad
 c_r=\frac{1+r}{1-r},                                    \label{p8:eq:cr-def}
\end{equation}
with almost-sure equality under the reflected digits
\(U_n^-=\tfrac12+(-1)^n\bigl(U_n-\tfrac12\bigr)\), which are again i.i.d.\
uniform.  Support, CDF and quantile transport are \cref{p7:cor:transport} and
\eqref{p7:eq:negative-support}; writing \(Q_q\) for the generalized inverse of
\(F_q\), we fix for the rest of this part the notation
\[
 \ell_r=-\frac{r}{1-r},
 \qquad
 u_r=\frac{1}{1-r},
 \qquad
 T_r(y)=\frac12+c_r\left(y-\frac12\right),
\]
so that \(T_r\) is the increasing affine bijection of \([0,1]\) onto
\([\ell_r,u_r]=\SupportOperator(X_{-r})\), and
\(F_{-r}=F_r\circ T_r^{-1}\), \(Q_{-r}=T_r\circ Q_r\).

\subsection{The correct negative-parameter density and the sign diagnosis}

The integrated source defines, as a total symbolic function,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde f_q(x)=
 \frac{F_q(x/q)-F_q((x-(1-q))/q)}{1-q}.                   \label{p8:eq:source-selected-f}
\end{equation}
For \(q>0\) it proves that this is the density.  At \(q<0\), division by \(q\) reverses
the CDF interval.  The next result resolves the open interpretation exactly.

\begin{theorem}[Radon--Nikodym density for every nonzero parameter]\label{p8:thm:all-sign-density}
For \(0<\lvert q\rvert<1\), the law of \(X_q\) has density
\begin{equation}
 g_q(x)=\frac{1}{1-q}\,
 \Probability\bigl(x-(1-q)\le qX_q'\le x\bigr),                  \label{p8:eq:density-probability}
\end{equation}
where \(X_q'\) is an independent copy.  Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 g_q(x)=\Sign(q)\,\widetilde f_q(x).}                     \label{p8:eq:density-sign}
\end{equation}
Thus for \(-1<q<0\), the repository's selected total function is not a probability
density but its negative.  In particular it integrates to \(-1\), while \(g_q\ge0\)
and integrates to \(1\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Condition on \(X_q'=y\) in \cref{p8:eq:affine-fixed-point}.  The conditional law is uniform
on the interval \([qy,qy+1-q]\), of length \(1-q>0\).  Averaging the conditional density
therefore gives \cref{p8:eq:density-probability}.  If \(q>0\), the event in that formula is
\[
 \frac{x-(1-q)}q\le X_q'\le\frac xq,
\]
which gives \(g_q=\widetilde f_q\).  If \(q<0\), the inequalities reverse and
\[
 g_q(x)=\frac{F_q((x-(1-q))/q)-F_q(x/q)}{1-q}
       =-\widetilde f_q(x).
\]
The CDF is continuous, so endpoint conventions do not matter.
\end{proof}

The density and all of its derivatives transport affinely,
\(g_{-r}(x)=c_r^{-1}g_r\bigl(T_r^{-1}(x)\bigr)\) and
\(g_{-r}^{(k)}(x)=c_r^{-(k+1)}g_r^{(k)}\bigl(T_r^{-1}(x)\bigr)\) for every
\(k\ge0\), so \(g_{-r}\in C_c^\infty(\RealNumbers)\) with support
\([\ell_r,u_r]\).  This is \cref{p7:cor:transport} and
\eqref{p7:eq:derivative-transport}.

\begin{corollary}[Norm and entropy transport]\label{p8:cor:norm-entropy}
For \(1\le p\le\infty\) and \(k\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
 \Norm{g_{-r}^{(k)}}_p
 =c_r^{1/p-k-1}\Norm{g_r^{(k)}}_p,                        \label{p8:eq:sobolev-scaling}
\end{equation}
with \(1/\infty=0\).  The differential entropy \(h(X_r)=-\int g_r\log g_r\) is
finite, with
\begin{equation}
 \log(1-r)\le h(X_r)\le0,                                  \label{p8:eq:entropy-finite}
\end{equation}
and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 h(X_{-r})=h(X_r)+\log c_r.                               \label{p8:eq:entropy-scaling}
\end{equation}
For every order \(\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)\) the R\'enyi entropy
\(h_\alpha(X)=(1-\alpha)^{-1}\log\int f_X^{\alpha}\) obeys the same law,
\(h_\alpha(X_{-r})=h_\alpha(X_r)+\log c_r\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use \eqref{p7:eq:derivative-transport} and the substitution
\(y=1/2+(x-1/2)/c_r\).  For \eqref{p8:eq:entropy-finite}:
\eqref{p8:eq:density-probability} gives \(0\le g_r\le1/(1-r)\), so
\(-\int g_r\log g_r\ge-\log\Norm{g_r}_\infty\ge\log(1-r)\), while Jensen's
inequality on the support \([0,1]\), of length one, gives
\(h(X_r)\le\log1=0\).  The two entropy identities are the Jacobian formula
for \(aX+b\) with \(a=c_r>0\): if \(f_X\) is the density of \(X\), then
\(aX+b\) has density \(a^{-1}f_X\bigl((\cdot-b)/a\bigr)\), so
\(\int\bigl(a^{-1}f_X((x-b)/a)\bigr)^{\alpha}\Differential x
 =a^{1-\alpha}\int f_X^{\alpha}\), which is
\(h_\alpha(aX+b)=h_\alpha(X)+\log a\), and \(\alpha\to1\) gives the Shannon
case.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Characteristic functions and sinc products}

Applying characteristic functions to the sign conjugacy gives the centered
transform scaling \(\psi_{-r}(t)=\psi_r(c_rt)\), the last clause of
\eqref{p7:eq:sign-law}.  On products it is the identity
\[
 \prod_{n\ge0}\SincRad\!\left(\frac{(1+r)r^nt}{2}\right)
 =\prod_{n\ge0}\SincRad\!\left(\frac{(1-r)r^nc_rt}{2}\right),
\]
immediate from \((1-r)c_r=1+r\).

\section{The exact negative dyadic law}

\subsection{Fabius, inverse Fabius, and Rvachev formulas}

Set \(r=1/2\).  Then \(c_r=3\), \(\ell_r=-1\), and \(u_r=2\).

The CDF, density and quantile of the negative dyadic law are
\cref{p7:cor:transport} at \(a=\tfrac12\) combined with the half-base bridge
\eqref{p8:eq:half-bridge}:
\[
 F_{-1/2}(x)=F\!\left(\frac{x+1}{3}\right),
 \qquad
 g_{-1/2}(x)=\frac23\RvachevUp\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{3}\right),
 \qquad
 Q_{-1/2}(u)=3F^{-1}(u)-1,
\]
on the support \([-1,2]\).  What the sign diagnosis adds is the value of the
source-selected total function there.

\begin{corollary}[Sign of the selected function at the negative dyadic base]
\label{p8:cor:negative-dyadic-sign}
For every real \(x\),
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde f_{-1/2}(x)=-\frac23\RvachevUp\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{3}\right). \label{p8:eq:negative-dyadic-selected}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Combine \cref{p8:eq:density-sign} with the density displayed above.
\end{proof}

This is a direct and unexpectedly economical link between a negative geometric base and
the inverse Fabius function.  It also means that every exact formula for \(F^{-1}\) or
its asymptotics is automatically an exact formula for the negative dyadic quantile.

\subsection{Thue--Morse derivative peaks on a stretched dyadic grid}

The frontier corpus proves the sharp Rvachev derivative identities
\begin{equation}
 \Norm{\RvachevUp^{(m)}}_\infty=2^{\binom{m+1}{2}},
 \qquad
 \RvachevUp^{(m)}(c_{m,j})=\ThueMorseSign{j}2^{\binom{m+1}{2}},       \label{p8:eq:up-peaks-baseline}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 c_{m,j}=-1+2^{-m}+j2^{1-m},
 \qquad 0\le j<2^m.                                      \label{p8:eq:cmj}
\end{equation}
It also proves higher-order flatness at this grid: \(\RvachevUp^{(k)}(c_{m,j})=0\) for
\(k>m\).  Transport gives a new negative-base atlas.

\begin{corollary}[Negative dyadic Thue--Morse atlas]\label{p8:cor:negative-thue-morse}
Define
\begin{equation}
 x_{m,j}=\frac{1+3c_{m,j}}2
 =-1+\frac{3}{2^{m+1}}+\frac{3j}{2^m}.                    \label{p8:eq:xmj}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 g_{-1/2}^{(m)}(x_{m,j})
 &=\ThueMorseSign{j}
   \left(\frac23\right)^{m+1}2^{\binom{m+1}{2}},          \label{p8:eq:negative-peak-values}\\
 \Norm{g_{-1/2}^{(m)}}_\infty
 &=\frac{2^{\binom{m+1}{2}+m+1}}{3^{m+1}},               \label{p8:eq:negative-peak-norm}\\
 g_{-1/2}^{(k)}(x_{m,j})&=0\qquad(k>m).                   \label{p8:eq:negative-flatness}
\end{align}
Thus the same Thue--Morse signs occur on a grid whose spacing is stretched from
\(2^{1-m}\) to \(3\cdot2^{-m}\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
From the negative dyadic density of \cref{p7:cor:transport},
\[
 g_{-1/2}^{(m)}(x)=\left(\frac23\right)^{m+1}
 \RvachevUp^{(m)}\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{3}\right).
\]
Set \((2x-1)/3=c_{m,j}\) and use \cref{p8:eq:up-peaks-baseline} and the higher-flatness
result.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Legendre-series transport}

The absorbed report assumed the Legendre expansion of \(\RvachevUp\) in
\(L^2\) and asserted its transport pointwise.  The assumption is not needed:
smoothness on the closed interval already forces absolute and uniform
convergence, so the identities below hold at every point.

\begin{proposition}[Legendre transport]\label{p8:prop:legendre-transport}
Let \(P_k\) be the Legendre polynomials on \([-1,1]\) and put
\[
 b_n=\frac{4n+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}\RvachevUp(t)P_{2n}(t)\Differential t,
 \qquad
 a_n^{(r)}=(4n+1)\int_0^1g_r(y)P_{2n}(2y-1)\Differential y
 \quad(0<r<1).
\]
Then \(b_n=\BigO(n^{-k})\) and \(a_n^{(r)}=\BigOAt{n^{-k}}{r}\) for every
\(k\), the even Legendre expansion
\begin{equation}
 \RvachevUp(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_nP_{2n}(t),
 \qquad -1\le t\le1,                                    \label{p8:eq:up-legendre}
\end{equation}
converges absolutely and uniformly, and so does
\(g_r(y)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_n^{(r)}P_{2n}(2y-1)\) on \([0,1]\).  Consequently the
negative dyadic density has the pointwise expansion
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 g_{-1/2}(x)=\frac23\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}
 b_nP_{2n}\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{3}\right),
 \qquad -1\le x\le2,}                                    \label{p8:eq:negative-legendre}
\end{equation}
and, for every \(0<r<1\) and \(\ell_r\le x\le u_r\),
\begin{equation}
 g_{-r}(x)=\frac1{c_r}\sum_{n\ge0}a_n^{(r)}
 P_{2n}\!\left(\frac{2x-1}{c_r}\right).                  \label{p8:eq:general-negative-legendre}
\end{equation}
No coefficients need to be recomputed: only the Jacobian and the affine
Legendre coordinate change.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(f\in C^\infty[-1,1]\) be even; the two cases are
\(f=\RvachevUp\) restricted to \([-1,1]\) and \(f(t)=g_r\bigl((t+1)/2\bigr)\),
both smooth on the closed interval because \(\RvachevUp\) and \(g_r\) are
\(C^\infty\) on \(\RealNumbers\) (\cref{p7:cor:transport} and
\eqref{p7:eq:spectral-zeta}) and both even because the two densities are
symmetric about their centers.  The Legendre operator
\(\mathcal L f=\bigl((1-t^2)f'\bigr)'\) satisfies
\(\mathcal L P_k=-k(k+1)P_k\), and it is symmetric on \(C^2[-1,1]\) with no
boundary condition, since the weight \(1-t^2\) vanishes at \(\pm1\):
\(\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal L f)g=-\int_{-1}^1(1-t^2)f'g'=\int_{-1}^1f\,\mathcal L g\).
Hence for every \(k\ge1\) and \(n\ge1\),
\[
 \int_{-1}^1fP_{2n}
 =\frac{(-1)^k}{\bigl(2n(2n+1)\bigr)^k}\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal L^kf)P_{2n},
 \qquad\text{so}\qquad
 \AbsoluteValue{\int_{-1}^1fP_{2n}}
 \le\frac{2\Norm{\mathcal L^kf}_\infty}{\bigl(2n(2n+1)\bigr)^k},
\]
using \(\sup_{[-1,1]}\AbsoluteValue{P_{2n}}=1\).  Multiplying by the
normalizing factor \((4n+1)/2\) gives coefficients of order \(n^{1-2k}\) for
every \(k\), which is the stated decay, and \(\sum_n\AbsoluteValue{b_n}<\infty\).
Since \(\AbsoluteValue{P_{2n}}\le1\) on \([-1,1]\), the series
\(\sum_nb_nP_{2n}\) converges absolutely and uniformly there to a continuous
function; by completeness of the Legendre polynomials in \(L^2(-1,1)\) its
\(L^2\) limit is \(f\) (the odd coefficients vanish by evenness), so the
continuous limit agrees with the continuous \(f\) almost everywhere, hence
everywhere.  The same argument gives the expansion of \(g_r\).  Finally
\(g_{-1/2}(x)=\tfrac23\RvachevUp\bigl((2x-1)/3\bigr)\) and
\(g_{-r}(x)=c_r^{-1}g_r\bigl(T_r^{-1}(x)\bigr)\) with
\(2T_r^{-1}(x)-1=(2x-1)/c_r\) (\cref{p7:cor:transport}); substituting the
uniformly convergent expansions gives \eqref{p8:eq:negative-legendre} and
\eqref{p8:eq:general-negative-legendre} pointwise.
\end{proof}

This supplies a direct bridge from the positive-$q$ Legendre theory to every negative
parameter.

\subsection{Exact transport of the Lambert--\texorpdfstring{$W_{-1}$}{W-1} endpoint phase}

Let \(L=\log2\).  The function
\(\lambda\mapsto\lambda2^{-\lambda}=\lambda\EulerE^{-L\lambda}\) increases on
\((0,1/L)\) to its maximum \(1/(\EulerE L)\) and decreases to \(0\)
afterwards, so for \(0<z<1/(\EulerE L)\) the equation
\begin{equation}
 z=\lambda2^{-\lambda}
\end{equation}
has exactly two positive solutions; \(\lambda(z)\) denotes the larger one,
\(\lambda(z)>1/L\).  Writing the equation as
\((-L\lambda)\EulerE^{-L\lambda}=-Lz\) with \(-Lz\in(-1/\EulerE,0)\), its two real
solutions are \(-L\lambda=W_0(-Lz)\in(-1,0)\) and \(-L\lambda=W_{-1}(-Lz)<-1\)
\cite{bib:corless1996}, and the larger \(\lambda\) is the second:
\begin{equation}
 \lambda(z)=-\frac1L W_{-1}(-Lz),
 \qquad 0<z<\frac1{\EulerE L}.                              \label{p8:eq:lambert-phase}
\end{equation}
The corpus's all-orders endpoint expansion of the Fabius function is written
in this coordinate, and it emphasizes that its periodic coefficient functions
must be evaluated at the \emph{exact} phase \(\lambda(z)\) rather than at a
phase with merely bounded error.  That expansion is imported here as
\statusexisting{}: it is neither restated nor reproved, and nothing below
depends on its form.  What this part proves is the transport of the
coordinate; the absorbed report presented the boxed formula below without a
statement or proof, and it is one change of variables.

\begin{proposition}[Exact transport of the endpoint coordinate]
\label{p8:prop:lambert-transport}
Write \(x=-1+\xi\) near the left endpoint of the support of \(X_{-1/2}\).
Then for every real \(\xi\) and every \(k\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
 F_{-1/2}(-1+\xi)=F(\xi/3),
 \qquad
 g_{-1/2}^{(k)}(-1+\xi)=3^{-(k+1)}g_{1/2}^{(k)}(\xi/3),       \label{p8:eq:endpoint-transport}
\end{equation}
and for \(0<\xi<3/(\EulerE L)\) the transported phase is
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \lambda_-(\xi)=\lambda(\xi/3)
 =-\frac1L W_{-1}\!\left(-\frac{L\xi}{3}\right).}        \label{p8:eq:negative-lambert-phase}
\end{equation}
Consequently, if \(F(z)=\mathcal E\bigl(z,\lambda(z)\bigr)+\rho(z)\) as
\(z\downarrow0\) for some expression \(\mathcal E\) and remainder \(\rho\)
--- in particular for the corpus's all-orders expansion with its one-periodic
coefficient functions of \(\lambda\) --- then
\(F_{-1/2}(-1+\xi)=\mathcal E\bigl(\xi/3,\lambda_-(\xi)\bigr)+\rho(\xi/3)\):
the coefficient functions are evaluated at \(\lambda_-\), the remainder bound
transfers verbatim, and each derivative acquires the factor \(3^{-k}\).  The
right endpoint follows from the symmetry of both laws about \(1/2\), and for
the quantile
\begin{equation}
 Q_{-1/2}(u)+1=3F^{-1}(u),\qquad 0<u<1.                    \label{p8:eq:inverse-endpoint-transport}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\(F_{-1/2}(x)=F\bigl((x+1)/3\bigr)\), \(Q_{-1/2}(u)=3F^{-1}(u)-1\) and
\(g_{-1/2}^{(k)}(x)=3^{-(k+1)}g_{1/2}^{(k)}\bigl((x+1)/3\bigr)\) are
\cref{p7:cor:transport} and \eqref{p7:eq:derivative-transport} at
\(a=\tfrac12\), where \(\lambda_{1/2}=3\) and \(\beta_{1/2}=1\); put
\(x=-1+\xi\).  The phase line is the definition of \(\lambda\) at the
argument \(\xi/3\), admissible exactly when \(\xi/3<1/(\EulerE L)\).  The
transfer statement is the substitution \(z=\xi/3\) in the assumed expansion,
and the derivative factors are those of \eqref{p8:eq:endpoint-transport}.
\end{proof}

\section{Shape theory: log-concavity and exact plateaux}

\subsection{Log-concavity for all real parameters}

\begin{definition}
A probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\RealNumbers\) is log-concave if for nonempty compact sets
\(A,B\) and \(0<\theta<1\),
\[
 \mu(\theta A+(1-\theta)B)
 \ge \mu(A)^\theta\mu(B)^{1-\theta}.
\]
An integrable function is log-concave when its logarithm is concave on its positivity
set, with the usual extended-value convention.
\end{definition}

In this sense the law of \(X_q\) is log-concave for every real
\(\lvert q\rvert<1\), including \(q=0\), where the density is
\(\IndicatorOf{[0,1]}\); for \(q\ne0\) the smooth density \(g_q\) is
log-concave on \(\RealNumbers\).  This is \cref{p7:thm:shape}: there the finite
partial sums \((1-q)\sum_{n\le N}q^nU_n\) are convolutions of uniform laws on
compact intervals, a negative coefficient merely reflects an interval, and
affine images and convolutions
preserve log-concavity by the Pr\'ekopa theorem \cite{bib:prekopa1973}.  Its proof there then passes to the limit
locally uniformly through the sinc-product tail bound.  This supplies the
global shape theorem that the repository's frontier list recorded as open
when the absorbed report was written; it implies
unimodality, and with reflection symmetry it places the mode at \(1/2\).  It
does \emph{not} by itself imply strict log-concavity: the same theorem
exhibits a whole parameter region where strictness is impossible.

\subsection{A dominant-digit plateau lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform convolution plateau]\label{p8:lem:uniform-plateau}
Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), independent of a random variable \(Y\) supported
on \([\alpha,\beta]\).  Let \(a>0\) and \(X=aU+Y\).  If \(a\ge\beta-\alpha\), then the
density of \(X\) is exactly \(1/a\) on
\begin{equation}
 [\beta,\alpha+a].                                        \label{p8:eq:general-plateau}
\end{equation}
When \(a>\beta-\alpha\), this is a nondegenerate interval.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Conditioning on \(Y\),
\[
 f_X(x)=\frac1a\Probability(x-a\le Y\le x).
\]
For \(x\in[\beta,\alpha+a]\), one has \(x\ge\beta\) and \(x-a\le\alpha\), so the event
contains the whole support of \(Y\) and has probability one.
\end{proof}

Applied to the fixed-point equation \(X_r=(1-r)U+rX_r'\) with \(\alpha=0\),
\(\beta=r\) and \(a=1-r\), the lemma gives the exact central plateaux of
\cref{p7:thm:shape}: for \(0<r\le1/2\) the positive density equals
\(1/(1-r)\) on \([r,1-r]\), the negative density equals \(1/(1+r)\) on
\([r^2/(1-r),\,1-r^2/(1-r)]\) --- the affine image of the first under
\cref{p7:cor:transport} --- each interval collapsing to the point \(x=1/2\) at
\(r=1/2\), and in either law the plateau carries mass \((1-2r)/(1-r)\).

Strictness above the transition, and the maximality of the plateau interval,
are Part~VI's conjecture on strict log-concavity in the overlapping regime,
recorded once in the discussion following \cref{p7:thm:shape}; by
\cref{p7:thm:sign-conjugacy} the negative cases follow from the positive ones.
The critical value \(r=1/2\) is structurally natural: it is exactly where the first
uniform digit and the entire tail have equal support length.  Proving strictness above
the transition likely requires an equality-case analysis for repeated Pr\'ekopa
convolution or a direct argument from the refinement equation.

\section{Residue-class decomposition and multiplication formulas}

\subsection{Decomposition into independent \texorpdfstring{$q^m$}{q^m} laws}

Splitting the defining series into residue classes \(n=mk+j\) writes \(X_q\)
as the weighted independent sum
\(X_q\doteqL[m]_q^{-1}\sum_{j<m}q^jX_{q^m}^{(j)}\), with the same weighted
identity for the centered variables, the transform law
\(\psi_q(t)=\prod_{j<m}\psi_{q^m}\bigl(q^jt/[m]_q\bigr)\) and the cumulant law
\(\cump_s(X_q)=\bigl([m]_{q^s}/[m]_q^s\bigr)\cump_s(X_{q^m})\).  All four are
\cref{p7:thm:multisection} and \eqref{p7:eq:multisection-transforms}, proved
there as identities of analytic germs valid outside the unit disc as well, and
identified with the Pochhammer dissection
\((a;q)_\infty=\prod_{r<m}(aq^r;q^m)_\infty\).

\subsection{Even--odd splitting}

For \(m=2\), \eqref{p7:eq:Y-multisection} becomes
\begin{align}
 X_r&\doteqL\frac{X_{r^2}^{(0)}+rX_{r^2}^{(1)}}{1+r},     \label{p8:eq:positive-even-odd}\\
 X_{-r}&\doteqL\frac{X_{r^2}^{(0)}-rX_{r^2}^{(1)}}{1-r}. \label{p8:eq:negative-even-odd}
\end{align}
Thus a negative-base law is a normalized difference of two independent positive-base
laws.  Combining this with \cref{p7:thm:sign-conjugacy} gives the distribution identity
\begin{equation}
 \frac{X_{r^2}^{(0)}-rX_{r^2}^{(1)}}{1-r}-\frac12
 \ \doteqL\
 c_r\left(
 \frac{X_{r^2}^{(0)}+rX_{r^2}^{(1)}}{1+r}-\frac12\right). \label{p8:eq:sum-difference-identity}
\end{equation}

For centered transforms, \(\psi_{q^2}\) is even, so
\begin{equation}
 \psi_{-r}(t)=
 \psi_{r^2}\!\left(\frac{t}{1-r}\right)
 \psi_{r^2}\!\left(\frac{rt}{1-r}\right).                \label{p8:eq:negative-even-odd-char}
\end{equation}
Together with \(\psi_{-r}(t)=\psi_r(c_rt)\) this is the sinc splitting
\eqref{p7:eq:sinc-splitting}, whose \(r=1/2\) case
\(\psi_{1/2}(3t)=\psi_{1/4}(2t)\psi_{1/4}(t)\) is precisely the interlacing of
the even and odd factors of the dyadic infinite sinc product into two
quarter-base products.

\subsection{Computational significance}

The residue formula provides a multiscale density algorithm.  Choose \(m\) so that
\(\lvert q\rvert^m\) is small.  The \(q^m\)-law then has a broad exact plateau and short
refinement depth; convolving its independently scaled copies reconstructs \(g_q\).  This
can outperform direct evaluation of a long sinc product when \(\lvert q\rvert\) is close
to one.  For negative \(q\), taking even \(m\) reduces every building block to a positive
parameter.

\section{Reciprocal bases and finite geometric normalization}

\subsection{Exact \texorpdfstring{$q\leftrightarrow q^{-1}$}{q <-> q^-1} reversal}

For an integer \(N\ge1\), define the normalized finite law
\begin{equation}
 X_{q,N}=\frac1{[N]_q}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}q^nU_n,             \label{p8:eq:finite-Xq}
\end{equation}
whenever \([N]_q\ne0\).  The coefficients sum to one, so \(\Expectation X_{q,N}=1/2\).  At
\(q=1\), the continuous extension is the arithmetic mean \(N^{-1}\sum U_n\).

\begin{theorem}[Finite reciprocal-base duality]\label{p8:thm:reciprocal-duality}
Let \(q\ne0\) and suppose both normalizations are defined.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{X_{q,N}\ \doteqL\ X_{1/q,N}.}                    \label{p8:eq:reciprocal-law}
\end{equation}
More strongly, if the digits on the reciprocal side are reversed, the two random
variables are equal almost surely.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The $q$-bracket reciprocity identity is
\begin{equation}
 [N]_{1/q}=q^{1-N}[N]_q.                                  \label{p8:eq:qbracket-reciprocity}
\end{equation}
Therefore
\[
 \frac{(1/q)^{N-1-n}}{[N]_{1/q}}
 =\frac{q^{-N+1+n}}{q^{1-N}[N]_q}
 =\frac{q^n}{[N]_q}.
\]
The coefficient of \(U_n\) at base \(q\) is exactly the coefficient of the reversed digit
\(U_{N-1-n}\) at base \(1/q\).  Since the digit vector is exchangeable, the laws agree;
using the reversed vector gives pathwise equality.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Canonical limits for \texorpdfstring{$\lvert q\rvert>1$}{|q|>1}}

\begin{theorem}[Reciprocal-base compactification]\label{p8:thm:outside-limit}
Let \(q\) be real with \(\lvert q\rvert>1\) and put \(p=1/q\), so that
\(0<\lvert p\rvert<1\); both normalizations \([N]_q\) and \([N]_p\) are then
nonzero for every \(N\ge1\).  Then, for every \(N\), \(X_{q,N}\doteqL X_{p,N}\),
and
\begin{equation}
 X_{q,N}\ \Longrightarrow\ X_p
 \qquad(N\to\infty).                                     \label{p8:eq:outside-limit}
\end{equation}
Thus the normalized finite laws at every real base outside the unit interval have a
canonical weak limit.  Explicitly,
\begin{align*}
 q=2&:\quad X_{q,N}\Longrightarrow X_{1/2},\\
 q=-2&:\quad X_{q,N}\Longrightarrow X_{-1/2}\doteqL3X_{1/2}-1,\\
 q=4&:\quad X_{q,N}\Longrightarrow X_{1/4},\\
 q=-4&:\quad X_{q,N}\Longrightarrow X_{-1/4}
 \doteqL\frac12+\frac53\left(X_{1/4}-\frac12\right).
\end{align*}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For real \(\lvert q\rvert>1\) one has \(q^N\ne1\), so \([N]_q\ne0\), and
\(\lvert p\rvert<1\) gives \([N]_p\ne0\); the identity in law is therefore
\cref{p8:thm:reciprocal-duality}.  Since \(\lvert p\rvert<1\),
\([N]_p\to(1-p)^{-1}\) and \(\sum_{n<N}p^nU_n\to\sum_{n\ge0}p^nU_n\) almost
surely (\cref{p0:prop:basic}), so
\(X_{p,N}=[N]_p^{-1}\sum_{n<N}p^nU_n\to(1-p)\sum_{n\ge0}p^nU_n=X_p\)
almost surely.  Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in law, and the
identity \(X_{q,N}\doteqL X_{p,N}\) transfers the weak limit to
\(X_{q,N}\).  The special cases use \cref{p7:thm:sign-conjugacy}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Exponential coupling rate]\label{p8:prop:finite-rate}
For \(0\le p<1\), there is a common-digit coupling such that
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{X_{p,N}-X_p}\le p^N\qquad\text{almost surely}.      \label{p8:eq:positive-finite-rate}
\end{equation}
For \(p=-r\), \(0<r<1\), and even \(N\), there is a coupling such that
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{X_{-r,N}-X_{-r}}\le c_rr^N.                         \label{p8:eq:negative-finite-rate}
\end{equation}
Hence the same bounds hold for the \(W_\infty\) Wasserstein distance.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For \(p\ge0\), write
\[
 A_N=(1-p)\sum_{n<N}p^nU_n,\qquad
 T_N=(1-p)\sum_{n\ge N}p^nU_n.
\]
Then \(0\le A_N\le1-p^N\), \(0\le T_N\le p^N\),
\(X_{p,N}=A_N/(1-p^N)\), and \(X_p=A_N+T_N\).  Hence
\[
 X_{p,N}-X_p=\frac{p^N}{1-p^N}A_N-T_N
\]
is the difference of two numbers in \([0,p^N]\).

For negative \(p=-r\), finite digit reflection (\cref{p7:thm:sign-conjugacy}) gives
\[
 X_{-r,N}-\frac12\ \doteqL\
 c_{r,N}\left(X_{r,N}-\frac12\right),
 \qquad
 c_{r,N}=c_r\frac{1-r^N}{1-(-r)^N}.
\]
When \(N\) is even, \(c_{r,N}=c_r\).  Couple both finite and infinite negative laws by
the same affine images of the positive coupling, and apply
\cref{p8:eq:positive-finite-rate}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Bell/$q$-bracket reciprocity}

Let \(u_1=1/2\), and for \(s\ge2\) let \(u_s\) be the $s$-th cumulant of a uniform
\(U\), so \(u_s=B_s/s\) for even \(s\) and \(u_s=0\) for odd \(s>1\).

\begin{theorem}[Finite cumulants and moments]\label{p8:thm:finite-cumulants}
For every admissible \(q,N\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \cump_s(X_{q,N})=u_s\frac{[N]_{q^s}}{[N]_q^s}.}          \label{p8:eq:finite-cumulants}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \Expectation X_{q,N}^k=
 \mathcal B_k\!\left(
 u_1,
 u_2\frac{[N]_{q^2}}{[N]_q^2},\ldots,
 u_k\frac{[N]_{q^k}}{[N]_q^k}
 \right).                                                  \label{p8:eq:finite-bell-moment}
\end{equation}
Every ratio in \cref{p8:eq:finite-cumulants} is invariant under
\(q\mapsto q^{-1}\), giving an algebraic Bell-polynomial proof of the moment part of
\cref{p8:thm:reciprocal-duality}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Cumulants add over independent variables and scale homogeneously, so
\[
 \cump_s(X_{q,N})=u_s\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}
 \left(\frac{q^n}{[N]_q}\right)^s
 =u_s\frac{[N]_{q^s}}{[N]_q^s}.
\]
Apply the moment--cumulant Bell formula.  Finally,
\[
 [N]_{q^{-s}}=q^{s(1-N)}[N]_{q^s}
\]
and \([N]_{q^{-1}}^s=q^{s(1-N)}[N]_q^s\), so the ratio is reciprocal-invariant.
\end{proof}

This reciprocity is the probability-law analogue of the involution underlying Gaussian
binomial reciprocity.  It suggests a systematic dictionary between finite geometric
uniform sums, symmetric functions of the coefficient multiset, and denominator-free
$q$-identities.  It is invariant at every finite \(N\), but its \(N\to\infty\)
limit is not one rational function of \(q\): the limit acquires a sign on
\(\lvert q\rvert>1\), and that sign is exactly what separates the reciprocal
germ from the reciprocal-base limit law
(\cref{p7:rem:two-meanings}).

\section{The Gaussian boundary \texorpdfstring{$\lvert q\rvert\uparrow1$}{|q| -> 1}}

\subsection{Sign-invariant standardization}

Cumulants and variance are \cref{p0:thm:cumulants} and
\eqref{p0:eq:variance}: for \(-1<q<1\),
\(\sigma_q^2=\Variance(X_q)=(1-q)/\bigl(12(1+q)\bigr)\).  Define
\begin{equation}
 Z_q=\frac{X_q-1/2}{\sigma_q}.                             \label{p8:eq:Zq}
\end{equation}
Since \(\sigma_{-r}=c_r\sigma_r\), the sign collapses under standardization,
\(Z_{-r}\doteqL Z_r\), so the standardized family depends only on
\(r=\lvert q\rvert\); this is \eqref{p7:eq:standard-sign-collapse}, whose
support-normalized refinement \eqref{p7:eq:Uq-def} says that every normalized
shape statistic is an even function of \(q\).

The centered characteristic function of \(Z_r\) has the useful normalized product
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_r(t)=\Expectation \EulerE^{itZ_r}
 =\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}
 \SincRad\!\left(\sqrt{3(1-r^2)}\,r^nt\right).              \label{p8:eq:standardized-sinc}
\end{equation}

\subsection{A quantitative central limit theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Berry--Esseen Gaussian boundary]\label{p8:thm:berry-esseen}
Let \(C_{\mathrm{BE}}\) be any universal constant valid in the classical
Berry--Esseen inequality for independent, non-identically distributed summands.  Then
for \(0<r<1\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}\AbsoluteValue{\Probability(Z_r\le x)-\PhiN(x)}
 \le
 C_{\mathrm{BE}}\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}
 \frac{(1-r^2)^{3/2}}{1-r^3}.}                            \label{p8:eq:BE-bound}
\end{equation}
The same bound holds for \(Z_{-r}\).  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 Z_{\pm r}\Longrightarrow N(0,1)
 \qquad(r\uparrow1),                                     \label{p8:eq:Gaussian-limit}
\end{equation}
and the right side of \cref{p8:eq:BE-bound} is
\begin{equation}
 C_{\mathrm{BE}}\sqrt{\frac32}\sqrt{1-r}
 \bigl(1+\BigO(1-r)\bigr).                               \label{p8:eq:BE-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write \(Y_q=\sum_{n\ge0}a_{n,q}V_n\) with
\(a_{n,q}=(1-q)q^n\) and \(r=\lvert q\rvert\).  Since
\[
 \Expectation\AbsoluteValue{V_n}^3=\frac1{32},
 \qquad
 \Variance(V_n)=\frac1{12},
\]
we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{n\ge0}\AbsoluteValue{a_{n,q}}^3&=\frac{\AbsoluteValue{1-q}^3}{1-r^3},\\
 \sum_{n\ge0}a_{n,q}^2&=\frac{(1-q)^2}{1-r^2}.
\end{align*}
The Berry--Esseen Lyapunov ratio is therefore
\begin{align*}
 \frac{\sum_n\Expectation\AbsoluteValue{a_{n,q}V_n}^3}
 {\left(\sum_n\Variance(a_{n,q}V_n)\right)^{3/2}}
 &=\frac{(1/32)}{(1/12)^{3/2}}
   \frac{(1-r^2)^{3/2}}{1-r^3}\\
 &=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\frac{(1-r^2)^{3/2}}{1-r^3}.
\end{align*}
The Berry--Esseen inequality for independent, non-identically distributed
summands \cite{bib:berry1941,bib:esseen1942,bib:petrov1975} is a finite-sum
statement, so it is applied to the truncations and the limit is taken
afterwards.  Put
\[
 S_N=\sum_{n<N}a_{n,q}V_n,
 \qquad
 s_N^2=\Variance(S_N)=\frac1{12}\sum_{n<N}a_{n,q}^2,
 \qquad
 Z^{(N)}=\frac{S_N}{s_N}.
\]
For each \(N\ge1\) the inequality gives
\(\sup_x\AbsoluteValue{\Probability(Z^{(N)}\le x)-\PhiN(x)}\le C_{\mathrm{BE}}L_N\)
with the truncated Lyapunov ratio
\[
 L_N=\frac{\sum_{n<N}\Expectation\AbsoluteValue{a_{n,q}V_n}^3}{s_N^3}
 =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\,
 \frac{(1-r^{3N})\,(1-r^2)^{3/2}}{(1-r^3)\,(1-r^{2N})^{3/2}} .
\]
As \(N\to\infty\), \(L_N\to L_\infty=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}(1-r^2)^{3/2}/(1-r^3)\),
the ratio \(L_N/L_\infty=(1-r^{3N})/(1-r^{2N})^{3/2}\) exceeding \(1\) for
every finite \(N\), so that no single truncation yields the boxed constant.
Now \(S_N\to Y_q\) almost surely (\cref{p0:prop:basic}) and
\(s_N\to\sigma_q\), so \(Z^{(N)}\to Z_r\) almost surely, hence in law; and
\(Z_r\) has a density (\cref{p8:thm:all-sign-density}), so its distribution
function is continuous and
\(\Probability(Z^{(N)}\le x)\to\Probability(Z_r\le x)\) for \emph{every}
\(x\).  Therefore, for each fixed \(x\),
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\Probability(Z_r\le x)-\PhiN(x)}
 =\lim_{N\to\infty}\AbsoluteValue{\Probability(Z^{(N)}\le x)-\PhiN(x)}
 \le C_{\mathrm{BE}}\lim_{N\to\infty}L_N
 =C_{\mathrm{BE}}L_\infty,
\]
and the supremum over \(x\) is \cref{p8:eq:BE-bound}.  The sign collapse
\eqref{p7:eq:standard-sign-collapse} handles \(-r\).  Expanding
\(1-r^2\sim2(1-r)\) and \(1-r^3\sim3(1-r)\) gives
\cref{p8:eq:BE-asymptotic}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Closed standardized Bernoulli cumulants}

\begin{corollary}[Low standardized cumulants and the order estimate]\label{p8:thm:standard-cumulants}
The even standardized cumulants
\(\lambda_{2m}(r)=\cump_{2m}(Z_r)=\cump_{2m}(Z_{-r})\) are
\eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants}, and all odd cumulants vanish.  In
particular,
\begin{align}
 \lambda_4(r)&=-\frac65\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2},              \label{p8:eq:lambda4}\\
 \lambda_6(r)&=\frac{48}{7}
 \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{1+r^2+r^4}.                            \label{p8:eq:lambda6}
\end{align}
For fixed \(m\ge2\), \(\lambda_{2m}(r)=\BigO((1-r)^{m-1})\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put \(m=2\) and \(m=3\) in \eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants} with
\(B_4=-1/30\) and \(B_6=1/42\).  Odd cumulants vanish by symmetry, and the
negative law has the same standardized distribution by
\eqref{p7:eq:standard-sign-collapse}.  Factoring
\(1-r^{2m}=(1-r^2)(1+r^2+\cdots+r^{2m-2})\) gives the order estimate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Bell-polynomial moment correction}

\begin{corollary}[First correction to Gaussian moments]\label{p8:cor:moment-correction}
For every fixed integer \(m\ge2\),
\begin{align}
 \Expectation Z_r^{2m}
 &=(2m-1)!!
 +\binom{2m}{4}(2m-5)!!\,\lambda_4(r)
 +\BigO((1-r)^2)                                          \label{p8:eq:moment-correction-1}\\
 &=(2m-1)!!
 -\frac65\binom{2m}{4}(2m-5)!!
  \frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}
 +\BigO((1-r)^2).                                         \label{p8:eq:moment-correction-2}
\end{align}
All odd moments vanish.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the moment--cumulant Bell expansion: \(\Expectation Z_r^{2m}\) is the sum
over set partitions of \(\{1,\dots,2m\}\) of the product of the cumulants
\(\lambda_{\AbsoluteValue B}\) over the blocks \(B\).  Blocks of odd size
contribute \(0\), since all odd cumulants vanish.  The Gaussian term consists
entirely of pair blocks (\(\lambda_2=1\)) and equals \((2m-1)!!\).  Since
\(\lambda_{2k}(r)=\BigO((1-r)^{k-1})\) by \cref{p8:thm:standard-cumulants},
a partition with blocks of sizes \(2k_1,\dots,2k_j\) contributes
\(\BigO\bigl((1-r)^{\sum_i(k_i-1)}\bigr)\); the only partitions of order
exactly \(1-r\) have one block of size four and \(m-2\) pairs, and their
number is
\[
 \binom{2m}{4}(2m-5)!!,
\]
with the convention \((-1)!!=1\) at \(m=2\), where the formula
\(\Expectation Z_r^4=3+\lambda_4(r)\) is exact.  Every block of size at least
six, and every product of two fourth cumulants, contributes
\(\BigO((1-r)^2)\); the implied constant depends on \(m\), through the
number of such partitions.  Insert \cref{p8:eq:lambda4}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quartic characteristic correction}

\begin{theorem}[First mod-Gaussian-type correction]\label{p8:thm:quartic-correction}
For \(T>0\) put \(r_0(T)=\sqrt{\max\{0,\,1-1/(3T^2)\}}\).  For
\(r_0(T)<r<1\) and \(\AbsoluteValue t\le T\) every factor of
\eqref{p8:eq:standardized-sinc} is positive, \(\log\Psi_r(t)\) is the
absolutely convergent sum of the logarithms of the factors, and
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \log\Psi_r(t)
 =-\frac{t^2}{2}
 -\frac{1-r^2}{20(1+r^2)}t^4
 +\BigO_T((1-r)^2),}                                      \label{p8:eq:quartic-logpsi}
\end{equation}
where the remainder term, written \(\varrho_r(t)\), is explicitly bounded by
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{\varrho_r(t)}
 \le\frac{27}{2600}\,\AbsoluteValue t^6\,\frac{(1-r^2)^2}{1+r^2+r^4}
 \le\frac{T^6(1-r)^2}{24}.                                 \label{p8:eq:quartic-remainder}
\end{equation}
The restriction on \(r\) cannot be dropped: \(\Psi_r\) vanishes at
\(t=\pi/\sqrt{3(1-r^2)}\), which lies in \([-T,T]\) as soon as
\(1-r^2\ge\pi^2/(3T^2)\) (at \(r=0\), \(\Psi_0(t)=\SincRad(\sqrt3\,t)\)
vanishes at \(t=\pi/\sqrt3\approx1.81\)), and there \(\log\Psi_r(t)\) is
undefined.  Consequently, for every fixed real \(t\),
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{r\uparrow1}
 \frac{\log\Psi_r(t)+t^2/2}{1-r}
 =-\frac{t^4}{20}.                                        \label{p8:eq:quartic-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put \(z_n=\sqrt{3(1-r^2)}\,r^nt\).  For \(r>r_0(T)\) and
\(\AbsoluteValue t\le T\) one has \(3(1-r^2)T^2<1\), hence
\(\AbsoluteValue{z_n}\le\AbsoluteValue{z_0}<1<\pi\) for every \(n\): all
factors of \eqref{p8:eq:standardized-sinc} are positive, and since
\(\sum_nz_n^2<\infty\) the logarithm of the product is the absolutely
convergent sum of the logarithms.  For \(\AbsoluteValue z<\pi\), Euler's product
\(\SincRad z=\prod_{k\ge1}\bigl(1-z^2/(\pi^2k^2)\bigr)\) gives the exact series
\begin{align*}
 \log\SincRad z
 &=-\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{\zeta(2m)}{m\,\pi^{2m}}\,z^{2m}
 =-\frac{z^2}{6}-\frac{z^4}{180}+R(z),\\
 \AbsoluteValue{R(z)}
 &\le z^6\sum_{m\ge3}\frac{\zeta(2m)}{m\,\pi^{2m}}
 \le\frac{z^6}{2600}
 \qquad(\AbsoluteValue z\le1),
\end{align*}
all terms having one sign; the constant is
\(\zeta(6)/(3\pi^6)+\zeta(8)/(4\pi^8)+\cdots=0.000381\ldots<1/2600\).
Summing over \(n\),
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{n\ge0}z_n^2&=3t^2,\\
 \sum_{n\ge0}z_n^4&=9t^4\frac{(1-r^2)^2}{1-r^4}
 =9t^4\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2},\\
 \sum_{n\ge0}\AbsoluteValue{z_n}^6
 &=27\AbsoluteValue t^6\frac{(1-r^2)^3}{1-r^6}
 =27\AbsoluteValue t^6\frac{(1-r^2)^2}{1+r^2+r^4},
\end{align*}
so \(\log\Psi_r(t)=-\tfrac12t^2-\tfrac1{20}\tfrac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}t^4
+\varrho_r(t)\) with \(\varrho_r(t)=\sum_nR(z_n)\), and
\(\AbsoluteValue{\varrho_r(t)}\le\tfrac1{2600}\sum_n\AbsoluteValue{z_n}^6\) is
the first bound of \eqref{p8:eq:quartic-remainder}; the second uses
\((1-r^2)^2\le4(1-r)^2\), \(1+r^2+r^4\ge1\), and \(108/2600<1/24\).  For the
limit \eqref{p8:eq:quartic-limit}, fix \(t\ne0\) (the case \(t=0\) is
trivial) and take \(T=\AbsoluteValue t\): the expansion applies for
\(r>r_0(\AbsoluteValue t)\), and
\((1-r^2)/(1+r^2)=(1-r)+\BigO((1-r)^2)\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The first Edgeworth correction, and the entropy deficit}

Let \(H_k\) be the probabilists' Hermite polynomial.  Fourier inversion of the
cumulant expansion of \cref{p8:thm:quartic-correction} predicts the first
Edgeworth correction, which we write with explicit remainder terms,
\begin{equation}
 f_{Z_r}(z)=\phiN(z)
 \left[1+\frac{\lambda_4(r)}{24}H_4(z)\right]
 +\mathcal R_r(z),                                        \label{p8:eq:formal-edgeworth-density}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \Probability(Z_r\le z)=\PhiN(z)
 -\frac{\lambda_4(r)}{24}H_3(z)\phiN(z)
 +\mathcal R_r^{F}(z),
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_r^{F}(z)=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\mathcal R_r ;    \label{p8:eq:formal-edgeworth-cdf}
\end{equation}
the two displays are consistent because
\(\frac{\Differential}{\Differential z}\bigl[H_3(z)\phiN(z)\bigr]=-H_4(z)\phiN(z)\).
The fixed-frequency theorem above does not control these remainders uniformly
in \(z\): that requires a high-frequency estimate uniform in \(r\), which the
absorbed report did not supply and therefore conjectured.  Part~XI supplies
it (\cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}), and the conjecture is a theorem of this
volume.

\begin{proposition}[Uniform first Edgeworth expansion]\label{p8:prop:edgeworth}
There are \(r_0<1\) and, for each pair of integers \(j,K\ge0\), constants
\(C_{j,K}\) and \(C_F\) such that for \(r_0<r<1\)
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{z\in\RealNumbers}(1+\AbsoluteValue z)^K
 \AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_r^{(j)}(z)}\le C_{j,K}(1-r)^2,
 \qquad
 \sup_{z\in\RealNumbers}\AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_r^{F}(z)}\le C_F(1-r)^2 .
                                                          \label{p8:eq:edgeworth-uniform}
\end{equation}
The next term of the expansion is
\(\phiN(z)\bigl[\lambda_6(r)H_6(z)/720+\lambda_4(r)^2H_8(z)/1152\bigr]\), after
which the remainder is \(\BigO((1-r)^3)\) in the same seminorms.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
This is \cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} read through
\cref{p0:tab:dictionary}: Part~XI's \(Z_h\) is \(Z_r\) at \(r=\EulerE^{-h}\),
its \(\lambda_{2m}(h)\) is \(\lambda_{2m}(r)\) (\cref{p0:prop:dictionary}),
and \(h=-\log r=(1-r)\bigl(1+\BigO(1-r)\bigr)\), so powers of \(h\) and of
\(1-r\) are interchangeable, up to constants, in every remainder.  In the
exact-cumulant Edgeworth polynomial \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial} the
multi-indices of weight at most \(1\) are the empty one and \(k_2=1\), giving
\(\mathcal E_{1,h}=1+\lambda_4H_4/4!\); those of weight \(2\) are \(k_3=1\)
and \(k_2=2\), giving \(\lambda_6H_6/6!+\lambda_4^2H_8/(2!\,(4!)^2)\), and
\(2\cdot24^2=1152\).  The density bound is \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-main} with
\(R=1\) (respectively \(R=2\)); the distribution-function bound is its case
\(j=0\), \(K=2\), integrated:
\(\AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_r^F(z)}\le\int_{\RealNumbers}\AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_r}
 \le C_{0,2}h^2\int_{\RealNumbers}(1+\AbsoluteValue x)^{-2}\Differential x
 =2C_{0,2}h^2\).
\end{proof}

The absorbed report stated \cref{p8:prop:edgeworth} as a conjecture; under
the convention of \cref{p0:sec:status} it is recorded here as a proposition
proved in Part~XI, and the same applies to the all-orders statement of
\cref{p8:rem:all-orders}.  The entropy deficit is a different matter: the
first Edgeworth term is now proved, but its use inside a relative entropy
needs global logarithmic control of \(f_{Z_r}/\phiN\), which Part~XI also
lacks (\cref{p11:conj:entropy}).

\begin{conjecture}[Entropy deficit]\label{p8:conj:entropy-deficit}
Let \(D(\LawOperator(Z_r)\Vert N(0,1))\) be relative entropy.  Then
\begin{equation}
 D(\LawOperator(Z_r)\Vert N(0,1))
 =\frac{\lambda_4(r)^2}{48}+o((1-r)^2)
 =\frac{3}{100}(1-r)^2+o((1-r)^2).                        \label{p8:eq:entropy-deficit}
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
 h(Z_r)=\frac12\log(2\pi e)-\frac{3}{100}(1-r)^2+o((1-r)^2).
\]
\end{conjecture}

The coefficient \(1/48\) follows formally by inserting
\(f/\phiN=1+(\lambda_4/24)H_4+\cdots\) into relative entropy and using
\(\Expectation_{\phiN}H_4^2=4!\).  This is the leading term \(d_2=3/100\) of
the full entropic expansion conjectured as \cref{p11:conj:entropy}; a proof
should combine \cref{p8:prop:edgeworth} with tail control supplied by
log-concavity (\cref{p7:thm:shape}) where \(f_{Z_r}/\phiN\) is small or large.

\section{Further conjectures and frontier directions}

\subsection{All-orders Gaussian asymptotics}

\begin{remark}[Complete Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite expansion: proved in Part~XI]
\label{p8:rem:all-orders}
The absorbed report conjectured that for every integer \(M\ge1\) the
standardized density has an expansion through order \((1-r)^M\) whose
coefficients are finite Bell polynomials in the exact cumulants
\(\lambda_4(r),\lambda_6(r),\ldots,\lambda_{2M+2}(r)\), expressed in the
Hermite basis, uniform with polynomial weights and differentiable termwise a
fixed number of times.  This is exactly \cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}
together with \cref{p11:prop:h-power-series}, with \(h=-\log r\) as the
expansion variable and the Bell-polynomial coefficient structure displayed in
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial}; following \cref{p0:sec:status} the
conjecture is demoted to this remark.  The analytic estimate the report
identified as crucial --- uniform control of \eqref{p8:eq:standardized-sinc}
outside the low-frequency window --- is \cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{A generic-$q$ Lambert--\texorpdfstring{$W$}{W} endpoint theory}

The all-orders endpoint programme is \cref{p7:conj:all-orders}, and its
transform-level half is already proved: the negative Laplace transform of
\(X_r\) is the geometric harmonic sum
\(\Expectation\EulerE^{-sX_r}=\prod_{n\ge0}\bigl(1-\EulerE^{-(1-r)r^ns}\bigr)
/\bigl((1-r)r^ns\bigr)\) --- the product formula \eqref{p0:eq:mgf} at
\(t=-s\), since \(E(-a)=(1-\EulerE^{-a})/a\), the interchange of expectation
and infinite product being justified there by locally uniform convergence ---
and \cref{p7:thm:cocycle-resolved} resolves its
logarithm exactly into a quadratic polynomial in \(\log s\), a real-analytic
one-periodic fluctuation in \(\log_{1/r}s\) with explicit Gamma--zeta Fourier
modes, and an exponentially small remainder.  What remains open is the
density-level saddle inversion, stated in the exact \(-W_{-1}\) coordinate as
\cref{p7:conj:all-orders}; the negative cases transfer by
\cref{p7:cor:transport}, which carries the left endpoint of \(F_{-r}\) to that
of \(F_r\) by \(x\mapsto(x-\ell_r)/c_r\).

\subsection{Legendre coefficients and endpoint saddles}

Because each \(g_q\) is compactly supported and smooth, its affine Legendre coefficients
decay faster than every power.  The precise stretched-exponential envelope should be
controlled by the same complex saddle geometry that governs endpoint flatness.

\begin{conjecture}[Legendre--Lambert asymptotic bridge]\label{p8:conj:legendre-lambert}
For the even Legendre coefficients of \(g_r\), the logarithm of the coefficient magnitude
has a complete asymptotic expansion whose principal scale is obtained by balancing the
large-degree Legendre boundary layer with the Lambert saddle of \(F_r\).  A smooth
log-periodic factor survives in the coefficient asymptotics.  Negative-base coefficients
obey exactly the same law after the affine normalization in
\cref{p8:eq:general-negative-legendre}.
\end{conjecture}

This would connect three parts of the existing program that are currently largely
parallel: endpoint Lambert asymptotics, Legendre expansions, and infinite sinc products.

\subsection{Reciprocal-base algebra and $q$-identities}

The coefficient multiset proof of \cref{p8:thm:reciprocal-duality} suggests a broader
principle: every symmetric polynomial or entire symmetric function of
\(\{q^n/[N]_q:0\le n<N\}\) is reciprocal-invariant.  Power sums give cumulants; elementary
symmetric functions give Gaussian-binomial expressions.

\begin{problem}[A probability proof of a full Gaussian-binomial reciprocity package]
\Cref{p7:sec:position-energy} and \eqref{p7:eq:lagrange-reversal} already give
the algebraic reciprocity, including
\(\GaussianBinomial{N}{k}{1/q}=q^{-k(N-k)}\GaussianBinomial{N}{k}{q}\) and the row reversal of the
$q$-Lagrange coefficients.  What is asked here is a probabilistic
realization: construct natural random variables or random polynomials whose elementary-symmetric
statistics of the finite geometric weights recover
\(\GaussianBinomial{N}{k}{q}\).  Then seek
mixed Bell/Gaussian identities obtained by converting between power sums and elementary
symmetric functions.
\end{problem}

\subsection{A formalization roadmap}

The strongest immediate formal targets are elementary enough to be realistic additions
to the existing Lean development:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2.2em]
\item replace the negative-parameter density ambiguity by the sign-corrected theorem
      \(g_q=\Sign(q)\widetilde f_q\);
\item prove finite reciprocal-base duality by coefficient extensionality and list
      \(q=\pm2,\pm4\) wrappers;
\item formalize the exact plateau theorem from the CDF tails.
\end{enumerate}
The remaining targets of the original list --- the reflected-digit coupling and
the affine pushforward \(\mu_{-r}=T_{r*}\mu_r\), the CDF, quantile, support and
smooth-density transports, the residue-class multiplication law with its
characteristic-function corollary, and the Bernoulli cumulant and
standardized-sign-collapse package --- are tranches of Part~VII's merged
roadmap and are listed there once.

Log-concavity may require additional convex-measure infrastructure.  Berry--Esseen and
uniform Edgeworth theory are longer-term targets, but the exact cumulant and quartic
formal-power-series identities can be separated from those analytic theorems.

\section{Conclusions}

The geometric-uniform family has more symmetry than is visible from the positive
parameter alone.  Centering turns every alternating geometric digit into a reflected
uniform digit, and this collapses the entire negative half of the parameter interval to
an affine copy of the positive half.  That one observation resolves the negative density
frontier, identifies the sign of the previously selected total function, and transports
Fabius, inverse Fabius, Rvachev, Legendre, Lambert--\(W\), sinc-product, and Thue--Morse
structures in one step.

Two further reorganizations complete the parameter picture.  Residue classes produce a
$q$-multiplication law, while finite digit reversal identifies \(q\) with \(q^{-1}\).
Thus negative parameters, bases outside the unit interval, and smaller positive bases
are not separate theories but affine or reciprocal views of the same laws.

Finally, the parameter edge \(\lvert q\rvert\uparrow1\) is a genuine Gaussian boundary.
The rate is controlled by a closed Berry--Esseen ratio, and the departure from normality
is encoded by Bernoulli cumulants and Bell partitions.  The quartic coefficient
\(-t^4/20\) is the first term of the all-orders Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite
expansion proved in Part~XI (\cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}), which
connects the probability family to the repository's existing Bell, Bernoulli,
Lambert, Legendre, and formal saddle machinery.

\appendix
\section{Auxiliary algebra}

\subsection{Support endpoints under negative affine transport}

Since \(T_r(y)=1/2+c_r(y-1/2)\),
\[
 T_r(0)=\frac{1-c_r}{2}=-\frac r{1-r},
 \qquad
 T_r(1)=\frac{1+c_r}{2}=\frac1{1-r}.
\]
For the positive plateau endpoint \(y=r\),
\[
 T_r(r)=\frac12+\frac{1+r}{1-r}\left(r-\frac12\right)
 =\frac{r^2}{1-r}.
\]
These identities explain the apparently asymmetric support and the symmetric central
plateau of the negative law.

\subsection{Finite negative/positive scale}

Digit reflection in \cref{p8:eq:finite-Xq} gives
\[
 X_{-r,N}-\frac12\ \doteqL\
 \frac{[N]_r}{[N]_{-r}}\left(X_{r,N}-\frac12\right),
\]
where
\[
 \frac{[N]_r}{[N]_{-r}}
 =\frac{1+r}{1-r}\frac{1-r^N}{1-(-r)^N}.
\]
For even \(N\), this is exactly \(c_r\); for odd \(N\), it converges exponentially to
\(c_r\).

\subsection{Low standardized cumulants}

The first values from \eqref{p0:eq:standardized-cumulants} are
\begin{align*}
 \lambda_2(r)&=1,\\
 \lambda_4(r)&=-\frac65\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2},\\
 \lambda_6(r)&=\frac{48}{7}\frac{(1-r^2)^2}{1+r^2+r^4},\\
 \lambda_8(r)&=-\frac{432}{5}
 \frac{(1-r^2)^3}{1+r^2+r^4+r^6}.
\end{align*}
The last coefficient uses \(B_8=-1/30\).  These feed directly into complete Bell
polynomials and higher Edgeworth terms.

\part{Cyclotomic Radial Expansions, Natural Boundaries, and Inverse Branches}



\begin{abstract}
The dyadic Rvachev up-function has Fourier transform
\(
 \prod_{j\ge 1}\SincRad(z/2^j)
\), and the surrounding repository develops its Fabius, Thue--Morse, $q$-series, Bell--Bernoulli, inverse, sampling, and Lambert-$W$ structures in considerable depth.  The current consolidated $q$-series frontier explicitly leaves two related tasks open: proving a generic natural boundary in the $q$-plane and constructing root-of-unity renormalizations.  This report resolves a concrete scalar version of both tasks for the complex geometric-uniform transform
\[
 \Phi(q,z)=\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad\bigl((1-q)q^jz\bigr),\qquad |q|<1.
\]

For a primitive $m$th root of unity $\omega$ and
\(d=\OrderOperator_{\mathrm{mult}}(\omega^2)=m/\gcd(m,2)\), we derive the radial expansion
\[
 \log\Phi(\omega(1-\delta),z)
 =-\frac{\mathscr A_\omega(z)}{\delta}+\mathscr B_\omega(z)+O(\delta),
\]
locally uniformly for $|(1-\omega)z|<\pi$.  The action is an explicit spectral dilogarithm,
\[
 \mathscr A_\omega(z)=\frac1{2d^2}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\Polylogarithm_2\!\left(\left(\frac{(1-\omega)z}{\pi n}\right)^{2d}\right).
\]
The action never vanishes for $0<|z|<\pi/2$ with $z$ real or purely imaginary.  Because roots of unity are dense, this proves that the unit circle is a natural boundary for $q\mapsto\Phi(q,z)$ throughout that entire frequency interval, on both slices.  The imaginary slice is the centered exponential germ $C_q(t)=\Phi(q,-\ImaginaryUnit t/2)$ of Part~VII, so the theorem settles \cref{p7:conj:natural-boundary} for every real $t$ with $0<|t|<\pi$ --- for all such $t$, not merely generic ones --- replacing that conjecture's cumulant-cancellation strategy by an explicit action.

A double scaling
\(q=\omega(1-\varepsilon^d)\), \(z=\sqrt\varepsilon\,w\)
then gives the locally uniform cyclotomic limit
\[
 \Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\varepsilon^d),\sqrt\varepsilon\,w\bigr)
 \longrightarrow \exp(-A_\omega w^{2d}),
 \qquad
 A_\omega=\frac{\zeta(2d)(1-\omega)^{2d}}{2d^2\pi^{2d}}.
\]
 We prove the first corrections and an all-orders Bell-polynomial expansion, identify the corresponding polyharmonic heat symbol, show that the reciprocal zero moments and Bernoulli cumulants collapse to a single order $2d$, derive the limiting Gould--Hopper Appell family, and construct formal inverse series both in the scaled frequency and in $q$ itself.  A universal analytic-germ theorem shows that the mechanism extends beyond sinc products to $q$-Pochhammer and other geometric products.  High-precision experiments, source code, CSV data, and figures accompany the report.
\end{abstract}

\section{Scope, status, and contribution boundary}

\subsection{The audited source landscape}

The requested source tree is a living research corpus rather than a single paper.  Its current top level contains the primary Fabius--Rvachev exposition, a mathematical glossary, a non-elementarity study, a Lean walkthrough, imported papers, an archive, and a semi-formalized frontier system.  During August 2026 many formerly separate frontier drafts were consolidated into thematic volumes.  Consequently, a novelty audit based only on old filenames would be misleading: the correct comparison target is the current consolidated mathematics, supplemented by historical inventories for paths that were absorbed or archived.

The audit used three layers.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item The current public GitHub tree, the current semi-formalized README, and the raw consolidated \emph{Exponents and $q$-Series Frontiers} source were inspected at theorem and open-problem level.
\item A preserved recursive ledger of every \texttt{*.tex} path under \texttt{Analysis/FabiusFunction/docs} at commit
\texttt{24da985eba70e46d862acdaddd476793a428213e} was used to retain coverage of the frozen archive and earlier source-paper layout.  The 57-path ledger is included in the companion archive as
\texttt{corpus\_inventory\_2026-08-27.txt}.
\item Prior frontier reports in the user's library were phrase- and formula-searched for the proposed concepts.  In particular, Stein--Koopman calculus, transfer determinants, fractional transforms, dyadic-comb interpolation, inverse-Lambert expansions, Appell deconvolution, and spectral zero-divisor theory were treated as occupied territory and are not presented here as new.
\end{enumerate}

The current consolidated $q$-series volume formulates a \emph{generic natural-boundary conjecture} for its geometric characteristic function and separately asks for \emph{root-of-unity renormalization}.  The present report targets precisely that remaining scalar analytic gap.  It does not claim to solve the full two-nome finite-law, matrix Mahler, or mixed Prouhet problem.

\begin{status}[Meaning of ``new'']
Throughout this report, \emph{new} means apparently new relative to the audited repository corpus.  It is not a claim of worldwide priority.  Classical ingredients such as Euler's sine product, Bernoulli cumulants, $q$-Pochhammer notation, and radial root-of-unity methods are cited and clearly separated from the deductions made here.
\end{status}

\subsection{Result ledger}

The principal contributions are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*.},leftmargin=3.4em]
\item An exact logarithmic and $q$-Pochhammer representation of the complex geometric sinc product, organized so that cyclotomic resonance is visible coefficient by coefficient.  The underlying product and the global spectral $q$-Pochhammer factorization now have exact Lean counterparts; the local master logarithm remains a manuscript theorem.
\item A two-term radial expansion at every nontrivial root of unity, with an explicit action $\mathscr A_\omega$ and constant term $\mathscr B_\omega$.
\item Three equivalent descriptions of $\mathscr A_\omega$: a resonant zeta series, an infinite spectral dilogarithm, and a cyclic projection integral.
\item A sign theorem for the action and, as a consequence, a proof that the unit circle is a natural boundary for every fixed real $0<|z|<\pi/2$.
\item A root-of-unity blow-up limit to $\exp(-A_\omega w^{2d})$, including subcritical corrections, the complete order-$\varepsilon^d$ layer, and an all-orders Bell-polynomial scheme.
\item A universal analytic-germ theorem that recovers both the sinc result and a root-scaled $q$-Pochhammer limit.
\item Spectral condensation: among all reciprocal zero power sums, exactly the $2d$th survives after cyclotomic scaling.
\item Bernoulli--Bell condensation: among all scaled cumulants, exactly the $2d$th survives, forcing an explicit sparse moment sequence.
\item A limiting Gould--Hopper/Appell family obtained from the inverse moment generating function.
\item Polyharmonic heat-kernel and Stokes-sector interpretations, distinguishing the genuinely dissipative roots $m\equiv2\pmod4$ from backward/rotated sectors.
\item Formal inverse series in the scaled frequency and in $q$, with explicit first corrections; sectorial analytic realization and monodromy remain open.
\item Reproducible high-precision tests whose fitted convergence exponents agree with the displayed asymptotic orders.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{status}[Current formal and analytic boundary]
The repository already defines the complex geometric sinc product and its
reciprocal-Gamma reflection factorization.  The global spectral
$q$-Pochhammer identity in \cref{p9:eq:qpoch-factor} is now machine-checked in
Lean; exact names and normalizations are recorded below.  No later
root-of-unity asymptotic, natural-boundary, condensation, Gould--Hopper, or
inverse-branch claim in this report is thereby Lean-verified.

There is also an analytic distinction inside the manuscript.  The fixed-index
cyclotomic expansions do not by themselves justify summation over an unbounded
index.  The proof of \cref{p9:thm:two-term-radial} closes this gap with a uniform
two-range estimate, splitting at $k\asymp\delta^{-1/2}$ and using geometric
decay beyond the cutoff.  By contrast, the inverse formulas below record
formal coefficients and sectorial targets, not established convergent analytic
germs at the boundary.
\end{status}

\section{The Fabius--Rvachev interface and its complex
\texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-extension}

\subsection{The dyadic probability law}

Let $V_0,V_1,\dots$ be independent random variables uniformly distributed on $[-1,1]$.  The centered dyadic random series
\begin{equation}
 Y_{1/2}=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-(j+1)}V_j
 \label{p9:eq:dyadic-series}
\end{equation}
has support $[-1,1]$ and density Rvachev's up-function $\RvachevUp$.  Its characteristic function, with the convention $\SincRad z=\sin z/z$, is
\begin{equation}
 \FourierAngular{\RvachevUp}(-z)
 =\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad\!\left(\frac{z}{2^{j+1}}\right).
 \label{p9:eq:up-transform}
\end{equation}
The Fabius distribution on $[0,1]$ is obtained by the affine change
\(X=(Y_{1/2}+1)/2\); this is \cref{p0:prop:fabius-point} in the canonical
normalization.  The repository develops this bridge, exact dyadic arithmetic, Thue--Morse derivative signs, moment and cumulant formulas, Legendre expansions, inverse asymptotics, and many related representations.  We use those structures only as motivation and normalization.

\subsection{The geometric family}

\begin{status}[Conventions of this part]
\label{p9:status:conventions}
This part is the one that works with \emph{complex} $q$, and its natural
frequency variable is therefore the one in which the sinc arguments carry no
factor of $\tfrac12$.  Concretely it uses seeds uniform on $[-1,1]$ and writes
$Y_q$ for what \cref{p0:def:family} calls $2\GeoLawCentered{q}$: for real
$0<q<1$,
\[
 Y_q=2\GeoLawCentered{q},
 \qquad
 \Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit zY_q}=\CharacteristicFunction{q}(2z),
\]
so every formula below converts to the canonical normalization by the single
substitution $z\mapsto t/2$, as recorded in \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}.  In
particular this part's cumulants are $2^{2m}$ times \eqref{p0:eq:cumulants}
and its variance is $(1-q)/(3(1+q))$, four times \eqref{p0:eq:variance}.  The
letter $Y_q$ denotes a different object in Parts~VII and~VIII --- there the
uncentered and the centered variable respectively --- which is why
\cref{p0:tab:dictionary} exists and why the notation catalogue's collision
register carries a row for $X,Y,Z$.
\end{status}

For real $0<q<1$, define
\begin{equation}
 Y_q=(1-q)\sum_{j\ge0}q^jV_j.
 \label{p9:eq:Yq}
\end{equation}
The coefficient sum is one, so $Y_q$ is again supported on $[-1,1]$.  Independence gives
\begin{equation}
 \Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit zY_q}
 =\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad\bigl((1-q)q^jz\bigr).
 \label{p9:eq:real-char}
\end{equation}
For complex $q$ there is generally no positive probability law, but the product itself remains a natural analytic object.

\begin{definition}[Complex $q$-Fabius--Rvachev sinc product]
For $q\in\DiskD=\SetOf{q\in\ComplexNumbers:|q|<1}$ and $z\in\ComplexNumbers$, set
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(q,z)=\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}
 \SincRad\bigl((1-q)q^jz\bigr).
 \label{p9:eq:Phi-def}
\end{equation}
Here $\SincRad0=1$ and the empty power is read as $q^{0}=1$ for every $q$,
including $q=0$.  Thus at $q=0$ the factor $j=0$ contributes $\SincRad z$ and
every factor with $j\ge1$ contributes $\SincRad0=1$; this is the convention
under which $\Phi(0,z)=\SincRad z$ below, and it matches the division-free
reading of the zero set in \cref{p9:eq:zeros}.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Holomorphy and normalization]\label{p9:prop:holomorphy-and-normalization}
The product in \cref{p9:eq:Phi-def} converges locally uniformly on $\DiskD\times\ComplexNumbers$ and defines a holomorphic function there.  Moreover,
\[
 \Phi(q,0)=1,
 \qquad
 \Phi(0,z)=\SincRad z,
 \qquad
 \Phi\left(\tfrac12,z\right)=\FourierAngular{\RvachevUp}(-z).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
On a compact set $|q|\le r<1$, $|z|\le R$, the $j$th argument is $O(r^j)$ uniformly.  Since $\SincRad w=1-w^2/6+O(w^4)$, the deviation of the $j$th factor from one is $O(r^{2j})$.  The Weierstrass criterion gives locally uniform convergence of the product and of its holomorphic finite approximants.  The three normalizations follow directly.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Exact Lean normalization dictionary]
Lean's existing product uses the frequency coordinate
\[
 \operatorname{geometricSincProduct}(q,u)
 =\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad\!\bigl(\pi q^j u\bigr).
\]
Consequently the present convention is exactly
\[
 \Phi(q,z)=\operatorname{geometricSincProduct}
 \left(q,\frac{(1-q)z}{\pi}\right).
\]
The definition and its module are
\begin{center}
\small
\path|Fabius.geometricSincProduct|\quad in\quad
\path|FabiusFunction.GeometricReciprocalGamma|.
\end{center}
At the dyadic point, the theorem
\begin{center}
\small
\path|Fabius.centeredSincProduct_eq_rvachevFourierProduct|
\end{center}
records the further coordinate conversion
\[
 \Phi\!\left(\tfrac12,z\right)
 =\operatorname{centeredSincProduct}(z)
 =\operatorname{rvachevFourierProduct}\!\left(\frac{z}{2\pi}\right).
\]
Thus the manuscript's Fourier variable and Lean's canonical Rvachev product
variable differ by the displayed factor $2\pi$.
\end{remark}

\section{Master logarithmic and
\texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-Pochhammer representations}

\subsection{The exact logarithmic series}

Euler's sine product and its logarithm give
\begin{equation}
 \SincRad w=\prod_{n\ge1}\left(1-\frac{w^2}{\pi^2n^2}\right),
 \qquad
 \log\SincRad w=-\sum_{k\ge1}c_kw^{2k},
 \label{p9:eq:sinc-log}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 c_k=\frac{\zeta(2k)}{k\pi^{2k}}>0.
 \label{p9:eq:ck}
\end{equation}
The logarithm is the branch normalized by $\log\SincRad0=0$ in $|w|<\pi$.

\begin{theorem}[Master logarithm]\label{p9:thm:master-logarithm}
On the domain
\[
 \Omega=\SetOf{(q,z)\in\DiskD\times\ComplexNumbers: |(1-q)z|<\pi},
\]
one has the absolutely and locally uniformly convergent expansion
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \log\Phi(q,z)
 =-\sum_{k\ge1}c_k
 \frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}z^{2k}.}
 \label{p9:eq:master-log}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $(q,z)\in\Omega$ every argument $(1-q)q^jz$ lies in the zero-free disk
$|w|<\pi$, so \cref{p9:eq:sinc-log} may be inserted factor by factor.  Fix a
compact $L\subset\Omega$ and choose $r<1$ and $\rho<1$ with $|q|\le r$ and
$|(1-q)z|\le\rho\pi$ on $L$.  Since $\zeta(2k)\le\zeta(2)$, so that
$c_k\le\zeta(2)/(k\pi^{2k})$, and since $|q|^{2jk}\le|q|^{2j}$ for $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j\ge0}\sum_{k\ge1}c_k\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)q^{j}z}^{2k}
 \le\sum_{j\ge0}r^{2j}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\zeta(2)}{k}\rho^{2k}
 =\frac{\zeta(2)}{1-r^{2}}\,\log\frac1{1-\rho^{2}}
 <\infty
 \label{p9:eq:master-majorant}
\end{equation}
uniformly on $L$.  The double family is therefore absolutely summable, so it
may be summed in either order; summing first over $j$ and using
$\sum_{j\ge0}q^{2kj}=(1-q^{2k})^{-1}$ gives \cref{p9:eq:master-log}.  The same
majorant, with the factor $\sum_jr^{2j}$ deleted, dominates the right-hand
side of \cref{p9:eq:master-log} and shows that it too converges absolutely and
uniformly on $L$.  The logarithm on the left is the sum of the individual
zero-normalized branches, which is the branch with
$\log\Phi(q,0)=0$.
\end{proof}

The coefficient
\begin{equation}
 R_k(q):=\frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}
 \label{p9:eq:Rk}
\end{equation}
is simultaneously a geometric power sum, a cumulant multiplier, and the source of every root-of-unity singularity.  The entire cyclotomic theory below is a careful organization of the resonances $q^{2k}=1$.

\subsection{A spectral \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-Pochhammer factorization}

Let $(a;Q)_\infty=\prod_{j\ge0}(1-aQ^j)$.  Reordering Euler's sine factors gives a second exact representation.

\begin{theorem}[Infinite spectral $q$-Pochhammer product]\label{p9:thm:infinite-spectral-pochhammer-product}
For every $q\in\DiskD$ and $z\in\ComplexNumbers$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Phi(q,z)=\prod_{n\ge1}
 \left(\frac{(1-q)^2z^2}{\pi^2n^2};q^2\right)_\infty.}
 \label{p9:eq:qpoch-factor}
\end{equation}
The double product is locally normally convergent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Euler's product to each sinc factor, obtaining the doubly indexed
product
\[
 \Phi(q,z)=\prod_{j\ge0}\prod_{n\ge1}\bigl(1+\alpha_{j,n}\bigr),
 \qquad
 \alpha_{j,n}=-\frac{(1-q)^2q^{2j}z^2}{\pi^2n^2}.
\]
Since $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}=\zeta(2)=\pi^{2}/6$ and $\sum_{j\ge0}|q|^{2j}
=(1-|q|^{2})^{-1}$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j\ge0}\sum_{n\ge1}\AbsoluteValue{\alpha_{j,n}}
 =\frac{\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}^{2}}{\pi^{2}}
  \cdot\frac{\zeta(2)}{1-\AbsoluteValue q^{2}}
 =\frac{\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}^{2}}{6\bigl(1-\AbsoluteValue q^{2}\bigr)},
 \label{p9:eq:qpoch-normal}
\end{equation}
which is finite for $|q|<1$ and bounded on compact subsets of
$\DiskD\times\ComplexNumbers$.  A product $\prod(1+\alpha_i)$ over a countable
index set with $\sum_i\AbsoluteValue{\alpha_i}<\infty$ converges
unconditionally, is unchanged by any bijective reindexing or by grouping the
factors into blocks, and its value equals either iterated product; this is the
standard criterion for normal convergence of infinite products, applied here
to the index set $\SetOf{(j,n)}$.  Grouping by $n$ and evaluating the inner
product over $j$ turns $\prod_{j\ge0}(1-(1-q)^{2}z^{2}q^{2j}/(\pi^{2}n^{2}))$
into the stated $q^{2}$-Pochhammer symbol.  Because
\cref{p9:eq:qpoch-normal} is uniform on compact sets, the convergence is
locally normal.  No hypothesis on the vanishing of individual Euler factors
is needed: absolute summability of the $\alpha_{j,n}$ is what licenses the
rearrangement, and a vanishing factor merely makes both sides zero.  Hence the
identity holds for every $q\in\DiskD$ and every $z\in\ComplexNumbers$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Lean crosswalk: global factorization]
The compiled theorem
\begin{center}
\small
\path|Fabius.geometricSincProduct_eq_tprod_complexQPochhammerInf|
\end{center}
in \path|FabiusFunction.RvachevPochhammerFactorization| states, for every
$q\in\ComplexNumbers$ with $|q|<1$ and every $u\in\ComplexNumbers$,
\[
 \operatorname{geometricSincProduct}(q,u)
 =\prod_{k\ge0}
 \left(\frac{u^2}{(k+1)^2};q^2\right)_\infty .
\]
Substituting $u=(1-q)z/\pi$ and reindexing $n=k+1$ gives
\cref{p9:eq:qpoch-factor} exactly.  Its proof is global in $u$, includes $q=0$
without division by a geometric scale, and remains valid when individual
Euler factors vanish.  The older dyadic theorem
\path|Fabius.rvachevFourierProduct_eq_tprod_complexQPochhammerInf| is now a
direct specialization of this variable-$q$ result.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Why dilogarithms appear]
Radial root-of-unity asymptotics of a single $q$-Pochhammer symbol are governed by a dilogarithmic action and a finite cyclic factor.  Formula \cref{p9:eq:qpoch-factor} superposes one such action for each spectral point $\pi n$.  The result is the infinite spectral dilogarithm obtained below.  Our direct proof from \cref{p9:eq:master-log} avoids branch bookkeeping and reduces the needed uniformity to the explicit two-range estimate in \cref{p9:thm:two-term-radial}.
\end{remark}

\section{Radial resonance at roots of unity}

\subsection{Cyclotomic notation}

Fix a primitive $m$th root
\begin{equation}
 \omega=\exp\left(\frac{2\pi\ImaginaryUnit h}{m}\right),
 \qquad (h,m)=1,
 \qquad m\ge2,
 \label{p9:eq:omega}
\end{equation}
and write
\begin{equation}
 d=\OrderOperator_{\mathrm{mult}}(\omega^2)=\frac{m}{\gcd(m,2)},
 \qquad
 a_\omega=1-\omega.
 \label{p9:eq:d-a}
\end{equation}
Thus $\omega^{2k}=1$ exactly when $d\mid k$.  We approach the root radially from inside the disk by
\begin{equation}
 q=\omega(1-\delta),
 \qquad \delta\downarrow0.
 \label{p9:eq:radial-q}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Resonant and nonresonant multipliers]\label{p9:lem:resonant-and-nonresonant-multipliers}
For fixed $k\ge1$,
\begin{align}
 \frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}
 &=\frac{a_\omega^{2k}}{1-\omega^{2k}}+O(\delta),
 && d\nmid k,
 \label{p9:eq:nonres-exp}\\[3pt]
 \frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}
 &=a_\omega^{2k}\left[
 \frac{1}{2k\delta}
 +\frac{\omega}{1-\omega}
 +\frac{2k-1}{4k}
 +O(\delta)
 \right],
 && d\mid k.
 \label{p9:eq:res-exp}
\end{align}
Both remainders are asserted here only for each fixed $k$; no uniformity in an
unbounded residue class is part of this lemma.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The nonresonant denominator tends to the nonzero number $1-\omega^{2k}$.  In the resonant case,
\begin{align*}
 (1-q)^{2k}
 &=a_\omega^{2k}
 \left(1+2k\frac{\omega}{a_\omega}\delta+O(k^2\delta^2)\right),\\
 1-q^{2k}
 &=1-(1-\delta)^{2k}
 =2k\delta-k(2k-1)\delta^2+O(k^3\delta^3).
\end{align*}
Divide the two expansions.  This proves the two fixed-$k$ statements.  Passing
from them to a summed expansion requires the separate uniform remainder
estimate isolated in the appendix.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The radial action and constant term}

\begin{definition}[Cyclotomic action]
For $|a_\omega z|<\pi$, define
\begin{equation}
 \Aact_\omega(z)
 =\sum_{\ell\ge1}
 \frac{c_{\ell d}}{2\ell d}
 a_\omega^{2\ell d}z^{2\ell d}.
 \label{p9:eq:action-series}
\end{equation}
Also define
\begin{align}
 \Bact_\omega(z)
 =&-\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\d\nmid k}}
 c_k\frac{a_\omega^{2k}}{1-\omega^{2k}}z^{2k}
 \label{p9:eq:B-first}\\
 &-\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\d\mid k}}
 c_ka_\omega^{2k}
 \left(\frac{\omega}{1-\omega}+\frac{2k-1}{4k}\right)z^{2k}.
 \label{p9:eq:B-second}
\end{align}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform multiplier estimates]
\label{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}
Write $a=a_\omega$ and $b=\omega/a$, and for $k\ge1$ and
$q=\omega(1-\delta)$ let
\begin{equation}
 S_k(\delta)
 =\frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}
 =\frac{(a+\omega\delta)^{2k}}{1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}}
 \label{p9:eq:Sk-delta}
\end{equation}
be the multiplier of $z^{2k}$ in \cref{p9:eq:master-log}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
