\item \emph{(Resonant factorization.)}  If $d\mid k$, then
\begin{equation}
 S_k(\delta)=\frac{a^{2k}}{2k\delta}\,H_k(\delta),
 \qquad
 H_k(\delta)=(1+b\delta)^{2k}\,
 \frac{2k\delta}{1-(1-\delta)^{2k}},
 \label{p9:eq:Hk}
\end{equation}
and $H_k$ extends holomorphically to the closed disc
$\AbsoluteValue\delta\le1/(4k)$, where
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{H_k(\delta)}\le M_1
 \DefinitionEquals2\EulerE^{\AbsoluteValue b/2},
 \qquad
 H_k(0)=1,
 \qquad
 \CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{1}H_k=2kb+\frac{2k-1}{2}.
 \label{p9:eq:Hk-bounds}
\end{equation}
\item \emph{(Nonresonant separation.)}  Suppose $d\ge2$ and $d\nmid k$.  Then
$\omega^{2k}$ is a $d$th root of unity different from $1$, and
\begin{equation}
 \gamma\DefinitionEquals
 \min_{\substack{1\le r<d\\0\le t\le1}}
 \AbsoluteValue{1-\omega^{2r}t}
 \ge\sin\frac{\pi}{d}>0 .
 \label{p9:eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
In particular $\AbsoluteValue{1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}}\ge\gamma$ for every
real $\delta\in[0,1]$.
\item \emph{(Nonresonant derivative.)}  Under the hypotheses of \textup{(ii)},
for $0\le\delta\le\delta_1\DefinitionEquals\AbsoluteValue a/2$,
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{S_k'(\delta)}
 \le 2k\,\Theta\,\AbsoluteValue{a+\omega\delta}^{2k},
 \qquad
 \Theta\DefinitionEquals
 \frac{2}{\gamma\AbsoluteValue a}+\frac1{\gamma^{2}} .
 \label{p9:eq:Sk-derivative}
\end{equation}
\item \emph{(Nonresonant analyticity.)}  Under the hypotheses of
\textup{(ii)}, put
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_0=2\sin\frac{\pi}{d},
 \qquad
 \lambda_\omega=\min\SetOf{\tfrac12,\
   \log\bigl(1+\tfrac{\gamma_0}{2}\bigr)} .
 \label{p9:eq:lambda-omega}
\end{equation}
Then $S_k$ is holomorphic on $\AbsoluteValue\delta\le\lambda_\omega/(2k)$ and
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{S_k(\delta)}
 \le M_2\AbsoluteValue a^{2k},
 \qquad
 M_2\DefinitionEquals
 \frac{2\EulerE^{\AbsoluteValue b/2}}{\gamma_0},
 \label{p9:eq:Sk-analytic}
\end{equation}
on that disc.
\item \emph{(Crude resonant lower bound.)}  If $d\mid k$ and $0<\delta\le1$,
then
\begin{equation}
 1-(1-\delta)^{2k}\ge1-\EulerE^{-2k\delta}
 \ge(1-\EulerE^{-1})\min(1,2k\delta).
 \label{p9:eq:tail-lower}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
When $d=1$ every index is resonant, parts \textup{(ii)}--\textup{(iv)}
are vacuous, and we then adopt the conventions $\gamma=\gamma_0=1$ and
$\lambda_\omega=\tfrac12$, so that the constants $\Theta$ and $M_2$ named
above are defined in every case.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, $1-q=1-\omega(1-\delta)=a+\omega\delta$ and
$q^{2k}=\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}$, which is \cref{p9:eq:Sk-delta}.

\emph{(i)}  If $d\mid k$ then $\omega^{2k}=1$, and \cref{p9:eq:Hk} is the
identity $(a+\omega\delta)^{2k}=a^{2k}(1+b\delta)^{2k}$ together with the
insertion of $2k\delta$.  Write $n=2k$.  From the binomial theorem,
\begin{equation}
 \frac{1-(1-\delta)^{n}}{n\delta}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}p_j(n)\delta^{j},
 \qquad
 p_j(n)=\frac{(-1)^{j}}{n}\binom{n}{j+1}
 =\frac{(-1)^{j}(n-1)\cdots(n-j)}{(j+1)!},
 \label{p9:eq:pj}
\end{equation}
so $p_0=1$, $p_1(n)=-(n-1)/2$ and $\AbsoluteValue{p_j(n)}\le n^{j}/(j+1)!$.
Hence for $n\AbsoluteValue\delta\le\tfrac12$,
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\frac{1-(1-\delta)^{n}}{n\delta}-1}
 \le\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(n\AbsoluteValue\delta)^{j}}{(j+1)!}
 =\frac{\EulerE^{x}-1-x}{x}\bigg|_{x=n\AbsoluteValue\delta}
 \le\frac{\EulerE^{1/2}-\tfrac32}{\tfrac12}
 <0.298<\frac12 ,
\]
the middle function being increasing in $x>0$.  Therefore the series
\cref{p9:eq:pj} is a nonvanishing holomorphic function on
$\AbsoluteValue\delta\le1/(2n)=1/(4k)$, its reciprocal
$G_n(\delta)=n\delta/(1-(1-\delta)^{n})$ is holomorphic there with
$\AbsoluteValue{G_n}\le(1-\tfrac12)^{-1}=2$, and
$\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{1}G_n=-p_1(n)=(n-1)/2$.  On the same disc
$\AbsoluteValue{(1+b\delta)^{n}}\le\EulerE^{n\AbsoluteValue b\AbsoluteValue\delta}
 \le\EulerE^{\AbsoluteValue b/2}$, which gives the bound in
\cref{p9:eq:Hk-bounds}; and
$\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{1}H_k=nb+(n-1)/2$ with $n=2k$, which is the
last assertion.

\emph{(ii)}  $\omega^{2}$ has multiplicative order $d$, so $\omega^{2k}$
depends only on $k\bmod d$ and equals $1$ exactly when $d\mid k$; for
$d\nmid k$ it is one of the numbers $\omega^{2r}$, $1\le r<d$.  Write
$\omega^{2r}=\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\phi}$.  The distance from $1$ to the
segment $\SetOf{\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\phi}t:0\le t\le1}$ equals
$\AbsoluteValue{\sin\phi}$ if $\cos\phi\ge0$ and equals $1$ if $\cos\phi<0$.
In the second case the distance is $1\ge\sin(\pi/d)$.  In the first case
$\phi=2\pi s/d$ with $s\not\equiv0\pmod d$, and writing $2s\equiv u\pmod{2d}$
with $0\le u<2d$ we get $\AbsoluteValue{\sin\phi}
 =\AbsoluteValue{\sin(\pi u/d)}$; here $u=0$ is excluded by
$s\not\equiv0\pmod d$, and $u=d$ forces $\phi=\pi$, hence $\cos\phi<0$, which
is the second case.  For the remaining $u$ we have
$\AbsoluteValue{\sin(\pi u/d)}\ge\sin(\pi/d)$.  Since
$(1-\delta)^{2k}\in[0,1]$ for real $\delta\in[0,1]$, the displayed lower bound
on $\AbsoluteValue{1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}}$ follows.

\emph{(iii)}  With $D_k(\delta)=1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}$ one has
$D_k'(\delta)=2k\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k-1}$, so
\[
 S_k'(\delta)
 =\frac{2k\omega(a+\omega\delta)^{2k-1}}{D_k(\delta)}
 -\frac{2k\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k-1}(a+\omega\delta)^{2k}}{D_k(\delta)^{2}} .
\]
For real $\delta\in[0,1]$ we have $\AbsoluteValue{(1-\delta)^{2k-1}}\le1$ and,
by \textup{(ii)}, $\AbsoluteValue{D_k}\ge\gamma$.  For
$0\le\delta\le\AbsoluteValue a/2$ also
$\AbsoluteValue{a+\omega\delta}\ge\AbsoluteValue a-\delta
 \ge\AbsoluteValue a/2$, so
$\AbsoluteValue{a+\omega\delta}^{2k-1}
 \le(2/\AbsoluteValue a)\AbsoluteValue{a+\omega\delta}^{2k}$.  Combining the
three bounds gives \cref{p9:eq:Sk-derivative}.

\emph{(iv)}  The minimum of $\AbsoluteValue{1-\eta}$ over $d$th roots of unity
$\eta\ne1$ is $\AbsoluteValue{1-\EulerE^{2\pi\ImaginaryUnit/d}}=2\sin(\pi/d)
=\gamma_0$.  For $\AbsoluteValue\delta\le\lambda_\omega/(2k)$,
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{(1-\delta)^{2k}-1}
 \le(1+\AbsoluteValue\delta)^{2k}-1
 \le\EulerE^{2k\AbsoluteValue\delta}-1
 \le\EulerE^{\lambda_\omega}-1\le\frac{\gamma_0}{2},
\]
so $\AbsoluteValue{1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}}
 \ge\gamma_0-\gamma_0/2=\gamma_0/2>0$; in particular the denominator does not
vanish and $S_k$ is holomorphic there.  The numerator obeys
$\AbsoluteValue{(a+\omega\delta)^{2k}}
 \le\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}\EulerE^{2k\AbsoluteValue b\AbsoluteValue\delta}
 \le\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}\EulerE^{\AbsoluteValue b/2}$, which gives
\cref{p9:eq:Sk-analytic}.

\emph{(v)}  $1-\delta\le\EulerE^{-\delta}$ gives the first inequality.  For the
second, $x\mapsto1-\EulerE^{-x}$ is concave with value $0$ at $x=0$, hence lies
above the chord $x\mapsto(1-\EulerE^{-1})x$ on $[0,1]$, and it is increasing,
hence at least $1-\EulerE^{-1}$ for $x\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform two-term radial root-of-unity expansion]
\label{p9:thm:two-term-radial}
Let $K$ be a compact subset of $\SetOf{z:|a_\omega z|<\pi}$.  Uniformly for $z\in K$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \log\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),z\bigr)
 =-\frac{\Aact_\omega(z)}{\delta}
 +\Bact_\omega(z)+O_K(\delta).}
 \label{p9:eq:two-term-radial}
\end{equation}
In particular, every nontrivial root of unity carries a full exponential-scale singularity unless $\Aact_\omega(z)=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $a=a_\omega$ and $b=\omega/a$, choose $0<\rho<\rho_1<1$ with
$|az|\le\rho\pi$ on $K$, and shrink $\delta_0>0$ so that
$\delta_0\le\min\SetOf{\tfrac1{64},\AbsoluteValue a/2}$ and
$|(a+\omega\delta)z|\le\rho_1\pi$ for $z\in K$ and $0\le\delta\le\delta_0$.
Then $(q,z)\in\Omega$ for $q=\omega(1-\delta)$ and $z\in K$, so
\cref{p9:eq:master-log} applies and
\[
 \log\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),z\bigr)
 =-\sum_{k\ge1}c_kS_k(\delta)z^{2k}
\]
with $S_k$ as in \cref{p9:eq:Sk-delta}.  We use the majorants
$c_k\AbsoluteValue{az}^{2k}\le\zeta(2)\rho^{2k}/k$ and
$c_k\AbsoluteValue{(a+\omega\delta)z}^{2k}\le\zeta(2)\rho_1^{2k}/k$, both
immediate from $c_k\le\zeta(2)/(k\pi^{2k})$.

\emph{Nonresonant indices.}  Assume $d\ge2$; for $d=1$ there are none.  For
$d\nmid k$ the function $S_k$ is real-analytic on $[0,\delta_0]$ and
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(iii)} applies, so the mean value
theorem gives, for $0\le\delta\le\delta_0$,
\begin{equation}
 c_k|z|^{2k}|S_k(\delta)-S_k(0)|
 \le 2k\Theta\,\delta\,
   c_k\max_{0\le s\le\delta}\AbsoluteValue{(a+\omega s)z}^{2k}
 \le C_K\delta\rho_1^{2k},
 \qquad
 C_K=2\zeta(2)\Theta .
 \label{p9:eq:nonres-uniform}
\end{equation}
Summing over $k$ bounds the total nonresonant deviation by
$C_K\rho_1^{2}(1-\rho_1^{2})^{-1}\delta=O_K(\delta)$, and the retained values
$S_k(0)=a^{2k}/(1-\omega^{2k})$ contribute exactly \cref{p9:eq:B-first}.

\emph{Resonant indices below the cutoff.}  Let $d\mid k$, put $n=2k$, and set
$N=\Floor{\delta^{-1/2}}$.  Since $\delta\le1/64$ we have
$N\le\delta^{-1/2}\le1/(8\delta)$, so every $k\le N$ satisfies
$\delta\le1/(8k)$, that is, $\delta$ lies within half the radius of the disc
of \cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(i)}.  Cauchy's estimate on that disc,
applied to $H_k$ with $\AbsoluteValue{H_k}\le M_1$ and radius $1/(4k)$, gives
for $\AbsoluteValue\delta\le1/(8k)$
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{H_k(\delta)-1
  -\bigl(\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{1}H_k\bigr)\delta}
 \le M_1\frac{(4k\delta)^{2}}{1-4k\delta}
 \le 32M_1k^{2}\delta^{2}.
\]
Dividing by $2k\delta$ and using \cref{p9:eq:Hk,p9:eq:Hk-bounds} therefore
yields the uniform expansion
\begin{equation}
 \frac{S_k(\delta)}{a^{2k}}
 =\frac1{2k\delta}+\frac{\omega}{a}
  +\frac{2k-1}{4k}+O(k\delta),
 \label{p9:eq:res-uniform}
\end{equation}
in which the implied constant is $16M_1$, independent of $k\le N$ and of
$\delta\le\delta_0$.  Multiplying by $c_k\AbsoluteValue{az}^{2k}$ bounds the
remainder of the $k$th term by
$16M_1\zeta(2)\rho^{2k}\delta$, so the sum
of these remainders over the resonant indices $k\le N$ is at most
$16M_1\zeta(2)\rho^{2}(1-\rho^{2})^{-1}\delta=O_K(\delta)$.  The three
retained terms of \cref{p9:eq:res-uniform}, summed over all resonant $k$,
produce exactly $-\Aact_\omega(z)/\delta$ and \cref{p9:eq:B-second}.

\emph{Resonant indices beyond the cutoff.}  By
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(v)},
\[
 c_k|z|^{2k}\AbsoluteValue{S_k(\delta)}
 \le\frac{\zeta(2)\rho_1^{2k}}
     {k\,(1-\EulerE^{-1})\min(1,2k\delta)}
 \le\frac{\zeta(2)}{1-\EulerE^{-1}}\rho_1^{2k}
   \left(\frac1k+\frac1{2k^{2}\delta}\right),
\]
while the corresponding subtracted terms satisfy
\[
 c_k\AbsoluteValue{az}^{2k}
 \left(\frac1{2k\delta}+\AbsoluteValue b+\frac{2k-1}{4k}\right)
 \le\zeta(2)\rho^{2k}
 \left(\frac1{2k^{2}\delta}+\frac{\AbsoluteValue b+1}{k}\right).
\]
Summing both over $k>N$ gives $O_K\bigl(\delta^{-1}\rho_1^{2N}\bigr)$, and
$\rho_1^{2N}\le\rho_1^{-2}(\rho_1^{2})^{\delta^{-1/2}}$, so by
\cref{p9:eq:exp-beats-power} this is $o_K(\delta^{M})$ for every $M$; in
particular it is $O_K(\delta)$.

Adding the three estimates proves \cref{p9:eq:two-term-radial}, with the
explicit constant
$2\zeta(2)\Theta\rho_1^{2}(1-\rho_1^{2})^{-1}
 +16M_1\zeta(2)\rho^{2}(1-\rho^{2})^{-1}+1$ for all sufficiently small
$\delta$, the first summand being absent when $d=1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Dilogarithmic and cyclic descriptions}

The action has two additional forms that expose its spectral and finite-cyclic content.

\begin{theorem}[Spectral dilogarithm]\label{p9:thm:spectral-dilogarithm}
For $|a_\omega z|<\pi$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Aact_\omega(z)
 =\frac{1}{2d^2}\sum_{n\ge1}
 \Polylogarithm_2\!\left(
 \left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}\right)^{2d}
 \right).}
 \label{p9:eq:spectral-dilog}
\end{equation}
The series converges absolutely and locally uniformly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $c_k=\zeta(2k)/(k\pi^{2k})$, the $\ell$th term of
\cref{p9:eq:action-series} is
\[
 \frac{c_{\ell d}}{2\ell d}a_\omega^{2\ell d}z^{2\ell d}
 =\frac{\zeta(2\ell d)}{2(\ell d)^{2}}
   \left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi}\right)^{2\ell d}
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{2(\ell d)^{2}}
   \left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}\right)^{2\ell d}.
\]
Let $K$ be a compact subset of $\SetOf{z:\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}<\pi}$ and
put $\rho=\max_{z\in K}\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}/\pi<1$.  Because
$\zeta(2\ell d)\le\zeta(2)$ for $\ell d\ge1$, the resulting double family is
absolutely summable, with
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\sum_{\ell\ge1}
 \frac1{2(\ell d)^{2}}
 \AbsoluteValue{\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}}^{2\ell d}
 =\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{\zeta(2\ell d)}{2(\ell d)^{2}}\rho^{2\ell d}
 \le\frac{\zeta(2)}{2d^{2}}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{\rho^{2\ell d}}{\ell^{2}}
 \le\frac{\zeta(2)^{2}}{2d^{2}}
 \label{p9:eq:dilog-majorant}
\end{equation}
uniformly for $z\in K$.  A summable double family may be summed in either
order, so
\[
 \Aact_\omega(z)
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\sum_{\ell\ge1}
 \frac1{2(\ell d)^2}
 \left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}\right)^{2\ell d}
 =\frac1{2d^2}\sum_{n\ge1}
 \Polylogarithm_2\!\left(\left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}\right)^{2d}\right),
\]
the inner sum being the defining series
$\Polylogarithm_2(x)=\sum_{\ell\ge1}x^{\ell}/\ell^{2}$ evaluated at
$x=(a_\omega z/(\pi n))^{2d}$, which satisfies $\AbsoluteValue x\le\rho^{2d}<1$.
Since the bound \cref{p9:eq:dilog-majorant} is uniform on $K$ and $K$ was an
arbitrary compact subset, the convergence is absolute and locally uniform.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclic projection formula]\label{p9:thm:cyclic-projection-formula}
For $|a_\omega z|<\pi$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Aact_\omega(z)
 =-\int_0^z
 \left[
 \frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}
 \log\SincRad(a_\omega\omega^rt)
 \right]\frac{\Differential t}{t}.}
 \label{p9:eq:cyclic-projection}
\end{equation}
Here every logarithm is the zero-normalized holomorphic branch from
\cref{p9:eq:sinc-log}, and the integral is taken along the straight segment from
$0$ to $z$ (equivalently, along any path in the disk).  The integrand has a
holomorphic removable extension at zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $z$ with $\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}<\pi$ and put
$\rho=\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}/\pi<1$.  For $t$ on the segment $[0,z]$ every
argument $a_\omega\omega^{r}t$ lies in $\SetOf{\AbsoluteValue w\le\rho\pi}$, so
\cref{p9:eq:sinc-log} applies to each of the $d$ logarithms and
\[
 \frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\log\SincRad(a_\omega\omega^rt)
 =-\sum_{k\ge1}c_ka_\omega^{2k}t^{2k}
 \left(\frac1d\sum_{r=0}^{d-1}\omega^{2kr}\right)
 =-\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\ d\mid k}}c_ka_\omega^{2k}t^{2k},
\]
because $\omega^{2}$ has order $d$, so the inner average is
$\IndicatorOf{d\mid k}$.  The surviving series has lowest term $t^{2d}$, so
after division by $t$ the integrand of \cref{p9:eq:cyclic-projection} is
$O(t^{2d-1})$ and extends holomorphically through $t=0$.  Parametrizing the
segment by $t=sz$ with $s\in[0,1]$ turns the integrand into
$-\sum_{d\mid k}c_ka_\omega^{2k}z^{2k}s^{2k-1}$, which is dominated by the
summable constants $\zeta(2)\rho^{2k}/k$ uniformly in $s\in[0,1]$ by
\cref{p9:eq:ck-majorant}.  Uniform convergence on the compact parameter
interval permits termwise integration, and
$\int_0^1s^{2k-1}\Differential s=1/(2k)$ turns the $k$th term into
$c_ka_\omega^{2k}z^{2k}/(2k)$.  Summing over $k=\ell d$ gives exactly
\cref{p9:eq:action-series}.  The integral is path independent inside the disc
because the integrand is holomorphic there.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Formula \cref{p9:eq:cyclic-projection} is a root-of-unity filter in the scale index.  The sinc function is even, so the relevant cycle is generated by $\omega^2$, not $\omega$; this explains the compression from order $m$ to $d=m/\gcd(m,2)$.
\end{remark}

\section{A natural-boundary theorem}

\subsection{The sign of the action}

The crucial point is that the action cannot vanish on a uniform real-frequency interval.

\begin{lemma}[Reality and sign of $a_\omega^{2d}$]\label{p9:lem:reality-and-sign}
The number $a_\omega^{2d}$ is real and nonzero.  For a primitive $m$th root,
\begin{equation}
 \Sign\bigl(a_\omega^{2d}\bigr)=
 \begin{cases}
 -1,&m\text{ odd},\\
 (-1)^{d+1},&m\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{p9:eq:sign-a}
\end{equation}
Thus it is positive exactly when $m\equiv2\pmod4$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $\omega=\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\theta}$.  Since
\(
 1-\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\theta}=-2\ImaginaryUnit\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\theta/2}\sin(\theta/2)
\),
\[
 a_\omega^{2d}=(-4)^d\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit d\theta}\sin^{2d}(\theta/2).
\]
If $m$ is odd then $d=m$ and $\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit d\theta}=1$, while $d$ is odd.  If $m$ is even then $d=m/2$, the primitive numerator $h$ is odd, and $\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit d\theta}=\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\pi h}=-1$.  The signs follow.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nonvanishing action on a universal interval]
\label{p9:thm:nonvanishing-action}
Let $\omega\ne1$ be a primitive $m$th root of unity and let $z$ be
\emph{either real or purely imaginary}, with
\begin{equation}
 0<|z|<\frac\pi2 .
 \label{p9:eq:zinterval}
\end{equation}
Then $\Aact_\omega(z)$ is real, nonzero, and
\begin{equation}
 \Sign\Aact_\omega(z)=
 \begin{cases}
  \Sign\bigl(a_\omega^{2d}\bigr), & z\in\RealNumbers,\\[0.25em]
  (-1)^{d}\Sign\bigl(a_\omega^{2d}\bigr),
   & z\in\ImaginaryUnit\RealNumbers .
 \end{cases}
 \label{p9:eq:sign-action}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Because $|a_\omega|\le2$, condition \cref{p9:eq:zinterval} implies
\(
 |a_\omega z/(\pi n)|<1
\) for every $n\ge1$.  Write $z=\varsigma$ in the real case and
$z=\ImaginaryUnit\varsigma$ with $\varsigma$ real in the imaginary case; in
both cases $z^{2d}=\epsilon\,\varsigma^{2d}$ with
$\epsilon=1$ and $\epsilon=(-1)^{d}$ respectively, because
$\ImaginaryUnit^{2d}=(-1)^{d}$.  Hence, by \cref{p9:eq:sign-a},
\[
 \left(\frac{a_\omega z}{\pi n}\right)^{2d}
 =a_\omega^{2d}\,\epsilon\left(\frac{\varsigma}{\pi n}\right)^{2d}
 =\sigma x_n,
 \qquad
 \sigma=\epsilon\Sign\bigl(a_\omega^{2d}\bigr)\in\SetOf{-1,1},
 \quad 0<x_n<1,
\]
the sign $\sigma$ being the same for every $n$ and the bound $x_n<1$ coming
from \cref{p9:eq:zinterval} exactly as in the real case, since
$|z|=|\varsigma|$.  For $0<x<1$, $\Polylogarithm_2(x)>0$ and
$\Polylogarithm_2(-x)<0$, and the series
\cref{p9:eq:spectral-dilog} converges absolutely.  Every summand therefore has
sign $\sigma$, so the sum is real and nonzero with that sign, which is
\cref{p9:eq:sign-action}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the imaginary slice is worth the extra line]
\label{p9:rem:two-slices}
The real slice $z\in\RealNumbers$ is the characteristic-function slice; the
imaginary slice $z\in\ImaginaryUnit\RealNumbers$ is the \emph{exponential}
slice, on which $\Phi$ becomes the centered moment generating germ of
Part~VII.  The two are transverse, and the natural-boundary statement that
Part~VII conjectures lives on the second one.  The only change in the proof is
the factor $\ImaginaryUnit^{2d}=(-1)^{d}$, which moves the common sign without
ever making it depend on $n$; that is what
\cref{p9:cor:germ-natural-boundary} needs.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Natural boundary}

\begin{theorem}[Natural boundary on a universal frequency interval]
\label{p9:thm:natural-boundary}
Fix $z$ either real or purely imaginary with $0<|z|<\pi/2$.  Then the
holomorphic function
\begin{equation}
 q\longmapsto\Phi(q,z),\qquad |q|<1,
 \label{p9:eq:qmap}
\end{equation}
admits no single-valued meromorphic continuation through any point of the unit
circle.  Explicitly: there exist no $\zeta_0$ with
$\AbsoluteValue{\zeta_0}=1$, no $\varrho>0$, and no function $F$ meromorphic on
the disc
$\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)=\SetOf{q:\AbsoluteValue{q-\zeta_0}<\varrho}$ such that
$F=\Phi(\cdot,z)$ on the connected set
$\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)\cap\DiskD$.  In particular the unit circle is a
natural boundary, and no continuation crosses a nontrivial boundary arc.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1: $\Phi(\cdot,z)$ is zero-free on $\DiskD$.}  For
$\AbsoluteValue q<1$ we have $\AbsoluteValue{1-q}<2$, hence
$\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}<2\cdot\pi/2=\pi$, so $(q,z)\in\Omega$ and
\cref{p9:eq:master-log} represents $\log\Phi(q,z)$ as a convergent series.
Therefore $\Phi(q,z)=\EulerE^{\log\Phi(q,z)}\ne0$ for every $q\in\DiskD$.  The
same inequality shows $\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}\le2\AbsoluteValue z<\pi$ for
every root of unity $\omega$, so $z$ lies in the common domain of
$\Aact_\omega$ and $\Bact_\omega$ and \cref{p9:eq:two-term-radial} may be
applied at $z$.

\emph{Step 2: no local continuation.}  Suppose such a triple
$(\zeta_0,\varrho,F)$ existed.  The lens $\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)\cap\DiskD$ is
a nonempty connected open set on which $F$ coincides with the zero-free
function $\Phi(\cdot,z)$, so $F$ does not vanish identically on the connected
disc $\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)$.  Roots of unity are dense on the unit circle,
so $\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)$ contains a root of unity $\omega\ne1$; fix one,
primitive of some order $m\ge2$.  For all sufficiently small $\delta>0$ the
radial point $\omega(1-\delta)$ lies in $\Delta(\zeta_0,\varrho)\cap\DiskD$, so
\begin{equation}
 F\bigl(\omega(1-\delta)\bigr)=\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),z\bigr).
 \label{p9:eq:F-radial}
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: the two growth rates are incompatible.}  Because $F$ is
meromorphic near $\omega$ and not identically zero, there are an integer $\nu$
and a function $G$ holomorphic near $\omega$ with $G(\omega)\ne0$ and
$F(q)=(q-\omega)^{\nu}G(q)$; this single formula covers a regular point
($\nu=0$), a zero ($\nu>0$) and a pole ($\nu<0$), and $\nu$ is finite in each
case.  Since $\AbsoluteValue{\omega(1-\delta)-\omega}=\delta$,
\begin{equation}
 \log\AbsoluteValue{F\bigl(\omega(1-\delta)\bigr)}
 =\nu\log\delta+O(1),
 \qquad\delta\downarrow0 .
 \label{p9:eq:mero-rate}
\end{equation}
On the other hand $A\DefinitionEquals\Aact_\omega(z)$ is real and nonzero by
\cref{p9:thm:nonvanishing-action}, and taking real parts in
\cref{p9:eq:two-term-radial} with $K=\SetOf z$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \log\AbsoluteValue{\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),z\bigr)}
 =-\frac{A}{\delta}+O(1).
 \label{p9:eq:mod-growth}
\end{equation}
By \cref{p9:eq:F-radial} the left-hand sides of
\cref{p9:eq:mero-rate,p9:eq:mod-growth} coincide.  But the right-hand side of
\cref{p9:eq:mero-rate} is $O(\log(1/\delta))$, whereas that of
\cref{p9:eq:mod-growth} tends to $-\infty$ at rate $\delta^{-1}$ when $A>0$ and
to $+\infty$ at rate $\delta^{-1}$ when $A<0$.  Dividing by $\delta^{-1}$ and
letting $\delta\downarrow0$ gives $-A=0$, contradicting $A\ne0$.

Hence no boundary point admits a single-valued meromorphic continuation.  A
continuation across a nontrivial arc would restrict to one at each of its
points, so none exists; and since a meromorphic continuation is in particular
weaker than a holomorphic one, the unit circle is a natural boundary.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The centered exponential germ of Part~VII]
\label{p9:cor:germ-natural-boundary}
For every real $t$ with $0<|t|<\pi$, the unit circle is a natural boundary for
\[
 q\longmapsto C_q(t)
 =\EulerE^{-t/2}\MomentGeneratingFunction{q}(t),
 \qquad |q|<1,
\]
the centered exponential germ of \cref{p7:eq:Cq}, and no single-valued
meromorphic continuation crosses a nontrivial boundary arc.  In particular
\cref{p7:conj:natural-boundary} holds on that interval, with its hypothesis
``generic fixed $t\ne0$'' replaced by the explicit punctured interval
$0<|t|<\pi$ and with no removable degeneracies to discard.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{p9:eq:Phi-def} and the dictionary \cref{p0:tab:dictionary},
$\Phi(q,z)=\CharacteristicFunction{q}(2z)
 =\Expectation\EulerE^{2\ImaginaryUnit z\GeoLawCentered{q}}$,
while $C_q(t)=\Expectation\EulerE^{t\GeoLawCentered{q}}$ by
\cref{p0:prop:mahler}.  Both expressions are entire in their argument, so
setting $z=-\ImaginaryUnit t/2$ gives the identity of holomorphic functions
\begin{equation}
 C_q(t)=\Phi\!\left(q,-\frac{\ImaginaryUnit t}{2}\right),
 \qquad t\in\ComplexNumbers,\ |q|<1 .
 \label{p9:eq:germ-slice}
\end{equation}
For real $t\ne0$ the frequency $-\ImaginaryUnit t/2$ is purely imaginary, and
the constraint $0<|z|<\pi/2$ of \cref{p9:thm:natural-boundary} reads
$0<|t|<\pi$.  Apply that theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the theorem]
The theorem gives an explicit, root-independent interval
$0<|z|<\pi/2$ on each of the two slices.  It does not classify exceptional
complex frequencies off them.  There the action can cross dilogarithm branch
cuts, and cancellation between spectral terms is a genuine possibility.
\end{remark}

\section{Cyclotomic blow-ups}

The fixed-frequency expansion diverges like $\delta^{-1}$.  A nontrivial local limit appears when the frequency shrinks at the exact resonant rate.

\subsection{Leading blow-up theorem}

Set
\begin{equation}
 q_\eps=\omega(1-\eps^d),
 \qquad
 z=\sqrt\eps\,w,
 \qquad \eps\downarrow0,
 \label{p9:eq:blowup-scaling}
\end{equation}
and define
\begin{equation}
 A_\omega
 =\frac{c_d a_\omega^{2d}}{2d}
 =\frac{\zeta(2d)a_\omega^{2d}}{2d^2\pi^{2d}}.
 \label{p9:eq:Aomega}
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform scaled-tail bound]\label{p9:lem:uniform-scaled-tail-bound}
For every compact set $W\subset\ComplexNumbers$ there are $C_W>0$ and $\eps_0>0$ such
that, for every integer $M\ge d$, every $w\in W$, and
$0<\eps\le\eps_0$, the tail of the master logarithm satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{k\ge M}c_k\eps^k|w|^{2k}
 \left|\frac{(a_\omega+\omega\eps^d)^{2k}}
 {1-\omega^{2k}(1-\eps^d)^{2k}}\right|
 \le C_W\eps^{M-d}.
 \label{p9:eq:scaled-tail}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $s=\eps^d$.  If $d\mid k$, then
\(
 1-(1-s)^{2k}\ge s
\).
If $d\nmid k$, the finitely many phases $\omega^{2k}\ne1$ keep
$|1-\omega^{2k}(1-s)^{2k}|$ uniformly away from zero.  After reducing
$\eps_0$ if necessary, both cases are therefore bounded below by $c_\omega s$
for a fixed $c_\omega>0$.  If $|w|\le R$ on $W$, then
$c_k\le\zeta(2)/(k\pi^{2k})$ turns the left side into at most
\[
 C\eps^{-d}\sum_{k\ge M}\frac1k
 \left(\frac{|a_\omega+\omega\eps^d|^2R^2}{\pi^2}\eps\right)^k.
\]
The parenthesized base is at most $B_W\eps<1/2$ for small $\eps$.
Summing the geometric tail proves \cref{p9:eq:scaled-tail}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclotomic blow-up limit]\label{p9:thm:cyclotomic-blow-limit}
Locally uniformly for $w\in\ComplexNumbers$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 \longrightarrow \exp(-A_\omega w^{2d}).}
 \label{p9:eq:blowup-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
In \cref{p9:eq:master-log}, the $k$th term acquires the factor $\eps^k$.  If $d\nmid k$, the multiplier \cref{p9:eq:Rk} remains bounded and the term tends to zero.  If $k=\ell d$, its multiplier is asymptotic to
\(
 a_\omega^{2k}/(2k\eps^d)
\), so the term has order $\eps^{(\ell-1)d}$.  Only $k=d$ survives, giving $-A_\omega w^{2d}$.  Taking $M=d+1$ in \cref{p9:eq:scaled-tail} makes every omitted term $O_W(\eps)$, which proves local uniformity and permits exponentiation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Subcritical and order-\texorpdfstring{$d$}{d} corrections}

For $1\le k<d$ define
\begin{equation}
 C_{k,\omega}
 =c_k\frac{a_\omega^{2k}}{1-\omega^{2k}},
 \label{p9:eq:Ck}
\end{equation}
and set
\begin{equation}
 \eta_\omega=\frac{2d\omega}{1-\omega}+\frac{2d-1}{2},
 \qquad
 D_\omega=\frac{c_{2d}a_\omega^{4d}}{4d}.
 \label{p9:eq:eta-D}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[First complete correction layers]\label{p9:thm:first-complete-correction-layers}
Uniformly on compact $w$-sets,
\begin{align}
 \log\Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 =&-A_\omega w^{2d}
 -\sum_{k=1}^{d-1}C_{k,\omega}\eps^kw^{2k}
 \label{p9:eq:correction-1}\\
 &-\eps^d\left(
 A_\omega\eta_\omega w^{2d}
 +D_\omega w^{4d}
 \right)
 +O(\eps^{d+1}).
 \label{p9:eq:correction-2}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $k<d$ there is no resonance, so the constant term of the multiplier gives \cref{p9:eq:Ck}.  At total order $\eps^d$, two and only two resonant sources contribute.  The next term in the $k=d$ multiplier is the constant in \cref{p9:eq:res-exp}, producing $A_\omega\eta_\omega w^{2d}$.  The leading pole of the $k=2d$ multiplier produces $D_\omega w^{4d}$.  Every omitted nonresonant term begins at $k=d+1$, and every later resonant term begins at order at least $2d$.  Taylor's theorem handles the finitely many displayed indices, while \cref{p9:eq:scaled-tail} with $M=2d+1$ handles the infinite remainder, giving $O(\eps^{d+1})$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{All orders and Bell polynomials}

Define the Laurent germ
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_k(\eps)
 =\frac{(a_\omega+\omega\eps^d)^{2k}}
 {1-\omega^{2k}(1-\eps^d)^{2k}}.
 \label{p9:eq:Rkeps}
\end{equation}
For $d\nmid k$ it is analytic at zero; for $d\mid k$ it has a simple pole in $\eps^d$.

\begin{theorem}[All-orders logarithmic expansion]
\label{p9:thm:all-orders}
There are even polynomials $L_n(w)$, with $\deg L_n\le2(n+d)$, such that for
every compact $W\subset\ComplexNumbers$ and every integer $N\ge1$ there are
$C_{W,N}>0$ and $\eps_{W,N}>0$ with
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{
  \log\Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)+A_\omega w^{2d}
  -\sum_{n=1}^{N}L_n(w)\eps^{n}}
 \le C_{W,N}\,\eps^{N+1}
 \label{p9:eq:all-log-quant}
\end{equation}
for all $w\in W$ and $0<\eps\le\eps_{W,N}$.  The constants depend on $N$ and
$W$, but not on $w$ or $\eps$.  We abbreviate this locally uniform
Poincar\'e expansion by
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 \sim -A_\omega w^{2d}+\sum_{n\ge1}L_n(w)\eps^n,
 \label{p9:eq:all-log}
\end{equation}
with no claim that the series on the right converges.  The coefficient is the
finite sum
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 L_n(w)=-\sum_{k=1}^{n+d}c_kw^{2k}
 \CoefficientExtraction{\eps}{n-k}\mathcal R_k(\eps).}
 \label{p9:eq:Ln}
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 \sim \EulerE^{-A_\omega w^{2d}}
 \left(1+\sum_{n\ge1}P_n(w)\eps^n\right),
 \label{p9:eq:all-Phi}
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 P_n(w)=\frac1{n!}
 B_n\bigl(1!L_1(w),2!L_2(w),\dots,n!L_n(w)\bigr),}
 \label{p9:eq:Bell-Pn}
\end{equation}
where $B_n$ is the complete exponential Bell polynomial.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $N\ge1$ and a compact $W$.  For small $\eps$ we have
$\AbsoluteValue{(1-q_\eps)\sqrt\eps\,w}<\pi$ on $W$, so \cref{p9:eq:master-log}
applies and $\log\Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 =-\sum_{k\ge1}c_kw^{2k}\eps^{k}\mathcal R_k(\eps)$ with $\mathcal R_k$ as in
\cref{p9:eq:Rkeps}.  The coefficient of $\eps^{n}$ in the $k$th term is the
Laurent coefficient of $\mathcal R_k$ with index $n-k$; since the lowest
exponent occurring in $\mathcal R_k$ is $-d$, only $k\le n+d$ contributes.
Hence \cref{p9:eq:Ln} is a finite sum and $\deg L_n\le2(n+d)$, so each $L_n$ is
bounded on $W$.

For the remainder, split at $k=N+d$.  Each of the finitely many germs
$f_k(\eps)=\eps^{d}\cdot\eps^{k}\mathcal R_k(\eps)$ with $1\le k\le N+d$ is
holomorphic at $\eps=0$, because $\eps^{k}\mathcal R_k$ has a pole of order at
most $d$ there.  Taylor's theorem applied to $f_k$ on a disc
$\AbsoluteValue\eps\le r_k$ gives
$\AbsoluteValue{f_k(\eps)-\sum_{j\le N+d}\CoefficientExtraction{\eps}{j}f_k
 \,\eps^{j}}\le c^{(k)}_N\eps^{N+d+1}$; dividing by $\eps^{d}$ shows that
$\eps^{k}\mathcal R_k(\eps)$ differs from its truncation through order
$\eps^{N}$ by at most $c^{(k)}_N\eps^{N+1}$.  There are at most $N+d$ such
indices, and multiplying by the bounded factor $c_kw^{2k}$ keeps the bound
uniform on $W$.  The indices $k\ge N+d+1$ are covered by
\cref{p9:eq:scaled-tail} with $M=N+d+1$, whose right-hand side is
$C_W\eps^{N+1}$.  Adding the two estimates gives \cref{p9:eq:all-log-quant}.
Formula \cref{p9:eq:Bell-Pn} is then the standard exponential formula for
exponentiating a formal series, applied coefficientwise to
\cref{p9:eq:all-log}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
This is a second Bell structure in the theory.  The repository's Bell polynomials encode moments from cumulants; here the same combinatorial transform encodes multiplicative cyclotomic corrections from logarithmic ones.  The two uses meet in \cref{p9:sec:bell-collapse}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Four small root orders}

\begin{example}[The root $\omega=-1$]
Here $m=2$, $d=1$, and $A_{-1}=1/3$.  Thus
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi(-1+\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)
 =-\frac{w^2}{3}
 +\eps\left(\frac{w^2}{6}-\frac{w^4}{45}\right)
 +O(\eps^2).
 \label{p9:eq:m2}
\end{equation}
The first cyclotomic limit is Gaussian.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Primitive cube root]
For $\omega=\EulerE^{2\pi\ImaginaryUnit/3}$, $d=3$ and $A_\omega=-1/630$.  Moreover
\[
 C_{1,\omega}=-\frac{\ImaginaryUnit}{2\sqrt3},
 \qquad
 C_{2,\omega}=-\frac{\ImaginaryUnit}{20\sqrt3}.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\eps^3),\sqrt\eps\,w\bigr)
 =\frac{w^6}{630}
 +\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\eps w^2}{2\sqrt3}
 +\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\eps^2w^4}{20\sqrt3}
 +O(\eps^3).
 \label{p9:eq:m3}
\end{equation}
The real-axis limit grows, so its transform interpretation belongs to rotated Stokes sectors.
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Fourth root]
For $\omega=\ImaginaryUnit$, $d=2$, $A_\omega=-1/180$, and $C_{1,\omega}=-\ImaginaryUnit/6$.  Therefore
\begin{align}
 \log\Phi\bigl(\ImaginaryUnit(1-\eps^2),\sqrt\eps\,w\bigr)
 =&\frac{w^4}{180}+\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\eps w^2}{6}
 \label{p9:eq:m4-first}\\
 &-\eps^2\left[
 \left(\frac1{360}-\frac{\ImaginaryUnit}{90}\right)w^4
 +\frac{w^8}{18900}
 \right]+O(\eps^3).
 \label{p9:eq:m4-second}
\end{align}
\end{example}

\begin{example}[Primitive sixth root]
For $\omega=\EulerE^{\pi\ImaginaryUnit/3}$, $d=3$, $A_\omega=1/17010$,
\[
 C_{1,\omega}=-\frac{\ImaginaryUnit}{6\sqrt3},
 \qquad
 C_{2,\omega}=\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\sqrt3}{540}.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\eps^3),\sqrt\eps\,w\bigr)
 =-\frac{w^6}{17010}
 +\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\eps w^2}{6\sqrt3}
 -\frac{\ImaginaryUnit\sqrt3\eps^2w^4}{540}
 +O(\eps^3).
 \label{p9:eq:m6}
\end{equation}
This is the first genuinely higher-order dissipative limit.
\end{example}

\section{A universal analytic-germ principle}

The sinc product is one instance of a more general mechanism.

\begin{theorem}[Universal resonant germ]
\label{p9:thm:universal-germ}
Let $h$ be entire with $h(0)=1$, and fix $R_h>0$ so small that $h$ has no zero
on the closed disc $\AbsoluteValue w\le R_h$.  There $h$ has a holomorphic
logarithm vanishing at the origin, and Cauchy's estimates give
\begin{equation}
 \log h(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_nz^n,
 \qquad
 \AbsoluteValue{b_n}\le M_hR_h^{-n},
 \qquad
 M_h=\max_{\AbsoluteValue w=R_h}\AbsoluteValue{\log h(w)} .
 \label{p9:eq:germ-log}
\end{equation}
For $|q|<1$ define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_h(q,z)=\prod_{j\ge0}h\bigl((1-q)q^jz\bigr).
 \label{p9:eq:Ph}
\end{equation}
Fix a root of unity $\omega\ne1$, of order $m\ge2$, put
\begin{equation}
 \gamma_h=\min\SetOf{\AbsoluteValue{1-\zeta t}:
   \zeta^{m}=1,\ \zeta\ne1,\ 0\le t\le1}>0,
 \label{p9:eq:gamma-h}
\end{equation}
and let
\begin{equation}
 r=\min\SetOf{n\ge1:b_n\ne0\ \text{and}\ \omega^n=1}.
 \label{p9:eq:r-germ}
\end{equation}
Assume this set is nonempty.  Along the radial approach
$q=\omega(1-\delta)$ with $\delta>0$ and $\delta\downarrow0$, interpret
$\delta^{1/r}$ as the positive real root.  Then, locally uniformly for $w$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \mathcal P_h\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),\delta^{1/r}w\bigr)
 \longrightarrow
 \exp\left(\frac{b_r(1-\omega)^r}{r}w^r\right).}
 \label{p9:eq:universal-germ}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
That $\gamma_h>0$ is clear: $\AbsoluteValue{1-\zeta t}$ is continuous and
positive on the compact set $(\mu_m\setminus\SetOf1)\times[0,1]$, since
$\zeta t=1$ with $t\in[0,1]$ forces $t=1$ and $\zeta=1$.

Write $a=1-\omega$ and $q=\omega(1-\delta)$, so that $1-q=a+\omega\delta$ and
$\AbsoluteValue{1-q}\le\AbsoluteValue a+\delta\le3$ for $0<\delta\le1$.  Let
$W\subset\ComplexNumbers$ be compact, $R_W=\max_W\AbsoluteValue w$, and restrict
to those $\delta$ with
\begin{equation}
 0<\delta\le\min\SetOf{1,\gamma_h},
 \qquad
 3R_W\delta^{1/r}\le\tfrac12R_h .
 \label{p9:eq:germ-domain}
\end{equation}
For $z=\delta^{1/r}w$ with $w\in W$ this gives
$\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)q^{j}z}\le\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}\le\tfrac12R_h<R_h$ for
every $j\ge0$: all arguments of $h$ lie in the disc on which $\log h$ is the
holomorphic branch of \cref{p9:eq:germ-log}, which is the domain of the
computation that follows.

Since $\AbsoluteValue{b_n}\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}^{n}
\AbsoluteValue q^{jn}\le M_h2^{-n}\AbsoluteValue q^{j}$ for $n\ge1$, the double
family is absolutely summable and
\[
 \log\mathcal P_h(q,z)
 =\sum_{j\ge0}\log h\bigl((1-q)q^{j}z\bigr)
 =\sum_{j\ge0}\sum_{n\ge1}b_n(1-q)^{n}q^{jn}z^{n}
 =\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\frac{(1-q)^{n}}{1-q^{n}}z^{n},
\]
each partial product of \cref{p9:eq:Ph} being the exponential of the
corresponding partial sum.  Put
$\theta=\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}/R_h\le\tfrac12$, so that
$\AbsoluteValue{b_n}\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)z}^{n}\le M_h\theta^{n}$ and
$\theta\le3R_W\delta^{1/r}/R_h$.

If $\omega^{n}\ne1$ then $q^{n}=\omega^{n}(1-\delta)^{n}$ with
$(1-\delta)^{n}\in[0,1]$, so $\AbsoluteValue{1-q^{n}}\ge\gamma_h$ by
\cref{p9:eq:gamma-h}; if $\omega^{n}=1$ then
$1-q^{n}=1-(1-\delta)^{n}\ge\delta$.  Since $\delta\le\gamma_h$, in both cases
$\AbsoluteValue{1-q^{n}}^{-1}\le\delta^{-1}$.  Hence the tail $n>r$ obeys
\[
 \sum_{n>r}\AbsoluteValue{b_n\frac{(1-q)^{n}}{1-q^{n}}z^{n}}
 \le\frac{M_h}{\delta}\sum_{n>r}\theta^{n}
 \le\frac{2M_h}{\delta}\theta^{r+1}
 \le\frac{2M_h}{\delta}
   \left(\frac{3R_W}{R_h}\right)^{r+1}\delta^{(r+1)/r}
 =O_W\bigl(\delta^{1/r}\bigr).
\]
For $1\le n<r$ with $b_n\ne0$ the index is nonresonant by the minimality in
\cref{p9:eq:r-germ}, so $\AbsoluteValue{1-q^{n}}\ge\gamma_h$ and the term is at
most $M_h\gamma_h^{-1}\theta^{n}=O_W(\delta^{n/r})=O_W(\delta^{1/r})$.
Finally $z^{r}=\delta w^{r}$, so the term $n=r$ equals
\[
 b_rw^{r}(a+\omega\delta)^{r}\,
 \frac{\delta}{1-(1-\delta)^{r}}
 \longrightarrow\frac{b_ra^{r}}{r}w^{r}
\]
uniformly on $W$, because $\delta/(1-(1-\delta)^{r})\to1/r$ and
$(a+\omega\delta)^{r}\to a^{r}$.  Adding the three estimates gives
$\log\mathcal P_h(\omega(1-\delta),\delta^{1/r}w)\to b_ra^{r}w^{r}/r$ uniformly
on $W$, and exponentiating, which is uniformly continuous on bounded sets,
gives \cref{p9:eq:universal-germ}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sinc and $q$-Pochhammer specializations]\label{p9:cor:sinc-and-pochhammer-specializations}
For $h(z)=\SincRad z$ one may take any $R_h<\pi$; only even coefficients
occur, with $b_{2k}=-c_k$, so the first resonance is
$r=\min\SetOf{2k:m\mid2k}=2d$ and
$b_r(1-\omega)^{r}/r=-c_da_\omega^{2d}/(2d)=-A_\omega$, recovering
\cref{p9:eq:blowup-limit}.  For $h(z)=1-z$ one may take any $R_h<1$; here
$b_n=-1/n$, so for a primitive $m$th root $r=m$ and
\begin{equation}
 \prod_{j\ge0}
 \left(1-(1-q)q^j\delta^{1/m}w\right)
 \longrightarrow
 \exp\left(-\frac{(1-\omega)^m}{m^2}w^m\right).
 \label{p9:eq:qpoch-germ-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}
The theorem separates three ingredients: the local Taylor support of $\log h$, the cyclic order of $\omega$, and the geometric denominator $1-q^n$.  It therefore applies to many $q$-analog kernels, not merely to the Fabius family.
\end{remark}

\section{Spectral zero condensation}

\subsection{The zero cloud}

For $0<|q|<1$, every sinc factor contributes the factor-labelled zeros
\begin{equation}
 z_{\ell,j}(q)=\frac{\pi\ell}{(1-q)q^j},
 \qquad \ell\in\IntegerNumbers\setminus\SetOf0,
 \quad j\ge0.
 \label{p9:eq:zeros}
\end{equation}
The division-free form
\[
 (1-q)q^jz=\pi\ell
\]
is valid also at $q=0$ and is the correct total statement there.  Distinct
pairs $(\ell,j)$ may describe the same geometric zero; throughout this
section reciprocal sums count the Euler factors with their resulting
multiplicity.
For positive $\ell$, define the reciprocal even power sum
\begin{equation}
 S_k(q)=\sum_{j\ge0}\sum_{\ell\ge1}z_{\ell,j}(q)^{-2k}.
 \label{p9:eq:Sk-def}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Exact reciprocal zero moments]\label{p9:prop:exact-reciprocal-zero-moments}
For every $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 S_k(q)=\frac{\zeta(2k)}{\pi^{2k}}
 \frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}.}
 \label{p9:eq:Sk}
\end{equation}
Moreover, the master logarithm is the canonical zero-moment expansion
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi(q,z)=-\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{S_k(q)}{k}z^{2k}.
 \label{p9:eq:log-Sk}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Insert \cref{p9:eq:zeros}, then separate the geometric and zeta sums.  The exact
identity
\[
 \frac{S_k(q)}{k}
 =c_k\frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}}
\]
makes \cref{p9:eq:log-Sk} identical to the master logarithm.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[One surviving spectral moment]\label{p9:thm:one-surviving-spectral-moment}
Under the cyclotomic scaling \cref{p9:eq:blowup-scaling},
\begin{equation}
 \eps^kS_k(q_\eps)\longrightarrow
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle
 \frac{\zeta(2d)}{\pi^{2d}}
 \frac{a_\omega^{2d}}{2d},&k=d,\\[7pt]
 0,&k\ne d.
 \end{cases}
 \label{p9:eq:spectral-collapse}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $d\nmid k$, the multiplier in \cref{p9:eq:Sk} remains bounded.  If $k=\ell d$, it grows like $\eps^{-d}$, so multiplication by $\eps^k$ gives $\eps^{(\ell-1)d}$.  Only $\ell=1$ survives.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Escaping zeros leave an exponential trace]
The limiting entire function $\EulerE^{-A_\omega w^{2d}}$ has no zeros.  The zero cloud of the rescaled sinc product escapes to infinity, but its $2d$th reciprocal moment remains finite and becomes the exponential factor in the Hadamard limit.  All other reciprocal moments disappear.
\end{remark}

\section{Bernoulli cumulants, Bell moments, and Appell collapse}
\label{p9:sec:bell-collapse}

\subsection{Complex moment functional}

For real $0<q<1$, the moment generating function of $Y_q$ is
\begin{equation}
 M(q,t)=\Expectation\EulerE^{tY_q}
 =\Phi(q,\ImaginaryUnit t)
 =\prod_{j\ge0}
 \frac{\sinh((1-q)q^jt)}{(1-q)q^jt}.
 \label{p9:eq:MGF}
\end{equation}
For complex $q$, \cref{p9:eq:MGF} defines an entire generating function and
hence a complex moment functional.  Its cumulants are defined for every
$q\in\DiskD$ by the coefficient prescription
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_n(q)\DefinitionEquals
 n!\,\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}\log M(q,t)\in\ComplexNumbers ,
 \label{p9:eq:kappa-def}
\end{equation}
the logarithm being the branch with $\log M(q,0)=0$; for real $0<q<1$ this is
the usual $n$th cumulant of $Y_q$.

\begin{proposition}[Bernoulli form of the cumulants]
\label{p9:prop:cumulants}
For every $q\in\DiskD$ and every $k\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_{2k}(q)
 =\frac{2^{2k-1}B_{2k}}{k}
 \frac{(1-q)^{2k}}{1-q^{2k}},
 \qquad
 \kappa_{2k+1}(q)=0.
 \label{p9:eq:cumulants}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Insert $z=\ImaginaryUnit t$ into \cref{p9:eq:master-log}, which is legitimate
for $\AbsoluteValue{(1-q)t}<\pi$, and use
$(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2k}=(-1)^{k}t^{2k}$:
\begin{equation}
 \log M(q,t)
 =\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k-1}c_kR_k(q)\,t^{2k},
 \label{p9:eq:logM-series}
\end{equation}
absolutely convergent there.  Only even powers occur, so
$\kappa_{2k+1}(q)=0$ and $\kappa_{2k}(q)=(2k)!\,(-1)^{k-1}c_kR_k(q)$.  Euler's
formula
\(
 \zeta(2k)=(-1)^{k+1}B_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}/\bigl(2\,(2k)!\bigr)
\)
in the Bernoulli convention \cref{p0:eq:bernoulli} converts
$c_k=\zeta(2k)/(k\pi^{2k})$ into
\[
 (2k)!\,(-1)^{k-1}c_k
 =(-1)^{k-1}\frac{(2k)!}{k\pi^{2k}}\cdot
   \frac{(-1)^{k+1}B_{2k}2^{2k}\pi^{2k}}{2\,(2k)!}
 =\frac{2^{2k}B_{2k}}{2k}
 =\frac{2^{2k-1}B_{2k}}{k},
\]
which is \cref{p9:eq:cumulants}.  For real $0<q<1$ this is exactly $2^{2k}$
times \cref{p0:eq:cumulants}, as \cref{p9:status:conventions} requires, since
$Y_q=2\GeoLawCentered q$ and the $n$th cumulant is homogeneous of degree $n$.
Both sides of \cref{p9:eq:cumulants} are rational in $q$ off the set
$q^{2k}=1$, so the identity for real $q$ already forces it for all
$q\in\DiskD$; the direct derivation above is recorded because it also fixes
the meaning of the left-hand side there.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Coefficientwise limits pass through products, exponentials and
reciprocals]
\label{p9:lem:formal-limits}
Let $f_\eps,f,g_\eps,g\in\ComplexNumbers[[t]]$ and suppose that
$\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}f_\eps\to\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}f$ and
$\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}g_\eps\to\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}g$ as
$\eps\downarrow0$, for every $n\ge0$.  Then, coefficientwise as
$\eps\downarrow0$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $f_\eps g_\eps\to fg$;
\item $\EulerE^{f_\eps}\to\EulerE^{f}$, provided $f_\eps(0)=f(0)=0$;
\item $1/f_\eps\to1/f$, provided $f_\eps(0)=f(0)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In each case the $n$th coefficient of the output is one fixed polynomial, with
coefficients not depending on $\eps$, in the first $n+1$ coefficients of the
input.  For \textup{(i)} this is the Cauchy product
$\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}(fg)=\sum_{i+j=n}f_ig_j$.  For \textup{(ii)} it is
the exponential formula
$\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}\EulerE^{f}
 =B_n(1!f_1,\dots,n!f_n)/n!$, with $B_n$ the complete exponential Bell
polynomial, which is the identity already used in \cref{p9:eq:Bell-Pn}.  For
\textup{(iii)} it is the recursion $h_0=1$,
$h_n=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_jh_{n-j}$, which exhibits
$h_n=\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}(1/f)$ as a polynomial in $f_1,\dots,f_n$.
Polynomials are continuous, so coefficientwise convergence is preserved.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cyclotomic cumulant condensation]
\label{p9:thm:cumulant-condensation}
Let $Z_\eps=\sqrt\eps\,Y_{q_\eps}$ at the level of formal moments.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_n(Z_\eps)\longrightarrow0
 \quad(n\ne2d),
 \label{p9:eq:kappa-vanish}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \kappa_{2d}(Z_\eps)\longrightarrow
 K_{2d,\omega}
 =\frac{2^{2d-2}B_{2d}a_\omega^{2d}}{d^2}.}
 \label{p9:eq:kappa-survive}
\end{equation}
Equivalently, coefficientwise near $t=0$,
\begin{equation}
 M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)
 \longrightarrow \exp(B_\omega t^{2d}),
 \qquad
 B_\omega=(-1)^{d+1}A_\omega
 =\frac{K_{2d,\omega}}{(2d)!}.
 \label{p9:eq:MGF-limit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Scaling by $\sqrt\eps$ multiplies the $n$th cumulant by $\eps^{n/2}$, so
$\kappa_n(Z_\eps)=\eps^{n/2}\kappa_n(q_\eps)$.  All odd cumulants vanish by
\cref{p9:prop:cumulants}, and for $n=2k$
\[
 \kappa_{2k}(Z_\eps)
 =\frac{2^{2k-1}B_{2k}}{k}\,\eps^{k}\mathcal R_k(\eps)
\]
with $\mathcal R_k$ as in \cref{p9:eq:Rkeps}.  If $d\nmid k$ then
$\mathcal R_k(\eps)\to a_\omega^{2k}/(1-\omega^{2k})$ stays bounded, so the
factor $\eps^{k}$ forces the limit $0$.  If $k=\ell d$ then
$1-(1-\eps^{d})^{2k}=2k\eps^{d}\bigl(1+O(\eps^{d})\bigr)$, so
\[
 \eps^{k}\mathcal R_k(\eps)
 =\frac{a_\omega^{2k}}{2k}\,\eps^{(\ell-1)d}
  \bigl(1+O(\eps^{d})\bigr),
\]
which tends to $0$ for $\ell\ge2$ and to $a_\omega^{2d}/(2d)$ for $\ell=1$.
This is \cref{p9:eq:kappa-vanish}, and at $k=d$ it gives
\[
 \kappa_{2d}(Z_\eps)\longrightarrow
 \frac{2^{2d-1}B_{2d}}{d}\cdot\frac{a_\omega^{2d}}{2d}
 =\frac{2^{2d-2}B_{2d}a_\omega^{2d}}{d^{2}}
 =K_{2d,\omega},
\]
which is \cref{p9:eq:kappa-survive}.  Consequently
$\log M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)
 =\sum_{k\ge1}\kappa_{2k}(Z_\eps)t^{2k}/(2k)!$ converges coefficientwise to
$K_{2d,\omega}t^{2d}/(2d)!$, and \cref{p9:lem:formal-limits}\textup{(ii)}
upgrades this to the coefficientwise limit \cref{p9:eq:MGF-limit} for $M$
itself, with $B_\omega=K_{2d,\omega}/(2d)!$.  Finally Euler's formula for
$\zeta(2d)$ gives
\[
 A_\omega=\frac{\zeta(2d)a_\omega^{2d}}{2d^{2}\pi^{2d}}
 =\frac{(-1)^{d+1}B_{2d}2^{2d}\pi^{2d}a_\omega^{2d}}
        {2\,(2d)!\cdot2d^{2}\pi^{2d}}
 =(-1)^{d+1}\frac{2^{2d-2}B_{2d}a_\omega^{2d}}{d^{2}\,(2d)!}
 =(-1)^{d+1}B_\omega ,
\]
which is the remaining identity of \cref{p9:eq:MGF-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Sparse Bell moment limit]\label{p9:cor:sparse-bell-moment-limit}
Let $m_n(q)$ be the moments generated by $M(q,t)$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \eps^{n/2}m_n(q_\eps)\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{unless }n=2dr,
 \label{p9:eq:mom-zero}
\end{equation}
and for $r\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \eps^{dr}m_{2dr}(q_\eps)
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{(2dr)!}{r!}B_\omega^r.}
 \label{p9:eq:mom-survive}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By definition $m_n(q)=n!\,\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}M(q,t)$, and replacing
$t$ by $\sqrt\eps\,t$ multiplies the $n$th coefficient by $\eps^{n/2}$, so
\[
 \eps^{n/2}m_n(q_\eps)
 =n!\,\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t).
\]
By \cref{p9:eq:MGF-limit} the right-hand side converges to
$n!\,\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}\EulerE^{B_\omega t^{2d}}$.  Expanding
$\EulerE^{B_\omega t^{2d}}=\sum_{r\ge0}B_\omega^{r}t^{2dr}/r!$ shows that this
vanishes unless $2d\mid n$ and equals $(2dr)!B_\omega^{r}/r!$ when $n=2dr$,
which is \cref{p9:eq:mom-zero,p9:eq:mom-survive}.  Equivalently, apply the
complete Bell polynomial to a cumulant list with exactly one nonzero entry.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Limiting Appell family}

Let $\mathcal A_n^{(q)}$ denote the inverse-moment Appell polynomials generated by
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\EulerE^{xt}}{M(q,t)}
 =\sum_{n\ge0}\mathcal A_n^{(q)}(x)\frac{t^n}{n!}.
 \label{p9:eq:Appell-q}
\end{equation}
Define the scaled family
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde{\mathcal A}_{n,\eps}(x)
 =\eps^{n/2}\mathcal A_n^{(q_\eps)}(x/\sqrt\eps).
 \label{p9:eq:Appell-scaled}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Gould--Hopper cyclotomic limit]\label{p9:thm:gould-hopper-cyclotomic-limit}
Coefficientwise as $\eps\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde{\mathcal A}_{n,\eps}(x)
 \longrightarrow H_n^{(d,B_\omega)}(x),
 \label{p9:eq:Appell-limit}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{n\ge0}H_n^{(d,B)}(x)\frac{t^n}{n!}
 =\EulerE^{xt-Bt^{2d}}
 \label{p9:eq:GH-gen}
\end{equation}
and explicitly
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 H_n^{(d,B)}(x)
 =n!\sum_{r=0}^{\Floor{n/(2d)}}
 \frac{(-B)^r x^{n-2dr}}{r!(n-2dr)!}.}
 \label{p9:eq:GH-explicit}
\end{equation}
These polynomials satisfy
\begin{equation}
 H_n^{(d,B)}=\EulerE^{-BD^{2d}}x^n,
 \qquad
 H_{n+1}^{(d,B)}=
 \left(x-2dB D^{2d-1}\right)H_n^{(d,B)},
 \quad D=\frac{\Differential}{\Differential x}.
 \label{p9:eq:GH-operator}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substituting $(x,t)\mapsto(x/\sqrt\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)$ in \cref{p9:eq:Appell-q}
leaves $\EulerE^{xt}$ unchanged and multiplies the $n$th Taylor coefficient by
$\eps^{n/2}$, so by \cref{p9:eq:Appell-scaled}
\[
 \sum_{n\ge0}\widetilde{\mathcal A}_{n,\eps}(x)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}
 =\frac{\EulerE^{xt}}{M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)} .
\]
The series $M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)$ has constant term $1$ and converges
coefficientwise to $\EulerE^{B_\omega t^{2d}}$ by \cref{p9:eq:MGF-limit}, so
\cref{p9:lem:formal-limits}\textup{(iii)} gives coefficientwise convergence of
its reciprocal, and then part~\textup{(i)}, applied with the
$\eps$-independent factor $\EulerE^{xt}$, gives
\[
 \CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}
 \frac{\EulerE^{xt}}{M(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,t)}
 \longrightarrow
 \CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}\EulerE^{xt-B_\omega t^{2d}}
\]
for every $n$.  Both sides are polynomials in $x$ of degree at most $n$;
expanding $\EulerE^{xt}=\sum_{j\ge0}x^{j}t^{j}/j!$ exhibits the coefficient of
$x^{j}$ in $\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}$ as
$\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n-j}$ of the reciprocal divided by $j!$, so the
convergence is also coefficient by coefficient in $x$, which is the assertion
of \cref{p9:eq:Appell-limit}.  Expanding
$\EulerE^{xt-Bt^{2d}}=\EulerE^{xt}\sum_{r\ge0}(-B)^{r}t^{2dr}/r!$ and reading
off $\CoefficientExtraction{t}{n}$ gives \cref{p9:eq:GH-explicit}.  For the
operator identities write $D=\frac{\Differential}{\Differential x}$ and note
$D^{j}\EulerE^{xt}=t^{j}\EulerE^{xt}$.  Hence
\[
 \sum_{n\ge0}\bigl(\EulerE^{-BD^{2d}}x^{n}\bigr)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}
 =\EulerE^{-BD^{2d}}\EulerE^{xt}
 =\EulerE^{-Bt^{2d}}\EulerE^{xt},
\]
which is \cref{p9:eq:GH-gen}, so $H_n^{(d,B)}=\EulerE^{-BD^{2d}}x^{n}$;  and
differentiating \cref{p9:eq:GH-gen} in $t$ gives
$\sum_nH_{n+1}^{(d,B)}t^{n}/n!
 =(x-2dBt^{2d-1})\EulerE^{xt-Bt^{2d}}
 =(x-2dBD^{2d-1})\EulerE^{xt-Bt^{2d}}$, whence
$H_{n+1}^{(d,B)}=(x-2dBD^{2d-1})H_n^{(d,B)}$.  Both identities are the content
of \cref{p9:eq:GH-operator}.
\end{proof}

\section{Polyharmonic heat symbols and Stokes sectors}

\subsection{Dissipative roots}

By \cref{p9:eq:sign-a}, $A_\omega>0$ exactly when the primitive root order satisfies $m\equiv2\pmod4$.  In that case the cyclotomic limit decays on the real frequency axis.

\begin{definition}[Cyclotomic polyharmonic kernel]
For $A>0$, $d\ge1$, and $\tau>0$, set
\begin{equation}
 K_{d,A}(x,\tau)
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}
 \EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}-\ImaginaryUnit x\xi}\Differential\xi.
 \label{p9:eq:heat-kernel}
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Polyharmonic semigroup]\label{p9:prop:polyharmonic-semigroup}
The kernel is Schwartz in $x$, has total mass one, and solves
\begin{equation}
 \partial_\tau K_{d,A}
 =(-1)^{d+1}A\,\partial_x^{2d}K_{d,A},
 \qquad
 K_{d,A}(\cdot,\tau)\to\delta_0
 \quad(\tau\downarrow0)
 \label{p9:eq:polyharmonic-PDE}
\end{equation}
in the distributional sense.  It obeys the scaling law
\begin{equation}
 K_{d,A}(x,\tau)
 =(A\tau)^{-1/(2d)}
 K_{d,1}\left(x(A\tau)^{-1/(2d)},1\right).
 \label{p9:eq:kernel-scaling}
\end{equation}
For $d=1$ it is Gaussian; for $d\ge2$ it necessarily changes sign.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Smoothness and the equation.}  Fix $\tau_0>0$.  For $\tau\ge\tau_0$ and
all integers $\alpha,\beta\ge0$,
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_\tau^{\alpha}\partial_x^{\beta}
   \EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}-\ImaginaryUnit x\xi}}
 =A^{\alpha}\AbsoluteValue\xi^{2d\alpha+\beta}
   \EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}}
 \le A^{\alpha}\AbsoluteValue\xi^{2d\alpha+\beta}
   \EulerE^{-\tau_0A\xi^{2d}},
\]
and the right-hand side is integrable in $\xi$ and independent of
$(x,\tau)$.  Differentiation under the integral sign is therefore legitimate,
and $K_{d,A}$ is $C^{\infty}$ on $\RealNumbers\times(0,\infty)$ with
\[
 \partial_\tau K_{d,A}
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}\bigl(-A\xi^{2d}\bigr)
   \EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}-\ImaginaryUnit x\xi}\Differential\xi,
 \qquad
 \partial_x^{2d}K_{d,A}
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}(-\ImaginaryUnit\xi)^{2d}
   \EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}-\ImaginaryUnit x\xi}\Differential\xi .
\]
Since $(-\ImaginaryUnit)^{2d}=(-1)^{d}$, multiplying the second identity by
$(-1)^{d+1}A$ reproduces the first, which is the equation in
\cref{p9:eq:polyharmonic-PDE}.

\emph{Schwartz class and mass.}  For fixed $\tau>0$ the function
$\xi\mapsto\xi^{\beta}\EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}}$ is Schwartz, so repeated
integration by parts in $\xi$ shows that
$x^{\alpha}\partial_x^{\beta}K_{d,A}(x,\tau)$ is bounded for all
$\alpha,\beta\ge0$; hence $K_{d,A}(\cdot,\tau)\in\mathcal S(\RealNumbers)$.
The symbol $\EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}}$ is even, so \cref{p9:eq:heat-kernel}
coincides with the inverse angular Fourier transform of
\cref{p0:eq:fourier}, and Fourier inversion for Schwartz functions gives
$\FourierAngularTransformOf{K_{d,A}(\cdot,\tau)}(\xi)
 =\EulerE^{-\tau A\xi^{2d}}$.  Evaluating at $\xi=0$ gives total mass
$\int_{\RealNumbers}K_{d,A}(x,\tau)\Differential x=1$.

\emph{Scaling and the initial value.}  The substitution
$\xi=(A\tau)^{-1/(2d)}u$ in \cref{p9:eq:heat-kernel} gives
\cref{p9:eq:kernel-scaling} directly.  For bounded continuous $\varphi$ that
law and $K_{d,1}(\cdot,1)\in L^{1}$ give
\[
 \int_{\RealNumbers}K_{d,A}(x,\tau)\varphi(x)\Differential x
 =\int_{\RealNumbers}K_{d,1}(y,1)\,
   \varphi\bigl(y(A\tau)^{1/(2d)}\bigr)\Differential y
 \longrightarrow\varphi(0)
 \qquad(\tau\downarrow0)
\]
by dominated convergence, which is the assertion
$K_{d,A}(\cdot,\tau)\to\delta_0$.  For $d=1$ the integral
\cref{p9:eq:heat-kernel} is the classical Gaussian.

\emph{Sign change for $d\ge2$.}  Suppose $K_{d,A}(\cdot,1)\ge0$.  Being
nonnegative with total mass one it is then the density of a probability
measure $\mu$, whose characteristic function is
$\varphi(\xi)=\EulerE^{-A\xi^{2d}}$.  For $\xi\ne0$,
\[
 \int_{\RealNumbers}\frac{2-2\cos(\xi x)}{\xi^{2}}\Differential\mu(x)
 =\frac{2-\varphi(\xi)-\varphi(-\xi)}{\xi^{2}}
 =\frac{2-2\EulerE^{-A\xi^{2d}}}{\xi^{2}}
 \longrightarrow0
 \qquad(\xi\to0),
\]
because $2d\ge4$.  The integrand is nonnegative and tends pointwise to
$x^{2}$, so Fatou's lemma gives
$\int_{\RealNumbers}x^{2}\Differential\mu(x)=0$, hence $\mu=\delta_0$ and
$\varphi\equiv1$ --- contradicting $\varphi(\xi)=\EulerE^{-A\xi^{2d}}$.
Therefore $K_{d,A}(\cdot,1)$ takes both signs, and by
\cref{p9:eq:kernel-scaling} so does $K_{d,A}(\cdot,\tau)$ for every $\tau>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The sixth-order Rvachev cyclotomic heat limit]\label{p9:cor:the-sixth-order-rvachev}
At a primitive sixth root, $d=3$ and $A_\omega=1/17010$.  The rescaled complex $q$-Fabius transform converges to $\EulerE^{-w^{6}/17010}$, the \emph{time-one} Fourier multiplier of
\begin{equation}
 \partial_\tau u=\frac1{17010}\partial_x^6u ;
 \label{p9:eq:sixth-pde}
\end{equation}
the multiplier at a general time $\tau>0$ is recovered from the same limit
after the substitution $w\mapsto\tau^{1/6}w$.
The associated fundamental solution has unit mass but is not of one sign: by
the preceding proposition it changes sign, and the classical oscillatory
asymptotics for polyharmonic kernels \cite{bib:evgrafov1970} show that it
in fact oscillates.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
At $\omega=\EulerE^{\pi\ImaginaryUnit/3}$ we have $m=6$, $\gcd(m,2)=2$ and
$d=3$, and $\theta=\pi/3$, so the computation in the proof of
\cref{p9:eq:sign-a} gives
\(
 a_\omega^{6}=(-4)^{3}\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit\pi}\sin^{6}(\pi/6)
 =(-64)(-1)\cdot2^{-6}=1 .
\)
Hence, by \cref{p9:eq:Aomega} and $\zeta(6)=\pi^{6}/945$,
\[
 A_\omega=\frac{\zeta(6)a_\omega^{6}}{2\cdot3^{2}\pi^{6}}
 =\frac1{945\cdot18}=\frac1{17010}>0 .
\]
\cref{p9:eq:blowup-limit} therefore gives
$\Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w)\to\EulerE^{-w^{6}/17010}$ locally uniformly in $w$.
By the proof of the preceding proposition,
$\FourierAngularTransformOf{K_{3,A_\omega}(\cdot,\tau)}(\xi)
 =\EulerE^{-\tau A_\omega\xi^{6}}$, whose value at $\tau=1$ is exactly the
limit just obtained; and by \cref{p9:eq:polyharmonic-PDE} with $d=3$ the
kernel solves \cref{p9:eq:sixth-pde}, since $(-1)^{d+1}=1$.  For a general
$\tau>0$ apply the same limit at the frequency $\tau^{1/6}w$, which is
legitimate because the convergence is locally uniform and $\tau^{1/6}W$ is
again compact.  The mass and sign statements are those of the preceding
proposition.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Backward roots and contour rotation}

If $A_\omega<0$ (all odd $m$ and all $m\equiv0\pmod4$), the real-axis symbol $\EulerE^{-A_\omega w^{2d}}$ grows.  It should not be interpreted as a tempered Fourier multiplier on $\RealNumbers$.  It is nevertheless an entire function with canonical decaying sectors
\begin{equation}
 \SetOf{w:\Re(A_\omega w^{2d})>0}.
 \label{p9:eq:stokes-sectors}
\end{equation}
More precisely, let $\Gamma$ be a piecewise smooth contour with two unbounded
ends and suppose that, outside a compact set,
\(
 \Re(A_\omega w^{2d})\ge c|w|^{2d}
\)
for some $c>0$.  Then
\[
 K_\Gamma(x,\tau)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma
 \EulerE^{-\tau A_\omega w^{2d}-\ImaginaryUnit xw}\Differential w
\]
converges absolutely and locally uniformly in $x\in\ComplexNumbers$ for $\tau>0$.
The degree-$2d$ decay dominates the linear $xw$ term, so differentiation under
the integral is justified and $K_\Gamma$ solves the same polyharmonic equation
as in \cref{p9:eq:polyharmonic-PDE}.  The sector boundaries
\(
 \Re(A_\omega w^{2d})=0
\)
are Stokes lines.  This produces a clean arithmetic/Stokes dichotomy: the residue class of $m$ modulo four determines whether the canonical radial blow-up is forward dissipative or backward/rotated.

\begin{problem}[Uniform Stokes connection]
Construct a single Riemann--Hilbert or steepest-descent description that connects the real dissipative kernels to the rotated kernels across the sign change of $A_\omega$, and determine the Stokes multipliers induced by the finite cyclic factor hidden in $\mathscr B_\omega$.
\end{problem}

\section{Inverse cyclotomic branches}

Throughout this section, $O(\eps^N)$ and $O(z^N)$ denote formal order: the
omitted series belongs to the corresponding principal ideal in the indicated
formal power-series ring.  No analytic remainder estimate is implicit.

\subsection{Inverse frequency at fixed radial scaling}

Fix a nonzero target $y\in\ComplexNumbers$ and a logarithm branch $\ell=\PrincipalLogarithm y$ with $\ell\ne0$:
\begin{equation}
 \ell=\PrincipalLogarithm y.
 \label{p9:eq:ell}
\end{equation}
Choose one of the $2d$ roots $w_0\ne0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 -A_\omega w_0^{2d}=\ell.
 \label{p9:eq:w0}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Formal inverse frequency series]\label{p9:prop:formal-inverse-frequency-series}
There is a unique formal series
$w(\eps)\in w_0+\eps\ComplexNumbers[[\eps]]$ which solves, coefficient by coefficient in
the formal expansion \cref{p9:eq:all-log},
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,w(\eps))=y,
 \qquad
 w(0)=w_0.
 \label{p9:eq:inverse-w}
\end{equation}
If $d\ge2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 w(\eps)=w_0
 -\frac{C_{1,\omega}}{2dA_\omega}
 w_0^{3-2d}\eps+O(\eps^2).}
 \label{p9:eq:w-first}
\end{equation}
For $d=1$,
\begin{equation}
 w(\eps)=w_0-\frac{\eta_\omega}{2}w_0\eps
 -\frac{D_\omega}{2A_\omega}w_0^3\eps+O(\eps^2).
 \label{p9:eq:w-first-d1}
\end{equation}
All higher coefficients are obtained recursively from \cref{p9:eq:Ln} and partial Bell polynomials.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Use the prescribed logarithm value $\ell$ and substitute a formal series for
$w$ in \cref{p9:eq:all-log}.  The derivative of the constant-term equation with
respect to $w$ is
\(
 -2dA_\omega w_0^{2d-1}\ne0
\), hence it is a unit and determines each successive coefficient
triangularly (equivalently, apply the formal implicit-function theorem).  At
order $\eps$, compare the derivative contribution with the
$-C_{1,\omega}w^2$ term when $d\ge2$.  For $d=1$, use the complete order-one
expression in \cref{p9:eq:correction-2}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Analytic realization remains open]
The proposition is formal: it does not assert a convergent germ in a full
complex neighborhood of $\eps=0$.  The denominators
$1-(1-\eps^d)^{2k}$ have complex singularities accumulating at the origin as
$k\to\infty$.  Thus the direct analytic implicit-function argument is not
available without proving cancellations among these singularities.  Any
analytic realization must supply such control, or else be formulated
sectorially or asymptotically with a uniform remainder estimate.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Inverse \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q} at small frequency}

The more unusual inverse asks for $q$ as a function of $z$ while the transform value is held fixed.

\begin{lemma}[The root-centered substitution is well defined]
\label{p9:lem:substitution-finite}
Let $\rho(s)\in\ComplexNumbers[[s]]$ with $\rho(0)\ne0$ and set
$\delta=z^{2d}\rho(z^{2})$ and $q=\omega(1-\delta)$.  Then for every $k\ge1$
the $k$th term $-c_kz^{2k}\mathcal R_k$ of \cref{p9:eq:master-log}, with
$\mathcal R_k$ as in \cref{p9:eq:Rkeps} and $\eps^{d}$ replaced by $\delta$, is
a well-defined element of $\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$ whose lowest occurring
power of $z$ is $z^{2k-2d}$ when $d\mid k$ and $z^{2k}$ otherwise.
Consequently $\CoefficientExtraction{z}{N}\log\Phi(q(z),z)$ receives
contributions only from the indices $k\le N/2+d$, the substitution is a
well-defined map $\ComplexNumbers[[s]]\to\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$, and its
constant term equals $-A_\omega/\rho(0)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The numerator $(a_\omega+\omega\delta)^{2k}$ is a power series in $\delta$ with
constant term $a_\omega^{2k}\ne0$, and $\delta\in z^{2d}\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$.
If $d\nmid k$ the denominator $1-\omega^{2k}(1-\delta)^{2k}$ has constant term
$1-\omega^{2k}\ne0$, hence is invertible in $\ComplexNumbers[[\delta]]$, and
$-c_kz^{2k}\mathcal R_k\in z^{2k}\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$.  If $d\mid k$ the
denominator is $1-(1-\delta)^{2k}=2k\delta\,u_k(\delta)$ with
$u_k\in\ComplexNumbers[[\delta]]$ and $u_k(0)=1$, so $u_k$ is invertible and
\[
 -c_kz^{2k}\mathcal R_k
 =-\frac{c_kz^{2k-2d}}{2k\,\rho(z^{2})}
   (a_\omega+\omega\delta)^{2k}u_k(\delta)^{-1}
 \in z^{2k-2d}\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]],
\]
$\rho$ being invertible because $\rho(0)\ne0$.  Since $d\mid k$ forces
$k\ge d$, the exponent $2k-2d$ is nonnegative in every case, so the sum over
$k$ lies in $\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$ and a term contributes to
$\CoefficientExtraction{z}{N}$ only when $2k-2d\le N$, that is $k\le N/2+d$.
The unique index with lowest power $z^{0}$ is $k=d$, and its contribution
there is $-c_da_\omega^{2d}/(2d\rho(0))=-A_\omega/\rho(0)$ by
\cref{p9:eq:Aomega}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Formal inverse $q$-series at a root of unity]
\label{p9:prop:inverse-q}
Assume $d\ge2$, fix $y$ and $\ell$ as above, and choose the root-centered coordinate
\begin{equation}
 q(z)=\omega(1-\delta(z)).
 \label{p9:eq:qz}
\end{equation}
There is a unique formal series
\[
 \rho(s)\in -\frac{A_\omega}{\ell}+s\ComplexNumbers[[s]],
 \qquad \delta(z)=z^{2d}\rho(z^2),
\]
such that, after substitution into the master logarithm on the prescribed
logarithm sheet, the identity
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(q(z),z)=y
 \label{p9:eq:q-inverse-eq}
\end{equation}
holds coefficient by coefficient.  Its first terms are
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \delta(z)=-\frac{A_\omega}{\ell}z^{2d}
 \left(1-\frac{C_{1,\omega}}{\ell}z^2+O(z^4)\right),}
 \label{p9:eq:delta-z}
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 q(z)=\omega\left[
 1+\frac{A_\omega}{\ell}z^{2d}
 -\frac{A_\omega C_{1,\omega}}{\ell^2}z^{2d+2}
 +O(z^{2d+4})
 \right].}
 \label{p9:eq:q-z-expansion}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{p9:lem:substitution-finite} the left-hand side of
\cref{p9:eq:q-inverse-eq}, read through the master logarithm on the prescribed
logarithm sheet, is a well-defined element
$\Lambda(\rho)\in\ComplexNumbers[[z^{2}]]$ whose coefficient of $z^{N}$ depends
polynomially on $\rho_0^{-1}$ and on finitely many $\rho_i$, and whose constant
term is $-A_\omega/\rho_0$.  The scalar equation $-A_\omega/\rho_0=\ell$ has the
unique solution $\rho_0=-A_\omega/\ell\ne0$, at which the derivative of
$\rho_0\mapsto-A_\omega/\rho_0$ equals $A_\omega/\rho_0^{2}\ne0$; so the formal
implicit-function theorem applies and determines $\rho_1,\rho_2,\dots$
triangularly from the coefficients of $z^{2},z^{4},\dots$.  The explicit
low-order coefficients are computed in
\cref{p9:app:inverse-coefficients}, which is the official derivation of
\cref{p9:eq:delta-z} and hence of \cref{p9:eq:q-z-expansion}: only the master
logarithm is used there, never the two-term radial expansion, whose $O(\delta)$
remainder is not an all-orders series.  No analytic remainder is claimed at any
step.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No convergent boundary germ is claimed]
The formal series is meaningful because every requested coefficient involves
only finitely many orders of the master expansion.  It does not by itself
define an analytic germ through $z=0$: the root-of-unity singular loci of the
individual denominators accumulate there.  Establishing sectorial sums, their
domains, and their Stokes transitions is a separate problem.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Formal branch geometry]
For the inverse-frequency problem, each fixed root $\omega$ and logarithm value
$\ell+2\pi\ImaginaryUnit k$ has $2d$ choices of $w_0$, and each choice produces one formal
series.  For the inverse-$q$ problem, fixing $\omega$ and a nonzero logarithm
value determines a unique formal series $\rho$.  Turning either algebraic
indexing into analytic continuation or monodromy requires sectorial
realizations and a careful separation of logarithm-sheet changes from
critical-value branching; neither is asserted here.
\end{remark}

\begin{status}[What an analytic inverse branch would require]
\label{p9:status:inverse-analytic}
The two propositions of this section are \statusproved{} as statements about
formal series and \statusopen{} as statements about functions; nothing in this
part asserts an analytic inverse branch.  The missing ingredient can be named
precisely.  For the inverse frequency $w(\eps)=\sum_{n\ge0}w_n\eps^{n}$ of
\cref{p9:eq:inverse-w} one would need constants $C,A>0$, an exponent $s\ge0$,
a sector
\[
 \Sigma=\SetOf{\eps\in\ComplexNumbers:
   0<\AbsoluteValue\eps<\eps_1,\ \AbsoluteValue{\arg\eps}<\vartheta},
\]
and a holomorphic $\mathbf w:\Sigma\to\ComplexNumbers$ with
$\Phi\bigl(q_\eps,\sqrt\eps\,\mathbf w(\eps)\bigr)=y$ on $\Sigma$ and
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{\mathbf w(\eps)-\sum_{n<N}w_n\eps^{n}}
 \le C\,A^{N}(N!)^{s}\AbsoluteValue\eps^{N}
 \qquad(\eps\in\Sigma,\ N\ge1);
 \label{p9:eq:gevrey-target}
\end{equation}
a Gevrey estimate of this shape, with $\vartheta>\pi s/2$, would identify
$\mathbf w$ as the Borel--Laplace sum of the formal series and would settle the
analytic realization.  The obstruction to producing \cref{p9:eq:gevrey-target}
by the present method is explicit rather than technical: the denominators
$1-(1-\eps^{d})^{2k}$ of \cref{p9:eq:Rkeps} vanish where $\eps^{d}=1-\zeta$
with $\zeta^{2k}=1$, and the nearest such point satisfies
$\AbsoluteValue{1-\zeta}=2\sin(\pi/(2k))\asymp1/k$, so the family
$\SetOf{\mathcal R_k}_{k\ge1}$ has no common disc of analyticity about
$\eps=0$ and no $k$-independent domain on which an implicit-function argument
could be run.  \cref{p9:thm:full-radial} does not repair this: it is an
asymptotic expansion at fixed frequency whose constants $C_{K,R}$ are allowed
to depend arbitrarily on the order $R$, and \cref{p9:eq:gevrey-target} is
exactly a statement about how those constants grow.  Proving a Gevrey version
of \cref{p9:thm:full-radial}, with $C_{K,R}\le CA^{R}(R!)^{s}$, is therefore
the missing estimate; it is the analytic content of the open problem
\emph{Cyclotomic inverse monodromy} stated below.
\end{status}

\section{Numerical experiments}

\subsection{Evaluation strategy}

Direct products are poorly conditioned near roots of unity.  The companion script evaluates the absolutely convergent master series \cref{p9:eq:master-log} with 80 decimal digits, and computes actions and constants from their own convergent series.  No numerical quadrature or random sampling is used.  The four main diagnostics are:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item the residual in the two-term fixed-frequency radial expansion;
\item the residual after removing every displayed blow-up correction through order $\eps^d$;
\item the error in the surviving Bernoulli cumulant and Bell moments;
\item the errors in the inverse frequency and inverse $q$ branches.
\end{enumerate}
