\begin{status}[Role of computation]
The numerical experiments do not substitute for proofs.  They check constants,
signs, and predicted asymptotic orders, and they are especially useful for
detecting missing resonant correction terms.  In particular, they do not prove
the uniform radial estimate established analytically above, convergence of
either formal inverse series, or any Lean theorem.  Only the global spectral
$q$-Pochhammer factorization has the exact Lean crosswalk recorded above; the
remaining cyclotomic assertions retain manuscript or frontier status according
to the boundary note at the start of the report.
\end{status}

\section{Connections with Thue--Morse and cyclic digital structure}

The original dyadic theory combines two kinds of scale symmetry.  The sinc product uses geometric scales $2^{-j}$, while the Thue--Morse polynomial
\(
 \prod_{j<N}(1-z^{2^j})
\)
encodes binary digit parity.  The cyclotomic analysis introduces a third viewpoint: a periodic character in the \emph{scale index} $j$.

At $q=\omega(1-\delta)$, the leading phases $q^j\approx\omega^j$ repeat with period $m$.  Because sinc is even, the logarithm sees $\omega^{2j}$ and the effective period is $d$.  The cyclic projector in \cref{p9:eq:cyclic-projection} is precisely the finite Fourier projection onto the resonant scale characters.  At $\omega=-1$, the period-two character collapses to $d=1$ and produces the Gaussian limit.  Higher roots produce higher-order heat symbols.

This does not identify the cyclotomic scale character with the Thue--Morse sequence itself: Thue--Morse parity is generated by binary digits of the \emph{summation index}, whereas $\omega^j$ is periodic in the \emph{scale position}.  A promising bridge is to combine the two characters in a two-nome product, exactly the larger problem left open in the repository.

\begin{problem}[Thue--Morse/cyclotomic coupling]
For finite products carrying both a Thue--Morse sign and a scale phase $\omega^j$, determine the resonant cumulant order, the analogue of $\mathscr A_\omega$, and whether Prouhet cancellation can suppress the leading spectral dilogarithm.  Classify the resulting limit symbols by the joint character group.
\end{problem}

\section{Further conjectures and research directions}

\subsection{Maximal natural-boundary domain}

\begin{problem}[Generic natural boundary and action-zero control]
Determine a precise exceptional set of frequencies for which enough
root-of-unity actions $\mathscr A_\omega(z)$ vanish to obstruct the
natural-boundary argument.  Prove at least a residual or full-measure generic
statement, and identify additional uniform arithmetic hypotheses that would
give an explicit complement.  A locally finite exceptional set is not assumed:
a countable union of discrete action-zero sets need not be locally finite.
\end{problem}

The theorem proved here covers $0<|z|<\pi/2$ uniformly.  Outside that interval,
the dilogarithm arguments may leave the unit disk or encounter branch cuts, and
the sign argument is unavailable.  On its defining disk each action is already
a nonzero analytic germ, since
\(
 \mathscr A_\omega(z)=A_\omega z^{2d}+O(z^{4d})
\)
with $A_\omega\ne0$, so its zeros there are discrete.  The genuine target is
simultaneous control of these zero sets across a dense family of roots, on
compatible larger frequency domains; a Baire-category argument might then
yield generic natural boundary, while arithmetic control of intersections
could sharpen ``generic'' to an explicit complement.

\subsection{Cyclic quantum dilogarithm in the finite term}

The leading action is dilogarithmic, while standard root-of-unity asymptotics of $q$-Pochhammer symbols also contain a finite cyclic quantum dilogarithm.  Formula \cref{p9:eq:B-first,p9:eq:B-second} should admit a factorized form obtained by multiplying the cyclic factors over $n$ in \cref{p9:eq:qpoch-factor}.

\begin{problem}[Spectral cyclic dilogarithm]
Find a convergent regularized product $\mathcal D_\omega(z)$ such that
\[
 \EulerE^{\mathscr B_\omega(z)}
 =\mathcal E_\omega(z)\mathcal D_\omega(z),
\]
where $\mathcal E_\omega$ is an elementary square-root factor and $\mathcal D_\omega$ is an infinite spectral product of finite cyclic quantum dilogarithms.  Determine its functional equations and zero divisor.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Irrational boundary phases and small divisors}

At an irrational point $q=\EulerE^{2\pi\ImaginaryUnit\alpha}$ there is no exact resonance, but denominators $1-q^{2k}$ can be arbitrarily small.  Diophantine properties of $\alpha$ should govern the boundary growth.

\begin{conjecture}[Diophantine phase transition]
For badly approximable $\alpha$, suitably Abel-regularized logarithms of $\Phi(r\EulerE^{2\pi\ImaginaryUnit\alpha},z)$ admit polynomial bounds as $r\uparrow1$ on a small frequency disk.  For Liouville $\alpha$, there exist frequency values with superpolynomial subsequential growth generated by near-resonant cumulants.
\end{conjecture}

This would interpolate between the exact root-of-unity action and generic natural-boundary behavior through small-divisor analysis.

\subsection{Arithmetic of the cyclotomic constants}

The constants
\[
 A_\omega=\frac{\zeta(2d)}{2d^2\pi^{2d}}(1-\omega)^{2d}
\]
are algebraic because $\zeta(2d)/\pi^{2d}$ is rational.  Their signs are elementary, but their Galois traces, norms, and divisibility encode nontrivial cyclotomic arithmetic.

\begin{problem}[Galois packets]
For fixed $m$, determine the trace and norm of $A_\omega$ over all primitive $m$th roots, and similarly for the correction coefficients $C_{k,\omega}$.  Relate their prime valuations to cyclotomic units and Bernoulli numerators.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Uniform double scaling in root order}

The present analysis fixes $m$.  When $m\to\infty$, the resonance order $d$ grows, $A_\omega$ becomes very small, and the limit exponent has increasing degree.  There should be a second asymptotic regime balancing $d$, $\eps$, and $w$.

\begin{problem}[Large-order cyclotomic saddle]
Determine a scaling in which
\(
 A_\omega w^{2d}
\)
remains nontrivial as $d\to\infty$, and identify whether the limiting profile is a hard cutoff, an extreme-value law, or a new Lambert-$W$ saddle.  Track the transition between polyharmonic kernels and the endpoint asymptotics already developed in the repository.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Inverse monodromy and branch braiding}

The formal inverse-frequency series have $2d$ algebraic choices on each
logarithm sheet.  If sectorial analytic realizations exist, continuation may
braid them around critical values of the frequency map, while winding the
target around zero changes the logarithm sheet.

\begin{problem}[Cyclotomic inverse monodromy]
First construct sectorial analytic realizations of the formal inverse branches.
Then determine their continuation around simple \emph{critical values}, where
inverse branches may transpose, and separately track the logarithm-sheet shift
$\ell\mapsto\ell+2\pi\ImaginaryUnit$ caused by winding around $y=0$.  The rotation
$w_0\mapsto\EulerE^{\pi\ImaginaryUnit/d}w_0$ permutes the $2d$ roots on a fixed nonzero
logarithm sheet; it should not be identified with the sheet shift without an
additional continuation argument.  Classify any resulting braid action and
its compatibility with the escaping zero cloud.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Two-nome extension}

The repository's open problem asks for a two-nome phase diagram and canonical root-of-unity limits.  The scalar theorem suggests the correct first invariant: identify the lowest Taylor monomial whose bidegree resonates with the pair of roots.  The universal germ calculation suggests studying
\[
 \prod_{j\ge0}h\bigl((1-\rho)\rho^jz,(1-\sigma)\sigma^jw\bigr),
\]
but the resonance set is now a lattice rather than a single arithmetic progression.  Its Newton polygon should determine the anisotropic scaling and the limiting exponential polynomial.

\begin{conjecture}[Newton-polygon resonance principle]
For an analytic two-variable germ, the canonical two-nome root-of-unity blow-up is determined by the lower convex hull of resonant Taylor exponents.  A single vertex gives a monomial exponential; an edge gives a genuinely multivariate exponential polynomial and a coupled polyharmonic PDE.
\end{conjecture}

\subsection{Formalization roadmap}

The new theory has a favorable dependency graph.
The product layer is already represented by
\path|Fabius.geometricSincProduct_eq_tprod_complexQPochhammerInf|, while the
general root-of-unity filter is available as \path|Fabius.sum_pow_eq_ite| and
\path|Fabius.sum_pow_mul_inv_pow_eq_ite|.  Thus the remaining roadmap begins
after these reusable foundations.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item \textbf{Finite algebra.}  Formalize $d=\OrderOperator_{\mathrm{mult}}(\omega^2)$, the resonant/nonresonant split, and the exact first two coefficients of \cref{p9:eq:res-exp}.
\item \textbf{Formal power series.}  Prove the coefficient identity \cref{p9:eq:Ln} in a Laurent-series ring; Bell exponentiation is already well suited to existing combinatorial infrastructure.
\item \textbf{Finite cyclic projection.}  Specialize the existing
root-of-unity filter to
\(
 d^{-1}\sum_{r<d}\omega^{2kr}=\IndicatorOf{d\mid k}
\)
and derive a finite-truncation version of \cref{p9:eq:cyclic-projection}.
\item \textbf{Analytic tails.}  Formalize the square-root cutoff proof of \cref{p9:thm:two-term-radial}, including the finite phase separation and exponential tail bound.
\item \textbf{Sign and natural boundary.}  Formalize the sign of $a_\omega^{2d}$ and $\Polylogarithm_2(\pm x)$ on $0<x<1$, then use the finite-order zero/pole contradiction.
\item \textbf{Moments.}  Reuse the repository's Bernoulli cumulant and Bell moment APIs to prove the one-cumulant limit.
\item \textbf{Inverse branches.}  Begin with formal coefficient recursion; defer the analytic implicit-function theorem until the local complex-analysis library is convenient.
\end{enumerate}

A compact first formal milestone would prove the blow-up limit and sparse moment formula without dilogarithms.  The natural-boundary theorem can then be added after both the analytic tail estimate and the sign representation are available in Lean.

\section{Conclusion}

The complex $q$-plane reveals a structure invisible on the positive real interval.  At every root of unity, the geometric sinc product organizes itself by the order of $\omega^2$.  Fixed frequencies see a spectral dilogarithmic action of size $1/\delta$; shrinking frequencies at the exact cyclotomic rate isolate one resonant coefficient and produce a pure exponential $\EulerE^{-A_\omega w^{2d}}$.  The same resonance appears simultaneously in the zero divisor, Bernoulli cumulants, Bell moments, and inverse Appell polynomials.

This organizes several themes of the Fabius--Rvachev corpus while explicitly
reusing its existing product, root-of-unity-filter, Bell, Appell, and dyadic
infrastructure.  The sinc product supplies the spectral side;
$q$-Pochhammer factorization explains the dilogarithmic action; Bell and
Bernoulli polynomials control formal corrections and moments; and root order
predicts a polyharmonic limit symbol.  The two-range estimate below completes
the radial theorem and hence the natural-boundary layer.  Constructing
sectorial inverse branches remains a separate analytic problem.

\appendix

\section{Uniform estimates behind the radial theorem}

Let $K\Subset\SetOf{z:|a_\omega z|<\pi}$ and choose $\rho<1$ such that
\(
 |a_\omega z|\le\rho\pi
\) on $K$.  The coefficient bound
\begin{equation}
 c_k|a_\omega z|^{2k}
 \le \frac{\zeta(2)}{k}\rho^{2k}
 \label{p9:eq:ck-majorant}
\end{equation}
provides the basic summable majorant.  When $d>1$, the nonresonant phases
$\omega^{2k}$ range over a finite set not containing one, and
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(ii)} bounds the denominator of
$S_k(\delta)$ below by the constant $\gamma\ge\sin(\pi/d)$, uniformly in $k$
and in $\delta\in[0,1]$.  Part~\textup{(iii)} of the same lemma bounds
$\AbsoluteValue{S_k'(\delta)}$ by
$2k\Theta\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega+\omega\delta}^{2k}$, the single factor $k$
cancelling the $1/k$ in \cref{p9:eq:ck-majorant}.  This is the detailed
justification of \cref{p9:eq:nonres-uniform}, with the explicit constant
$C_K=2\zeta(2)\Theta$ and
$\Theta=2/(\gamma\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega})+\gamma^{-2}$; when $d=1$ the
nonresonant part is empty.

For resonant $k$, the cutoff $N=\Floor{\delta^{-1/2}}$ is deliberately
smaller than the tempting scale $\delta^{-1}$.  On $k\le N$ the true expansion
parameter $k\delta$ tends uniformly to zero, so Taylor's theorem with remainder
gives \cref{p9:eq:res-uniform}.  On $k>N$, geometric decay wins against every
power of $\delta$: for each $M>0$ and $0<r<1$,
\begin{equation}
 \delta^{-M}r^{\,\delta^{-1/2}}\longrightarrow0.
 \label{p9:eq:exp-beats-power}
\end{equation}
This proves, rather than merely predicts, the uniform $O_K(\delta)$ remainder
in \cref{p9:thm:two-term-radial}.

The same cutoff method can be repeated to any prescribed finite order, once
the order-dependent Taylor constants are kept explicit.  The uniform bounds of
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier} are exactly what is needed, because they
control every Taylor coefficient of the multipliers, not merely the first two.
Define, for $r\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 B_{r,\omega}(z)
 =-\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\ d\nmid k}}c_k
   \CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r}S_k\;z^{2k}
  -\sum_{\substack{k\ge1\\ d\mid k}}
   \frac{c_ka_\omega^{2k}}{2k}
   \CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r+1}H_k\;z^{2k},
 \label{p9:eq:Br-def}
\end{equation}
with $S_k$ and $H_k$ as in \cref{p9:eq:Sk-delta,p9:eq:Hk}.

\begin{theorem}[All-orders fixed-frequency radial expansion]
\label{p9:thm:full-radial}
Every series \cref{p9:eq:Br-def} converges absolutely and locally uniformly on
$\SetOf{z:\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}<\pi}$, and $B_{0,\omega}=\Bact_\omega$.
Moreover, for every compact
$K\Subset\SetOf{z:\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}<\pi}$ and every integer $R\ge0$
there are $C_{K,R}>0$ and $\delta_{K,R}>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{
  \log\Phi\bigl(\omega(1-\delta),z\bigr)
  +\frac{\Aact_\omega(z)}{\delta}
  -\sum_{r=0}^{R}B_{r,\omega}(z)\delta^{r}}
 \le C_{K,R}\,\delta^{R+1}
 \label{p9:eq:full-radial-quant}
\end{equation}
for all $z\in K$ and $0<\delta\le\delta_{K,R}$.  We abbreviate this by the
locally uniform Poincar\'e expansion
\begin{equation}
 \log\Phi(\omega(1-\delta),z)
 \sim -\frac{\Aact_\omega(z)}{\delta}
 +\sum_{r\ge0}B_{r,\omega}(z)\delta^r .
 \label{p9:eq:full-radial}
\end{equation}
The constant $C_{K,R}$ is allowed to depend on $R$; no claim is made that the
series in \cref{p9:eq:full-radial} converges, nor that its constants grow at
any prescribed rate in $R$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $0<\rho<\rho_1<1$ with $\AbsoluteValue{a_\omega z}\le\rho\pi$ on $K$ and
$\AbsoluteValue{(a_\omega+\omega\delta)z}\le\rho_1\pi$ for $z\in K$ and
$0\le\delta\le\delta_0$, and abbreviate $a=a_\omega$, $b=\omega/a$.

\emph{Step 1: coefficient bounds.}  By
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(i)}, $H_k$ is holomorphic with
$\AbsoluteValue{H_k}\le M_1$ on the closed disc
$\AbsoluteValue\delta\le1/(4k)$, so Cauchy's estimates give
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r}H_k}\le M_1(4k)^{r},
 \qquad
 \AbsoluteValue{H_k(\delta)-\sum_{r=0}^{R+1}
   \CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r}H_k\;\delta^{r}}
 \le 2M_1(4k\delta)^{R+2}
 \label{p9:eq:Hk-taylor}
\end{equation}
for $0\le\delta\le1/(8k)$, the second bound being the geometric estimate of
the Taylor tail on half the radius.  By
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(iv)}, for $d\nmid k$ the function
$S_k$ is holomorphic with $\AbsoluteValue{S_k}\le M_2\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}$ on
$\AbsoluteValue\delta\le\lambda_\omega/(2k)$, so likewise
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r}S_k}
 \le M_2\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}
   \Bigl(\frac{2k}{\lambda_\omega}\Bigr)^{r},
 \qquad
 \AbsoluteValue{S_k(\delta)-\sum_{r=0}^{R}
   \CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{r}S_k\;\delta^{r}}
 \le 2M_2\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}
   \Bigl(\frac{2k\delta}{\lambda_\omega}\Bigr)^{R+1}
 \label{p9:eq:Sk-taylor}
\end{equation}
for $0\le\delta\le\lambda_\omega/(4k)$.  Combining the left-hand bounds with
\cref{p9:eq:ck-majorant} dominates the two families in \cref{p9:eq:Br-def} by
$M_2\zeta(2)(2/\lambda_\omega)^{r}k^{r-1}\rho^{2k}$ and by
$M_14^{r+1}\zeta(2)k^{r-1}\rho^{2k}/2$ respectively, both summable in $k$
because $\rho<1$, and uniformly so on $K$.  Hence each $B_{r,\omega}$
converges absolutely and locally uniformly.  For $r=0$ the coefficients are
$\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{0}S_k=a^{2k}/(1-\omega^{2k})$ and, by
\cref{p9:eq:Hk-bounds}, $\CoefficientExtraction{\delta}{1}H_k=2kb+(2k-1)/2$,
so \cref{p9:eq:Br-def} reduces termwise to
\cref{p9:eq:B-first,p9:eq:B-second}; that is $B_{0,\omega}=\Bact_\omega$.

Note also that, for $d\mid k$, expanding $H_k$ through order $\delta^{R+1}$ and
dividing by $2k\delta$ expands $S_k$ through order $\delta^{R}$ starting at
$\delta^{-1}$, with coefficient $a^{2k}/(2k)$ there; multiplied by
$-c_kz^{2k}$ and summed over the resonant $k$, that coefficient reproduces
exactly $-\Aact_\omega(z)$ by \cref{p9:eq:action-series}.  Thus the three
displayed objects in \cref{p9:eq:full-radial-quant} are the true sum, its
$\delta^{-1}$ coefficient, and its coefficients of $\delta^{0},\dots,\delta^{R}$.

\emph{Step 2: the remainder below the cutoff.}  Split every sum over $k$ at
$N=\Floor{\delta^{-1/2}}$, and shrink $\delta_{K,R}\le\delta_0$ so that
$\delta_{K,R}\le\min\SetOf{1/64,\lambda_\omega^{2}/16}$, which is
positive because $\lambda_\omega>0$ by \cref{p9:eq:lambda-omega} and the
convention recorded in \cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}; then
$N\le\delta^{-1/2}\le\min\SetOf{1/(8\delta),\lambda_\omega/(4\delta)}$, so
\cref{p9:eq:Hk-taylor,p9:eq:Sk-taylor} apply for every $k\le N$.  Using
$S_k=a^{2k}H_k/(2k\delta)$ in the resonant case and
\cref{p9:eq:ck-majorant} throughout, the resonant part of the left-hand side
of \cref{p9:eq:full-radial-quant} restricted to $k\le N$ is at most
\[
 \sum_{\substack{d\mid k,\;k\le N}}
 \frac{c_k\AbsoluteValue{az}^{2k}}{2k\delta}\cdot2M_1(4k\delta)^{R+2}
 \le M_1\zeta(2)4^{R+2}\,\delta^{R+1}\sum_{k\ge1}k^{R}\rho^{2k},
\]
and the nonresonant part at most
\[
 \sum_{\substack{d\nmid k,\;k\le N}}
 c_k\AbsoluteValue z^{2k}\cdot
 2M_2\AbsoluteValue a^{2k}
 \Bigl(\frac{2k\delta}{\lambda_\omega}\Bigr)^{R+1}
 \le 2M_2\zeta(2)
 \Bigl(\frac{2}{\lambda_\omega}\Bigr)^{R+1}\delta^{R+1}
 \sum_{k\ge1}k^{R}\rho^{2k}.
\]
Both sums over $k$ are finite because $\rho<1$, so this contribution is
$O_{K,R}(\delta^{R+1})$.

\emph{Step 3: the remainder beyond the cutoff.}  For $k>N$ the true terms are
bounded exactly as in the proof of \cref{p9:thm:two-term-radial}: by
\cref{p9:lem:uniform-multiplier}\textup{(ii)} and \textup{(v)},
\[
 c_k\AbsoluteValue z^{2k}\AbsoluteValue{S_k(\delta)}
 \le C\rho_1^{2k}\Bigl(\frac1k+\frac1{k^{2}\delta}\Bigr),
\]
with $C$ depending only on $\gamma$ and $\omega$.  The subtracted terms with
index $k>N$ --- the $k$th term of $\Aact_\omega(z)/\delta$ together with the
$k$th terms of $B_{0,\omega},\dots,B_{R,\omega}$ --- are bounded, after
summation over $0\le r\le R$ and using the left-hand bounds of
\cref{p9:eq:Hk-taylor,p9:eq:Sk-taylor} together with $\delta\le1$, by
$C_R\,\rho^{2k}k^{R}\bigl(1+(k\delta)^{-1}\bigr)$.  Summing both over $k>N$
gives $O_R\bigl(\delta^{-1}N^{R}\rho_1^{2N}\bigr)$, and
$\rho_1^{2N}\le\rho_1^{-2}(\rho_1^{2})^{\delta^{-1/2}}$, so by
\cref{p9:eq:exp-beats-power} this is $o(\delta^{M})$ for every $M>0$; in
particular it is $O(\delta^{R+1})$.

Adding the estimates of Steps~2 and~3 proves
\cref{p9:eq:full-radial-quant}, and \cref{p9:eq:full-radial} is its
abbreviation.
\end{proof}

The bound obtained above for $C_{K,R}$ grows like $4^{R}R!$, the factorial
entering through $\sum_kk^{R}\rho^{2k}$.  Whether it can be held to a Gevrey
rate is a separate question, and an open one; it is what an analytic --- as opposed to
asymptotic --- theory of the inverse branches would need, as recorded in
\cref{p9:status:inverse-analytic}.

\section{A direct coefficient derivation for the inverse
\texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-branch}
\label{p9:app:inverse-coefficients}

Set
\(
 \delta=\rho z^{2d}
\).  The $k=d$ term in the logarithm is
\begin{align}
 -c_dz^{2d}
 \frac{(a_\omega+\omega\rho z^{2d})^{2d}}
 {1-(1-\rho z^{2d})^{2d}}
 &=-\frac{A_\omega}{\rho}
 +O(z^{2d}).
 \label{p9:eq:rho-leading}
\end{align}
For $1\le k<d$, the nonresonant terms are
\begin{equation}
 -C_{k,\omega}z^{2k}+O(z^{2k+2d}).
 \label{p9:eq:rho-nonres}
\end{equation}
Write
\begin{equation}
 \rho(z)=\rho_0+\rho_1z^2+O(z^4),
 \qquad
 \rho_0=-\frac{A_\omega}{\ell}.
 \label{p9:eq:rho-series}
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 -\frac{A_\omega}{\rho(z)}
 =\ell+\ell\left(-\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_0}\right)z^2+O(z^4).
\]
Matching the $-C_{1,\omega}z^2$ term gives
\(
 \rho_1/\rho_0=-C_{1,\omega}/\ell
\), which is \cref{p9:eq:delta-z}.  Higher coefficients follow triangularly because the derivative in $\rho$ never vanishes at $\rho_0$.

\part{Parameter Flow, Convex Order, and Large Deviations}




\begin{abstract}
Let $U_0,U_1,\ldots$ be independent $\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]$ variables and
\[
  X_q=(1-q)\sum_{j\ge0}q^jU_j,\qquad 0<q<1.
\]
At $q=1/2$ the density of $X_q$ is the standard centered Rvachev
$\RvachevUp$-function, and hence lies on the usual Fabius--Rvachev bridge.  The
current ProveIt corpus already contains an extensive theory of this family:
its infinite-sinc transform, Bernoulli cumulants, $q$-Pochhammer
factorizations, parameter limits, fixed-base endpoint asymptotics, finite
prefix transport, and a first Gaussian correction.  After a source-level
crosswalk against that corpus, this report develops a different parameter
layer.

First, for $0<r<s<1$ we construct an explicit probability kernel
$p_{r,s}$ whose generating function is
\[
  P_{r,s}(z)=\frac{1-s}{1-r}\frac{1-rz}{1-sz}.
\]
It transports the geometric coefficient profile at $r$ to that at $s$ and
forms a convolution cocycle.  A random tail shift with law $p_{r,s}$ gives an
explicit martingale coupling, proving the universal convex-order flow
$X_s\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}X_r$.  The kernels are the increments of an
inhomogeneous compound-Poisson subordinator with geometric jump law.

Second, writing $q=\EulerE^{-\delta}$, we prove a full large-deviation principle at
speed $1/\delta$.  Its limiting scaled cumulant transform is
\[
 \Lambda(\theta)=\int_0^\infty
     \log\!\left(\frac{\sinh(\theta \EulerE^{-t})}{\theta \EulerE^{-t}}\right)\Differential t
 =\int_0^\theta\frac{\log(\sinh u/u)}{u}\Differential u,
\]
and the rate is $I=\Lambda^*$.  The finite-$q$ transform is an exact midpoint
Riemann sum.  Midpoint Euler--Maclaurin therefore yields an all-orders
expansion containing only even powers of $\delta$ and Bernoulli polynomials
at $1/2$; in particular
\[
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)=\Lambda(\theta)
 -\frac{\delta^2\theta^2}{24}\Lambda''(\theta)+O(\delta^4).
\]
The rate has an explicit rational Taylor series at the origin and a new
Lambert-$W_{-1}$ boundary law as $x\uparrow1$.

Third, we prove a uniform all-orders Edgeworth expansion for the
\emph{continuous} limit $q\uparrow1$, valid after any fixed number of density
derivatives.  This is distinct from the discrete $\mathrm{Fup}_n$ Edgeworth
theorem already present in the repository.  Exact Bernoulli cumulants produce
the Hermite coefficients, and a geometric infinite-sinc tail lemma supplies
the global Fourier control.  Numerical experiments reproduce the predicted
orders $1,2,3,4$ and the midpoint orders $2,4$.  The report closes with a
moderate-deviation bridge, a sharp saddlepoint conjecture, the exact sign
pattern of the rate series --- the absorbed report's positivity conjecture is
refuted at degree $24$ ---, and a formalization roadmap.  All theorem proofs here are paper-level arguments;
no claim of Lean verification is made.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Main claims of the report}

The central claims are the following.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{R\arabic*.}]
\item An exact coefficient kernel $p_{r,s}$, its cocycle, its
compound-Poisson generator, and an explicit martingale proof of
$X_s\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}X_r$.
\item An all-orders midpoint Euler--Maclaurin expansion for the scaled
$q\uparrow1$ cumulant transform.
\item A G\"artner--Ellis large-deviation principle with an explicit integral
transform, rational central rate series, and Lambert-$W_{-1}$ edge inversion.
\item A differentiated, uniform, all-orders Edgeworth expansion for the
continuous geometric family.
\item Matching between central and large deviations, together with
saddlepoint and transseries conjectures and the refutation of the rate-series
positivity conjecture.
\end{enumerate}

The constructions extend verbatim to many bounded seed distributions.  The
uniform seed is singled out because it is exactly the Fabius--Rvachev case
and because its cumulant transform is controlled by Bernoulli numbers.

\section{The geometric-uniform law and the Fabius--Rvachev point}
\label{p10:sec:setup}

\subsection{Random series, transforms, and fixed point}

Let $U_0,U_1,\dots$ be independent variables with density
$\frac12\IndicatorOf{[-1,1]}$.  For $0<q<1$ define
\begin{equation}
  X_q=(1-q)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q^jU_j.
  \label{p10:eq:Xq}
\end{equation}
Since $X_q=2\GeoLawCentered q$ by \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}, \cref{p0:prop:basic}
gives that the series converges absolutely for every realization (its terms
are dominated by $(1-q)q^j$), that $\Expectation X_q=0$, and that
$\AbsoluteValue{X_q}\le1$ with support exactly $[-1,1]$.  Its distribution
solves
\begin{equation}
  X_q\overset{d}= (1-q)U+qX_q',
  \label{p10:eq:perpetuity}
\end{equation}
where $X_q'$ is an independent copy, and by \cref{p0:prop:fixed-point},
transported by \cref{p0:lem:transport} with $\alpha=2$, it is the unique
solution of \eqref{p10:eq:perpetuity} with finite first moment --- in
particular the unique compactly supported one.  We use
\[
 \SincRad z=\frac{\sin z}{z},\qquad
 \sinhc z=\frac{\sinh z}{z},
\]
with their continuous values at zero.  The characteristic and moment
generating functions are
\begin{align}
 \phi_q(t)&=\Expectation \EulerE^{itX_q}
   =\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}\SincRad\bigl((1-q)q^jt\bigr),
   \label{p10:eq:cf}\\
 M_q(t)&=\Expectation \EulerE^{tX_q}
   =\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}\sinhc\bigl((1-q)q^jt\bigr).
   \label{p10:eq:mgf}
\end{align}
At $q=1/2$ the first product is
$\prod_{k\ge1}\SincRad(t/2^k)$, the standard Fourier transform of the centered
Rvachev $\RvachevUp$-function.  Thus $X_{1/2}$ is exactly the centered up-law; the
usual piecewise shift/reflection relation then connects its density to the
Fabius function \cite{bib:fabius1966,bib:rvachev1990,bib:arias2018}.

\subsection{Bernoulli cumulants}

Let $B_n$ denote the Bernoulli numbers with $B_2=1/6$.  Since
\begin{equation}
 \log\sinhc z
 =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}
   \frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m(2m)!}z^{2m},
 \qquad |z|<\pi,
 \label{p10:eq:logsinhc-series}
\end{equation}
the even cumulants of $U$ and $X_q$ are
\begin{align}
 \kappa_{2m}(U)&=\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m},
 \label{p10:eq:uniform-cumulants}\\
 \kappa_{2m}(X_q)&=\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m}
     \frac{(1-q)^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}},
 \qquad \kappa_{2m+1}(X_q)=0.
 \label{p10:eq:Xq-cumulants}
\end{align}
In particular
\begin{equation}
 \sigma_q^2:=\Variance(X_q)=\frac{1-q}{3(1+q)}.
 \label{p10:eq:variance}
\end{equation}
The moments are complete Bell polynomials in the cumulants \cite{bib:comtet1974}, so every even
moment is a rational function of $q$ with Bernoulli input.  This exact
cumulant layer is part of the established corpus; our use of it below is to
build the new parameter asymptotics.

\subsection{The natural small parameter}

Set
\begin{equation}
 q=\EulerE^{-\delta},\qquad \delta=-\log q.
 \label{p10:eq:delta}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 1-q=\delta s_\delta \EulerE^{-\delta/2},
 \qquad
 s_\delta:=\frac{2\sinh(\delta/2)}{\delta}
 =1+\frac{\delta^2}{24}+\frac{\delta^4}{1920}+O(\delta^6).
 \label{p10:eq:sdelta}
\end{equation}
This exact half-step factorization is the source of the midpoint
Euler--Maclaurin cancellation in \cref{p10:sec:midpoint}.  Notice also
\begin{equation}
 \sigma_q^2=\frac13\tanh\frac{\delta}{2}
 =\frac{\delta}{6}-\frac{\delta^3}{72}
   +\frac{\delta^5}{720}+O(\delta^7).
 \label{p10:eq:variance-delta}
\end{equation}
Thus the unstandardized law collapses to zero at scale $\sqrt\delta$, while
its standardized form tends to a Gaussian.

\section{An exact parameter-flow kernel and martingale transport}
\label{p10:sec:transport}

The finite-prefix transport theory already in the corpus orders successive
truncations.  Here the number of factors is infinite and the parameter itself
moves.  The key observation is that the geometric coefficient profile admits
an exact stochastic factorization.

\subsection{Coefficient cocycle}

Write
\begin{equation}
 a_j(q)=(1-q)q^j,
 \qquad
 A_q(z)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(q)z^j=\frac{1-q}{1-qz}.
 \label{p10:eq:coefficient-pgf}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Parameter-flow kernel]
\label{p10:thm:kernel}
For $0<r<s<1$, define a probability mass function on $\NaturalNumbers$ by
\begin{equation}
 p_{r,s}(0)=\frac{1-s}{1-r},\qquad
 p_{r,s}(k)=\frac{(s-r)(1-s)}{1-r}s^{k-1},\quad k\ge1.
 \label{p10:eq:prs}
\end{equation}
Its probability generating function is
\begin{equation}
 P_{r,s}(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}p_{r,s}(k)z^k
 =\frac{1-s}{1-r}\frac{1-rz}{1-sz}.
 \label{p10:eq:Prs}
\end{equation}
The geometric coefficient profiles satisfy
\begin{equation}
 a(s)=p_{r,s}*a(r),
 \qquad A_s(z)=P_{r,s}(z)A_r(z),
 \label{p10:eq:coefficient-convolution}
\end{equation}
and the kernels form the convolution cocycle
\begin{equation}
 p_{r,t}=p_{s,t}*p_{r,s},
 \qquad 0<r<s<t<1.
 \label{p10:eq:cocycle}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The coefficients in \eqref{p10:eq:prs} are nonnegative and
\[
 p_{r,s}(0)+\sum_{k\ge1}p_{r,s}(k)
 =\frac{1-s}{1-r}+\frac{s-r}{1-r}=1.
\]
Dividing the two rational functions in \eqref{p10:eq:coefficient-pgf} gives
\[
 \frac{A_s(z)}{A_r(z)}
 =\frac{1-s}{1-r}\frac{1-rz}{1-sz},
\]
whose geometric-series expansion is exactly \eqref{p10:eq:prs}.  This proves
\eqref{p10:eq:coefficient-convolution}.  The cocycle follows immediately from
$P_{r,t}=A_t/A_r=(A_t/A_s)(A_s/A_r)$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Compound-Poisson interpretation}

The cocycle is not merely algebraic.  Differentiating its logarithm in the
upper parameter gives
\begin{align}
 \frac{\partial}{\partial s}\log P_{r,s}(z)
 &=\frac{z}{1-sz}-\frac{1}{1-s}
 \notag\\
 &=\sum_{k\ge1}s^{k-1}(z^k-1).
 \label{p10:eq:levy-generator}
\end{align}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 P_{r,s}(z)=
 \exp\left\{\int_r^s\sum_{k\ge1}u^{k-1}(z^k-1)\Differential u\right\}.
 \label{p10:eq:compound-poisson-pgf}
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}[Inhomogeneous geometric-jump subordinator]
\label{p10:prop:subordinator}
There exists an increasing process $(N_q)_{0<q<1}$ with independent
increments such that $N_s-N_r$ has law $p_{r,s}$.  At parameter value $u$,
jumps occur with total intensity $(1-u)^{-1}\Differential u$, and conditional on a
jump the size has geometric law
\begin{equation}
 \Probability\{J=k\mid u\}=(1-u)u^{k-1},\qquad k\ge1.
 \label{p10:eq:geometric-jumps}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The process is constructed, not merely read off \eqref{p10:eq:compound-poisson-pgf}.
Let $\mathcal N$ be a Poisson random measure on $(0,1)\times\SetOf{1,2,\ldots}$
with intensity $\nu(\Differential u,\SetOf k)=u^{k-1}\Differential u$.  For
$0<r<s<1$ the intensity of the strip $(r,s]\times\SetOf{1,2,\ldots}$ is
\[
 \sum_{k\ge1}\int_r^su^{k-1}\Differential u
 =\int_r^s\frac{\Differential u}{1-u}
 =\log\frac{1-r}{1-s}<\infty,
\]
so $\mathcal N$ has finitely many points in every such strip almost surely
(the mass diverges only as $s\uparrow1$, which is why the process is indexed by
$q<1$).  Put
\[
 N_q=\int_{(0,q]\times\SetOf{1,2,\ldots}}k\,\mathcal N(\Differential u,\Differential k),
 \qquad 0<q<1,
\]
a finite sum of the jump sizes in $(0,q]$.  It is nondecreasing in $q$, and
since $\mathcal N$ restricted to disjoint strips is independent, the increments
over disjoint parameter intervals are independent.  The exponential formula
for Poisson random measures gives, for $0\le z\le1$,
\[
 \Expectation z^{N_s-N_r}
 =\exp\left\{\int_r^s\sum_{k\ge1}u^{k-1}(z^k-1)\Differential u\right\}
 =P_{r,s}(z)
\]
by \eqref{p10:eq:compound-poisson-pgf}, so $N_s-N_r$ has law $p_{r,s}$; the
cocycle \eqref{p10:eq:cocycle} is then the additivity of increments.  At
parameter value $u$ the total jump rate is $\sum_{k\ge1}u^{k-1}=(1-u)^{-1}$,
and normalizing the intensity by it gives \eqref{p10:eq:geometric-jumps}.
\end{proof}

The expected number of jumps between $r$ and $s$ is
$\log((1-r)/(1-s))$.  Thus the apparently static operation of making the
coefficient sequence more diffuse is governed by a simple pure-jump flow.

\subsection{Explicit martingale coupling}

The kernel acts by random shifts of the independent environment.  This gives
a direct convex-order proof, stronger than a comparison of finitely many
moments.

\begin{theorem}[Tail-shift martingale transport]
\label{p10:thm:martingale-transport}
Let $V_0,V_1,\ldots$ be iid integrable real random variables and define
\begin{equation}
 X_q^{(V)}=(1-q)\sum_{j\ge0}q^jV_j.
 \label{p10:eq:general-seed}
\end{equation}
For $0<r<s<1$, let $N$ be independent of the sequence and have law
$p_{r,s}$.  Put
\begin{equation}
 Y_{r,s}=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(r)V_{j+N}.
 \label{p10:eq:Yrs}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 Y_{r,s}\overset d=X_r^{(V)},
 \qquad
 \Expectation\!\left[Y_{r,s}\mid V_0,V_1,\ldots\right]=X_s^{(V)}.
 \label{p10:eq:martingale-coupling}
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 X_s^{(V)}\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}X_r^{(V)}.
 \label{p10:eq:convex-order}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, the series defining $X_q^{(V)}$ and $Y_{r,s}$ converge absolutely
almost surely: since $\sum_ja_j(q)=1$,
$\Expectation\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(q)\AbsoluteValue{V_j}=\Expectation\AbsoluteValue V<\infty$,
so $\sum_ja_j(q)\AbsoluteValue{V_j}<\infty$ a.s., and the same holds for every
shifted tail.  For every fixed $n$, the tail $(V_n,V_{n+1},\ldots)$ has the same
joint law as the original iid sequence, hence the conditional-on-$N=n$ variable
in \eqref{p10:eq:Yrs} has law $X_r^{(V)}$.  Thus $Y_{r,s}\overset d=X_r^{(V)}$.
Conditioning instead on the entire environment, the interchange of the two
sums below is Fubini's theorem for the signed double series, justified by the
integrable majorant
\[
 \Expectation\sum_{n\ge0}p_{r,s}(n)\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(r)\AbsoluteValue{V_{j+n}}
 =\sum_{n\ge0}p_{r,s}(n)\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(r)\,\Expectation\AbsoluteValue V
 =\Expectation\AbsoluteValue V<\infty ;
\]
it gives
\begin{align*}
 \Expectation[Y_{r,s}\mid(V_j)_{j\ge0}]
 &=\sum_{n\ge0}p_{r,s}(n)\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(r)V_{j+n}\\
 &=\sum_{k\ge0}\left(\sum_{n=0}^{k}p_{r,s}(n)a_{k-n}(r)\right)V_k\\
 &=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k(s)V_k
 =X_s^{(V)},
\end{align*}
where the penultimate equality is \eqref{p10:eq:coefficient-convolution}.
Therefore $X_s^{(V)}$ is the conditional expectation of a variable having
law $X_r^{(V)}$.  Jensen's inequality yields
$\Expectation\Phi(X_s^{(V)})\le\Expectation\Phi(X_r^{(V)})$ for every convex $\Phi$ for which
the expectations exist, which is exactly convex order.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Stop-loss and moment inequalities]
\label{p10:cor:stoploss}
For $0<r<s<1$ and every $t\in\RealNumbers$,
\begin{equation}
 \Expectation(X_s-t)_+\le \Expectation(X_r-t)_+.
 \label{p10:eq:stoploss}
\end{equation}
If the seed is centered and has finite variance, then
\begin{equation}
 \Variance(X_q^{(V)})=\Variance(V)\frac{1-q}{1+q},
 \label{p10:eq:general-variance}
\end{equation}
and this variance is strictly decreasing unless $V$ is degenerate.  All
even convex moments that exist are nonincreasing in $q$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Why the proof is genuinely infinite-dimensional]
\label{p10:rem:infinite-dimensional}
The right shift of an infinite coefficient sequence is not a finite
permutation.  Nevertheless every shifted iid tail produces exactly the same
weighted-sum law.  Averaging over the shift kernel therefore supplies the
martingale directly and bypasses finite-dimensional approximation.  The
finite-prefix convex-order chain in the repository and the parameter flow
\eqref{p10:eq:convex-order} are complementary rather than duplicate statements.
\end{remark}

\section{The scaled cumulant transform as a midpoint \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-integral}
\label{p10:sec:midpoint}

\subsection{Exact half-step representation}

For the uniform seed set
\begin{equation}
 g(z)=\log\sinhc z=\log\frac{\sinh z}{z}.
 \label{p10:eq:gdef}
\end{equation}
The scaled cumulant generating function at large-deviation speed
$1/\delta$ is
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)
 :=\delta\log\Expectation\exp\!\left(\frac{\theta X_{\EulerE^{-\delta}}}{\delta}\right).
 \label{p10:eq:scaled-cgf}
\end{equation}
Using \eqref{p10:eq:sdelta}, the $j$th argument of $g$ is
\[
 \frac{\theta(1-\EulerE^{-\delta})\EulerE^{-j\delta}}{\delta}
 =\theta s_\delta \EulerE^{-(j+1/2)\delta}.
\]
Hence the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\quad
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)
 =\delta\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}
 g\!\left(\theta s_\delta \EulerE^{-(j+1/2)\delta}\right).
 \quad}
 \label{p10:eq:midpoint-sum}
\end{equation}
This is a midpoint Riemann sum on the logarithmic scale.  It is the reason the
first correction is $O(\delta^2)$ rather than $O(\delta)$.

\subsection{Limit transform}

\begin{theorem}[Limiting scaled cumulant transform]
\label{p10:thm:lambda-limit}
Uniformly for $\theta$ in compact subsets of $\RealNumbers$,
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)\longrightarrow
 \Lambda(\theta):=\int_0^\infty g(\theta \EulerE^{-t})\Differential t
 =\int_0^\theta\frac{g(u)}{u}\Differential u.
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda}
\end{equation}
More precisely, with $s_\delta$ as in \eqref{p10:eq:sdelta}, for every
$\theta\in\RealNumbers$ and every $\delta>0$,
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{\Lambda_\delta(\theta)-\Lambda(\theta)}
 \le\frac{s_\delta\,\delta^2\AbsoluteValue\theta}{6},
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-rate}
\end{equation}
so the convergence is of order $\delta^2$, locally uniformly.
The function $\Lambda$ is even, real analytic, and strictly convex, with
\begin{align}
 \Lambda'(\theta)&=\frac{1}{\theta}
    \log\frac{\sinh\theta}{\theta},
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-prime}\\
 \Lambda''(\theta)&=
 \frac{\theta\coth\theta-
       \log(\sinh\theta/\theta)-1}{\theta^2}>0,
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-second}\\
 \Lambda'(\RealNumbers)&=(-1,1).
 \label{p10:eq:gradient-range}
\end{align}
At the origin,
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda(\theta)=
 \sum_{m\ge1}
 \frac{2^{2m-2}B_{2m}}{m^2(2m)!}\theta^{2m}
 =\frac{\theta^2}{12}-\frac{\theta^4}{720}
  +\frac{\theta^6}{17010}-\cdots.
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-Bernoulli}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Elementary facts about $g$.}  On $(0,\infty)$,
$g'(u)=\coth u-u^{-1}$ and $g''(u)=u^{-2}-\sinh^{-2}u$; $g''$ decreases from
$g''(0)=\tfrac13$ to $0$, so $0<g''\le\tfrac13$ and, integrating from $0$,
$0<g'(u)\le u/3$.  With the Euler operator $D=u\,\Differential/\Differential u$
one has $Dg(u)=u\coth u-1$ and $D^2g(u)=u\,(Dg)'(u)=u\coth u-u^2\sinh^{-2}u$,
both nonnegative, with $Dg(u)\le u$ because $\coth u\le1+u^{-1}$.  All of
$g,Dg,D^2g$ are $O(u^2)$ as $u\to0$, by \eqref{p10:eq:logsinhc-series}.

\emph{The two integrals in \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda}.}  For $\theta\ne0$ the
substitution $u=\AbsoluteValue\theta\EulerE^{-t}$ turns
$\int_0^\infty g(\theta\EulerE^{-t})\Differential t$ into
$\int_0^{\AbsoluteValue\theta}g(u)u^{-1}\Differential u$, which is absolutely
convergent because $g(u)/u=O(u)$ at $0$; both sides are even in $\theta$.

\emph{The rate \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-rate}.}  By evenness take $\theta>0$ and
put $w=\theta s_\delta$ and $f(t)=g(w\EulerE^{-t})$, so that
\eqref{p10:eq:midpoint-sum} reads
$\Lambda_\delta(\theta)=\delta\sum_{j\ge0}f((j+\tfrac12)\delta)$ and
$\int_0^\infty f=\Lambda(w)$.  The chain rule gives
$f''(t)=D^2g(w\EulerE^{-t})\ge0$, so $f\in C^2[0,\infty)$ with
\[
 \int_0^\infty\AbsoluteValue{f''(t)}\Differential t
 =\int_0^{w}D^2g(u)\frac{\Differential u}{u}
 =\int_0^{w}(Dg)'(u)\Differential u=Dg(w)=w\coth w-1\le w .
\]
On each cell $[j\delta,(j+1)\delta]$ with midpoint $m_j$, the midpoint rule
has the Peano representation
$\int_{j\delta}^{(j+1)\delta}f-\delta f(m_j)
 =\int_{j\delta}^{(j+1)\delta}f''(t)k_j(t)\Differential t$
with the kernel $k_j(t)=\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac\delta2-\AbsoluteValue{t-m_j}\bigr)^2$,
$0\le k_j\le\delta^2/8$.  Summing over $j$,
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\Lambda_\delta(\theta)-\Lambda(\theta s_\delta)}
 \le\frac{\delta^2}{8}\int_0^\infty\AbsoluteValue{f''}
 \le\frac{\delta^2}{8}\,\theta s_\delta .
\]
Next, $\Lambda'(u)=g(u)/u$ (fundamental theorem of calculus applied to the
second integral in \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda}), and
$0\le g(u)/u<1$ for $u>0$ because $g(u)=\int_0^ug'<u$; hence
$\AbsoluteValue{\Lambda(\theta s_\delta)-\Lambda(\theta)}\le\theta(s_\delta-1)$.
Finally $s_\delta-1=\sum_{k\ge1}(\delta/2)^{2k}/(2k+1)!$ and
$\tfrac{\delta^2}{24}s_\delta=\sum_{k\ge1}(\delta/2)^{2k}/(6\,(2k-1)!)$ with
$(2k+1)!\ge6\,(2k-1)!$, so $s_\delta-1\le\delta^2s_\delta/24$.  Adding the two
estimates gives $\delta^2\theta s_\delta(\tfrac18+\tfrac1{24})
=\delta^2\theta s_\delta/6$, which is \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-rate}; the
convergence in \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda} follows.

\emph{Regularity, derivatives, and convexity.}  From
$\Lambda'(\theta)=g(\theta)/\theta$ one reads off
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-prime}, and differentiating once more gives
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-second}, whose numerator is
$Dg(\theta)-g(\theta)=\int_0^\theta\bigl(g'(\theta)-g'(u)\bigr)\Differential u>0$
for $\theta>0$ because $g'$ is strictly increasing; at the origin
$\Lambda''(0)=g''(0)/2=\tfrac16$ (the series \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-Bernoulli}).
Hence $\Lambda''>0$ everywhere, and $\Lambda$ is real analytic on
$\RealNumbers$ because $g(u)/u$ is (the entire function $\sinh u/u$ is
strictly positive on the real axis).  The integral representation
$\Lambda''(\theta)=\int_0^\infty\EulerE^{-2t}g''(\theta\EulerE^{-t})\Differential t$
is also legitimate: the $\theta$-derivatives of the integrand are
$\EulerE^{-t}g'(\theta\EulerE^{-t})$ and $\EulerE^{-2t}g''(\theta\EulerE^{-t})$,
dominated for $\AbsoluteValue\theta\le R$ by $R\EulerE^{-2t}/3$ and
$\EulerE^{-2t}/3$ respectively, so differentiation under the integral sign is
covered by dominated convergence.  Finally
$g(\theta)=\theta-\log(2\theta)+O(\EulerE^{-2\theta})$ as
$\theta\to+\infty$, so $\Lambda'(\theta)=g(\theta)/\theta\to1$ while staying
below $1$; oddness gives the lower endpoint, and strict monotonicity of
$\Lambda'$ gives \eqref{p10:eq:gradient-range}.  Integrating
\eqref{p10:eq:logsinhc-series} termwise on $\AbsoluteValue\theta<\pi$ gives
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-Bernoulli}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{All-orders midpoint Euler--Maclaurin expansion}

Let $B_n(x)$ be the Bernoulli polynomials and let
$D=\theta\frac{\Differential}{\Differential\theta}$ be the Euler operator.

\begin{theorem}[All-order midpoint expansion]
\label{p10:thm:midpoint-EM}
For every integer $N\ge1$ and every compact $K\subset\RealNumbers$,
\begin{align}
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)
 &=\Lambda(\theta s_\delta)
 +\sum_{m=1}^{N-1}
   \frac{B_{2m}(1/2)}{(2m)!}\delta^{2m}
   D^{2m-1}g(\theta s_\delta)
 +O_{K,N}(\delta^{2N})
 \label{p10:eq:EM-all-orders}
\end{align}
uniformly for $\theta\in K$.  In particular the expansion contains only
even powers of $\delta$.  The first two nontrivial terms are
\begin{align}
 \Lambda_\delta(\theta)
 &=\Lambda(\theta)
 -\frac{\delta^2\theta^2}{24}\Lambda''(\theta)
 +\delta^4 C_4(\theta)+O_K(\delta^6),
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-two-corrections}\\
 C_4(\theta)
 &=\frac{7D^3g-10D^2g+5Dg-2g}{5760}(\theta).
 \label{p10:eq:C4}
\end{align}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Derivatives of the summand.}  Put $w=\theta s_\delta$ and
$f(t)=f_{\delta,\theta}(t)=g(w\EulerE^{-t})$.  Under $u=w\EulerE^{-t}$ one has
$\Differential/\Differential t=-u\,\Differential/\Differential u=-D$, so by
induction
\begin{equation}
 f^{(n)}(t)=(-1)^n\,(D^ng)(w\EulerE^{-t}),
 \qquad
 f^{(n)}(0)=(-1)^n\,D^ng(w),
 \label{p10:eq:f-derivatives-D}
\end{equation}
which is the identity $f^{(2m-1)}(0)=-D^{2m-1}g(\theta s_\delta)$ used below.
On $\AbsoluteValue u<\pi$ the series \eqref{p10:eq:logsinhc-series} gives
$D^ng(u)=\sum_{m\ge1}(2m)^n\frac{2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m(2m)!}u^{2m}=O(u^2)$, and
$D^ng$ is continuous on $\RealNumbers$; hence every $f^{(n)}(t)$ is
$O(\EulerE^{-2t})$ as $t\to\infty$, so all derivatives of $f$ vanish at
infinity and are integrable on $[0,\infty)$, and the quantity
\begin{equation}
 V_n(w)\DefinitionEquals\int_0^\infty\AbsoluteValue{f^{(n)}(t)}\Differential t
 =\int_0^{\AbsoluteValue w}\AbsoluteValue{D^ng(u)}\frac{\Differential u}{u}
 \label{p10:eq:Vn}
\end{equation}
is finite, continuous, and nondecreasing in $\AbsoluteValue w$.

\emph{Midpoint Euler--Maclaurin with kernel remainder.}  For
$F\in C^{2N}[0,1]$ and $\omega\in[0,1]$ the Bernoulli-polynomial expansion
\cite{bib:olver1974}
\[
 F(\omega)=\int_0^1F
 +\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\frac{B_k(\omega)}{k!}\bigl[F^{(k-1)}(1)-F^{(k-1)}(0)\bigr]
 -\frac1{(2N)!}\int_0^1\widetilde B_{2N}(\omega-x)F^{(2N)}(x)\Differential x,
\]
with $\widetilde B_n$ the $1$-periodic Bernoulli function, applied on the
cell $[j\delta,(j+1)\delta]$ to $F(x)=f((j+x)\delta)$ at $\omega=\tfrac12$
gives, after multiplication by $\delta$,
\[
 \delta f\bigl((j+\tfrac12)\delta\bigr)
 =\int_{j\delta}^{(j+1)\delta}f
 +\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\frac{B_k(\tfrac12)}{k!}\delta^k
   \bigl[f^{(k-1)}\bigr]_{j\delta}^{(j+1)\delta}
 -\frac{\delta^{2N}}{(2N)!}\int_{j\delta}^{(j+1)\delta}
   \widetilde B_{2N}\!\left(\frac t\delta-\frac12\right)f^{(2N)}(t)\Differential t,
\]
where $\widetilde B_{2N}(\tfrac12-t/\delta+j)=\widetilde B_{2N}(t/\delta-\tfrac12)$
by periodicity and evenness.  Summing over $j\ge0$, the bracketed terms
telescope to $-f^{(k-1)}(0)$ because $f^{(k-1)}(t)\to0$, and the odd Bernoulli
values $B_{2m+1}(\tfrac12)$ vanish.  Hence the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \delta\sum_{j\ge0}f\bigl((j+\tfrac12)\delta\bigr)
 =\int_0^\infty f
 -\sum_{m=1}^{N}\frac{B_{2m}(\tfrac12)}{(2m)!}\delta^{2m}f^{(2m-1)}(0)
 -R_N,
 \label{p10:eq:midpoint-EM-proof}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 R_N=\frac{\delta^{2N}}{(2N)!}\int_0^\infty
   \widetilde B_{2N}\!\left(\frac t\delta-\frac12\right)f^{(2N)}(t)\Differential t .
\]
Since $\sup\AbsoluteValue{\widetilde B_{2N}}=\AbsoluteValue{B_{2N}}$, the
remainder obeys
\begin{equation}
 \AbsoluteValue{R_N}\le\frac{\AbsoluteValue{B_{2N}}}{(2N)!}\,\delta^{2N}\,V_{2N}(\theta s_\delta),
 \label{p10:eq:midpoint-EM-remainder}
\end{equation}
and for $\theta\in K$ and $0<\delta\le1$ the right side is at most
$\frac{\AbsoluteValue{B_{2N}}}{(2N)!}\delta^{2N}V_{2N}(s_1\max_K\AbsoluteValue\theta)$
with $s_1=2\sinh\tfrac12$, a bound of the form $O_{K,N}(\delta^{2N})$.  The
integral in \eqref{p10:eq:midpoint-EM-proof} is $\Lambda(\theta s_\delta)$, and
\eqref{p10:eq:f-derivatives-D} converts $-f^{(2m-1)}(0)$ into
$+D^{2m-1}g(\theta s_\delta)$; the term $m=N$ is itself $O_{K,N}(\delta^{2N})$
by continuity of $D^{2N-1}g$, and absorbing it gives \eqref{p10:eq:EM-all-orders}.
The even-power structure is the vanishing of $B_{2m+1}(\tfrac12)$; explicitly
$B_{2m}(\tfrac12)=(2^{1-2m}-1)B_{2m}$, so $B_2(\tfrac12)=-\tfrac1{12}$ and
$B_4(\tfrac12)=\tfrac7{240}$.

\emph{The first two corrections.}  Write $\theta s_\delta=\theta\EulerE^{\lambda}$
with
\[
 \lambda=\log s_\delta=\frac{\delta^2}{24}-\frac{\delta^4}{2880}+O(\delta^6),
\]
from $s_\delta=1+\delta^2/24+\delta^4/1920+O(\delta^6)$ in \eqref{p10:eq:sdelta}.
Because $D\Lambda=\theta\Lambda'=g$ and $D^2\Lambda=Dg$, Taylor expansion along
the Euler flow gives
$\Lambda(\theta\EulerE^\lambda)=\Lambda+\lambda g+\tfrac12\lambda^2Dg+O(\delta^6)$,
and likewise $Dg(\theta\EulerE^\lambda)=Dg+\lambda D^2g+O(\delta^4)$, all
evaluated at $\theta$.  Inserting these into \eqref{p10:eq:EM-all-orders} with
$N=3$:
\begin{align*}
 \Lambda(\theta s_\delta)&=\Lambda+\frac{\delta^2}{24}g
  +\delta^4\Bigl(-\frac{g}{2880}+\frac{Dg}{1152}\Bigr)+O(\delta^6),\\
 \frac{B_2(\tfrac12)}{2!}\delta^2Dg(\theta s_\delta)
 &=-\frac{\delta^2}{24}Dg-\frac{\delta^4}{576}D^2g+O(\delta^6),\\
 \frac{B_4(\tfrac12)}{4!}\delta^4D^3g(\theta s_\delta)
 &=\frac{7\delta^4}{5760}D^3g+O(\delta^6).
\end{align*}
The $\delta^2$ terms combine to $\frac{\delta^2}{24}(g-Dg)$, and
$Dg-g=\theta g'(\theta)-g(\theta)=\theta^2\Lambda''(\theta)$ by
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-second}, which is the first correction in
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-two-corrections}.  The $\delta^4$ terms combine to
$\frac{-2g+5Dg-10D^2g+7D^3g}{5760}$, which is \eqref{p10:eq:C4}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A q-calculus reading]
\label{p10:rem:q-calculus}
Equation \eqref{p10:eq:midpoint-sum} is a logarithmic Jackson-type sum whose mesh
is $\delta=-\log q$, and it is the exponential factor $\EulerE^{-\delta/2}$ of the
exact factorization \eqref{p10:eq:sdelta} that centers the sampling at half
steps; the residual amplitude $s_\delta$ moves no node and only rescales the
argument, $\theta\mapsto\theta s_\delta$.  The resulting coefficients are Bernoulli polynomials at
$1/2$, not merely Bernoulli numbers at zero.  This provides a direct bridge
between the repository's $q$-product layer and its Bernoulli/Euler--Maclaurin
layer \cite{bib:gasper2004}.
\end{remark}

\section{A large-deviation principle as \texorpdfstring{$q\uparrow1$}{q tends to 1}}
\label{p10:sec:LDP}

\subsection{The rate function}

\begin{theorem}[Large-deviation principle]
\label{p10:thm:LDP}
The family $X_{\EulerE^{-\delta}}$ satisfies a large-deviation principle on $\RealNumbers$
with speed $1/\delta$ and good rate function
\begin{equation}
 I(x)=\sup_{\theta\in\RealNumbers}\{\theta x-\Lambda(\theta)\}.
 \label{p10:eq:rate-Legendre}
\end{equation}
The function $I$ is even, strictly convex on $(-1,1)$, satisfies $I(0)=0$,
and is infinite for $|x|\ge1$.  For $|x|<1$, let $\theta_x$ be the unique
solution of
\begin{equation}
 x=\Lambda'(\theta_x)
 =\frac1{\theta_x}\log\frac{\sinh\theta_x}{\theta_x}.
 \label{p10:eq:saddle-equation}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 I(x)=\theta_xx-\Lambda(\theta_x),
 \qquad I'(x)=\theta_x,
 \qquad I''(x)=\frac1{\Lambda''(\theta_x)}.
 \label{p10:eq:rate-parametric}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The hypotheses of the G\"artner--Ellis theorem
\cite{bib:ellis1984,bib:dembo1998} are checked one by one.  The scaled
logarithmic moment generating functions of the family at speed $1/\delta$ are
exactly $\Lambda_\delta$ in \eqref{p10:eq:scaled-cgf}, and
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-rate} gives $\Lambda_\delta(\theta)\to\Lambda(\theta)$ for
\emph{every} $\theta\in\RealNumbers$, not only on compacts.  The limit
$\Lambda$ is finite on all of $\RealNumbers$, so its effective domain is
$\RealNumbers$, whose boundary is empty; $\Lambda$ is differentiable there by
\cref{p10:thm:lambda-limit}.  Hence $\Lambda$ is lower semicontinuous and
essentially smooth, the steepness condition being vacuous, and $0$ is an
interior point of the domain.  Since every $X_{\EulerE^{-\delta}}$ is
supported in the fixed compact interval $[-1,1]$, the family is exponentially
tight.  The theorem therefore gives the full large-deviation principle, upper
and lower bounds included, with the good rate function
\eqref{p10:eq:rate-Legendre}; $I$ is even because $\Lambda$ is, and
$I(0)=0$ because $\Lambda\ge0=\Lambda(0)$ and $\Lambda'(0)=0$.

For the parametric form, $\Lambda'$ is real analytic with $\Lambda''>0$ and
range $(-1,1)$ by \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-second}--\eqref{p10:eq:gradient-range},
so for $\AbsoluteValue x<1$ the saddle equation \eqref{p10:eq:saddle-equation}
has exactly one solution $\theta_x$, and by the implicit function theorem
$x\mapsto\theta_x$ is real analytic on $(-1,1)$ with
$\theta_x'=1/\Lambda''(\theta_x)$.  The concave function
$\theta\mapsto\theta x-\Lambda(\theta)$ has its maximum at its unique critical
point $\theta_x$, giving $I(x)=\theta_xx-\Lambda(\theta_x)$; differentiating,
$I'(x)=\theta_x+\theta_x'\bigl(x-\Lambda'(\theta_x)\bigr)=\theta_x$ and
$I''(x)=\theta_x'=1/\Lambda''(\theta_x)>0$, which is
\eqref{p10:eq:rate-parametric} and the strict convexity of $I$ on $(-1,1)$.
Outside $[-1,1]$ the rate is infinite by support.  At $x=1$,
$\theta-\Lambda(\theta)\to\infty$ as $\theta\to\infty$ by the expansion
\eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-large} proved in \cref{p10:thm:Lambert-edge}; hence
$I(1)=\infty$, and similarly at $-1$.
\end{proof}

Part~XI proves the same principle on its own compact scale, and the two
statements are exact transcriptions of one another rather than two theorems.
By \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}, $X_q=2\GeoLawCentered q$, so the standardized
variable $X_q/\sigma_q$, with $\sigma_q$ as in \eqref{p10:eq:variance}, is
$\GeoLawStandard q$, which is Part~XI's $Z_h$ at $h=\delta$; by
\eqref{p10:eq:variance-delta},
$\sqrt\delta/\sigma_q=\sqrt6\,(1+O(\delta^2))$, so Part~XI's compact variable
$Y_h=\sqrt\delta\,Z_h$ of \eqref{p11:eq:Yh} is
$\sqrt6\,X_{\EulerE^{-\delta}}(1+O(\delta^2))$.  Accordingly
\cref{p11:thm:compact-ldp} is the present theorem after $y=\sqrt6\,x$: the
two speeds $1/h$ and $1/\delta$ coincide, the transforms are related by
$\Lambda_{\mathrm{XI}}(s)=\Lambda(\sqrt6\,s)$, because
\eqref{p11:eq:Lambda-J} reads $\Lambda_{\mathrm{XI}}(s)=J(\sqrt6\,s)$ and
$J=\Lambda$ by \cref{p10:prop:CLambda-closed}, and the rate functions by
$I_{\mathrm{XI}}(y)=I(y/\sqrt6)$; in particular
\eqref{p10:eq:gradient-range} becomes the range $(-\sqrt6,\sqrt6)$ of
\eqref{p11:eq:rate-support}, and \eqref{p10:eq:I-center-series} becomes
\eqref{p11:eq:I-center-series}.  Under the same substitution the parametric
identities \eqref{p10:eq:rate-parametric} are \cref{p11:thm:rate-parametric}:
the saddle $\theta_x$ of \eqref{p10:eq:saddle-equation} is Part~XI's $a$, the
level is $y(a)=\sqrt6\,\ell(a)/a$ of \eqref{p11:eq:y-a}, and
$I(x)=\theta_xx-\Lambda(\theta_x)$ is \eqref{p11:eq:I-parametric}.  Both
coordinates are carried by the volume on purpose: the present one has
support $[-1,1]$ and is the one used in \cref{p10:sec:Lambert} and
\cref{p10:sec:matching}, while Part~XI's has support
$[-\sqrt6,\sqrt6]$ and is the one in which its Edgeworth matching is stated.

Thus for regular sets $A$ the logarithmic probability scale is
\begin{equation}
 \Probability\{X_q\in A\}
 =\exp\left[-\frac{\inf_{x\in A}I(x)+o(1)}{-\log q}\right].
 \label{p10:eq:LDP-heuristic}
\end{equation}
This is a parameter-concentration law, not the fixed-$q$ spatial endpoint
asymptotic already developed in the corpus.

\subsection{Central rate series}

The inverse saddle map in \eqref{p10:eq:saddle-equation} is analytic at zero.
Series reversion gives
\begin{align}
 \theta_x={}&6x+\frac{36}{5}x^3+\frac{1656}{175}x^5
 +\frac{9504}{875}x^7+\frac{709344}{67375}x^9
 +\frac{18086976}{1990625}x^{11}
 +O(x^{13}),
 \label{p10:eq:theta-center-series}\\
 I(x)={}&3x^2+\frac95x^4+\frac{276}{175}x^6
 +\frac{1188}{875}x^8+\frac{354672}{336875}x^{10}
 +\frac{1507248}{1990625}x^{12}
 +O(x^{14}).
 \label{p10:eq:I-center-series}
\end{align}
All displayed coefficients are positive, and the companion symbolic script
checks positivity through the $x^{16}$ coefficient.  The pattern does not
persist.

\begin{remark}[Sign pattern and radius of the rate series]
\label{p10:rem:rate-signs}
Write $I(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}c_nx^{2n}$.  The absorbed report conjectured that
every $c_n$ is strictly positive.  That conjecture is \emph{false}: exact
rational reversion of \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-Bernoulli}, carried out for this
volume to order $x^{28}$ and reproducing the eight coefficients of the appendix,
gives $c_9,c_{10},c_{11}>0$ but
\begin{gather*}
 c_{12}=-\frac{3032147123502547968}{3562005918173828125}
 =-0.85124707\ldots,\\
 c_{13}=-\frac{58363635922427846541312}{89139198102300048828125}
 =-0.65474715\ldots,
\end{gather*}
while $c_{14}>0$ again; the values are listed in the appendix.  The sign of
$c_{12}$ was confirmed independently of the series arithmetic by evaluating
$I$ from its exact saddle at sixty digits: at $x=0.3$ the residual
$I(x)-\sum_{n\le11}c_nx^{2n}=-2.514\times10^{-13}$ agrees with
$c_{12}x^{24}+c_{13}x^{26}+c_{14}x^{28}=-2.526\times10^{-13}$ to the size of the
first omitted term.  Convexity of $I$ is of course unaffected.

The radius of convergence $R_I$ of the series is positive, because $\theta_x$
is the analytic inverse of $\Lambda'$ at a point where $\Lambda''\ne0$, and
$R_I\le1$, because $I$ is real analytic on $(-1,1)$ and $I(x)\to\infty$ as
$x\uparrow1$ (\cref{p10:thm:Lambert-edge}), whereas a radius larger than $1$
would make the series bounded near $x=1$.  The fourteen computed values of
$c_n^{1/(2n)}$ lie between $0.92$ and $1.74$ and cluster near $1$, consistent
with $R_I=1$; the exact value is not determined here, and because the signs
alternate irregularly Pringsheim's theorem does not apply.
\end{remark}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/fabius_q_frontiers_report/figures/rate_function_lambert.pdf}
\caption{The exact parametric rate $I(x)$, its rational center expansion, and
the Lambert-$W_{-1}$ boundary approximation.  The latter is already visually
indistinguishable from the exact curve for $x\gtrsim0.8$.}
\label{p10:fig:rate}
\end{figure}

\section{Lambert-\texorpdfstring{$W_{-1}$}{W(-1)} behavior at the rate boundary}
\label{p10:sec:Lambert}

The fixed-base Fabius endpoint theory uses Lambert $W$ to invert flat spatial
tails.  The rate function develops a second, conceptually different Lambert
mechanism: the saddle parameter diverges as the deviation level approaches
the fixed support boundary.

\subsection{Asymptotics of the limiting transform}

For $u>0$,
\begin{equation}
 g(u)=u-\log(2u)+\log(1-\EulerE^{-2u}).
 \label{p10:eq:g-large}
\end{equation}
Define the convergent constant
\begin{equation}
 \cL=
 \int_0^1\frac{\log(\sinh u/u)}{u}\Differential u-1
 +\int_1^\infty\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-2u})}{u}\Differential u.
 \label{p10:eq:CLambda}
\end{equation}
Numerically,
\begin{equation}
 \cL=-0.96892042396303131827115715418362428628\ldots.
 \label{p10:eq:CLambda-value}
\end{equation}

The constant \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda} is not a new transcendental.  Throughout,
Bernoulli numbers are those of \eqref{p0:eq:bernoulli}, so that
\eqref{p10:eq:logsinhc-series} holds, and $\gamma_1$ denotes the \emph{first
Stieltjes constant} in the convention fixed by Part~XI in
\eqref{p11:eq:stieltjes-convention}, namely the one in which
$\zeta(1+s)=s^{-1}+\gamma-\gamma_1s+O(s^2)$; in that convention
$\gamma_1=-0.0728158454836767248605\ldots$.

\begin{proposition}[Closed form of the endpoint constant]
\label{p10:prop:CLambda-closed}
The limiting transform \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda} is Part~XI's transform $J$ of
\eqref{p11:eq:ell-J}: one has $\Lambda=J$ on all of $\RealNumbers$.  The
constant \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda} has the closed form
\begin{equation}
 \cL=\mathfrak C-\frac{(\log2)^2}{2}
    =\gamma_1+\frac{\gamma^2}{2}-\frac{\pi^2}{12}-\frac{(\log2)^2}{2},
 \label{p10:eq:CLambda-closed}
\end{equation}
where $\gamma$ is Euler's constant, $\gamma_1$ is the first Stieltjes
constant of \eqref{p11:eq:stieltjes-convention}, and $\mathfrak C$ is the
renormalized Mellin constant \eqref{p11:eq:Cstar} of Part~XI.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The integrand of \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda} is $g(u)/u$ with $g=\log\sinhc$ from
\eqref{p10:eq:gdef}, and Part~XI's $\ell$ in \eqref{p11:eq:ell-J} is the same
function of the same variable.  Hence
$\Lambda(\theta)=\int_0^\theta g(u)u^{-1}\Differential u
 =\int_0^\theta\ell(v)v^{-1}\Differential v=J(\theta)$, both sides being even.

For the constant, substitute $x=2u$, under which $\Differential u/u
=\Differential x/x$.  By \eqref{p10:eq:g-large},
\[
 \int_0^1\frac{g(u)}{u}\Differential u
 =1+\int_0^1\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-2u})-\log(2u)}{u}\Differential u
 =1+\int_0^2\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\Differential x,
\]
while the second integral of \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda} becomes
$\int_2^\infty\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})x^{-1}\Differential x$.  The two occurrences
of $1$ in \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda} cancel, so
\begin{equation}
 \cL=\int_0^2\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\Differential x
     +\int_2^\infty\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})}{x}\Differential x .
 \label{p10:eq:CLambda-halved}
\end{equation}
This is \eqref{p11:eq:Cstar-integral} with the splitting point $2$ in place
of $1$, and the two differ by an elementary integral:
\[
 \mathfrak C-\cL
 =\int_1^2\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})}{x}\Differential x
  -\int_1^2\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\Differential x
 =\int_1^2\frac{\log x}{x}\Differential x
 =\frac{(\log2)^2}{2}.
\]
\cref{p11:lem:J-asymptotic} identifies $\mathfrak C$ with the finite part of
$-\Gamma(s)\zeta(s+1)$ at $s=0$, computed there from
\eqref{p11:eq:mellin-log1mexp} and \eqref{p11:eq:stieltjes-convention} as
\eqref{p11:eq:mellin-finite-part}, giving
$\mathfrak C=\gamma_1+\tfrac12\gamma^2-\tfrac1{12}\pi^2$.  This proves
\eqref{p10:eq:CLambda-closed}.

The same statement read through the two logarithmic variables explains why a
$(\log2)^2$ appears at all.  \cref{p11:lem:J-asymptotic} expands $J$ in
$L=\log(2a)$, giving $J(\theta)=\theta-\tfrac12L^2+\mathfrak C
+O(\EulerE^{-2\theta}/\theta)$, whereas \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-large} expands the
same function in $\log\theta$.  Since
$\tfrac12L^2=\tfrac12(\log\theta)^2+(\log2)\log\theta+\tfrac12(\log2)^2$, the
elementary terms agree and the constants must differ by exactly
$\tfrac12(\log2)^2$, the additive constant of such an expansion being unique
because $\theta$, $(\log\theta)^2$, $\log\theta$ and $1$ are asymptotically
independent and the remainder vanishes.
\end{proof}

Numerically \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda-closed} reproduces
\eqref{p10:eq:CLambda-value}: by \eqref{p11:eq:Cstar},
$\mathfrak C=-0.72869391700393060593\ldots$, and subtracting
$\tfrac12(\log2)^2=0.24022650695910071233\ldots$ gives
$-0.96892042396303131827\ldots$.  The closed form and the two absolutely
convergent integrals of \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda} were evaluated independently
to sixty decimal places and agree to that precision.

\begin{theorem}[Transform and saddle endpoint]
\label{p10:thm:Lambert-edge}
As $\theta\to+\infty$,
\begin{align}
 \Lambda(\theta)
 &=\theta-\frac12(\log\theta)^2
   -(\log2)\log\theta+\cL
   +O\!\left(\frac{\EulerE^{-2\theta}}{\theta}\right),
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-large}\\
 1-\Lambda'(\theta)
 &=\frac{\log(2\theta)}{\theta}
   +O\!\left(\frac{\EulerE^{-2\theta}}{\theta}\right).
 \label{p10:eq:Lambda-prime-large}
\end{align}
Let $\eta=1-x\downarrow0$ and
\begin{equation}
 \theta_0(\eta)=-\frac1\eta W_{-1}(-\eta/2).
 \label{p10:eq:theta-Lambert}
\end{equation}
Then, with $L_\eta=\log\theta_0(\eta)$, the exact saddle satisfies, for
$0<\eta\le\tfrac12$,
\begin{equation}
 \theta_{1-\eta}=\theta_0(\eta)\,(1+\varepsilon_\eta),
 \qquad
 0<\varepsilon_\eta\le
 \frac{2\,\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(\eta)}}{\bigl(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(\eta)}\bigr)L_\eta},
 \label{p10:eq:theta-Lambert-error}
\end{equation}
in particular $\theta_{1-\eta}=\theta_0(\eta)\bigl(1+O(\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(\eta)}/L_\eta)\bigr)$,
and
\begin{equation}
 I(1-\eta)
 =\frac12L_\eta^2+(\log2-1)L_\eta
   -\log2-\cL+O\bigl(\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(\eta)}\bigr),
 \label{p10:eq:I-Lambert}
\end{equation}
the remainder being at most $4\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(\eta)}$ in absolute value for
$0<\eta\le\tfrac12$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Integrate \eqref{p10:eq:g-large} from $1$ to $\theta$.  The elementary terms give
$\theta-\frac12(\log\theta)^2-(\log2)\log\theta$, while the two convergent
remainders combine exactly into \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda}, leaving the tail
\[
 T(\theta)\DefinitionEquals\int_\theta^\infty\frac{-\log(1-\EulerE^{-2u})}{u}\Differential u,
 \qquad
 0<T(\theta)\le\frac{\EulerE^{-2\theta}}{2\theta\,(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta})},
\]
so that $\Lambda(\theta)=\theta-\frac12(\log\theta)^2-(\log2)\log\theta+\cL+T(\theta)$
exactly; this is \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-large}, and dividing
\eqref{p10:eq:g-large} by $\theta$ gives \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-prime-large}.

For $\theta>0$ the saddle equation $1-\eta=\Lambda'(\theta)=g(\theta)/\theta$
is, by \eqref{p10:eq:g-large}, equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 \eta\theta=\log(2\theta)-\log(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta}).
 \label{p10:eq:edge-saddle-exact}
\end{equation}
Dropping the exponentially small last term yields
$\eta\theta=\log(2\theta)$, equivalent to
$(-\eta\theta)\EulerE^{-\eta\theta}=-\eta/2$.  The diverging positive solution is
\eqref{p10:eq:theta-Lambert} on branch $W_{-1}$ \cite{bib:corless1996}; it is a
decreasing function of $\eta$ with $\theta_0(\tfrac12)=4.3065\ldots$, so
$\theta_0\ge4$ for $0<\eta\le\tfrac12$.

\emph{The displacement.}  Write $\theta=\theta_0(1+\varepsilon)$ and use
$\eta\theta_0=\log(2\theta_0)$: equation \eqref{p10:eq:edge-saddle-exact} becomes
\[
 h(\varepsilon)\DefinitionEquals\varepsilon\log(2\theta_0)-\log(1+\varepsilon)
 =r(\varepsilon)\DefinitionEquals-\log\bigl(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0(1+\varepsilon)}\bigr).
\]
For $\varepsilon\ge0$ the left side is increasing (its derivative is
$\log(2\theta_0)-(1+\varepsilon)^{-1}>0$ because $\log(2\theta_0)>1$) with
$h(0)=0$, while $r$ is positive and decreasing; hence $h-r$ increases
strictly from $-r(0)<0$ to $+\infty$ on $[0,\infty)$ and has exactly one zero
$\varepsilon_\eta>0$ there.  Since \eqref{p10:eq:edge-saddle-exact} has the
unique solution $\theta_{1-\eta}$, this zero is it, which gives the positivity
in \eqref{p10:eq:theta-Lambert-error}.  For the upper bound,
$\log(1+\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon$ gives
$\varepsilon_\eta\bigl(\log(2\theta_0)-1\bigr)\le h(\varepsilon_\eta)
 =r(\varepsilon_\eta)\le r(0)\le\EulerE^{-2\theta_0}/(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0})$,
and $\log(2\theta_0)-1=L_\eta+\log2-1\ge L_\eta/2$ as soon as
$L_\eta\ge2(1-\log2)$, i.e.\ $\theta_0\ge1.85$, which holds for
$\eta\le\tfrac12$.

\emph{The edge law.}  Put $\theta_x=\theta_{1-\eta}$ and $x=1-\eta$.  By
\eqref{p10:eq:rate-parametric} and the exact form of \eqref{p10:eq:Lambda-large},
\[
 I(1-\eta)=\theta_xx-\Lambda(\theta_x)
 =-\eta\theta_x+\frac12(\log\theta_x)^2+(\log2)\log\theta_x-\cL-T(\theta_x),
\]
and substituting \eqref{p10:eq:edge-saddle-exact} for $\eta\theta_x$,
\[
 I(1-\eta)=\frac12(\log\theta_x)^2+(\log2-1)\log\theta_x-\log2-\cL
 +\log\bigl(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_x}\bigr)-T(\theta_x),
\]
an identity with no error term.  The last two terms are together at most
$\bigl(1+\tfrac1{2\theta_0}\bigr)\EulerE^{-2\theta_0}/(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0})$ in
absolute value, since $\theta_x\ge\theta_0$.  Finally
$\log\theta_x=L_\eta+\log(1+\varepsilon_\eta)$ with
$0<\log(1+\varepsilon_\eta)\le\varepsilon_\eta$, so replacing $\theta_x$ by
$\theta_0$ in the two elementary terms changes them by
$\bigl(L_\eta+\log2-1+\tfrac12\log(1+\varepsilon_\eta)\bigr)\log(1+\varepsilon_\eta)
 \le L_\eta\varepsilon_\eta
 \le2\EulerE^{-2\theta_0}/(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0})$
by \eqref{p10:eq:theta-Lambert-error}.  Adding the two bounds gives a
remainder of at most $(3+\tfrac1{2\theta_0})\EulerE^{-2\theta_0}/(1-\EulerE^{-2\theta_0})
 \le4\EulerE^{-2\theta_0}$ for $\theta_0\ge4$, which is \eqref{p10:eq:I-Lambert}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Double logarithmic geometry]
\label{p10:rem:double-log}
The standard branch expansion gives
\[
 -W_{-1}(-\eta/2)
 =\log(2/\eta)+\log\log(2/\eta)+o(1),
\]
and consequently
\[
 L_\eta=\log(1/\eta)+\log\log(1/\eta)
 +o(\log\log(1/\eta)).
\]
Thus the rate diverges primarily like $\tfrac12\log^2(1/\eta)$,
with a forced $\log(1/\eta)\log\log(1/\eta)$ correction.  This is the parameter-LDP
counterpart of the log-squared endpoint structures elsewhere in the
Fabius--Rvachev theory.
\end{remark}

The edge law \eqref{p10:eq:I-Lambert} is \cref{p11:thm:rate-edge} written in
the coordinate of this part.  The edge parameters agree, because
$y=\sqrt6\,x$ turns Part~XI's $1-y/\sqrt6$ into $\eta=1-x$, and Part~XI's
Lambert variable \eqref{p11:eq:wdelta} is, by \eqref{p10:eq:theta-Lambert}
and $\eta\theta_0=\log(2\theta_0)$,
\[
 w(\eta)=-W_{-1}(-\eta/2)=\eta\,\theta_0(\eta)=\log\bigl(2\theta_0(\eta)\bigr)
 =L_\eta+\log2 .
\]
Substituting this together with \eqref{p10:eq:CLambda-closed} into
\eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-main} returns \eqref{p10:eq:I-Lambert} identically:
\[
 \tfrac12w(\eta)^2-w(\eta)-\mathfrak C
 =\tfrac12L_\eta^2+(\log2-1)L_\eta-\log2
  +\tfrac12(\log2)^2-\mathfrak C
 =\tfrac12L_\eta^2+(\log2-1)L_\eta-\log2-\cL .
\]
Part~XI's \eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-a} states the same exponentially small error
at the exact saddle $a=\theta_{1-\eta}$; \eqref{p10:eq:I-Lambert} carries it
over to the Lambert approximation $\theta_0(\eta)$ through the explicit
displacement bound \eqref{p10:eq:theta-Lambert-error}, at the price of the
constant $4$.

\section{Uniform all-orders Edgeworth expansion for \texorpdfstring{$q\uparrow1$}{q tends to 1}}
\label{p10:sec:Edgeworth}

\subsection{Standardized infinite-sinc product}

Set
\begin{equation}
 Z_q=\frac{X_q}{\sigma_q},
 \qquad b_q=\frac{1-q}{\sigma_q}=\sqrt{3(1-q^2)}.
 \label{p10:eq:Zq-bq}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \chi_q(t):=\Expectation \EulerE^{itZ_q}
 =\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad(b_qq^jt).
 \label{p10:eq:standardized-cf}
\end{equation}
This standardized layer is shared with Part~XI, and the two parts use the
same variable, not merely proportional ones.  Indeed $X_q=2\GeoLawCentered q$
by \cref{p0:tab:dictionary}, so $\sigma_q$ of \eqref{p10:eq:variance} is
twice the canonical standard deviation and $Z_q=\GeoLawStandard q$; with
$r=q=\EulerE^{-\delta}$ and $h=\delta$ this is exactly Part~XI's $Z_h$ of
\eqref{p11:eq:h-r-sigma-Z}.  Consequently $b_q=a_h=\sqrt{3(1-q^2)}$ and
$\chi_q=\Psi_h$ of \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-product}, and everything proved in
\cref{p11:sec:edgeworth} applies to $\chi_q$ verbatim after the substitution
$h=\delta$.

Let $\lambda_n(q)$ be the standardized cumulants of $Z_q$.  From
\eqref{p10:eq:Xq-cumulants}, for $m\ge2$,
\begin{align}
 \lambda_{2m}(q)
 &=\frac{3^m2^{2m-1}B_{2m}}{m}
   \frac{(1-q^2)^m}{1-q^{2m}}
 \label{p10:eq:lambda-q}\\
 &=\frac{3^m2^{3m-2}B_{2m}}{m}
   \frac{\sinh^m\delta}{\sinh(m\delta)},
 \qquad q=\EulerE^{-\delta}.
 \label{p10:eq:lambda-delta}
\end{align}
Therefore $\lambda_{2m}=O(\delta^{m-1})$.  Both forms are
\cref{p11:prop:exact-cumulants}, where they are proved; they are repeated
here because the hyperbolic parity of \eqref{p10:eq:lambda-delta} is read off
below.  The first values are
\begin{align}
 \lambda_4&=-\frac65\tanh\delta
 =-\frac65\delta+\frac25\delta^3+O(\delta^5),
 \label{p10:eq:lambda4}\\
 \lambda_6&=\frac{64}{7}\delta^2-\frac{64}{7}\delta^4+O(\delta^6),
 \label{p10:eq:lambda6}\\
 \lambda_8&=-\frac{864}{5}\delta^3+\frac{1728}{5}\delta^5+O(\delta^7).
 \label{p10:eq:lambda8}
\end{align}

\subsection{Weighted Hermite polynomial}

Let $H_n$ denote the probabilists' Hermite polynomials,
$\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\EulerE^{-x^2/2}$, and let a multi-index
$\bm{k}=(k_2,k_3,\ldots)$ have Edgeworth weight and Hermite degree
% ed.: the absorbed source typeset this weight with the corpus binary
% digit-sum macro, which means wt_2 and is used with that meaning in
% Parts I--IV and VII of this volume.  The local letter w of Part XI's
% weight display replaces it here.
\begin{equation}
 w(\bm{k})=\sum_{m\ge2}(m-1)k_m,
 \qquad
 |\bm{k}|_*=\sum_{m\ge2}mk_m.
 \label{p10:eq:edgeworth-weight}
\end{equation}
For $R\ge0$ define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E_{R,q}(x)=
 \sum_{w(\bm{k})\le R}
 H_{2|\bm{k}|_*}(x)
 \prod_{m\ge2}\frac1{k_m!}
 \left(\frac{\lambda_{2m}(q)}{(2m)!}\right)^{k_m}.
 \label{p10:eq:edgeworth-polynomial}
\end{equation}
Only finitely many indices contribute.  Keeping exact finite-$q$ cumulants is
useful: it automatically resums many higher powers of $\delta$.  The weight
$w$ and the degree $|\bm{k}|_*$ are Part~XI's $w$ and $\nu$ of
\eqref{p11:eq:weights}, so \eqref{p10:eq:edgeworth-polynomial} is
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial} at $h=\delta$:
$\mathcal E_{R,q}=\mathcal E_{R,h}$.

\subsection{Global Fourier bounds}

\begin{remark}[Geometric infinite-sinc tails]
\label{p10:lem:sinc-tail}
The global frequency control needed below is proved once, in Part~XI, for the
very same product: by \eqref{p10:eq:standardized-cf} and
\cref{p0:tab:dictionary} one has $\chi_q=\Psi_h$ at $h=\delta$, so
\cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope} applies verbatim.  In the letters of this part
it gives, for each $q_0\in(0,1)$ and each integer $L\ge0$, positive constants
$c,C_L$ such that for $q_0\le q<1$
\begin{equation}
 |\chi_q(t)|\le
 \begin{cases}
   \EulerE^{-ct^2},& |t|\le b_q^{-1},\\[1mm]
   C_L\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{c}{1-q}\right)
   (1+b_q|t|)^{-L},& |t|\ge b_q^{-1}.
 \end{cases}
 \label{p10:eq:sinc-tail-bound}
\end{equation}
The first line is \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-envelope} together with the exact
identity \eqref{p11:eq:S-gaussian}, which is where the normalization
$\sum_{j\ge0}(b_qq^j)^2=3$ enters; the exponential factor on the second line
is \eqref{p11:eq:S-outer} combined with $1-q^2\asymp\delta$; and the
polynomial factor is the elementary bound $|\SincRad u|\le|u|^{-1}$ applied
to the first $L$ factors of the product.  \Cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope} is
strictly stronger than \eqref{p10:eq:sinc-tail-bound} in two respects that
the sup-norm statement below does not display: it bounds every fixed
frequency derivative $\partial_t^{\,p}\Psi_h$, which is what a
Schwartz-seminorm conclusion needs, and on the outer zone the proof of
\cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} sharpens the tail to
$\EulerE^{-c/\delta}(1+|t|)^{-N}$ for every prescribed $N$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The differentiated theorem}

\begin{remark}[Continuous-parameter Edgeworth expansion]
\label{p10:thm:Edgeworth}
The differentiated Edgeworth expansion this part uses is the sup-norm
specialization of the theorem proved in Part~XI, and the volume states it
only once.  Since $Z_q$ is Part~XI's $Z_h$ at $h=\delta$ and
$\mathcal E_{R,q}=\mathcal E_{R,h}$, \cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} with
$j=r$ and $K=0$ reads: writing $f_q$ for the density of $Z_q$, for every pair
of nonnegative integers $R$ and $r$ there exist $q_{R,r}<1$ and
$C_{R,r}<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}
 \left|
 f_q^{(r)}(x)-
 \frac{\Differential^r}{\Differential x^r}
 \bigl[\phi(x)\mathcal E_{R,q}(x)\bigr]
 \right|
 \le C_{R,r}\,\delta^{R+1},
 \qquad q_{R,r}<q<1,
 \label{p10:eq:Edgeworth-theorem}
\end{equation}
where $\delta=-\log q$.  Part~XI's \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-main} is strictly
stronger, since it carries an arbitrary fixed polynomial weight $(1+|x|)^K$
alongside the $r$ spatial derivatives; \eqref{p10:eq:Edgeworth-theorem} is
its $K=0$ corollary.

One ingredient deserves to be named, because the report absorbed into this
part used it as an assumption rather than proving it.  Its low-frequency step
was the expansion
\[
 \log\chi_q(t)
 =-\frac{t^2}{2}
 +\sum_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac{\lambda_{2m}(q)}{(2m)!}(it)^{2m}
 +\rho_{R,q}(t),
 \qquad
 |\rho_{R,q}(t)|\le C_R\delta^{R+1}\bigl(1+|t|^{2R+4}\bigr),
\]
with the frequency window on which it holds left to be arranged afterwards.
Nothing in this volume rests on that as an assumption: the estimate is
\cref{p11:lem:cumulant-remainder}, proved there on the explicit window
$b_q|t|\le\varepsilon_0$ for any fixed $\varepsilon_0<\pi$, and for every
fixed frequency derivative, as \eqref{p11:eq:logpsi-trunc} and
\eqref{p11:eq:rho-bound} at $h=\delta$.  (Part~XI writes $\delta$ for that
frequency-split constant; it is unrelated to the $\delta=-\log q$ of this
part, which is why it is called $\varepsilon_0$ here.)  The global envelope
that accompanies it is \cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}, quoted above as
\eqref{p10:eq:sinc-tail-bound}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{First explicit corrections}

Expanding the exact-cumulant form in the natural variable $\delta$ gives
\begin{equation}
 f_q(x)=\phi(x)
 \left[1+\delta Q_1(x)+\delta^2Q_2(x)+\delta^3Q_3(x)
 +O_{C^r}(\delta^4)\right],
 \label{p10:eq:explicit-edgeworth}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align}
 Q_1&=-\frac1{20}H_4,
 \label{p10:eq:Q1}\\
 Q_2&=\frac4{315}H_6+\frac1{800}H_8,
 \label{p10:eq:Q2}\\
 Q_3&=\frac1{60}H_4-\frac3{700}H_8
      -\frac1{1575}H_{10}-\frac1{48000}H_{12}.
 \label{p10:eq:Q3}
\end{align}
The absence of an $H_4$ term in $Q_2$ and of an $H_6$ term in $Q_3$ reflects
the hyperbolic parity visible in \eqref{p10:eq:lambda-delta}.  If one instead
uses $1-q$ as the small parameter, these cancellations are obscured by the
change of variables.  The same three orders appear in Part~XI as
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-three-orders}, written in $h=\delta$ and with the
remainder measured in every fixed Schwartz seminorm; the parity reading above
is what this part adds to them.

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/fabius_q_frontiers_report/figures/edgeworth_errors.pdf}
\caption{Sup-norm density errors from direct Fourier inversion.  Fitted
slopes $1.02$, $2.05$, $3.07$, and $4.10$ agree with
\eqref{p10:eq:Edgeworth-theorem} and \cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}.}
