\section{Preliminaries: Fabius, Rvachev, and the geometric \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-family}\label{p11:sec:prelim}

\subsection{Random-series identities}
Write \(V_n=U_n-1/2\), so that \(V_n\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1/2,1/2]\).  Then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:centered-X}
 X_r-\frac12=(1-r)\sum_{n\ge0}r^nV_n.
\end{equation}
The variance follows immediately:
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:variance}
 \sigma_r^2=\frac{(1-r)^2}{12}\sum_{n\ge0}r^{2n}
 =\frac{1-r}{12(1+r)}.
\end{equation}
The moment generating function of \(V_n\) is \(\sinh(t/2)/(t/2)\), while its characteristic function is \(\SincRad(t/2)=\sin(t/2)/(t/2)\).  Hence the standardized characteristic function is
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Psi-product}
 \Psi_h(t)=\Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit tZ_h}
 =\prod_{n=0}^{\infty}\SincRad\!\left(a_hr^nt\right),
 \qquad
 a_h=\sqrt{3(1-r^2)},\quad r=\EulerE^{-h}.
\end{equation}
The normalization is exact because
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:quadratic-sum}
 \sum_{n\ge0}(a_hr^n)^2=3.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Smoothness and Fourier conventions}
We use
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:fourier-convention}
 \FourierAngular{f}(-t)=\int_{\RealNumbers}\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit tx}f(x)\,\Differential x,
 \qquad
 f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}\FourierAngular{f}(-t)\,\Differential t.
\end{equation}
For every fixed \(h>0\), the product \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-product} decays faster than every negative power, and therefore \(Z_h\) has a compactly supported \(C^\infty\) density \(f_h\) \cite{bib:jessen1935,bib:arias1982}.  A quantitative version is proved in \Cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}.

The probabilists' Hermite polynomials are
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Hermite}
 H_n(x)=(-1)^n\EulerE^{x^2/2}\frac{\Differential^n}{\Differential x^n}\EulerE^{-x^2/2},
 \qquad
 \phiN(x)=\frac{\EulerE^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.
\end{equation}
Thus \(\phiN^{(n)}=(-1)^nH_n\phiN\), and Fourier inversion in the
positive-exponent convention \eqref{p11:eq:fourier-convention} gives
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:hermite-inversion}
 \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}
 \EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}(\ImaginaryUnit t)^n\EulerE^{-t^2/2}\,\Differential t
 =H_n(x)\phiN(x).
\end{equation}

\subsection{Cumulants of a centered uniform variable}
With Bernoulli numbers defined by
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:bernoulli-generating}
 \frac{z}{\EulerE^z-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}B_n\frac{z^n}{n!},
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:uniform-cumulants}
 \log\frac{\sinh(z/2)}{z/2}
 =\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\frac{z^{2m}}{(2m)!},
 \qquad \AbsoluteValue z<2\pi.
\end{equation}
Accordingly, the \(2m\)-th cumulant of \(V_n\) is \(B_{2m}/(2m)\), and all odd cumulants vanish.

\section{Exact cumulants and the Bernoulli--Bell bridge}\label{p11:sec:cumulants}

\begin{proposition}[Exact standardized cumulants]\label{p11:prop:exact-cumulants}
For every \(m\ge2\), the standardized cumulant of order \(2m\) of \(Z_h\) is
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:lambda-r}
 \lambda_{2m}(r)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,12^m
  \frac{(1-r^2)^m}{1-r^{2m}}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for \(r=\EulerE^{-h}\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:lambda-h-hyperbolic}
 \boxed{
 \lambda_{2m}(h)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,12^m2^{m-1}
  \frac{\sinh^m h}{\sinh(mh)}.}
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\lambda_{2m}(h)=\BigO(h^{m-1})\) as \(h\downarrow0\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Cumulants add under independent summation and scale homogeneously.  From \eqref{p11:eq:centered-X} and \eqref{p11:eq:uniform-cumulants},
\[
 \kappa_{2m}(X_r-1/2)
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}(1-r)^{2m}\sum_{n\ge0}r^{2mn}
 =\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\frac{(1-r)^{2m}}{1-r^{2m}}.
\]
Dividing by \(\sigma_r^{2m}\), with \eqref{p11:eq:variance}, proves \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-r}.  Since
\[
 1-\EulerE^{-2h}=2\EulerE^{-h}\sinh h,
 \qquad
 1-\EulerE^{-2mh}=2\EulerE^{-mh}\sinh(mh),
\]
the exponential factors cancel and give \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-h-hyperbolic}.  Finally \(\sinh^mh/\sinh(mh)\sim h^{m-1}/m\).
\end{proof}

The hyperbolic representation makes a second layer of structure visible.  Set
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ck-dmk}
 c_k=\frac{2^{2k-1}B_{2k}}{k(2k)!},
 \qquad
 d_{m,k}=c_k\bigl(m-m^{2k}\bigr).
\end{equation}
The classical identity
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:log-sinh}
 \log\frac{\sinh z}{z}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}c_kz^{2k},
 \qquad \AbsoluteValue z<\pi,
\end{equation}
turns every cumulant into an exponential Bell series.

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli--Bell expansion of every cumulant]\label{p11:thm:cumulant-bell}
Let \(Y_\ell\) denote the complete exponential Bell polynomial, characterized by
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:bell-def}
 \exp\!\left(\sum_{k\ge1}x_k\frac{z^k}{k!}\right)
 =\sum_{\ell\ge0}Y_\ell(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)\frac{z^\ell}{\ell!}.
\end{equation}
For \(m\ge2\), define
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Am}
 A_m=\frac{B_{2m}}{2m}\,12^m\frac{2^{m-1}}{m}.
\end{equation}
Then, for every \(h\) with \(0<h<\pi/m\),
\begin{align}
 \lambda_{2m}(h)
 &=A_mh^{m-1}
   \exp\!\left(\sum_{k\ge1}d_{m,k}h^{2k}\right)\label{p11:eq:lambda-exponential}\\
 &=A_mh^{m-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{Y_\ell(1!d_{m,1},2!d_{m,2},\ldots,\ell!d_{m,\ell})}{\ell!}
 h^{2\ell}.\label{p11:eq:lambda-bell}
\end{align}
Thus the complete continuous-parameter cumulant calculus is generated by Bernoulli numbers followed by one Bell-polynomial exponentiation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Rewrite \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-h-hyperbolic} as
\[
 \lambda_{2m}(h)=A_mh^{m-1}
 \left(\frac{\sinh h}{h}\right)^m\frac{mh}{\sinh(mh)}.
\]
Taking logarithms of the factor after \(A_mh^{m-1}\) and applying \eqref{p11:eq:log-sinh} gives
\[
 m\log\frac{\sinh h}{h}-\log\frac{\sinh(mh)}{mh}
 =\sum_{k\ge1}c_k(m-m^{2k})h^{2k},
\]
which is \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-exponential}.  Apply \eqref{p11:eq:bell-def} with \(z=h^2\) and \(x_k=k!d_{m,k}\).

The stated range is exact and cannot be replaced by a single interval
independent of \(m\).  By \Cref{p0:lem:log-sinhc} the series
\eqref{p11:eq:log-sinh} has radius exactly \(\pi\); it is applied here at the
two arguments \(h\) and \(mh\), and the second is the binding one, so
\eqref{p11:eq:lambda-exponential} and \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-bell} converge
precisely for \(0<h<\pi/m\).  The threshold degenerates as \(m\to\infty\),
which is harmless downstream: \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} and
\Cref{p11:prop:h-power-series} use \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-bell} only for
\(2\le m\le R+1\) with \(R\) fixed in advance, hence only for
\(0<h<\pi/(R+1)\).
\end{proof}

The first cumulants, useful later, are
\begin{align}
 \lambda_4(h)&=-\frac65\tanh h
 =-\frac65h+\frac25h^3-\frac4{25}h^5+\BigO(h^7),\label{p11:eq:lambda4}\\
 \lambda_6(h)&=\frac{192}{7}\frac{\sinh^3h}{\sinh3h}
 =\frac{64}{7}h^2-\frac{64}{7}h^4+\BigO(h^6),\label{p11:eq:lambda6}\\
 \lambda_8(h)&=-\frac{3456}{5}\frac{\sinh^4h}{\sinh4h}
 =-\frac{864}{5}h^3+\frac{1728}{5}h^5+\BigO(h^7).\label{p11:eq:lambda8}
\end{align}

\section{All-orders Edgeworth expansion in Schwartz seminorms}\label{p11:sec:edgeworth}

\subsection{The exact-cumulant Edgeworth polynomial}
For a multi-index \(\bm k=(k_2,\ldots,k_{R+1})\in\NaturalNumbers^R\), define its Edgeworth weight and Hermite degree by
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:weights}
 w(\bm k)=\sum_{m=2}^{R+1}(m-1)k_m,
 \qquad
 \nu(\bm k)=\sum_{m=2}^{R+1}mk_m.
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial}
 \mathcal E_{R,h}(x)=
 \sum_{\substack{\bm k\in\NaturalNumbers^R\\w(\bm k)\le R}}
 H_{2\nu(\bm k)}(x)
 \prod_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac1{k_m!}
 \left(\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)}{(2m)!}\right)^{k_m}.
\end{equation}
The zero multi-index contributes \(1\).  The polynomial uses the \emph{exact} cumulants, not their truncated power series.  This makes the theorem compact and automatically incorporates many higher-order parameter terms.

For integers \(j,K\ge0\), write
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:schwartz-seminorm}
 \Norm{g}_{j,K}=\sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}(1+\AbsoluteValue x)^K\AbsoluteValue{g^{(j)}(x)}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[All-orders continuous-parameter Edgeworth expansion]\label{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}
Fix integers \(R,j,K\ge0\).  There exist \(h_0>0\) and \(C_{R,j,K}<\infty\) such that, for \(0<h\le h_0\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:edgeworth-main}
 \boxed{
 \Norm{f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}}_{j,K}
 \le C_{R,j,K}h^{R+1}.}
\end{equation}
Consequently \(f_h\) has a complete asymptotic expansion in the Schwartz topology, and every coefficient is an explicit Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite polynomial.
\end{theorem}

Relative to the classical Edgeworth framework \cite{bib:bhattacharya2010,bib:petrov1975}, this theorem strengthens the usual local statement in three ways: it is uniform on all of \(\RealNumbers\), survives any fixed number of spatial derivatives, and carries arbitrary fixed polynomial weights.

The passage from the exact-cumulant polynomial \(\mathcal E_{R,h}\) to a
genuine power series in \(h\) --- which is what the last sentence of the
theorem asserts, and what the quantile expansion below consumes --- requires
re-expanding each \(\lambda_{2m}(h)\) and re-truncating.  That change of
remainder is estimated once, here.

\begin{proposition}[Re-expansion in powers of \(h\)]\label{p11:prop:h-power-series}
Let \(P_N\) be the polynomial defined by \eqref{p11:eq:coefficient-extraction}.
For every \(R\ge0\) the difference
\(\mathcal E_{R,h}-\sum_{N=0}^{R}h^NP_N\) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree at
most \(D_R=4R\), all of whose coefficients are \(\BigOAt{h^{R+1}}{R}\) as
\(h\downarrow0\).  Consequently, for all \(j,K\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:E-vs-power-series}
 \Norm{f_h-\phiN\sum_{N=0}^{R}h^NP_N}_{j,K}\le C_{R,j,K}h^{R+1},
\end{equation}
so \(f_h\) does have a complete asymptotic expansion in powers of \(h\) in
every Schwartz seminorm, with coefficients \(\phiN P_N\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The term of \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial} indexed by \(\bm k\) is
\[
 H_{2\nu(\bm k)}(x)\prod_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac1{k_m!}
 \left(\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)}{(2m)!}\right)^{k_m}.
\]
Its \(x\)-independent factor is real analytic in \(h\) on \(0<h<\pi/(R+1)\) by
\Cref{p11:thm:cumulant-bell}, and vanishes to order \(w(\bm k)\) at \(h=0\)
because \(\lambda_{2m}(h)=A_mh^{m-1}(1+\BigO(h^2))\).  Only the finitely many
\(\bm k\) with \(w(\bm k)\le R\) occur, so Taylor's theorem with remainder at
order \(R\), applied to each such coefficient function of \(h\), replaces every
coefficient by a polynomial in \(h\) of degree \(R\) up to
\(\BigOAt{h^{R+1}}{R}\).  The Hermite degrees are bounded by
\(2\nu(\bm k)=2\bigl(w(\bm k)+\sum_mk_m\bigr)\le4w(\bm k)\le4R\), because
\(m-1\ge1\) gives \(\sum_mk_m\le w(\bm k)\); this is \(D_R\).  That the
resulting coefficient of \(h^N\) equals \(P_N\) for every \(N\le R\),
independently of \(R\), is \eqref{p11:eq:coefficient-extraction}: multi-indices
with \(w(\bm k)\ge R+1\) cannot contribute to \(h^N\) with \(N\le R\).
Finally \(\Norm{\phiN\,x^{d}}_{j,K}<\infty\) for every \(d\le4R\), so
multiplying the coefficient bound by \(\phiN\) and adding
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-main} gives \eqref{p11:eq:E-vs-power-series}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Global sinc-product bounds}
The proof starts with a uniform frequency envelope.

\begin{lemma}[Global sinc envelope]\label{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}
The constant \(c=\tfrac16\) is admissible throughout.  First,
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:sinc-basic-envelope}
 \AbsoluteValue{\SincRad u}\le\exp\bigl(-c\min(u^2,1)\bigr),\qquad u\in\RealNumbers.
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Sht}
 S_h(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}\min\bigl((a_hr^nt)^2,1\bigr).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Psi-envelope}
 \AbsoluteValue{\Psi_h(t)}\le\EulerE^{-cS_h(t)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, with the same \(c\) and with \(A_h\) the support constant of
\eqref{p11:eq:standardized-support}, for every integer \(q\ge0\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Psi-derivative-envelope}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h(t)}
 \le\bigl(\EulerE^{c}A_h\bigr)^{q}\,\EulerE^{-cS_h(t)},
 \qquad
 A_h=\sum_{n\ge0}a_hr^n=\sqrt{3\coth(h/2)},
 \quad A_h\le\sqrt{\frac{13}{2h}}\ \ (0<h\le1).
\end{equation}
Since \(A_h\le\sqrt{13/(2h)}\), this implies the weaker form
\(\AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h}\le
 C_qh^{-q/2}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^q\EulerE^{-cS_h}\) in which the estimate is
quoted elsewhere; the sharper form carries no factor \((1+\AbsoluteValue t)^q\).
Finally, for any fixed \(0<\delta<1\) and with
\(c_\delta=\tfrac12\min(\delta^2,\EulerE^{-2})\),
\begin{align}
 S_h(t)&=3t^2,
 &&\AbsoluteValue t\le a_h^{-1},\label{p11:eq:S-gaussian}\\
 S_h(t)&\ge c_\delta h^{-1},
 &&\AbsoluteValue t\ge\delta a_h^{-1},\label{p11:eq:S-outer}\\
 S_h(t)&\ge\frac{\log(a_h\AbsoluteValue t)}{h}+\frac{\EulerE^{-2}}{2h},
 &&a_h\AbsoluteValue t\ge1,\ 0<h\le1.\label{p11:eq:S-power}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The scalar envelope.}  From the Euler product
\(\SincRad u=\prod_{k\ge1}\bigl(1-u^2/(k\pi)^2\bigr)\) and
\(\log(1-x)\le-x\),
\[
 \log\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad u}
 \le-\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{u^2}{k^2\pi^2}=-\frac{u^2}{6},
 \qquad\AbsoluteValue u<\pi,
\]
which gives \eqref{p11:eq:sinc-basic-envelope} with \(c=\tfrac16\) on
\(\AbsoluteValue u\le1\).  For \(\AbsoluteValue u\ge1\) the function
\(\SincRad\) decreases on \([1,\pi]\) and satisfies
\(\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad u}\le\AbsoluteValue u^{-1}\le\pi^{-1}\) beyond, so
\[
 \sup_{\AbsoluteValue u\ge1}\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad u}
 =\sin1=0.8414709\ldots<0.8464817\ldots=\EulerE^{-1/6},
\]
which is \eqref{p11:eq:sinc-basic-envelope} on \(\AbsoluteValue u\ge1\).
Multiplying the factors of \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-product} proves
\eqref{p11:eq:Psi-envelope}.

\emph{Derivatives.}  Write \(\alpha_n=a_hr^n\) and
\(\Psi_{h,N}(t)=\prod_{n<N}\SincRad(\alpha_nt)\).  By
\cref{p0:prop:products} the partial products converge to \(\Psi_h\) locally
uniformly on \(\ComplexNumbers\), and every \(\Psi_{h,N}\) is entire; by
Weierstrass' theorem \(\partial_t^q\Psi_{h,N}\to\partial_t^q\Psi_h\) locally
uniformly for every \(q\).  It therefore suffices to bound the partial
products uniformly in \(N\), and no interchange beyond this needs to be
assumed.  Since \(\SincRad u=\int_0^1\cos(us)\Differential s\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:sinc-derivative-sup}
 \Norm{\SincRad^{(m)}}_\infty\le\int_0^1s^m\Differential s=\frac1{m+1}\le1 .
\end{equation}
Applying the multinomial form of Leibniz's rule to a finite product --- which,
unlike the informal count ``one factor per differentiation'', allows several
derivatives to land on the same factor ---
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_{h,N}(t)}
 \le\sum_{\substack{(m_n)_{n<N}\in\NaturalNumbers^{N}\\ \sum_nm_n=q}}
   \frac{q!}{\prod_nm_n!}
   \prod_{n:\,m_n\ge1}\alpha_n^{m_n}
   \prod_{n:\,m_n=0}\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad(\alpha_nt)},
\]
where \eqref{p11:eq:sinc-derivative-sup} was used on each differentiated
factor.  At most \(q\) indices carry \(m_n\ge1\), and each index contributes at
most \(1\) to \(S_h\), so by \eqref{p11:eq:sinc-basic-envelope} the
undifferentiated block is at most
\(\EulerE^{cq}\EulerE^{-cS_h(t)}\).  What remains is the multinomial expansion
of \(\bigl(\sum_{n<N}\alpha_n\bigr)^q\).  Letting \(N\to\infty\) and using
\[
 \sum_{n\ge0}a_hr^n=\frac{a_h}{1-r}
 =\sqrt{\frac{3(1-r^2)}{(1-r)^2}}
 =\sqrt{\frac{3(1+r)}{1-r}}=\sqrt{3\coth(h/2)}=A_h
\]
gives \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-derivative-envelope}; and since \(x\coth x\) increases,
\(hA_h^2=3h\coth(h/2)\le3\coth(\tfrac12)=6.4918\ldots<\tfrac{13}2\) for
\(0<h\le1\).

\emph{Lower bounds for \(S_h\).}  If \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le1\), every term in
\eqref{p11:eq:Sht} is quadratic, so \eqref{p11:eq:quadratic-sum} gives
\eqref{p11:eq:S-gaussian}.  If
\(\delta a_h^{-1}\le\AbsoluteValue t\le a_h^{-1}\), then by
\eqref{p11:eq:S-gaussian}, \(a_h^2=3(1-r^2)\) and \(1-\EulerE^{-2h}\le2h\),
\[
 S_h(t)=3t^2\ge\frac{3\delta^2}{a_h^2}
 =\frac{\delta^2}{1-\EulerE^{-2h}}\ge\frac{\delta^2}{2h}\ge\frac{c_\delta}{h}.
\]
If \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t>1\), let \(n_1\ge1\) be least with
\(a_hr^{n_1}\AbsoluteValue t<1\); the indices \(n<n_1\) contribute exactly
\(1\) each, so \(S_h(t)\ge n_1>h^{-1}\log(a_h\AbsoluteValue t)\), while
\(a_hr^{n_1}\AbsoluteValue t\ge r\,a_hr^{n_1-1}\AbsoluteValue t\ge r\) makes
the quadratic tail
\[
 \sum_{n\ge n_1}(a_hr^n t)^2
 =\frac{(a_hr^{n_1}t)^2}{1-r^2}\ge\frac{r^2}{1-r^2}
 =\frac1{\EulerE^{2h}-1}\ge\frac{\EulerE^{-2h}}{2h}
 \qquad(\text{by }\EulerE^{x}-1\le x\EulerE^{x}).
\]
Adding the two blocks gives \eqref{p11:eq:S-power} for \(0<h\le1\).  It also
gives \eqref{p11:eq:S-outer} on this range for \(0<h\le1\), because
\(\EulerE^{-2h}/(2h)\ge\EulerE^{-2}/(2h)\ge c_\delta/h\); and for \(h>1\) one
has \(S_h(t)\ge1\ge h^{-1}\ge c_\delta h^{-1}\) since \(c_\delta<1\).  Thus
\eqref{p11:eq:S-outer} holds for every \(h>0\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Low-frequency cumulant control}
\begin{lemma}[Uniform cumulant remainder]\label{p11:lem:cumulant-remainder}
Fix \(R,q\ge0\) and \(0<\delta<\pi\).  Uniformly for \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:logpsi-trunc}
 \log\Psi_h(t)
 =-\frac{t^2}{2}
 +\sum_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)}{(2m)!}(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2m}
 +\rho_{R,h}(t),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:rho-bound}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\rho_{R,h}(t)}
 \le C_{R,q,\delta}h^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{2R+4}.
\end{equation}
The identity and the bound hold verbatim for complex \(t\) with
\(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta\), the logarithm being the principal branch;
only holomorphy of \(\log\SincRad\) on \(\AbsoluteValue z<\pi\) is used.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(\SincRad z=\sinhc(\ImaginaryUnit z)\), \eqref{p11:eq:log-sinh} gives
\(\log\SincRad z=\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^kc_kz^{2k}\) on \(\AbsoluteValue z<\pi\),
where the logarithm is holomorphic because \(\SincRad\) has no zero there.  Put
\[
 g_R(z)=\log\SincRad z-\sum_{k=1}^{R+1}(-1)^kc_kz^{2k},
\]
holomorphic on \(\AbsoluteValue z<\pi\) and vanishing to order \(2R+4\) at the
origin, so \(g_R(z)=z^{2R+4}\tilde g_R(z)\) with \(\tilde g_R\) holomorphic
there.  Fix \(\delta<\delta'<\pi\) and set
\(M=\sup_{\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta'}\AbsoluteValue{\tilde g_R(z)}<\infty\).
Cauchy's estimate on circles of radius \(\delta'-\delta\) gives
\(\AbsoluteValue{\tilde g_R^{(i)}(z)}\le i!\,M(\delta'-\delta)^{-i}\) for
\(\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta\); expanding \(\partial_z^q(z^{2R+4}\tilde g_R)\)
by Leibniz's rule and using \(\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta\) to absorb the lower
powers therefore yields the derivative-uniform remainder estimate
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:gR-derivative}
 \AbsoluteValue{g_R^{(q)}(z)}\le C_{R,q,\delta}\,
 \AbsoluteValue z^{\max(0,\,2R+4-q)},
 \qquad\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta,\ q\ge0 .
\end{equation}
This is the statement that ``differentiation lowers powers of \(t\)'', now
proved rather than asserted.

For \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta\) all factors of \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-product}
are zero free, so \(\log\Psi_h(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}\log\SincRad(a_hr^nt)\), the
series converging locally uniformly (its \(n\)th term is
\(\BigO((a_hr^n)^2t^2)\)) and hence differentiable term by term.  Splitting
each summand into its polynomial part and \(g_R\) gives
\eqref{p11:eq:logpsi-trunc} with
\(\rho_{R,h}(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}g_R(a_hr^nt)\), because
\[
 (-1)^kc_k\,\frac{a_h^{2k}}{1-r^{2k}}\,t^{2k}
 =\frac{B_{2k}}{2k}\,\frac{12^k}{(2k)!}\,
   \frac{(1-r^2)^k}{1-r^{2k}}\,(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2k}
 =\frac{\lambda_{2k}(h)}{(2k)!}(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2k}
\]
by \eqref{p11:eq:ck-dmk}, \(a_h^2=3(1-r^2)\) and
\Cref{p11:prop:exact-cumulants}; the term \(k=1\) is \(-t^2/2\) since
\(\lambda_2=1\).

For the bound, \(\partial_t^q\rho_{R,h}(t)=\sum_n(a_hr^n)^qg_R^{(q)}(a_hr^nt)\).
Because \(a_h^2=3(1-\EulerE^{-2h})\le6h\) and
\(1-\EulerE^{-x}\ge x/2\) for \(0\le x\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:geometric-power-sum}
 \sum_{n\ge0}(a_hr^n)^{2k}=\frac{a_h^{2k}}{1-r^{2k}}
 \le\frac{(6h)^{k}}{kh}=\frac{6^{k}}{k}\,h^{k-1}
 \qquad(2kh\le1).
\end{equation}
If \(q\le2R+4\), \eqref{p11:eq:gR-derivative} and
\eqref{p11:eq:geometric-power-sum} at \(k=R+2\) give
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\rho_{R,h}(t)}
 \le C_{R,q,\delta}\AbsoluteValue t^{2R+4-q}
 \sum_{n\ge0}(a_hr^n)^{2R+4}
 \le C_{R,q,\delta}\,\frac{6^{R+2}}{R+2}\,h^{R+1}
 \AbsoluteValue t^{2R+4-q};
\]
if \(q>2R+4\), the same two displays give
\(\AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\rho_{R,h}}\le C\sum_n(a_hr^n)^{q}
 \le C'h^{q/2-1}\le C'h^{R+1}\) for \(h\le1\), since
\(q/2-1\ge R+\tfrac32\).  Both cases are \eqref{p11:eq:rho-bound}.  Every step
uses only \(\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta\) and holomorphy, so the argument is
unchanged for complex \(t\) with \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the Edgeworth theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}]
Let
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:approx-transform}
 A_{R,h}(t)=\EulerE^{-t^2/2}
 \sum_{\substack{\bm k\in\NaturalNumbers^R\\w(\bm k)\le R}}
 \prod_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac1{k_m!}
 \left(\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2m}}{(2m)!}\right)^{k_m}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{p11:eq:hermite-inversion}, its inverse Fourier transform is \(\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}\).

Fix \(\varepsilon=\dfrac1{8(R+2)}\), so that \(\varepsilon<\tfrac14\) and
\(\varepsilon(2R+4)=\tfrac14<R+1\), and split the frequency axis into
\[
 \mathcal Z_0=\{\AbsoluteValue t\le h^{-\varepsilon}\},\qquad
 \mathcal Z_1=\{h^{-\varepsilon}<\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta/a_h\},\qquad
 \mathcal Z_2=\{\AbsoluteValue t>\delta/a_h\},
\]
where \(0<\delta<1\) is fixed.

On \(\mathcal Z_0\) we work on the closed complex discs
\(D_t=\SetOf{z:\AbsoluteValue{z-t}\le1}\), \(t\in\mathcal Z_0\).  Since
\(a_h^2=3(1-\EulerE^{-2h})\le6h\), we have
\(a_h(h^{-\varepsilon}+1)\le\sqrt{6h}\,(h^{-\varepsilon}+1)\to0\) because
\(\varepsilon<\tfrac12\), so for small \(h\) every such disc lies in the
window \(a_h\AbsoluteValue z\le\delta\) on which
\Cref{p11:lem:cumulant-remainder} is valid.  There write
\(\Psi_h=\EulerE^{-z^2/2}\EulerE^{u}\) with \(u=P_h+\rho_{R,h}\) and
\(P_h(z)=\sum_{m=2}^{R+1}\lambda_{2m}(h)(\ImaginaryUnit z)^{2m}/(2m)!\), and
\(A_{R,h}=\EulerE^{-z^2/2}\Sigma_{R,h}\) with \(\Sigma_{R,h}\) the sum in
\eqref{p11:eq:approx-transform}; then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Z0-split}
 \EulerE^{z^2/2}\bigl(\Psi_h-A_{R,h}\bigr)(z)
 =\bigl(\EulerE^{P_h}-\Sigma_{R,h}\bigr)
 +\EulerE^{P_h}\bigl(\EulerE^{\rho_{R,h}}-1\bigr).
\end{equation}

The omitted monomials form an infinite family of unbounded degree in \(z\), so
they must be summed, not merely counted.  Put
\(\theta=h\,(1+\AbsoluteValue z^2)^2\) and
\[
 C^\ast_R=\max_{2\le m\le R+1}\ \sup_{0<h\le1}
 \frac{\AbsoluteValue{\lambda_{2m}(h)}}{(2m)!\,h^{m-1}},
\]
which is finite because by \Cref{p11:prop:exact-cumulants} the function
\(\sinh^mh/\sinh(mh)\) is continuous on \((0,1]\) with limit \(h^{m-1}/m\) at
the origin.  Since \(\AbsoluteValue z^{2m}\le(1+\AbsoluteValue z^2)^{2m-2}\)
for \(m\ge2\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:beta-grading}
 \beta_m\DefinitionEquals
 \frac{\AbsoluteValue{\lambda_{2m}(h)}\,\AbsoluteValue z^{2m}}{(2m)!}
 \le C^\ast_R\,\theta^{\,m-1},
 \qquad 2\le m\le R+1 .
\end{equation}
In the expansion
\(\EulerE^{P_h}=\sum_{\bm k\in\NaturalNumbers^R}\prod_mk_m!^{-1}
 \bigl(\lambda_{2m}(\ImaginaryUnit z)^{2m}/(2m)!\bigr)^{k_m}\) the multi-index
\(\bm k\) contributes at most \(\prod_m\beta_m^{k_m}/k_m!\le
 (\max(1,C^\ast_R)\,\theta)^{w(\bm k)}\), because \(m-1\ge1\) forces
\(\sum_mk_m\le w(\bm k)\); and at most \((W+1)^R\) multi-indices have
\(w(\bm k)=W\).  Hence, once \(\max(1,C^\ast_R)\theta\le\tfrac12\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:weight-tail}
 \AbsoluteValue{\EulerE^{P_h}-\Sigma_{R,h}}
 \le\sum_{W\ge R+1}(W+1)^R\bigl(\max(1,C^\ast_R)\theta\bigr)^{W}
 \le C_R\,\theta^{R+1}
 =C_R\,h^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue z^2)^{2R+2}.
\end{equation}
On \(\mathcal Z_0\) and its discs, \(1+\AbsoluteValue z^2\le4h^{-2\varepsilon}\)
for small \(h\), so \(\theta\le16h^{1-4\varepsilon}\to0\) and the hypothesis of
\eqref{p11:eq:weight-tail} holds; the same estimate gives
\(\AbsoluteValue{P_h}\le\sum_{m}\beta_m\le2C^\ast_R\theta\le1\), while
\eqref{p11:eq:rho-bound} with \(q=0\) gives
\(\AbsoluteValue{\rho_{R,h}}\le
 C_Rh^{R+1-\varepsilon(2R+4)}=C_Rh^{R+3/4}\le1\).  Therefore the second term of
\eqref{p11:eq:Z0-split} is at most
\(\EulerE^{2}\AbsoluteValue{\rho_{R,h}}\le
 C_Rh^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue z)^{2R+4}\).  Finally
\(\AbsoluteValue{\EulerE^{-z^2/2}}=\EulerE^{-\Re(z^2)/2}
 \le\EulerE^{1/2}\EulerE^{\AbsoluteValue t}\EulerE^{-t^2/2}
 \le\EulerE^{3/2}\EulerE^{-t^2/4}\) for \(\AbsoluteValue{z-t}\le1\), and
\((1+\AbsoluteValue z)\le2+\AbsoluteValue t\), so
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Z0-sup}
 \sup_{\AbsoluteValue{z-t}\le1}
 \AbsoluteValue{(\Psi_h-A_{R,h})(z)}
 \le C_Rh^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{4R+4}\EulerE^{-t^2/4},
 \qquad t\in\mathcal Z_0 .
\end{equation}
Both \(\Psi_h\) and \(A_{R,h}\) are entire, so Cauchy's estimate
\(\AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^qg(t)}\le q!\sup_{\AbsoluteValue{z-t}=1}
 \AbsoluteValue{g(z)}\) upgrades \eqref{p11:eq:Z0-sup} to every frequency
derivative at once, with no Fa\`a di Bruno bookkeeping:
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:central-transform-error}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q(\Psi_h-A_{R,h})(t)}
 \le C h^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^M\EulerE^{-t^2/4}
 \qquad(t\in\mathcal Z_0),
\end{equation}
with \(M=4R+4\) and \(C=C(R,q)\).  The right side is integrable with norm
\(\BigO(h^{R+1})\).

On \(\mathcal Z_1\) one has \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t\le\delta<1\), so
\eqref{p11:eq:S-gaussian} gives \(S_h(t)=3t^2\) and
\eqref{p11:eq:Psi-derivative-envelope} gives
\(\AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h(t)}\le(\EulerE^{c}A_h)^q\EulerE^{-t^2/2}\)
with \(c=\tfrac16\).  The approximant \(A_{R,h}\) is \(\EulerE^{-t^2/2}\) times
a polynomial of degree at most \(4R\) whose coefficients are bounded uniformly
for \(0<h\le1\).  Hence for all \(j,q\ge0\)
\[
 \int_{\mathcal Z_1}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{j}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q(\Psi_h-A_{R,h})}\Differential t
 \le C_{j,q,R}\,h^{-q/2}
 \int_{\AbsoluteValue t>h^{-\varepsilon}}
 (1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{j+4R}\EulerE^{-t^2/2}\Differential t
 =\BigO\bigl(\EulerE^{-h^{-2\varepsilon}/4}\bigr),
\]
which is \(\BigO(h^N)\) for every \(N\).

On \(\mathcal Z_2\) the estimate must be made, not merely indicated; split it
at \(a_h\AbsoluteValue t=1\).  For
\(\delta a_h^{-1}<\AbsoluteValue t\le a_h^{-1}\), \eqref{p11:eq:S-outer} gives
\(S_h\ge c_\delta h^{-1}\), the zone has length at most \(2a_h^{-1}\), and
\((1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{j}\le(1+a_h^{-1})^{j}\); since \(a_h^{-1}\le(3h)^{-1/2}\)
for \(h\le1\), the corresponding integral of
\((1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{j}\AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h}\) is at most
\(C_{j,q}h^{-(j+q+1)/2}\EulerE^{-cc_\delta/h}\).

For \(\AbsoluteValue t>a_h^{-1}\) put \(T=a_h\AbsoluteValue t\ge1\).  Then
\eqref{p11:eq:S-power} and \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-derivative-envelope} give the
explicit outer decay
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:outer-power-decay}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h(t)}
 \le\bigl(\EulerE^{c}A_h\bigr)^{q}\,
   \EulerE^{-c\EulerE^{-2}/(2h)}\,T^{-c/h},
 \qquad c=\tfrac16,
\end{equation}
a power of \(T\) whose exponent \(c/h\) diverges: this is the precise form of
``the number of sinc factors with argument at least one grows like
\(h^{-1}\log(a_h\AbsoluteValue t)\)''.  Using \(1+\AbsoluteValue t\le2T/a_h\)
there (legitimate since \(\AbsoluteValue t\ge a_h^{-1}\ge1\) for \(h\le\tfrac16\))
and substituting \(t=T/a_h\),
\[
 \int_{\AbsoluteValue t>a_h^{-1}}(1+\AbsoluteValue t)^{j}
 \AbsoluteValue{\partial_t^q\Psi_h}\Differential t
 \le\frac{2^{j+1}\bigl(\EulerE^{c}A_h\bigr)^{q}}{a_h^{\,j+1}}
 \EulerE^{-c\EulerE^{-2}/(2h)}\int_1^\infty T^{\,j-c/h}\Differential T
 \le\frac{2^{j+2}\bigl(\EulerE^{c}A_h\bigr)^{q}}{a_h^{\,j+1}}
 \EulerE^{-c\EulerE^{-2}/(2h)}
\]
as soon as \(c/h\ge j+2\), that is \(h\le\frac1{6(j+2)}\).  The prefactor is
\(\BigO(h^{-(j+q+1)/2})\) and is absorbed by
\(\EulerE^{-\EulerE^{-2}/(12h)}\).  The approximant \(A_{R,h}\) carries the
factor \(\EulerE^{-t^2/2}\) with \(\AbsoluteValue t>a_h^{-1}\ge(6h)^{-1/2}\)
and is smaller still.  The quantifiers now match the statement of the theorem:
\(R\), \(j\) and \(K\) are fixed first, only derivative orders \(q\le K\) are
needed, and \(h_0\) is then constrained by
\(h_0\le\min\bigl(\tfrac16,\tfrac1{6(j+2)}\bigr)\) together with the finitely
many smallness conditions used on \(\mathcal Z_0\); no bound is required for an
unquantified \(N\).

Collecting the three zones and applying Leibniz's rule --- which writes
\(\partial_t^q[(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}g]\) as a combination of
\(t^{\,j-i}\partial_t^{\,q-i}g\) with \(0\le i\le\min(j,q)\) --- we obtain, for
every fixed \(q\) and \(j\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:fourier-derivative-L1}
 \Norm{\partial_t^q\bigl[(\ImaginaryUnit t)^j(\Psi_h-A_{R,h})\bigr]}_{L^1(\RealNumbers)}
 \le C_{R,j,q}h^{R+1}.
\end{equation}

It remains to convert \eqref{p11:eq:fourier-derivative-L1} into the seminorm
bound; since the Schwartz-topology claim rests entirely on this step, it is
written out.  Let \(g=f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}\), so that
\(\FourierAngular{g}(-t)=\Psi_h-A_{R,h}=:G(t)\) by
\eqref{p11:eq:hermite-inversion}, and \(G\) together with all its derivatives
is integrable by the three zone estimates.  By
\eqref{p11:eq:fourier-convention},
\(g^{(j)}(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int(-\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}
 \EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}G(t)\Differential t\).  From
\(x\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}
 =\ImaginaryUnit\,\partial_t\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}\), \(K\) integrations
by parts --- with no boundary contribution, because
\(\partial_t^{i}[(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}G(t)]\to0\) as
\(\AbsoluteValue t\to\infty\) for \(i\le K\) --- give
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:weighted-inversion}
 x^{K}g^{(j)}(x)
 =\frac{(-\ImaginaryUnit)^{K}}{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}
   \EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit tx}\,
   \partial_t^{K}\bigl[(-\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}G(t)\bigr]\Differential t,
 \qquad
 \sup_{x}\AbsoluteValue{x^{K}g^{(j)}(x)}
 \le\frac1{2\pi}\Norm{\partial_t^{K}
   \bigl[(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}G\bigr]}_{L^1}.
\end{equation}
The case \(K=0\) is plain Fourier inversion.  Since
\((1+\AbsoluteValue x)^{K}\le2^{K}(1+\AbsoluteValue x^{K})\),
\[
 \Norm{g}_{j,K}
 \le\frac{2^{K}}{2\pi}\left(
   \Norm{(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}G}_{L^1}
   +\Norm{\partial_t^{K}\bigl[(\ImaginaryUnit t)^{j}G\bigr]}_{L^1}\right)
 \le C_{R,j,K}h^{R+1}
\]
by \eqref{p11:eq:fourier-derivative-L1} with \(q=0\) and \(q=K\).  This is
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-main}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{First explicit orders}
Expanding the exact-cumulant polynomial in powers of \(h\) gives
\begin{align}
 f_h(x)=\phiN(x)\Bigg[1
 &-\frac{h}{20}H_4(x)\notag\\
 &+h^2\left(\frac4{315}H_6(x)+\frac1{800}H_8(x)\right)\notag\\
 &+h^3\left(\frac1{60}H_4(x)-\frac3{700}H_8(x)
 -\frac1{1575}H_{10}(x)-\frac1{48000}H_{12}(x)\right)
 \Bigg]+\BigO_{\mathcal S}(h^4).\label{p11:eq:edgeworth-three-orders}
\end{align}
Here \(\BigO_{\mathcal S}\) means an error of that order in every fixed Schwartz seminorm.  The second-order terms are the familiar Bell combination
\[
 \frac{\lambda_6}{6!}H_6+\frac12\left(\frac{\lambda_4}{4!}\right)^2H_8,
\]
but \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} establishes the complete continuous-parameter hierarchy and its global analytic control.

\section{CDF and inverse-distribution asymptotics}\label{p11:sec:quantiles}

\subsection{Uniform CDF expansion}
Because the error in \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} has polynomially weighted uniform control, it is integrable with the same order.  Since
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:integrate-hermite}
 \int_{-\infty}^xH_n(u)\phiN(u)\,\Differential u=-H_{n-1}(x)\phiN(x),\qquad n\ge1,
\end{equation}
we obtain the following.

\begin{corollary}[All-orders CDF expansion]\label{p11:cor:cdf-edgeworth}
Let \(F_h(x)=\Probability(Z_h\le x)\).  For every \(R\ge0\), uniformly in \(x\in\RealNumbers\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:cdf-general}
 F_h(x)=\PhiN(x)-\phiN(x)
 \sum_{\substack{\bm k\in\NaturalNumbers^R\\1\le w(\bm k)\le R}}
 H_{2\nu(\bm k)-1}(x)
 \prod_{m=2}^{R+1}\frac1{k_m!}
 \left(\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)}{(2m)!}\right)^{k_m}
 +\BigO(h^{R+1}).
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every fixed \(K\ge0\) the error term
\(\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)\) in \eqref{p11:eq:cdf-general} obeys the weighted bound
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:cdf-weighted-error}
 \sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}
 (1+\AbsoluteValue x)^{K}\AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)}
 \le C_{R,K}h^{R+1}.
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(D_{R,h}\) be the right-hand side of \eqref{p11:eq:cdf-general} without
the error term, and \(\mathcal R_{R,h}=F_h-D_{R,h}\).  Since the zero
multi-index contributes \(H_0=1\) to \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial},
\eqref{p11:eq:integrate-hermite} gives
\(D_{R,h}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}\), whence
\(\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}(f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h})\).

The weighted claim does \emph{not} follow from
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-main} alone: integrating a density error of size
\(h^{R+1}(1+\AbsoluteValue x)^{-K-1}\) from \(-\infty\) leaves, for a generic
integrand, a constant that no polynomial weight can beat.  What makes it true
here is the exact cancellation of total mass,
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:mass-cancellation}
 \int_{\RealNumbers}\bigl(f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}\bigr)\Differential x=0,
\end{equation}
which holds because \(\int f_h=1\), \(\int\phiN=1\), and \(\int H_n\phiN=0\)
for every \(n\ge1\), so that only the zero multi-index of
\eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-polynomial} survives integration.

Granted \eqref{p11:eq:mass-cancellation}, integrate from the near side of the
axis.  For \(x\ge0\),
\(\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)=-\int_x^{\infty}(f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h})\), so by
\Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} with \(j=0\) and weight \(K+1\),
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)}
 \le\Norm{f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}}_{0,K+1}
   \int_x^{\infty}\frac{\Differential u}{(1+u)^{K+1}}
 =\frac{\Norm{f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h}}_{0,K+1}}{K\,(1+x)^{K}}
\]
for \(K\ge1\), and symmetrically for \(x\le0\) from
\(\mathcal R_{R,h}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}(f_h-\phiN\mathcal E_{R,h})\).  For
\(K=0\) the same two formulas give the unweighted statement
\eqref{p11:eq:cdf-general}.  This proves
\eqref{p11:eq:cdf-weighted-error}.
\end{proof}

Through second order,
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:cdf-second-order}
 F_h(x)=\PhiN(x)+\phiN(x)\left[
 \frac{h}{20}H_3(x)
 -h^2\left(\frac4{315}H_5(x)+\frac1{800}H_7(x)\right)
 \right]+\BigO_{\mathrm{weighted}}(h^3).
\end{equation}

\subsection{Central Cornish--Fisher inversion}
Let \(Q_h(u)=F_h^{-1}(u)\), \(0<u<1\), and \(z=\PhiN^{-1}(u)\).  The inverse Fabius function is the special member \(r=1/2\) after the appropriate affine normalization; the theorem below is an inverse-distribution asymptotic at the opposite, Gaussian boundary \(r\uparrow1\).

\begin{theorem}[All-orders central quantile expansion]\label{p11:thm:quantile-expansion}
Fix \(0<\eta<1/2\) and \(R\ge1\).  Uniformly for \(u\in[\eta,1-\eta]\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:quantile-general}
 Q_h(u)=z+\sum_{n=1}^{R}h^nq_n(z)+\BigO_{R,\eta}(h^{R+1}),
 \qquad z=\PhiN^{-1}(u),
\end{equation}
where each \(q_n\) is an explicitly computable polynomial.  The first two are
\begin{align}
 q_1(z)&=-\frac1{20}H_3(z),\label{p11:eq:q1}\\
 q_2(z)&=\frac{zH_3(z)^2}{800}-\frac{H_4(z)H_3(z)}{400}
 +\frac4{315}H_5(z)+\frac1{800}H_7(z).\label{p11:eq:q2}
\end{align}
All higher \(q_n\) follow recursively by coefficient extraction from \eqref{p11:eq:quantile-recursion} below.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{A window with a uniform lower bound on the density.}  Let
\(z_\eta=\PhiN^{-1}(1-\eta)\) and \(I_\eta=[-z_\eta-1,\,z_\eta+1]\); for
\(u\in[\eta,1-\eta]\) the normal quantile \(z=\PhiN^{-1}(u)\) lies in
\([-z_\eta,z_\eta]\).  Put \(2c_\eta=\phiN(z_\eta+1)>0\).  By
\Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} with \(R=j=K=0\) (where
\(\mathcal E_{0,h}\equiv1\)) we have \(\Norm{f_h-\phiN}_\infty\le C_0h\), so
\(f_h\ge c_\eta\) on \(I_\eta\) once \(h\le h_1(\eta)\).  Hence \(F_h\) is
strictly increasing on \(I_\eta\) with \(F_h'\ge c_\eta\), and \(Q_h\) is well
defined and smooth on \(F_h(I_\eta)\supseteq[\eta,1-\eta]\).  This much is the
implicit function theorem; by itself it produces no expansion, and in
particular no uniform remainder.  The next two steps supply both.

\emph{An approximate inverse.}  By \Cref{p11:cor:cdf-edgeworth} together with
the re-expansion of \Cref{p11:prop:h-power-series}, applied to the
\(h\)-dependent coefficients in \eqref{p11:eq:cdf-general}, there are
polynomials \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) with
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:cdf-graded}
 \sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}
 \left\lvert F_h(x)-\PhiN(x)-\phiN(x)\sum_{n=1}^{N}h^nA_n(x)\right\rvert
 \le C_Nh^{N+1}
\end{equation}
for every \(N\).  Let \(q_1,\ldots,q_N\) be given by
\eqref{p11:eq:quantile-recursion} below and set
\(\widetilde Q_N(h,z)=z+\sum_{n=1}^{N}h^nq_n(z)\).  The functions
\(\PhiN,\phiN,A_n,q_n\) are smooth, so on the compact set \(I_\eta\) they and
their derivatives through order \(N+1\) are bounded by some
\(B=B(N,\eta)\).  Since \(\widetilde Q_N(h,z)-z=\BigO(h)\) uniformly for
\(z\in[-z_\eta,z_\eta]\), the increment stays in \(I_\eta\) for small \(h\) and
Taylor expansion of \(\PhiN\) and of \(\phiN A_n\) about \(z\) in that
increment, truncated after order \(N\), is legitimate with remainder
\(\BigOAt{h^{N+1}}{N,\eta}\).  Recursion
\eqref{p11:eq:quantile-recursion} says precisely that the coefficients of
\(h^1,\ldots,h^N\) in the resulting expansion of
\(F_h(\widetilde Q_N(h,z))-\PhiN(z)\) all vanish.  Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:approx-inverse}
 \sup_{u\in[\eta,1-\eta]}
 \AbsoluteValue{F_h\bigl(\widetilde Q_N(h,z)\bigr)-u}
 \le C_{N,\eta}\,h^{N+1}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Transfer to the exact quantile.}  For small \(h\) both
\(\widetilde Q_N(h,z)\) and \(Q_h(u)\) lie in \(I_\eta\), where
\(F_h'\ge c_\eta\).  The mean value theorem and \(F_h(Q_h(u))=u\) give
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{Q_h(u)-\widetilde Q_N(h,z)}
 \le\frac1{c_\eta}
   \AbsoluteValue{F_h\bigl(\widetilde Q_N(h,z)\bigr)-F_h\bigl(Q_h(u)\bigr)}
 \le\frac{C_{N,\eta}}{c_\eta}\,h^{N+1},
\]
uniformly in \(u\in[\eta,1-\eta]\); the remainder order survives because the
lower bound \(F_h'\ge c_\eta\) is uniform on the window.  Taking \(N=R\) proves
\eqref{p11:eq:quantile-general}.

For the explicit recursion, write
\[
 F_h(x)=\PhiN(x)+\phiN(x)\sum_{n\ge1}h^nA_n(x),
 \qquad
 q_{<N}(h,z)=\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}h^nq_n(z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:quantile-recursion}
 q_N(z)=-[h^N]\left\{
 \frac{\PhiN(z+q_{<N})-\PhiN(z)}{\phiN(z)}
 +\frac{\phiN(z+q_{<N})}{\phiN(z)}
  \sum_{n=1}^{N}h^nA_n(z+q_{<N})
 \right\},
\end{equation}
where \([h^N]\) extracts the coefficient.  Equivalently, insert \(q_{<N}+h^Nq_N\) into the identity \(F_h(Q_h(u))=u\) and isolate the unique linear contribution \(h^Nq_N\).  This is a Fa\`a di Bruno/Bell recursion and proves all-orders computability.

From \eqref{p11:eq:cdf-second-order},
\[
 A_1=\frac1{20}H_3,
 \qquad
 A_2=-\frac4{315}H_5-\frac1{800}H_7.
\]
At first order, \(q_1=-A_1\), giving \eqref{p11:eq:q1}.  At second order,
\[
 q_2=-\left[\frac12\frac{\phiN'}{\phiN}q_1^2
 +\frac{(\phiN A_1)'}{\phiN}q_1+A_2\right].
\]
Use \(\phiN'/\phiN=-z\), \((\phiN H_3)'=-\phiN H_4\), and \eqref{p11:eq:q1}; simplification gives \eqref{p11:eq:q2}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Connection to Lagrange inversion]
The recursion \eqref{p11:eq:quantile-recursion} is a moving-base analogue of Lagrange inversion: the base map is \(\PhiN\), and the perturbation is organized by Hermite polynomials.  It provides a concrete meeting point between the repository's inverse-function program, Bell polynomials, and its geometric-comb interpolation program.
\end{remark}

\section{Moderate deviations and the compact-scale large-deviation principle}\label{p11:sec:ldp}

\subsection{Gaussian moderate deviations}
\begin{theorem}[Moderate-deviation principle]\label{p11:thm:moderate-deviations}
Let \(b_h\to\infty\) and \(hb_h^2\to0\) as \(h\downarrow0\).  Then \(Z_h/b_h\) satisfies a large-deviation principle with speed \(b_h^2\) and good rate function
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:moderate-rate}
 I_{\mathrm{mod}}(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for each Borel set \(A\), the usual LDP upper and lower bounds hold with speed \(b_h^2\) and rate \(x^2/2\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Avoid the cumulant series, whose radius of convergence would itself have to be
controlled, and use the exact product form instead.  By
\eqref{p11:eq:centered-X} and \cref{p0:prop:dictionary}\,(ii), the coefficient
of \(V_n\) in \(Z_h\) is \(2a_hr^n\), so with
\(\ell(a)=\log(\sinh a/a)\) as in \eqref{p11:eq:ell-J} below,
\[
 \frac1{b_h^2}\log\Expectation\EulerE^{tb_hZ_h}
 =\frac1{b_h^2}\sum_{n\ge0}\ell\bigl(a_hr^n\,tb_h\bigr).
\]
The Euler product \(\sinh z/z=\prod_{k\ge1}(1+z^2/(k\pi)^2)\) together with
\(0\le x-\log(1+x)\le x^2/2\) for \(x\ge0\) gives a two-sided estimate valid
for \emph{all} real \(z\), with no smallness restriction:
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ell-quartic}
 0\le\frac{z^2}{6}-\ell(z)
 \le\frac{z^4}{2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(k\pi)^4}
 =\frac{z^4}{2}\cdot\frac{\zeta(4)}{\pi^4}
 =\frac{z^4}{180},
 \qquad z\in\RealNumbers .
\end{equation}
Summing \eqref{p11:eq:ell-quartic} over \(n\), using
\(\sum_n(a_hr^n)^2=3\) from \eqref{p11:eq:quadratic-sum} and
\[
 \sum_{n\ge0}(a_hr^n)^4=\frac{a_h^4}{1-r^4}
 =\frac{9(1-r^2)}{1+r^2}\le18h ,
\]
we obtain the explicit, locally uniform estimate
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:md-uniform}
 \left\lvert\frac1{b_h^2}\log\Expectation\EulerE^{tb_hZ_h}
 -\frac{t^2}{2}\right\rvert
 \le\frac{t^4}{10}\,hb_h^2
 \qquad(t\in\RealNumbers),
\end{equation}
whose right side tends to \(0\) uniformly on compact \(t\)-sets exactly under
the hypothesis \(hb_h^2\to0\).  The limit \(t\mapsto t^2/2\) is finite and
differentiable on all of \(\RealNumbers\), hence lower semicontinuous and
essentially smooth (its essential domain has empty boundary), so the
G\"artner--Ellis theorem \cite{bib:dembo1998} applies in its full form and
gives the LDP at speed \(b_h^2\) with the good rate function
\(\sup_t\{tx-t^2/2\}=x^2/2\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The compact scale}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Yh}
 Y_h=\sqrt h\,Z_h.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{p11:eq:standardized-support}, its support converges to \([-\sqrt6,\sqrt6]\).  Put
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ell-J}
 \ell(a)=\log\frac{\sinh a}{a},\qquad \ell(0)=0,
 \qquad
 J(a)=\int_0^a\frac{\ell(v)}{v}\,\Differential v.
\end{equation}
The function \(J\) is even, because \(\ell(v)/v\) is odd.

\begin{theorem}[Compact-scale LDP]\label{p11:thm:compact-ldp}
The family \((Y_h)_{h\downarrow0}\) satisfies a large-deviation principle with speed \(h^{-1}\) and good convex rate function
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:rate-legendre}
 I(y)=\sup_{s\in\RealNumbers}\{sy-\Lambda(s)\},
\end{equation}
where
\begin{align}
 \Lambda(s)
 &=\int_0^1\frac{\ell(\sqrt6\,su)}{u}\,\Differential u\label{p11:eq:Lambda-integral}\\
 &=J(\sqrt6\,s).\label{p11:eq:Lambda-J}
\end{align}
The function \(\Lambda\) is even, real analytic, and strictly convex.  Its derivative maps \(\RealNumbers\) bijectively onto \((-\sqrt6,\sqrt6)\).  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:rate-support}
 I(y)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \AbsoluteValue y<\sqrt6,
 \qquad
 I(y)=\infty\quad\text{for }\AbsoluteValue y\ge\sqrt6.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The limiting generator, by a two-sided Riemann bracket.}  The
coefficient of \(V_n\) in \(Z_h\) is \(2a_hr^n\), so
\(\log\Expectation\EulerE^{\theta Z_h}=\sum_{n\ge0}\ell(a_hr^n\theta)\); at
\(\theta=s/\sqrt h\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ldp-riemann}
 \Lambda_h(s)\DefinitionEquals
 h\log\Expectation\exp\!\left(\frac{sY_h}{h}\right)
 =h\sum_{n\ge0}\ell\bigl(\beta_hs\EulerE^{-nh}\bigr),
 \qquad
 \beta_h=\frac{a_h}{\sqrt h}
 =\sqrt{\frac{3(1-\EulerE^{-2h})}{h}}\longrightarrow\sqrt6 .
\end{equation}
(The scale is written \(\beta_h\), not \(b_h\), to keep it distinct from the
moderate-deviation scale of \Cref{p11:thm:moderate-deviations}.)  Fix
\(s>0\).  Because \(\ell\) is even, nonnegative, and increasing on
\([0,\infty)\), the function
\(\varphi_h(x)=\ell(\beta_hs\EulerE^{-x})\) is nonnegative and
\emph{decreasing} on \([0,\infty)\); for such a function the Riemann sum
brackets the integral,
\[
 \int_0^{\infty}\varphi_h
 \le h\sum_{n\ge0}\varphi_h(nh)
 \le\int_0^{\infty}\varphi_h+h\,\varphi_h(0),
\]
so no domination argument and no fixed majorant are needed even though
\(\beta_h\) moves with \(h\).  Substituting \(u=\EulerE^{-x}\) turns
\(\int_0^\infty\varphi_h\) into
\(\int_0^1\ell(\beta_hsu)\Differential u/u=J(\beta_hs)\), giving
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ldp-bracket}
 J(\beta_hs)\le\Lambda_h(s)\le J(\beta_hs)+h\,\ell(\beta_hs).
\end{equation}
Both \(J\) and \(\ell\) are continuous, \(\beta_h\to\sqrt6\), and
\(h\,\ell(\beta_hs)\to0\) for each fixed \(s\); hence
\(\Lambda_h(s)\to J(\sqrt6\,s)=\Lambda(s)\), which is
\eqref{p11:eq:Lambda-integral} after \(u=\EulerE^{-x}\) and
\eqref{p11:eq:Lambda-J} after \(v=\sqrt6\,su\).  The case \(s<0\) follows from
evenness of \(\ell\), and \(s=0\) is trivial.  This verifies the hypothesis of
the G\"artner--Ellis theorem for every \(s\in\RealNumbers\).

\emph{Regularity of \(\Lambda\), without differentiating under an integral.}
The function \(v\mapsto\ell(v)/v\), set to \(0\) at \(v=0\), is real analytic
on \(\RealNumbers\): \(\sinh v/v\) is entire and strictly positive on
\(\RealNumbers\), so \(\ell\) is real analytic and vanishes to second order at
the origin.  Hence its primitive \(J\), and therefore
\(\Lambda=J(\sqrt6\,\cdot)\), are real analytic on all of \(\RealNumbers\);
evenness of \(\Lambda\) follows from that of \(J\).  For strict convexity,
\(\Lambda''(s)=6J''(\sqrt6\,s)\) and
\(J'(a)=\ell(a)/a=\bigl(\ell(a)-\ell(0)\bigr)/(a-0)\) is the difference
quotient of \(\ell\) based at the origin.  Now \(\ell\) is the logarithmic
moment generating function of \(2V\) with \(V\) uniform on
\([-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]\), a nondegenerate variable, so \(\ell\) is strictly
convex; a difference quotient of a strictly convex function from a fixed base
point is strictly increasing, so \(J''>0\) and \(\Lambda''>0\).

\emph{Derivative range, essential smoothness, and the support of \(I\).}  From
\(\ell(a)=a-\log(2a)+\log(1-\EulerE^{-2a})\) one gets \(\ell(a)/a\to1\) as
\(a\to+\infty\), so \(\Lambda'(s)=\sqrt6\,\ell(\sqrt6\,s)/(\sqrt6\,s)\)
increases strictly from \(-\sqrt6\) to \(\sqrt6\) and
\(\Lambda'(\RealNumbers)=(-\sqrt6,\sqrt6)\) exactly.  Since \(\Lambda\) is
finite and differentiable on all of \(\RealNumbers\), its essential domain is
\(\RealNumbers\) and has empty boundary; \(\Lambda\) is therefore lower
semicontinuous and essentially smooth, and the steepness condition is vacuous.
Consequently the G\"artner--Ellis theorem \cite{bib:dembo1998} yields the
\emph{full} large-deviation principle, lower bound included, with the good
convex rate function \eqref{p11:eq:rate-legendre}; \(I\) is good because
\(\Lambda\) is finite everywhere, and in any case
\(\AbsoluteValue{Y_h}\le\sqrt h\,A_h=\sqrt{3h\coth(h/2)}\le\sqrt{13/2}\) for
\(0<h\le1\), so the family is exponentially tight.  Finally \(I\) is finite
exactly on the derivative range: for \(\AbsoluteValue y<\sqrt6\) the saddle
equation \(\Lambda'(s)=y\) is solvable and \(I(y)\) is the finite value there,
while at \(y=\sqrt6\), writing \(a=\sqrt6\,s\),
\[
 \sqrt6\,s-\Lambda(s)=a-J(a)
 =\int_0^{a}\left(1-\frac{\ell(v)}{v}\right)\Differential v
 \ge\int_1^{a}\frac{\log(2v)}{v}\Differential v
 \longrightarrow\infty
\]
because \(1-\ell(v)/v=\bigl(\log(2v)-\log(1-\EulerE^{-2v})\bigr)/v\ge\log(2v)/v\)
for \(v\ge1\); a fortiori \(I(y)=\infty\) for \(y>\sqrt6\).  This is
\eqref{p11:eq:rate-support}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact saddle parametrization}
\begin{theorem}[Parametric rate formula]\label{p11:thm:rate-parametric}
For \(a>0\), define
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:y-a}
 y(a)=\sqrt6\frac{\ell(a)}{a}.
\end{equation}
Then \(y(a)\) is strictly increasing from \(0\) to \(\sqrt6\), and
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:I-parametric}
 \boxed{
 I(y(a))=\ell(a)-J(a).}
\end{equation}
The negative half of the rate function follows by symmetry.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set \(a=\sqrt6s\).  Since \(J'(a)=\ell(a)/a\), the saddle equation \(y=\Lambda'(s)\) becomes \eqref{p11:eq:y-a}.  Strict convexity of \(\Lambda\) makes \(y(a)\) strictly increasing.  At the saddle,
\[
 sy-\Lambda(s)
 =\frac{a}{\sqrt6}\left(\sqrt6\frac{\ell(a)}a\right)-J(a)
 =\ell(a)-J(a).
\]
\end{proof}

The Taylor expansion
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Lambda-series}
 \Lambda(s)=\frac{s^2}{2}-\frac{s^4}{20}+\frac4{315}s^6
 -\frac3{700}s^8+\frac{16}{9625}s^{10}+\BigO(s^{12})
\end{equation}
reuses exactly the Bernoulli coefficients that drive the Edgeworth expansion.  Series reversion gives
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:I-center-series}
 I(y)=\frac{y^2}{2}+\frac{y^4}{20}+\frac{23}{3150}y^6
 +\frac{11}{10500}y^8+\frac{821}{6063750}y^{10}+\BigO(y^{12}).
\end{equation}
The positive quartic term shows how compact support makes deviations more expensive than Gaussian ones as soon as one leaves the infinitesimal center.

\section{Lambert--\texorpdfstring{$W$}{W} inversion at the limiting support edge}\label{p11:sec:lambert-edge}

The parametric formula in \Cref{p11:thm:rate-parametric} permits a precise edge analysis.  It is here that the Gaussian boundary, the lower real branch of Lambert \(W\) \cite{bib:corless1996}, and the zeta/Stieltjes constants meet.

\subsection{A renormalized Mellin constant}
Use the standard Stieltjes convention
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:stieltjes-convention}
 \zeta(1+s)=\frac1s+\gamma-\gamma_1s+\BigO(s^2).
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Cstar}
 \mathfrak C=\gamma_1+\frac{\gamma^2}{2}-\frac{\pi^2}{12}
 =-0.7286939170039306059\ldots.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Large-saddle expansion of \(J\)]\label{p11:lem:J-asymptotic}
As \(a\to+\infty\), with \(L=\log(2a)\),
\begin{align}
 \ell(a)&=a-L+\BigO(\EulerE^{-2a}),\label{p11:eq:ell-large}\\
 J(a)&=a-\frac12L^2+\mathfrak C+\BigO(\EulerE^{-2a}/a).\label{p11:eq:J-large}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first identity follows from
\[
 \ell(a)=a-\log(2a)+\log(1-\EulerE^{-2a}).
\]
For the second, put \(x=2v\) in \eqref{p11:eq:ell-J}:
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:J-renormalized}
 J(a)=a+\int_0^{2a}\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\,\Differential x.
\end{equation}
The Mellin transform
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:mellin-log1mexp}
 \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})\,\Differential x
 =-\Gamma(s)\zeta(s+1),\qquad \Re s>0,
\end{equation}
continues meromorphically to \(s=0\).  Using
\[
 \Gamma(s)=\frac1s-\gamma+
 \left(\frac{\gamma^2}{2}+\frac{\pi^2}{12}\right)s+\BigO(s^2)
\]
and \eqref{p11:eq:stieltjes-convention},
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:mellin-finite-part}
 -\Gamma(s)\zeta(s+1)
 =-\frac1{s^2}+\mathfrak C+\BigO(s).
\end{equation}
More explicitly, the finite part in \eqref{p11:eq:mellin-finite-part} is the absolutely convergent quantity
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Cstar-integral}
 \mathfrak C=
 \int_0^1\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\,\Differential x
 +\int_1^\infty\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})}{x}\,\Differential x.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for \(A>1\),
\[
 \int_0^A\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\,\Differential x
 +\frac12\log^2A
 =\int_0^1\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})-\log x}{x}\,\Differential x
 +\int_1^A\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})}{x}\,\Differential x.
\]
Taking \(A=2a\) and subtracting \eqref{p11:eq:Cstar-integral} leaves
\[
 -\int_{2a}^\infty\frac{\log(1-\EulerE^{-x})}{x}\,\Differential x
 =\BigO(\EulerE^{-2a}/a),
\]
which proves \eqref{p11:eq:J-large}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The lower Lambert branch}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:delta-edge}
 \delta=1-\frac{y}{\sqrt6},\qquad y\uparrow\sqrt6.
\end{equation}
From \eqref{p11:eq:y-a},
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:delta-a-exact}
 a\delta=\log(2a)-\log(1-\EulerE^{-2a}).
\end{equation}
The exponentially small second term is the sole difference from the exactly Lambert-invertible equation \(a\delta=\log(2a)\).

\begin{theorem}[Lambert--\(W_{-1}\) support-edge rate]\label{p11:thm:rate-edge}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:wdelta}
 w(\delta)=-W_{-1}(-\delta/2),\qquad \delta\downarrow0.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:edge-rate-main}
 \boxed{
 I\!\left(\sqrt6(1-\delta)\right)
 =\frac12w(\delta)^2-w(\delta)-\mathfrak C+o(1).}
\end{equation}
More precisely, if \(a\) is the exact saddle determined by \eqref{p11:eq:delta-a-exact}, then
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:edge-rate-a}
 I(y(a))=\frac12\log^2(2a)-\log(2a)-\mathfrak C+\BigO(\EulerE^{-2a}).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Subtract \eqref{p11:eq:J-large} from \eqref{p11:eq:ell-large} and use \eqref{p11:eq:I-parametric}; this proves \eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-a}.  Ignoring the exponentially small term in \eqref{p11:eq:delta-a-exact}, write \(L=\log(2a)\).  The equation \(a\delta=L\) and \(2a=\EulerE^L\) give
\[
 Le^{-L}=\frac\delta2,
 \qquad
 L=-W_{-1}(-\delta/2)=w(\delta).
\]
For the exact equation, put \(L=\log(2a)\) and \(F(L)=L\EulerE^{-L}\).  Multiplying \eqref{p11:eq:delta-a-exact} by \(\EulerE^{-L}\) gives
\[
 \frac{\delta}{2}=F(L)-\EulerE^{-L}\log(1-\EulerE^{-\EulerE^L}).
\]
If \(w=w(\delta)\), then \(F(w)=\delta/2\).  Since \(F'(u)=(1-u)\EulerE^{-u}\), the mean-value theorem and \(-\log(1-z)\asymp z\) yield
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:L-w-sharp}
 L-w=\BigO\!\left(\frac{\EulerE^{-\EulerE^w}}{w}\right).
\end{equation}
In particular \(w(L-w)=o(1)\), so substituting \(L=w+\BigO(\EulerE^{-\EulerE^w}/w)\) into \eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-a} proves \eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A new three-way connection]
The coefficient \(\mathfrak C\) comes from the finite part of \(-\Gamma(s)\zeta(s+1)\) at \(s=0\), the saddle coordinate comes from an infinite geometric uniform convolution, and the edge inversion is controlled by \(W_{-1}\).  This is distinct from the fixed-\(r\) periodic Lambert--\(W\) endpoint expansion in the repository: here \(r\uparrow1\) first, producing a smooth nonperiodic limiting rate, and only then does the compact coordinate approach its support edge.
\end{remark}

\section{Quadratic \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-Gevrey and Denjoy--Carleman regularity}\label{p11:sec:carleman}

\subsection{A convention for global ultradifferentiable classes}
Let \(M=(M_n)_{n\ge0}\) be positive with \(M_0=1\).  Define the global Roumieu class
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:roumieu-class}
 \mathcal B^{\{M\}}(\RealNumbers)=\left\{f\in C^\infty(\RealNumbers):
 \exists C,A>0\ \forall n\ge0,
 \Norm{f^{(n)}}_\infty\le CA^nM_n\right\}.
\end{equation}
For log-convex \(M\), the Denjoy--Carleman criterion in this convention \cite{bib:komatsu1973} says that the class is quasianalytic exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:carleman-criterion}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{M_{n-1}}{M_n}=\infty.
\end{equation}
A Gevrey class of finite order \(s\) corresponds, up to exponential factors, to \(M_n=(n!)^s\).

\subsection{The Rvachev function}
The exact norm identity is not imported here as an axiom: in this volume it is
\Cref{p6:thm:exact-derivative-norm} specialized to \(a=2\), where
\(h_2=\RvachevUp\).  Combining
\eqref{p6:eq:exact-derivative-norm-closed} and
\eqref{p6:eq:exact-derivative-L1} at \(a=2\), and using
\(\Norm{h_2}_\infty=1\), gives
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:up-exact-norm}
 \Norm{\RvachevUp^{(n)}}_\infty
 =\Norm{\RvachevUp^{(n)}}_1
 =2^{n(n+1)/2}.
\end{equation}
Its finite signed derivative decomposition is
\eqref{p6:eq:ha-derivative-hierarchy}, indexed by the signed Thue--Morse
sequence \cite{bib:allouche1999}.  Thus automatic-sequence cancellation and
support tiling produce an exact global smoothness scale, and the two theorems
of this section are \statusproved{} within the volume rather than
\statusexisting.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp Denjoy--Carleman class of \(\RvachevUp\)]\label{p11:thm:carleman-up}
Let
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Mup}
 M_n^{\RvachevUp}=2^{n(n+1)/2}.
\end{equation}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \(\RvachevUp\in\mathcal B^{\{M^{\RvachevUp}\}}(\RealNumbers)\), with the sharp constants \(C=A=1\).
\item The class is optimal modulo the natural exponential equivalence of weight sequences: if \(\RvachevUp\in\mathcal B^{\{N\}}\), then \(N_n\ge C^{-1}A^{-n}M_n^{\RvachevUp}\) for suitable \(C,A>0\).
\item \(\RvachevUp\) belongs to no Gevrey class of finite order.
\item \(\mathcal B^{\{M^{\RvachevUp}\}}\) is nonquasianalytic, since
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:up-carleman-sum}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{M_{n-1}^{\RvachevUp}}{M_n^{\RvachevUp}}
 =\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}=1.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Parts (i) and (ii) are immediate from the equality \eqref{p11:eq:up-exact-norm}.  If \(\RvachevUp\) were Gevrey of finite order \(s\), then for some \(C,A\),
\[
 2^{n(n+1)/2}\le CA^n(n!)^s.
\]
The logarithm of the left side is \((\log2)n^2/2+\BigO(n)\), whereas the right side has logarithm \(\BigO(n\log n)\), a contradiction.  Finally
\[
 M_n^{\RvachevUp}/M_{n-1}^{\RvachevUp}=2^n,
\]
which is increasing in \(n\); together with \(M_0^{\RvachevUp}=1\) this is the
log-convexity hypothesis under which \eqref{p11:eq:carleman-criterion} was
stated, and which must be verified before the criterion is used.  The sum
\eqref{p11:eq:up-carleman-sum} is then finite, so the Denjoy--Carleman
criterion proves nonquasianalyticity.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Quadratic \(q\)-Gevrey scale]
In this report, a derivative weight with
\[
 \log M_n=\frac{\log(1/q)}2n^2+\BigO(n),\qquad 0<q<1,
\]
is called \emph{quadratic \(q\)-Gevrey}.  This terminology is descriptive and is not intended to replace other established \(q\)-Gevrey conventions.
\end{definition}
For \(\RvachevUp\), \(q=1/2\).  The name records the same quadratic exponent that appears in \(q\)-Pochhammer products, Stieltjes--Wigert moments, and log-Gaussian Fourier envelopes.

\subsection{Separated-base atomic functions}
For the general atomic functions \(h_a\), \(a\ge2\), \Cref{p6:thm:exact-derivative-norm} proves
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ha-exact-norm}
 \Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_\infty
 =\frac{a^{n(n+3)/2+1}}{2^{n+1}},
 \qquad
 \Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_1=a^{n(n+1)/2}.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp class for \(h_a\), \(a\ge2\)]\label{p11:thm:carleman-ha}
Set
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:Ma}
 M_n^{(a)}=\frac{a^{n(n+3)/2}}{2^n}.
\end{equation}
Then \(h_a\in\mathcal B^{\{M^{(a)}\}}\) sharply modulo exponential equivalence, belongs to no finite Gevrey class, and its class is nonquasianalytic because
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:ha-carleman-sum}
 \sum_{n\ge1}\frac{M_{n-1}^{(a)}}{M_n^{(a)}}
 =\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{2}{a^{n+1}}<\infty.
\end{equation}
Its quadratic \(q\)-Gevrey parameter is \(q=a^{-1}\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The \emph{first} identity in \eqref{p11:eq:ha-exact-norm} says
\(\Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_\infty=(a/2)M_n^{(a)}\), so
\(h_a\in\mathcal B^{\{M^{(a)}\}}\) with \(C=a/2\), \(A=1\), and conversely
\(h_a\in\mathcal B^{\{N\}}\) forces \(N_n\ge(2/a)C^{-1}A^{-n}M_n^{(a)}\); this
is membership together with optimality.  (The second identity in
\eqref{p11:eq:ha-exact-norm}, the \(L^1\) norm \(a^{n(n+1)/2}\), is \emph{not}
\((a/2)M_n^{(a)}\) --- at \(a=3\), \(n=1\) the two are \(3\) and \(27/4\) --- and
it enters only through the Fourier envelope
\eqref{p11:eq:fourier-from-carleman}.)  Quadratic growth again excludes every
finite Gevrey order.  Finally \(M_0^{(a)}=1\) and
\(M_n^{(a)}/M_{n-1}^{(a)}=a^{n+1}/2\) is increasing, so \(M^{(a)}\) is
log-convex and \eqref{p11:eq:carleman-criterion} may be applied; summing the
reciprocals gives \eqref{p11:eq:ha-carleman-sum}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Associated functions and Fourier decay}
For a weight \(M\), define its associated function
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:associated-function}
 \omega_M(t)=\sup_{n\ge0}\log\frac{t^n}{M_n}.
\end{equation}
For \(M_n^{\RvachevUp}=2^{n(n+1)/2}\), elementary optimization gives
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:omega-up}
 \omega_{M^{\RvachevUp}}(t)
 =\frac{(\log t)^2}{2\log2}-\frac12\log t+\BigO(1),
 \qquad t\to\infty.
\end{equation}
Integration by parts and \eqref{p11:eq:up-exact-norm} therefore imply a log-Gaussian Fourier envelope
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:fourier-from-carleman}
 \AbsoluteValue{\FourierAngular{\RvachevUp}(-\xi)}
 \le C\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\log(C'\AbsoluteValue\xi))^2}{2\log2}
 +\BigO(\log\AbsoluteValue\xi)\right].
\end{equation}
For \(h_a\), the coefficient \((2\log a)^{-1}\) replaces \((2\log2)^{-1}\).  The repository develops the Fourier envelope by product methods; the new point here is that the same quadratic law is precisely the associated function of the optimal Denjoy--Carleman class.  The derivative and Fourier pictures are Legendre dual.

\section{Numerical experiments}\label{p11:sec:numerics}

\subsection{Method}
The exact standardized characteristic function \eqref{p11:eq:Psi-product} was evaluated on a centered FFT frequency grid.  The infinite product was truncated at the first index \(N\) whose sinc argument
fell below \(10^{-14}\); by \eqref{p11:eq:sinc-basic-envelope} the discarded
tail multiplies the product by a factor in
\(\bigl[\exp\bigl(-10^{-28}/(6(1-r^2))\bigr),\,1\bigr]\), which for every
tabulated \(h\ge0.05\) is within \(10^{-27}\) of \(1\) and so far below the
smallest reported error, \(1.83\times10^{-7}\).  Fourier inversion used
\(2^{15}\) grid points with physical spacing \(0.002\), i.e. a window
\(\AbsoluteValue x\le32.768\); since \(Z_h\) is supported in
\(\AbsoluteValue x\le A_h=\sqrt{3\coth(h/2)}\), which is \(10.96\) at
\(h=0.05\) and smaller for larger \(h\), the window contains the whole support
and there is no wrap-around.  The numerical density mass was
\(0.99999999999926\) for every reported \(h\).  No Monte Carlo sampling was
used.

\section{Conjectures and frontier directions}\label{p11:sec:conjectures}

The theorems above open several directions that are not merely requests for more coefficients.  They concern matching between asymptotic regimes, local symbolic regularity, and arithmetic structure.

\subsection{A matched four-regime asymptotic theory}
\begin{conjecture}[Uniform saddlepoint local large deviations]\label{p11:conj:local-ldp}
For every compact \(K\subset(-\sqrt6,\sqrt6)\), the density of \(Y_h\) has the uniform saddlepoint expansion
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:local-ldp-conj}
 f_{Y_h}(y)
 \sim \frac{\exp[-I(y)/h]}{\sqrt{2\pi h\,\Lambda''(s(y))}}
 \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}h^nA_n(y),
 \qquad y\in K,
\end{equation}
where \(s(y)\) is the unique solution of \(\Lambda'(s)=y\), and each \(A_n\) is an explicit differential polynomial in \(\Lambda\).
\end{conjecture}

\Cref{p10:conj:saddlepoint} is the same conjecture in Part~X's coordinate, obtained by the substitution \(y=\sqrt6\,x\) of \Cref{p0:tab:dictionary}; the density picks up the Jacobian \(\sqrt6\) and \(\Lambda''(s(y))=6\Lambda''(\theta_x)\), so the two prefactors agree.

\begin{conjecture}[Edgeworth--large-deviation matching]\label{p11:conj:matching}
When \(y=\sqrt h\,x\to0\), the saddlepoint expansion \eqref{p11:eq:local-ldp-conj}, re-expanded in \(h\), matches the Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite Edgeworth series term by term.  In the overlap \(1\ll x\ll h^{-1/2}\), it matches the Gaussian moderate-deviation expansion.  This matching is Borel summable in a sector of the complex \(x\)-plane avoiding the images of the nearest sinc zeros.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Double matching at the compact edge]\label{p11:conj:edge-matching}
There is a two-parameter uniform asymptotic that matches the compact-scale Lambert--\(W\) law \eqref{p11:eq:edge-rate-main} to the fixed-\(r\) endpoint asymptotic with its periodic logarithmic profile.  The crossover occurs when \(\delta\downarrow0\) and \(h\downarrow0\) jointly so that the exact saddle reaches the first geometric lattice scale before the continuum Riemann-sum approximation loses uniformity.
\end{conjecture}

The last conjecture should reveal how the periodic fluctuations at fixed \(r\) disappear in the continuum \(r\uparrow1\) limit.  Poisson summation in the logarithmic index is a promising mechanism: nonzero Fourier modes should be exponentially small in \(1/h\) in the interior but become visible near the edge.

\subsection{Beyond all orders and sinc-zero geometry}
\begin{conjecture}[Resurgent frequency corrections]\label{p11:conj:resurgence}
After optimal truncation of the continuous Edgeworth series, the remainder is controlled by complex saddles associated with the nearest zeros of \(\SincRad(a_hr^nt)\).  Their actions form a geometric lattice, and the Stokes multipliers admit a \(q\)-product description.  The first exponentially small scale is \(\exp(-C/h)\), consistent with the outer-frequency estimate in \Cref{p11:lem:sinc-envelope}.
\end{conjecture}

A practical route is to apply logarithmic Poisson summation to
\[
 \sum_{n\ge0}\log\SincRad(a_h\EulerE^{-nh}t)
\]
and isolate its nonzero dual modes.  This should be the Gaussian-boundary counterpart of the periodic endpoint profiles already present at fixed base.

\subsection{Entropy and information geometry}
The repository conjectures the leading entropy deficit.  \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz} supplies the missing local expansion, but a complete proof still requires global logarithmic control where \(f_h/\phiN\) is small or large.

\begin{conjecture}[Full entropic expansion]\label{p11:conj:entropy}
The relative entropy has a complete expansion
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:entropy-series}
 D(\LawOperator(Z_h)\Vert N(0,1))
 \sim \sum_{n\ge2}d_nh^n,
 \qquad d_2=\frac3{100},
\end{equation}
where every \(d_n\) is a finite contraction of Bernoulli-generated Edgeworth coefficients using Hermite orthogonality.  The same holds for Fisher information and for Rényi divergences in a nontrivial interval of orders.
\end{conjecture}

A proof should combine the weighted Edgeworth theorem with a saddlepoint majorant on the scale \(x=O(h^{-1/2})\).  The LDP from \Cref{p11:thm:compact-ldp} provides exactly the missing tail geometry.

\subsection{Local symbolic Carleman spectra}
The global weight in \Cref{p11:thm:carleman-ha} is sharp, but local derivative growth can be much smaller at points whose symbolic orbit repeatedly enters regions where the base profile is tiny.

\begin{problem}[Multifractal local regularity]\label{p11:prob:local-carleman}
For \(a\ge2\) and \(x\) in the symbolic attractor, determine the spectrum of
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:local-growth-spectrum}
 \underline\alpha(x)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\AbsoluteValue{h_a^{(n)}(x)}}{n^2},
 \qquad
 \overline\alpha(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\AbsoluteValue{h_a^{(n)}(x)}}{n^2}.
\end{equation}
Relate the Hausdorff dimensions of level sets to recurrence rates of the digit shift and to thermodynamic pressure.
\end{problem}

\begin{conjecture}[Typical quadratic exponent]\label{p11:conj:typical-carleman}
For the natural Bernoulli measure on the symbolic attractor of \(h_a\),
\[
 \underline\alpha(x)=\overline\alpha(x)=\frac12\log a
\]
for almost every \(x\), while exceptional recurrent orbits realize a nontrivial interval of lower subleading exponents.
\end{conjecture}

\subsection{The overlapping phase \texorpdfstring{$1<a<2$}{1<a<2}}
The exact norm formula uses disjoint cylinder supports and therefore stops at
\(a=2\).  Fourier methods still give the matching upper bound, and in fact with
a linear rather than an \(n\log n\) correction.  Write
\(T=2\pi\AbsoluteValue\xi\) and \(L=\log_aT\), and use
\(\AbsoluteValue{\SincRad u}\le\min(1,\AbsoluteValue u^{-1})\) in Part~VI's
product \(\FourierTwoPi{h_a}(\xi)=\prod_{j\ge1}\SincRad(Ta^{-j})\), keeping
only the \(N=\Floor{L}\) factors whose argument is at least \(1\):
for \(T\ge a\), with \(\phi=L-N\in[0,1)\),
\[
 \AbsoluteValue{\FourierTwoPi{h_a}(\xi)}
 \le\frac{a^{N(N+1)/2}}{T^{N}}
 =\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log a}{2}\bigl(L^2-L-\phi^2+\phi\bigr)\right)
 \le a^{1/8}\,T^{1/2}
   \exp\!\left(-\frac{\log^2T}{2\log a}\right),
\]
since \(\phi^2-\phi\ge-\tfrac14\).  Hence, substituting \(T=\EulerE^{v}\),
\[
 \Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_\infty
 \le\int_{\RealNumbers}
   (2\pi\AbsoluteValue\xi)^{n}
   \AbsoluteValue{\FourierTwoPi{h_a}(\xi)}\Differential\xi
 \le\frac{a^{n+1}}{\pi(n+1)}
  +\frac{a^{1/8}}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
   \EulerE^{(n+3/2)v-v^{2}/(2\log a)}\Differential v,
\]
and completing the square in the Gaussian integral gives
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:overlap-upper}
 \log\Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_\infty\le\frac{\log a}{2}n^2+\BigOAt{n}{a},
 \qquad 1<a<2 .
\end{equation}
This much is \statusproved.  It is one half of \eqref{p11:eq:overlap-conj}; the
matching lower bound, which the disjointness argument supplies only for
\(a\ge2\), is what the following conjecture asserts.

\begin{conjecture}[Sharp quadratic exponent under overlap]\label{p11:conj:overlap-growth}
For every \(1<a<2\),
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:overlap-conj}
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1{n^2}\log\Norm{h_a^{(n)}}_\infty
 =\frac12\log a.
\end{equation}
The subleading term changes at parameters with exceptional Bernoulli-convolution overlap, and may encode arithmetic properties of \(a\).
\end{conjecture}

This conjecture would extend the quadratic \(q\)-Gevrey classification through the entire smooth geometric family, while leaving room for arithmetic phase transitions in the \(n\log n\) or linear term.

\subsection{Arithmetic and Thue--Morse directions}
\begin{conjecture}[Cumulant-coefficient denominators]\label{p11:conj:cumulant-denominators}
After the natural normalization by \((2m)!\), the coefficients in the \(h\)-expansion \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-bell} have denominators controlled by von Staudt--Clausen primes from the Bernoulli numbers and by the divisors of \(m^{2k}-m\).  There is a finite-prime valuation formula compatible with the dyadic arithmetic of \(F(2^{-n})\).
\end{conjecture}

\begin{problem}[Automatic-sequence Edgeworth analogs]
Replace the uniform digits in \eqref{p11:eq:Xr-def} by signed or block-dependent digits generated by Thue--Morse and other automatic sequences.  Determine when a Gaussian boundary survives, how automatic cancellations alter the first nonzero cumulant, and whether the resulting Edgeworth polynomials inherit finite-kernel recurrences.
\end{problem}

\begin{problem}[Legendre--Hermite contraction]
The repository develops compact-support Legendre and Jacobi expansions, whereas the Gaussian boundary naturally selects the Hermite basis.  Determine a joint limit in the polynomial degree and in \(h\downarrow0\) under which the appropriately rescaled Legendre/Jacobi coefficients contract to the Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite Edgeworth coefficients.  A successful contraction formula would connect the global compact-support spectral theory to the local Gaussian asymptotic theory without passing through pointwise Fourier inversion.
\end{problem}

\subsection{Formalization targets}
The analytic arguments naturally split into reusable lemmas suitable for Lean or another proof assistant:
\begin{enumerate}
\item exact cumulant algebra and hyperbolic simplification;
\item the global sinc envelope and geometric power-sum bounds;
\item weighted Fourier inversion from \(W^{K,1}\) estimates;
\item the Riemann-sum limit for \(\Lambda_h\);
\item strict convexity and Legendre duality;
\item the Mellin finite-part computation of \(\mathfrak C\);
\item the Carleman ratio test for the exact norm sequence.
\end{enumerate}
The most delicate formalization component is the all-orders bookkeeping in \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}; encoding the weight \(w(\bm k)\) as a graded finite-support map should make the Bell combinatorics manageable.

\section{Promising research program}\label{p11:sec:program}

A productive sequence of projects, ordered by mathematical dependency rather than by perceived difficulty, is:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{P\arabic*.}]
\item \textbf{Local saddlepoint theorem.}  Prove \Cref{p11:conj:local-ldp} by complex Fourier inversion around the unique imaginary saddle.  Establish uniformity on compact subsets of the open limiting support.
\item \textbf{Central matching.}  Expand the saddlepoint coefficients at \(y=0\) and identify them combinatorially with the Bernoulli--Bell--Hermite coefficients of \Cref{p11:thm:edgeworth-schwartz}.
\item \textbf{Entropic CLT with coefficients.}  Combine weighted central control and the compact-scale LDP to prove \Cref{p11:conj:entropy}, first through \(h^3\), then to all orders.
\item \textbf{Logarithmic Poisson modes.}  Derive the exponentially small correction between the geometric Riemann sum and its continuum integral.  Identify the first dual mode and its Stokes geometry.
\item \textbf{Edge crossover.}  Construct the double-scaling asymptotic of \Cref{p11:conj:edge-matching}, retaining the fixed-base periodic phase until it is exponentially suppressed.
\item \textbf{Overlapping quadratic regularity.}  Prove \eqref{p11:eq:overlap-conj}; investigate whether Pisot, Salem, or exact-overlap parameters alter subleading derivative growth.
\item \textbf{Local Carleman thermodynamics.}  Translate the exact symbolic derivative formula into a subadditive pressure problem and compute the multifractal spectrum in \Cref{p11:prob:local-carleman}.
\item \textbf{Arithmetic coefficient package.}  Implement exact Bernoulli--Bell coefficient generation, valuation analysis, and conjecture discovery for \eqref{p11:eq:lambda-bell} and the quantile polynomials.
\item \textbf{Legendre--Hermite contraction.}  Derive the double-scaling limit in the preceding problem and use it to transfer spectral estimates between compact-support and Gaussian-boundary regimes.
\end{enumerate}

The first five projects form a single asymptotic arc from the Gaussian center to the fixed-parameter endpoint.  Projects six through eight exploit the independent but structurally parallel quadratic growth appearing in derivatives, \(q\)-products, and arithmetic denominators; the ninth connects the repository's orthogonal-polynomial and Gaussian asymptotic languages.

\section{Conclusion}
The geometric-uniform deformation turns the Fabius/Rvachev pair into a parameterized laboratory in which several asymptotic languages coexist.  The exact cumulants make Bernoulli numbers primary; exponential composition turns them into Bell polynomials; Fourier inversion turns Bell monomials into Hermite corrections; inversion of the CDF produces Cornish--Fisher polynomials; rescaling to the compact support produces a G\"artner--Ellis rate; and approaching that support edge produces the lower Lambert branch and a Stieltjes constant.  Independently, the Thue--Morse derivative hierarchy produces an exact quadratic-exponential Carleman weight, whose Legendre dual is the log-Gaussian Fourier envelope.

The central result is therefore not only a missing Edgeworth estimate.  It is a bridge between the repository's probability, \(q\)-series, inverse-function, Lambert--\(W\), Bernoulli/Bell, Fourier-product, and automatic-sequence components.  The large-deviation and quadratic \(q\)-Gevrey theorems show that the same geometric scaling controls both the parameter boundary \(r\uparrow1\) and the derivative order \(n\to\infty\), but through different Legendre transforms.  This duality appears to be a fertile organizing principle for the next phase of the Fabius--Rvachev program.

\section{Explicit Hermite polynomials and third-order formulas}\label{p11:app:hermite}
The probabilists' Hermite polynomials used above begin
\begin{align*}
H_3(x)&=x^3-3x,\\
H_4(x)&=x^4-6x^2+3,\\
H_5(x)&=x^5-10x^3+15x,\\
H_6(x)&=x^6-15x^4+45x^2-15,\\
H_7(x)&=x^7-21x^5+105x^3-105x,\\
H_8(x)&=x^8-28x^6+210x^4-420x^2+105.
\end{align*}
The third-order CDF expansion obtained by integrating \eqref{p11:eq:edgeworth-three-orders} is
\begin{align}\label{p11:eq:cdf-third-order}
F_h(x)=\PhiN(x)+\phiN(x)\Bigg[&\frac h{20}H_3(x)
-h^2\left(\frac4{315}H_5(x)+\frac1{800}H_7(x)\right)\notag\\
&+h^3\left(-\frac1{60}H_3(x)+\frac3{700}H_7(x)
+\frac1{1575}H_9(x)+\frac1{48000}H_{11}(x)\right)\Bigg]\notag\\
&+\BigO_{\mathrm{weighted}}(h^4).
\end{align}

\section{A coefficient-extraction form of the full Edgeworth series}\label{p11:app:coefficient}
Treat \(h\) as a formal variable and write the cumulant expansions from \Cref{p11:thm:cumulant-bell} as
\[
 \lambda_{2m}(h)=\sum_{n\ge m-1}\lambda_{2m,n}h^n.
\]
Then the coefficient of \(h^N\) in the density expansion is
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:coefficient-extraction}
 P_N(x)=[h^N]\exp_{\mathcal H}\!\left(
 \sum_{m\ge2}\frac{\lambda_{2m}(h)}{(2m)!}\,H_{2m}\right),
\end{equation}
where \(\exp_{\mathcal H}\) means that multiplication is performed before replacing \((\ImaginaryUnit t)^{2k}\) by \(H_{2k}(x)\).  More explicitly,
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:PN-explicit}
 P_N(x)=
 \sum_{\substack{k_2,k_3,\ldots\ge0\\
 n_{m,j}\ge0\\
 \sum_{m,j}jn_{m,j}=N\\
 \sum_jn_{m,j}=k_m}}
 H_{2\sum_mmk_m}(x)
 \prod_{m\ge2}\frac1{k_m!(2m)!^{k_m}}
 \frac{k_m!}{\prod_jn_{m,j}!}
 \prod_j\lambda_{2m,j}^{n_{m,j}}.
\end{equation}
Only finitely many indices occur for each \(N\), because \(\lambda_{2m,j}=0\) for \(j<m-1\).  Formula \eqref{p11:eq:PN-explicit} is suitable for exact symbolic generation.

\section{Large-deviation series derivation}\label{p11:app:ldp-series}
From \eqref{p11:eq:log-sinh},
\begin{align*}
\Lambda(s)
&=\int_0^1\sum_{k\ge1}c_k(\sqrt6\,su)^{2k}\frac{\Differential u}{u}\\
&=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{c_k6^k}{2k}s^{2k}.
\end{align*}
This yields \eqref{p11:eq:Lambda-series}.  To compute \(I\), solve \(y=\Lambda'(s)\) recursively:
\begin{equation}\label{p11:eq:s-of-y}
 s(y)=y+\frac15y^3+\frac{23}{525}y^5+\frac{22}{2625}y^7
 +\frac{821}{606375}y^9+\BigO(y^{11}).
\end{equation}
Substitution into \(I(y)=ys(y)-\Lambda(s(y))\) gives \eqref{p11:eq:I-center-series}.
