\part{Flat Parameter Response and Smooth $q$-Dynamics at the Fabius Point}



\begin{abstract}
This report develops three new, mutually reinforcing directions in the Fabius--Rvachev
system.  The first concerns the normalized geometric-uniform family
\[
 X_q=(1-q)\sum_{j\ge0}q^jU_j,
 \qquad 0<q<1,
\]
whose half-base member is the Fabius distribution.  We prove that its density is jointly
\(C^\infty\) in the parameter and space variables, but that the exact central plateau for
\(q\le1/2\) produces a continuum of flat nonanalytic fronts.  Every mixed derivative of the
plateau defect vanishes on those fronts, while the defect is strictly positive immediately on
the other side.  In particular,
\[
 \left.\partial_q^r f_q\!\left(\tfrac12\right)\right|_{q=1/2}
 =2^{r+1}r!\qquad(r\ge0),
\]
yet the Taylor series does not represent the right-hand germ.  This gives a parameter-space
counterpart of the classical nowhere-analytic smoothness of the Fabius function.

The second direction is a linear-response or susceptibility theory at \(q=1/2\).  A pathwise
parameter derivative yields a canonical signed tangent measure.  We derive its contractive
resolvent expansion, exact CDF and density refinement equations, conditional-transport form,
infinite-sinc Fourier transform, Bernoulli cumulants, Bell-polynomial moment jets, and a
rational shifted-Legendre spectrum.  The first several exact Legendre coefficients are
computed; a tempting alternating-sign pattern is shown to fail at degree \(16\).

The third direction treats composition dynamics.  We prove a \(C^\infty\) flat Koenigs
linearization theorem for the inverse Fabius map at the midpoint, statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\),
which the absorbed report had left as a hypothesis.  Together with the established strict
convexity of \(F\), exact midpoint--endpoint transfer,
and complete affine midpoint jet, it gives a unique global \(C^\infty\) diffeomorphism
\(\Theta:(0,1)\to\RealNumbers\) satisfying
\[
 \Theta(F(x))=2\Theta(x),\qquad
 \Theta(F^{-1}(x))=\tfrac12\Theta(x),\qquad
 \Theta'(1/2)=1.
\]
The coordinate differs from \(x-1/2\) by a nonzero flat function.  Consequently
inverse
iterates have the beyond-all-orders expansion
\[
 F^{-n}(x)=\frac12+2^{-n}\Theta(x)+\BigO_{x,N}(2^{-Nn})
 \quad\text{for every }N,
\]
with no intermediate algebraic correction terms.  Finally, the known quadratic endpoint law
is converted into a logarithmic B\"ottcher-type height, giving an exact
doubling cocycle and a double-exponential asymptotic for forward iterates, and its quotient
by \(-\Theta\) is an exact one-periodic dynamical factor.  The
report ends with explicit conjectures, numerical checks, and a Lean formalization roadmap.
\end{abstract}

\section{Scope, corpus audit, and novelty boundary}

\subsection{What was surveyed}

The anti-duplication audit used the live documentation tree under
\path{Analysis/FabiusFunction/docs}, with the following hierarchy.

\begin{enumerate}

\path{Fabius_Function_and_Rvachev_Up/Fabius_Function_and_Rvachev_Up.tex},
its mathematical glossary, and the separate non-elementarity article were treated as the
formalization-backed baseline.
\item The canonical
\path{semi-formalized-research-frontiers/semi-formalized-research-frontiers.tex}
was treated as the principal index of deductions, experiments, and open obligations not yet
promoted to the primary exposition.
\item The current draft manifest and the thematic consolidation directories were used as the
index of later work on Thue--Morse formulae, exponent sequences and \(q\)-series, finite sinc
products, atomic functions beyond the dyadic case, signed/reciprocal \(q\)-Fabius orbits,
Lambert \(W\), spectra and arithmetic, transforms, inverse and sampling problems,
Legendre/Lagrange/Rvachev representations, and Fourier decay.
\item The frozen archive was inspected as provenance, not counted as a separate source of new

The live frontier README records that eleven former notebooks were consolidated into six
canonical thematic syntheses plus a gap register, preserving distinct arguments, numerical
evidence, warnings, and proof obligations while compressing redundant repetitions
\cite{bib:repo2026o}.  The current manifest adds the larger thematic draft volumes and recent
representation reports \cite{bib:repo2026p}.  Accordingly, the phrase \emph{new result} below
means ``not found in the active primary exposition, canonical frontier volume, or current
manifest under the audited concepts and equivalent terminology.''  It is not a claim of
absolute priority over all mathematical literature.

\begin{statusbox}{Repository-novel axes identified by the audit}
Exact searches in the active primary and canonical frontier sources found no Fabius-specific
Koenigs/Schr\"oder conjugacy, no B\"ottcher treatment of composition orbits, and no systematic
parameter derivative/linear-response theory for the geometric-uniform family.  The corpus does
contain the ingredients used here: the geometric law and its smooth density, the exact plateau
phase, the midpoint transfer, inverse midpoint defect identities, strict shape theorems,
Bernoulli--Bell machinery, Legendre expansions, and sharp endpoint asymptotics.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Existing inputs deliberately not reproved from first principles}

We use the following results from the repository as named inputs.

\begin{itemize}
\item The bounded Fabius function \(F\) is \(C^\infty\), strictly increasing on \([0,1]\),
constant outside that interval, symmetric by \(F(1-x)=1-F(x)\), and satisfies
\[
 F'(x)=2F(2x)\quad(0\le x\le1/2).
\]
It is strictly convex on \([0,1/2]\), strictly concave on \([1/2,1]\), and all positive-order
endpoint derivatives vanish \cite{bib:repo2026n}.
\item The exact midpoint transfer is
\begin{equation}
 F\!\left(\frac12+h\right)=\frac12+2h-F(h),\qquad
 F\!\left(\frac12-h\right)=\frac12-2h+F(h),
 \quad 0\le h\le\frac12,
 \label{p12:eq:midpoint-transfer-input}
\end{equation}
and \(F^{(k)}(1/2)=0\) for every \(k\ge2\) \cite{bib:repo2026n}.
\item For \(0<q<1\), the normalized geometric-uniform law has a compactly supported
\(C^\infty\) density \(f_q\), a continuous CDF \(F_q\), reflection symmetry, exact support
\([0,1]\), and the affine refinement equation stated in \cref{p12:sec:qfamily}
\cite{bib:repo2026n}.
\item At the dyadic endpoint,
\begin{equation}
 \log F(2^{-t})\sim-\frac{\log2}{2}\,t^2\qquad(t\to\infty),
 \label{p12:eq:dyadic-leading-input}
\end{equation}
while the sharp expansion contains a nonconstant periodic correction in an exact lower-Lambert
phase \cite{bib:repo2026n,bib:repo2026o}.
\end{itemize}

Everything labeled \statusproved{} is derived in this report from these inputs and standard
real/Fourier analysis.  Conditional statements and conjectures are explicitly separated.  No
new theorem in this report has an exact current Lean counterpart; the formal files listed
below certify inputs only.

\section{Conventions of this part}
\label{p12:sec:qfamily}

This part works in the canonical normalization of Part~0, restricted to
$0<q<1$.  In the notation of \cref{p0:def:family} it writes
\begin{equation}
 c_j(q)=(1-q)q^j,
 \qquad
 X_q=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j(q)U_j=\GeoLaw{q},
 \qquad
 Z_q=X_q-\frac12=\GeoLawCentered{q},
 \label{p12:eq:q-law}
\end{equation}
with $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$ independent and uniform on $[0,1]$, and
\[
 F_q(x)=\Probability(X_q\le x),\qquad f_q(x)=F_q'(x),
\]
so $F_q=G_q$ and $f_q=g_q$ in Part~0's letters.  Everything this part needs
from the shared layer is proved there: $X_q\in[0,1]$ with
$\Expectation X_q=\tfrac12$ (\cref{p0:prop:basic}), the identification
$F_{1/2}=\FabiusBounded$ with $f_{1/2}=2\RvachevUp(2\cdot-1)$
(\cref{p0:prop:fabius-point}), the independent-copy decomposition
\begin{equation}
 X_q\overset d=(1-q)U_0+qX_q'
 \label{p12:eq:affine-copy}
\end{equation}
together with its uniqueness (\cref{p0:prop:fixed-point}), and the centered
characteristic function
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_q(t)=\Expectation\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit tZ_q}
 =\prod_{j\ge0}\SincRad\!\left(\frac{c_j(q)t}{2}\right)
 =\CharacteristicFunction{q}(t)
 \label{p12:eq:centered-sinc-product}
\end{equation}
with its locally uniform convergence in $(q,t)$ (\cref{p0:prop:products}).
Cumulants and variance are \cref{p0:thm:cumulants} and
\eqref{p0:eq:variance}.  The one consequence of \eqref{p12:eq:affine-copy}
that this part uses and Part~0 does not record is the pair of exact
distribution and density relations obtained by conditioning on $U_0$,
\begin{align}
 F_q(x)
 &=\int_0^1F_q\!\left(\frac{x-(1-q)u}{q}\right)\Differential u,
 \label{p12:eq:q-cdf-integral}\\
 f_q(x)
 &=\frac{F_q(x/q)-F_q((x-(1-q))/q)}{1-q},
 \label{p12:eq:q-density-difference}
\end{align}
the second being the $u$-derivative of the first after the substitution
$u\mapsto(x-qy)/(1-q)$; both are used throughout this part's response
calculus.

\section{Joint smoothness and flat nonanalytic parameter fronts}
\label{p12:sec:fronts}

\subsection{Uniform Schwartz bounds in the parameter}

The repository proves smoothness in \(x\) for each fixed \(q\).  The first new step is to make
the parameter dependence simultaneous.

\begin{theorem}[Joint smoothness of the geometric-uniform density]
\label{p12:thm:joint-smoothness}
The map
\[
 (q,x)\longmapsto f_q(x)
\]
is \(C^\infty\) on \((0,1)\times\RealNumbers\).  More quantitatively, for every compact
\(K\Subset(0,1)\) and every \(a,b,N\in\NaturalNumbers\),
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{q\in K}\sup_{t\in\RealNumbers}
 (1+|t|)^N
 \left|\partial_q^a\partial_t^b\Phi_q(t)\right|<\infty.
 \label{p12:eq:uniform-schwartz}
\end{equation}
Consequently \(q\mapsto f_q\) is \(C^\infty\) as a map from \((0,1)\) into every
\(C^m(\RealNumbers)\), and all parameter derivatives are supported in \([0,1]\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Weights.}  Fix \(K=[\alpha,\beta]\Subset(0,1)\).  Differentiating
\(c_j(q)=q^j-q^{j+1}\) termwise, for \(0\le l\le r\) and \(j\ge l\),
\(\sup_K|\partial_q^lc_j|\le2(j+1)^l\beta^{\,j-l}\).  Hence
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j\ge0}\sup_{q\in K}|\partial_q^r c_j(q)|<\infty
 \qquad(r\ge0),
 \label{p12:eq:weight-derivative-sum}
\end{equation}
and in particular \(q\mapsto X_q\) is \(C^\infty\) in \(L^\infty\) under the
common-digit coupling.  Put
\(\varepsilon_j^{(r)}=\max\bigl(\sup_Kc_j,\max_{1\le l\le r}\sup_K|\partial_q^lc_j|\bigr)\),
a summable sequence for each \(r\).

\emph{One factor.}  Since \(\SincRad z=\int_0^1\cos(zs)\Differential s\),
differentiation under the integral gives, for real \(z\) and every \(m\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|\SincRad^{(m)}(z)\bigr|\le\int_0^1s^m\Differential s=\frac1{m+1}.
 \label{p12:eq:sinc-derivative-bound}
\end{equation}
Let \(F_j(q,t)=\SincRad(c_j(q)t/2)\).  Then
\(\partial_t^bF_j=(c_j/2)^b\SincRad^{(b)}(c_jt/2)\), and applying \(\partial_q^k\) by
the Leibniz and Fa\`a di Bruno formulas produces a finite sum of terms, each a
product of factors \(\partial_q^lc_j\) (\(l\le k\)) with a factor
\((t/2)^i\SincRad^{(b+i)}(c_jt/2)\), \(i\le k\).  Every term with
\((k,b)\ne(0,0)\) contains at least one factor \(c_j\) or \(\partial_q^lc_j\) with
\(l\ge1\), and the remaining weight factors are bounded uniformly in \(j\) and
\(q\in K\).  With \eqref{p12:eq:sinc-derivative-bound} this gives
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|\partial_q^k\partial_t^bF_j(q,t)\bigr|\le C_{k,b}(1+|t|)^k\varepsilon_j^{(k)}
 \quad\bigl((k,b)\ne(0,0)\bigr),
 \qquad
 |F_j(q,t)|\le\min\left(1,\frac{2}{c_j(q)|t|}\right).
 \label{p12:eq:factor-derivative-bound}
\end{equation}

\emph{The tail.}  For \(M\le M'\) let \(P_{M,M'}=\prod_{M\le j<M'}F_j\).  By the
Leibniz rule, \(\partial_q^a\partial_t^bP_{M,M'}\) is a sum, over the ways of
distributing the \(a\) parameter and \(b\) frequency derivatives among the
factors, of multinomial coefficients times products in which at most \(a+b\)
factors are marked by a derivative.  Bounding every unmarked factor by \(1\)
and every marked one by \eqref{p12:eq:factor-derivative-bound}, and grouping
the terms by the set \(S\) of marked indices (\(|S|\le a+b\)), one obtains
\begin{equation}
 \bigl|\partial_q^a\partial_t^bP_{M,M'}(q,t)\bigr|
 \le C_{a,b}(1+|t|)^a\sum_{s\le a+b}\frac1{s!}\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge M}\varepsilon_j^{(a)}\Bigr)^{s}
 \le C'_{a,b}(1+|t|)^a,
 \label{p12:eq:tail-derivative-bound}
\end{equation}
uniformly in \(M\le M'\) and \(q\in K\).  As \(M'\to\infty\), \(P_{M,M'}\)
converges locally uniformly in \((q,t)\) to \(P_M=\prod_{j\ge M}F_j\)
(\cref{p0:prop:products}); since all mixed derivatives of order \(\le m+1\)
are bounded uniformly in \(M'\) on compact sets, the derivatives of order
\(\le m\) are equicontinuous, and the Arzel\`a--Ascoli theorem together with
the uniqueness of the limit shows that the convergence holds in \(C^m\) on
compact sets for every \(m\).  Hence \(P_M\) is \(C^\infty\) and satisfies
\eqref{p12:eq:tail-derivative-bound}.

\emph{The prefix.}  For \(\Phi_{q,M}=\prod_{j<M}F_j\) and \(|t|\ge1\), a term of the
Leibniz expansion of \(\partial_q^{a'}\partial_t^{b'}\Phi_{q,M}\) has at most
\(a'+b'\) marked factors, each \(\le C(1+|t|)^{a'}\), and at least
\(M-a'-b'\) unmarked ones, each \(\le2/(c_j|t|)\le2/((1-\beta)\alpha^M|t|)\)
because \(c_j(q)\ge(1-\beta)\alpha^j\ge(1-\beta)\alpha^M\) for \(j<M\).  Thus
\(|\partial_q^{a'}\partial_t^{b'}\Phi_{q,M}|\le C_{M,a',b'}(1+|t|)^{a'-(M-a'-b')}\)
on \(K\times\RealNumbers\), the case \(|t|\le1\) being trivial.

\emph{The product.}  Writing \(\Phi_q=\Phi_{q,M}P_M\) and applying the Leibniz
rule once more, each term is bounded by
\(C(1+|t|)^{2a'+b'-M}(1+|t|)^{a-a'}\le C(1+|t|)^{2a+b-M}\).  Choosing
\(M\ge N+2a+b\) proves \eqref{p12:eq:uniform-schwartz}.

\emph{Inversion.}  The characteristic function of \(X_q=Z_q+\tfrac12\) is
\(\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit t/2}\Phi_q(t)\), so that in the angular convention
\eqref{p0:eq:fourier} of Part~0 one has
\(\FourierAngular{f_q}(t)=\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit t/2}\Phi_q(t)\), and since
\(\Phi_q\in L^1\) by \eqref{p12:eq:uniform-schwartz} with \(N=2\),
\[
 f_q(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit t(x-1/2)}\Phi_q(t)\Differential t .
\]
Applying \(\partial_q^a\partial_x^b\) to the integrand gives
\((2\pi)^{-1}(-\ImaginaryUnit t)^b\EulerE^{-\ImaginaryUnit t(x-1/2)}\partial_q^a\Phi_q(t)\),
whose modulus is bounded, uniformly for \((q,x)\in K\times\RealNumbers\), by
\((2\pi)^{-1}|t|^b\sup_K|\partial_q^a\Phi_q(t)|\le C_{a,b}(1+|t|)^{-2}\) by
\eqref{p12:eq:uniform-schwartz} with \(N=b+2\).  Differentiation under the
integral sign is therefore justified by dominated convergence, \(f\) is
jointly \(C^\infty\), and
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{q\in K}\sup_{x\in\RealNumbers}\bigl|\partial_q^a\partial_x^bf_q(x)\bigr|
 \le\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\RealNumbers}(1+|t|)^b\sup_{q\in K}|\partial_q^a\Phi_q(t)|\Differential t
 <\infty .
 \label{p12:eq:density-derivative-bound}
\end{equation}
Since \(F_q\) is identically zero to the left of zero and identically one to
the right of one for all \(q\in(0,1)\), every parameter derivative of the
density vanishes off \([0,1]\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The theorem is a smooth, not analytic, parameter statement.  The next results show that this
distinction is essential, not technical.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The exact plateau and its moving boundary}

For \(q\le1/2\), the head interval \((1-q)U_0\) is at least as long as the support \([0,q]\)
of the tail \(qX_q'\).  The convolution therefore has a central plateau.  This plateau is
already present in the repository's general-base analysis.  Its parameter-space consequence
is new.

\begin{proposition}[Exact plateau and edge defects]
\label{p12:prop:plateau-defect}
For \(0<q\le1/2\),
\begin{equation}
 f_q(x)=\frac1{1-q}
 \qquad(q\le x\le1-q).
 \label{p12:eq:plateau}
\end{equation}
Fix \(x\in(0,1/2)\), and define
\(
 \Delta(q,x)=(1-q)^{-1}-f_q(x).
\)
Then, in the full neighborhood \(0<q<1-x\) of the left front \(q=x\),
\begin{equation}
 \Delta(q,x)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&0<q\le x,\\[2mm]
  \displaystyle\frac{F_q((q-x)/q)}{1-q},&x<q<1-x.
 \end{cases}
 \label{p12:eq:left-front-defect}
\end{equation}
At the meeting point \(x=1/2\),
\begin{equation}
 \Delta\!\left(q,\frac12\right)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&0<q\le1/2,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\frac{2F_q((2q-1)/(2q))}{1-q},&1/2<q<1.
 \end{cases}
 \label{p12:eq:center-front-defect}
\end{equation}
The right front is obtained by \(x\mapsto1-x\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If \(q\le x\le1-q\), then \(x/q\ge1\) and
\((x-(1-q))/q\le0\).  Formula \eqref{p12:eq:q-density-difference} gives
\eqref{p12:eq:plateau}.

Now let \(x<1/2\).  For \(x<q<1-x\), the second CDF argument in
\eqref{p12:eq:q-density-difference} is negative, while \(x/q\in(0,1)\).  Thus
\[
 f_q(x)=\frac{F_q(x/q)}{1-q}
 =\frac{1-F_q(1-x/q)}{1-q},
\]
which is \eqref{p12:eq:left-front-defect}.  At \(x=1/2\), reflection makes the two missing edge
masses equal and gives \eqref{p12:eq:center-front-defect}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Flat nonanalytic fronts]
\label{p12:thm:flat-fronts}
The defect \(\Delta(q,x)=(1-q)^{-1}-f_q(x)\) is flat on each plateau front:
\begin{align}
 \partial_q^r\partial_x^s\Delta(q,x)\big|_{q=x}&=0
 &&(0<x<1/2),
 \label{p12:eq:left-front-flat}\\
 \partial_q^r\partial_x^s\Delta(q,x)\big|_{q=1-x}&=0
 &&(1/2<x<1),
 \label{p12:eq:right-front-flat}
\end{align}
for all \(r,s\ge0\), and the same statement holds at \((q,x)=(1/2,1/2)\).
Nevertheless \(\Delta\) is strictly positive immediately outside the plateau.  Therefore:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \((q,x)\mapsto f_q(x)\) is not real analytic at any point of the two fronts;
\item for every fixed \(x\in(0,1)\), the section \(q\mapsto f_q(x)\) is not real analytic at
\(q_c=\min(x,1-x)\);
\item the \(C^\infty(\RealNumbers)\)-valued map \(q\mapsto f_q\) is not real analytic at any
\(q\in(0,1/2]\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{p12:thm:joint-smoothness}, \(\Delta\) is jointly \(C^\infty\).  On one open side of
each front it is identically zero by \eqref{p12:eq:plateau}.  Every mixed derivative is therefore
zero on that side and, by continuity, on the boundary.  This proves flatness.

For \(x<1/2\) and \(q>x\) sufficiently close to \(x\), formula
\eqref{p12:eq:left-front-defect} has a positive argument.  The support of \(X_q\) is the entire
interval \([0,1]\), and a direct finite-digit event also shows \(F_q(y)>0\) for every
\(y>0\); hence the defect is strictly positive.  The center formula is similarly positive
for \(q>1/2\).

A real-analytic function whose full Taylor series is zero at a point vanishes in a
neighborhood.  Thus the positive defect contradicts analyticity in one or two variables.  For
the function-space statement, a map \(q\mapsto f_q\in C^\infty(\RealNumbers)\) is called real
analytic at \(q_0\) if there are \(\varphi_n\in C^\infty(\RealNumbers)\) and \(r>0\) such that
\(f_q=\sum_{n\ge0}\varphi_n(q-q_0)^n\) for \(|q-q_0|<r\), the series converging in every
seminorm \(\sup_{[-A,A]}|\partial_x^m\cdot|\); this is the standard notion for a map into a
Fr\'echet space.  Composing such a map with a continuous linear functional yields an ordinary
real-analytic scalar function, because the functional passes termwise through the convergent
series.  Apply this to the evaluation functional at \(x=q_0\) when \(q_0<1/2\), or at
\(x=1/2\) when \(q_0=1/2\): the resulting scalar function \(q\mapsto f_q(x)\) would be real
analytic at \(q_0\), contradicting (2).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact front jets]
\label{p12:cor:front-jets}
For every \(r\ge0\),
\begin{align}
 \left.\partial_q^r f_q(x)\right|_{q=x}
 &=\frac{r!}{(1-x)^{r+1}},&&0<x<1/2,
 \label{p12:eq:left-front-qjet}\\
 \left.\partial_q^r f_q(x)\right|_{q=1-x}
 &=\frac{r!}{x^{r+1}},&&1/2<x<1,
 \label{p12:eq:right-front-qjet}\\
 \left.\partial_q^r f_q\!\left(\frac12\right)\right|_{q=1/2}
 &=2^{r+1}r!.
 \label{p12:eq:center-qjet}
\end{align}
Every mixed jet containing at least one \(x\)-derivative vanishes on the front.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Subtract the flat defect from \((1-q)^{-1}\) and differentiate.  The last statement follows
because the plateau branch has no \(x\)-dependence.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A smooth phase transition]
At \((1/2,1/2)\), the Taylor series in \(q-1/2\) is exactly the convergent Taylor series of
\((1-q)^{-1}\).  It therefore predicts the plateau continuation on both sides, while the true
right-hand function is smaller by the positive, flat term in
\eqref{p12:eq:center-front-defect}.  This is a particularly transparent example of a convergent
Taylor series that fails to represent its \(C^\infty\) function.
\end{remark}

\section{The first \texorpdfstring{\(q\)}{q}-response at the Fabius point}
\label{p12:sec:response}

\subsection{Pathwise differentiation and the tangent measure}

Differentiate the weights in the common-digit coupling.  At \(q=1/2\),
\begin{equation}
 d_j:=c_j'(1/2)=
 \begin{cases}
 -1,&j=0,\\
 0,&j=1,\\
 (j-1)2^{-j},&j\ge2.
 \end{cases}
 \qquad \sum_{j\ge0}d_j=0.
 \label{p12:eq:dj}
\end{equation}
Define
\begin{equation}
 X=X_{1/2},\qquad Z=X-\frac12,
 \qquad V=\sum_{j\ge0}d_jU_j
       =\sum_{j\ge0}d_j\left(U_j-\frac12\right).
 \label{p12:eq:XV}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Pathwise linear response]
\label{p12:thm:pathwise-response}
For every \(\varphi\in C^1(\RealNumbers)\) whose derivative is bounded,
\begin{equation}
 \left.\frac{\Differential}{\Differential q}\Expectation\varphi(X_q)\right|_{q=1/2}
 =\Expectation\bigl[\varphi'(X)V\bigr].
 \label{p12:eq:pathwise-response}
\end{equation}
There is a unique compactly supported smooth signed density
\begin{equation}
 \rho(x)=\left.\partial_q f_q(x)\right|_{q=1/2}
 \label{p12:eq:rho-def}
\end{equation}
representing this functional, and its cumulative response
\begin{equation}
 G(x)=\left.\partial_qF_q(x)\right|_{q=1/2}
      =\int_{-\infty}^{x}\rho(t)\Differential t
 \label{p12:eq:G-def}
\end{equation}
satisfies
\begin{gather}
 G(1-x)=-G(x),\qquad \rho(1-x)=\rho(x),
 \label{p12:eq:tangent-symmetry}\\
 \int\rho=0,
 \qquad \int\left(x-\frac12\right)\rho(x)\Differential x=0,
 \qquad \rho\!\left(\frac12\right)=4.
 \label{p12:eq:tangent-normalizations}
\end{gather}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(K\) be a compact neighborhood of \(1/2\) in \((0,1)\).  By
\eqref{p12:eq:weight-derivative-sum}, \(q\mapsto X_q(\omega)=\sum_jc_j(q)U_j(\omega)\) is
\(C^1\) on \(K\) for every \(\omega\), with derivative \(\sum_jc_j'(q)U_j\), and the mean value
theorem gives the \(\omega\)-independent bound
\[
 \left|\frac{\varphi(X_{q+h})-\varphi(X_q)}{h}\right|
 \le\|\varphi'\|_\infty\sup_{q'\in K}\Bigl|\sum_jc_j'(q')U_j\Bigr|
 \le\|\varphi'\|_\infty\sum_j\sup_K|c_j'|<\infty
\]
for \(q,q+h\in K\).  Dominated convergence therefore permits the limit \(h\to0\) inside the
expectation, and the chain rule gives \eqref{p12:eq:pathwise-response} with \(V=\sum_jd_jU_j\).
On the other hand \(\Expectation\varphi(X_q)=\int_0^1\varphi f_q\), and
\eqref{p12:eq:density-derivative-bound} with \((a,b)=(1,0)\) lets one differentiate under the
integral: the functional is represented by \(\rho=\partial_qf_q|_{q=1/2}\), which is smooth and
supported in \([0,1]\) by \cref{p12:thm:joint-smoothness}.  It is the only continuous compactly
supported representative, since a continuous compactly supported function integrating to zero
against every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty\) vanishes.  Likewise
\(F_q(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xf_q\) may be differentiated in \(q\) under the integral, the integrand
\(\partial_qf_q\) being jointly continuous and supported in \([0,1]\), which gives
\eqref{p12:eq:G-def}.

Replacing every digit by \(1-U_j\) sends \(X\) to \(1-X\) and, because \(\sum d_j=0\), sends
\(V\) to \(-V\).  This gives \eqref{p12:eq:tangent-symmetry}.  Total mass and mean are independent
of \(q\), proving the two integral identities.  The center value is the case \(r=1\) of
\eqref{p12:eq:center-qjet}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A contractive susceptibility resolvent}

The response is not only a derivative of an infinite product; it is the solution of a
contractive fixed-point equation.

Let \(\mathcal M_0\) be the space of finite signed measures of total mass zero and finite first
moment, equipped with the Kantorovich--Rubinstein norm
\begin{equation}
 \|\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}
 =\sup\left\{\left|\int\phi\Differential\eta\right|:
 \phi(0)=0,\ \Lip(\phi)\le1\right\}.
 \label{p12:eq:KR}
\end{equation}
For \(0<q<1\), define
\begin{equation}
 \langle\phi,R_q\eta\rangle
 =\int_0^1\int\phi((1-q)u+qx)\Differential\eta(x)\Differential u.
 \label{p12:eq:Rq}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Susceptibility series]
\label{p12:thm:susceptibility}
The operator \(R_q\) preserves \(\mathcal M_0\) and is a contraction there:
\begin{equation}
 \|R_q\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\le q\|\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}.
 \label{p12:eq:Rq-contraction}
\end{equation}
Let \(\mu_q\) be the law of \(X_q\).  The derivative
\(\nu_q=\partial_q\mu_q\) exists in total variation (and hence in the KR norm), has smooth
compactly supported density \(\partial_qf_q\), and has total mass zero.  Define the finite
zero-mass measure
\begin{equation}
 \sigma_q:=\nu_q-R_q\nu_q.
 \label{p12:eq:sigmaq-measure}
\end{equation}
For every \(\phi\in C_c^1(\RealNumbers)\), this measure has the source formula
\begin{equation}
 \langle\phi,\sigma_q\rangle
 =\int_0^1\int
 \phi'((1-q)u+qx)(x-u)\Differential\mu_q(x)\Differential u.
 \label{p12:eq:sigmaq}
\end{equation}
It has a smooth compactly supported density.  Moreover, \(\nu_q\) is the unique zero-mass
solution of
\begin{equation}
 \nu_q=R_q\nu_q+\sigma_q,
 \label{p12:eq:linear-response-fixed}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \nu_q=(I-R_q)^{-1}\sigma_q
      =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R_q^n\sigma_q}
 \label{p12:eq:susceptibility-series}
\end{equation}
with convergence in \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write
\[
 T_q\phi(x)=\int_0^1\phi((1-q)u+qx)\Differential u.
\]
If \(\Lip(\phi)\le1\), then \(T_q\phi\) has Lipschitz constant at most \(q\).
It need not vanish at the KR basepoint.  Since \(\eta(\RealNumbers)=0\), however,
\[
 \int T_q\phi\Differential\eta
 =\int\bigl(T_q\phi-T_q\phi(0)\bigr)\Differential\eta,
\]
and the parenthesized function does vanish at zero.  Thus
\(
\|R_q\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\le q\|\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}
\), proving \eqref{p12:eq:Rq-contraction}; preservation of total mass is immediate.

\emph{Differentiability in total variation.}  Fix a compact \(K\Subset(0,1)\) containing
\(q\) in its interior.  Taylor's formula with integral remainder in the parameter gives, for
\(q+h\in K\) and every \(x\),
\[
 f_{q+h}(x)-f_q(x)-h\,\partial_qf_q(x)
 =\int_0^h(h-s)\,\partial_q^2f_{q+s}(x)\Differential s,
\]
and all functions involved vanish off \([0,1]\).  Integrating in \(x\) over \([0,1]\) and using
\eqref{p12:eq:density-derivative-bound} with \((a,b)=(2,0)\),
\[
 \bigl\|f_{q+h}-f_q-h\,\partial_qf_q\bigr\|_{L^1(\RealNumbers)}
 \le\frac{h^2}{2}\sup_{q'\in K}\sup_x|\partial_q^2f_{q'}(x)|,
\]
which is differentiability of \(q\mapsto\mu_q=f_q\Differential x\) in total variation with
derivative \(\nu_q=\partial_qf_q\Differential x\); its total mass is
\(\partial_q\int f_q=0\).  Convergence in total variation implies convergence in the KR norm
for zero-mass measures carried by \([0,1]\): a test function with \(\phi(0)=0\) and
\(\Lip(\phi)\le1\) satisfies \(|\phi|\le1\) on \([0,1]\), so
\(\|\eta\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\le\|\eta\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\) there.  The measure \(R_q\nu_q\) has the
smooth compactly supported density \(y\mapsto q^{-1}\int_0^1\partial_qf_q((y-(1-q)u)/q)\Differential u\),
so \(\sigma_q\) in \eqref{p12:eq:sigmaq-measure} is well defined, has zero mass, and has a
smooth density supported in \([0,1]\).

\emph{The source formula.}  For \(\phi\in C_c^1(\RealNumbers)\) the fixed point
\eqref{p12:eq:affine-copy} reads
\(\int\phi\Differential\mu_q=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1\phi((1-q)u+qx)f_q(x)\Differential x\Differential u\).
The integrand is jointly \(C^1\) in \((q,u,x)\) on the compact set \(K\times[0,1]^2\), so the
right side may be differentiated in \(q\) under the integral.  The derivative falling on
\(f_q\) gives \(\langle\phi,R_q\nu_q\rangle\); the derivative falling on the affine argument
gives \(\int_0^1\!\int\phi'((1-q)u+qx)(x-u)\Differential\mu_q(x)\Differential u\).  Since the left
side differentiates to \(\langle\phi,\nu_q\rangle\), this is \eqref{p12:eq:linear-response-fixed}
with the source \eqref{p12:eq:sigmaq}.

\emph{Uniqueness and the series.}  If \(\eta\in\mathcal M_0\) solves
\(\eta=R_q\eta+\sigma_q\), then \(\eta-\nu_q=R_q(\eta-\nu_q)\), so by
\eqref{p12:eq:Rq-contraction} \(\|\eta-\nu_q\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\le q\|\eta-\nu_q\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\),
forcing \(\|\eta-\nu_q\|_{\mathrm{KR}}=0\) and hence \(\eta=\nu_q\), because a finite signed
measure with finite first moment that integrates every Lipschitz function to zero is zero.
For the series, note that \((\mathcal M_0,\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{KR}})\) is not complete, so a
Neumann-series argument is not available; instead iterate \eqref{p12:eq:linear-response-fixed}
to the exact identity
\[
 \nu_q-\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}R_q^n\sigma_q=R_q^N\nu_q,
 \qquad
 \Bigl\|\nu_q-\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}R_q^n\sigma_q\Bigr\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\le q^N\|\nu_q\|_{\mathrm{KR}}\longrightarrow0,
\]
which is \eqref{p12:eq:susceptibility-series}, the resolvent notation standing for the unique
solution just identified.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Higher response hierarchy]
\label{p12:cor:higher-response}
For \(s\ge0\) the measure \(\nu_q^{(s)}=\partial_q^s\mu_q\) exists in total variation and has
the smooth density \(\partial_q^sf_q\) supported in \([0,1]\); it has zero mass for \(s\ge1\).
For \(j\ge0\) and a finite signed measure \(\eta\) carried by \([0,1]\), define
\(R_q^{(j)}\eta\) by
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \langle\phi,R_q^{(j)}\eta\rangle
 &=\int_0^1\!\int\phi^{(j)}\bigl((1-q)u+qx\bigr)(x-u)^j\Differential\eta(x)\Differential u\\
 &=\int_0^1\!\int\partial_q^j\bigl[\phi((1-q)u+qx)\bigr]\Differential\eta(x)\Differential u,
 \qquad\phi\in C_c^\infty(\RealNumbers),
\end{aligned}
 \label{p12:eq:Rq-derivative-operator}
\end{equation}
so that \(R_q^{(0)}=R_q\).  If \(\eta=h\Differential x\) with \(h\in C^\infty\) supported in
\([0,1]\), then \(R_q^{(j)}\eta\) is the finite signed measure with smooth density
\((-1)^jH_{q,j}^{(j)}\) supported in \([0,1]\), where
\begin{equation}
 H_{q,j}(y)=q^{-j-1}\int_0^1(y-u)^j\,h\!\left(\frac{y-(1-q)u}{q}\right)\Differential u,
 \label{p12:eq:Rq-derivative-density}
\end{equation}
and it has zero mass when \(j\ge1\).  For every \(s\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
 (I-R_q)\nu_q^{(s)}
 =\sum_{j=1}^{s}\binom{s}{j}R_q^{(j)}\nu_q^{(s-j)}
 \DefinitionEquals S_{q,s},
 \label{p12:eq:higher-distributional}
\end{equation}
where \(S_{q,s}\) is a finite zero-mass measure with smooth density supported in \([0,1]\),
and consequently
\begin{equation}
 \nu_q^{(s)}=(I-R_q)^{-1}S_{q,s}
 =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}R_q^nS_{q,s}
 \label{p12:eq:higher-resolvent}
\end{equation}
with convergence in the KR norm, \(\nu_q^{(s)}\) being the unique zero-mass solution of
\(\nu=R_q\nu+S_{q,s}\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first assertion is the Taylor argument of the proof of \cref{p12:thm:susceptibility}
applied to \(\partial_q^{s-1}f_q\), using \eqref{p12:eq:density-derivative-bound} with
\((a,b)=(s+1,0)\); zero mass follows from \(\int f_q=1\).  In
\eqref{p12:eq:Rq-derivative-operator} the two expressions agree because the argument
\((1-q)u+qx\) is affine in \(q\) with \(q\)-derivative \(x-u\), and the right side is a
continuous linear functional on \(C_c^\infty\) since \(\eta\) is finite and carried by
\([0,1]\).  For \(\eta=h\Differential x\), substitute \(y=(1-q)u+qx\), so that
\(x=(y-(1-q)u)/q\), \(\Differential x=\Differential y/q\) and \(x-u=(y-u)/q\):
\[
 \langle\phi,R_q^{(j)}\eta\rangle
 =\int_{\RealNumbers}\phi^{(j)}(y)H_{q,j}(y)\Differential y
 =(-1)^j\int_{\RealNumbers}\phi(y)H_{q,j}^{(j)}(y)\Differential y,
\]
after \(j\) integrations by parts, \(H_{q,j}\) being smooth and supported in \([0,1]\)
because \(y=(1-q)u+qx\in[0,1]\) whenever \(u,x\in[0,1]\).  This is
\eqref{p12:eq:Rq-derivative-density}; for \(j\ge1\) the density is a derivative of a compactly
supported function, so its integral vanishes.

For \eqref{p12:eq:higher-distributional}, write the fixed point as
\(\int\phi\Differential\mu_q=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1\phi((1-q)u+qx)f_q(x)\Differential x\Differential u\).
The integrand is jointly \(C^\infty\) on \(K\times[0,1]^2\) for every compact \(K\Subset(0,1)\), so
the right side may be differentiated \(s\) times in \(q\) under the integral, and the Leibniz
rule distributes the derivatives between the argument and \(f_q\):
\[
 \langle\phi,\nu_q^{(s)}\rangle
 =\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom sj\int_0^1\!\int_0^1\partial_q^j\bigl[\phi((1-q)u+qx)\bigr]\,
   \partial_q^{s-j}f_q(x)\Differential x\Differential u
 =\sum_{j=0}^{s}\binom sj\langle\phi,R_q^{(j)}\nu_q^{(s-j)}\rangle .
\]
Moving the \(j=0\) term to the left gives \eqref{p12:eq:higher-distributional}, and by the
density formula each summand of \(S_{q,s}\) is a finite zero-mass measure with smooth density
supported in \([0,1]\).  The uniqueness and telescoping arguments of
\cref{p12:thm:susceptibility}, which used only the contraction \eqref{p12:eq:Rq-contraction}
and the fact that \(\nu_q^{(s)}\in\mathcal M_0\), then give \eqref{p12:eq:higher-resolvent}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact refinement equations for the tangent CDF and density}

Put \(f=F'\).  Differentiating \eqref{p12:eq:q-cdf-integral} at \(q=1/2\), then changing variables
from \(u\) to \(v=2x-u\), gives the following.

\begin{theorem}[Tangent refinement system]
\label{p12:thm:tangent-refinement}
Here \(F\equiv0\) on \((-\infty,0]\) and \(F\equiv1\) on \([1,\infty)\), while \(f\), \(G\)
and \(\rho\) vanish off \([0,1]\); these are the values the four functions take on
\(\RealNumbers\), because \(F_q\) is constant off \([0,1]\) for every \(q\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 G(x)=\int_{2x-1}^{2x}G(v)\Differential v
      +4\int_{2x-1}^{2x}(x-v)f(v)\Differential v.}
 \label{p12:eq:G-refinement}
\end{equation}
The source can be written without \(f\) as
\begin{equation}
 4F(x)-4xF(2x)-4(1-x)F(2x-1).
 \label{p12:eq:G-source-F}
\end{equation}
Differentiation in \(x\) yields
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \rho(x)=2\bigl(G(2x)-G(2x-1)\bigr)+2f(x)
 -8x f(2x)-8(1-x)f(2x-1).}
 \label{p12:eq:rho-refinement}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put \(A(q,u,x)=(x-(1-q)u)/q\), so that
\(\partial_qA=\bigl(uq-(x-(1-q)u)\bigr)/q^2=(u-x)/q^2\) and
\(A(\tfrac12,u,x)=2x-u\), \(\partial_qA|_{q=1/2}=4(u-x)\).  The map \((q,y)\mapsto F_q(y)\)
is jointly \(C^\infty\), since \(F_q(y)=\int_{-\infty}^yf_q\) and \(\partial_qf_q\) is jointly
continuous with support in \([0,1]\) (\cref{p12:thm:joint-smoothness}); hence
\((q,u)\mapsto F_q(A(q,u,x))\) is jointly \(C^1\) on a compact neighborhood of
\(\{\tfrac12\}\times[0,1]\), and \eqref{p12:eq:q-cdf-integral} may be differentiated in \(q\)
under the integral over \([0,1]\).  With \(G_q=\partial_qF_q\) and \(f_q=\partial_yF_q\) this
gives, at \(q=\tfrac12\),
\[
 G(x)=\int_0^1G(2x-u)\Differential u
      +4\int_0^1(u-x)f(2x-u)\Differential u,
\]
and the substitution \(v=2x-u\), under which \(u-x=x-v\), is
\eqref{p12:eq:G-refinement}.  Integrating the source by parts,
\(4\int_{2x-1}^{2x}(x-v)f(v)\Differential v
 =4\bigl[(x-v)F(v)\bigr]_{2x-1}^{2x}+4\int_{2x-1}^{2x}F(v)\Differential v\),
and the half-base CDF identity \(F(x)=\int_{2x-1}^{2x}F(v)\Differential v\)
(the case \(q=\tfrac12\) of \eqref{p12:eq:q-cdf-integral}) turns this into
\eqref{p12:eq:G-source-F}.  Finally, \(G\) and \(v\mapsto(x-v)f(v)\) are continuous on
\(\RealNumbers\), so the Leibniz rule for the variable limits applies to
\eqref{p12:eq:G-refinement} and gives
\[
 G'(x)=2G(2x)-2G(2x-1)+4\int_{2x-1}^{2x}f(v)\Differential v
 +4\bigl[2(x-2x)f(2x)-2(x-2x+1)f(2x-1)\bigr],
\]
where \(4\int_{2x-1}^{2x}f=4\bigl(F(2x)-F(2x-1)\bigr)=2f(x)\) by the case
\(q=\tfrac12\) of \eqref{p12:eq:q-density-difference}; this is \eqref{p12:eq:rho-refinement}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
At \(x=1/2\), the boundary values of \(f\) vanish and \(G(0)=G(1)=0\); hence
\eqref{p12:eq:rho-refinement} immediately recovers \(\rho(1/2)=2f(1/2)=4\).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Conditional transport form}

\begin{proposition}[Canonical velocity field and conditional versions]
\label{p12:prop:velocity-field}
Let
\(
 \widetilde b(x)=\Expectation[V\mid X=x]
\)
be any regular conditional version.  The half-base density is strictly positive on
\((0,1)\), and every such version agrees Lebesgue-a.e. there with the canonical representative
\begin{equation}
 b_*(x):=-\frac{G(x)}{f(x)}.
 \label{p12:eq:canonical-velocity}
\end{equation}
The function \(b_*\) is smooth and odd on \((0,1)\), and it satisfies the pointwise identities
\begin{equation}
 b_*(x)f(x)=-G(x),
 \qquad
 \rho(x)=-\frac{\Differential}{\Differential x}\bigl(b_*(x)f(x)\bigr),
 \qquad b_*(1-x)=-b_*(x).
 \label{p12:eq:velocity-form}
\end{equation}
For an arbitrary regular conditional version, the product identity holds only a.e. and the
continuity equation only distributionally:
\[
 \widetilde b\,f=-G\quad\text{a.e. on }(0,1),
 \qquad \rho=-(\widetilde b\,f)' \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\RealNumbers).
\]
Thus the \(q\)-response is a one-dimensional continuity equation with canonical velocity
\(b_*\); null-set changes to a conditional version carry no pointwise content.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For a smooth compactly supported test function,
\[
 \int\varphi(x)\rho(x)\Differential x
 =\Expectation[\varphi'(X)V]
 =\int\varphi'(x)\widetilde b(x)f(x)\Differential x.
\]
Hence \(\rho=-(\widetilde b f)'\) in distributions.  Extend
\(\widetilde b f\) by zero off \([0,1]\).  Since \(V\) is bounded, this product is integrable
and compactly supported; \(G\) is also compactly supported because \(\int\rho=0\).  Therefore
\((\widetilde b f+G)'=0\) on \(\RealNumbers\), and compact support forces
\(\widetilde b f=-G\) a.e.

At half base, \(f(x)=2\bigl(F(2x)-F(2x-1)\bigr)\) by \eqref{p12:eq:q-density-difference}, and
this is strictly positive for \(0<x<1\): if \(x\le\tfrac12\) then \(F(2x-1)=0<F(2x)\), and if
\(x\ge\tfrac12\) then \(F(2x)=1>F(2x-1)\), because \(F\) is strictly increasing on \([0,1]\)
and constant outside it (a repository input listed in \cref{p12:sec:audit}; equivalently,
\(\RvachevUp>0\) on \((-1,1)\)).  Thus \(\mu\) and Lebesgue measure have the
same null sets in the interior, and every conditional version equals
\(b_*=-G/f\) there a.e.  Smoothness follows from smoothness of \(G,f\) and interior positivity.
Finally, \(G(1-x)=-G(x)\) and \(f(1-x)=f(x)\), so the canonical representative is odd.
Its product with \(f\) equals \(-G\) pointwise, and differentiation yields the pointwise
continuity equation.
\end{proof}

\section{Fourier, Bernoulli--Bell, and Legendre faces of the response}
\label{p12:sec:spectral}

\subsection{A marked infinite-sinc product}

At \(q=1/2\), write \(c_j=2^{-j-1}\).  The centered Fourier transform of the tangent density
is the parameter derivative of \(\Phi_q\).

\begin{theorem}[Tangent sinc product]
\label{p12:thm:tangent-sinc}
For every real or complex \(t\),
\begin{equation}
 \dot\Phi(t):=\left.\partial_q\Phi_q(t)\right|_{q=1/2}
 =\sum_{j\ge0}d_j\frac t2\,
 \SincRad'\!\left(\frac{t}{2^{j+2}}\right)
 \prod_{k\ne j}\SincRad\!\left(\frac{t}{2^{k+2}}\right),
 \label{p12:eq:marked-sinc}
\end{equation}
where \(d_j\) is given by \eqref{p12:eq:dj}.  Off the zero set of \(\Phi\), this is equivalently
\begin{equation}
 \dot\Phi(t)=\Phi(t)
 \sum_{j\ge0}d_j\frac t2
 \left[
 \cot\!\left(\frac{c_jt}{2}\right)-\frac{2}{c_jt}
 \right].
 \label{p12:eq:log-sinc-response}
\end{equation}
The apparent poles in \eqref{p12:eq:log-sinc-response} are removable after multiplication by
\(\Phi\), as certified by the entire expression \eqref{p12:eq:marked-sinc}.  The noncentered
Fourier transform is \(\FourierAngular{\rho}(-t)=\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit t/2}\dot\Phi(t)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Allow \(q\) and \(t\) to be complex, with \(|q|\le\varrho<1\) and \(|t|\le R\).  From the
Taylor series, \(|\SincRad z-1|\le\sum_{k\ge1}|z|^{2k}/(2k+1)!\le\tfrac16|z|^2\EulerE^{|z|}\)
and \(|\SincRad'(z)|\le\sum_{k\ge1}2k|z|^{2k-1}/(2k+1)!\le\tfrac13|z|\EulerE^{|z|}\) for all
complex \(z\).  With \(z_j=c_j(q)t/2\) and \(|c_j(q)|\le2\varrho^j\) one gets
\(\sum_j|\SincRad z_j-1|\le\tfrac{R^2}6\EulerE^{R}\sum_j\varrho^{2j}<\infty\), uniformly on the
set considered.  By the Weierstrass criterion the product
\eqref{p12:eq:centered-sinc-product} converges uniformly there, so \(\Phi_q(t)\) is holomorphic
in \((q,t)\) on \(\{|q|<1\}\times\ComplexNumbers\) and, by Weierstrass' theorem on uniformly
convergent sequences of holomorphic functions, \(\partial_q\) of the limit is the locally
uniform limit of \(\partial_q\) of the partial products.  The latter is, by the product rule,
\(\sum_{j<M}c_j'(q)\tfrac t2\SincRad'(c_jt/2)\prod_{k<M,\,k\ne j}\SincRad(c_kt/2)\), which at
\(q=\tfrac12\) is the \(M\)-th partial sum of \eqref{p12:eq:marked-sinc} because
\(c_j'(\tfrac12)=d_j\) and \(c_j(\tfrac12)t/2=t/2^{j+2}\).  The series converges locally
uniformly in \(t\in\ComplexNumbers\) on its own: since
\(\prod_{k\ne j}|\SincRad(t/2^{k+2})|\le\prod_k(1+\tfrac{R^2}{6\cdot4^{k+2}}\EulerE^{R})\le\EulerE^{R^2\EulerE^R/72}\),
its \(j\)-th term is bounded by
\(|d_j|\,\tfrac R2\cdot\tfrac{R}{3\cdot2^{j+2}}\EulerE^{R}\EulerE^{R^2\EulerE^R/72}=O(j\,4^{-j})\).
Hence \eqref{p12:eq:marked-sinc} holds for every complex \(t\), and both sides are entire.  The
logarithmic form \eqref{p12:eq:log-sinc-response} uses
\(\SincRad'(z)/\SincRad(z)=\cot z-z^{-1}\) off the zeros of \(\Phi\), and the statement about
\(\FourierAngular{\rho}\) is the \(q\)-derivative of the relation
\(\FourierAngular{f_q}(-t)=\EulerE^{\ImaginaryUnit t/2}\Phi_q(t)\) from the proof of
\cref{p12:thm:joint-smoothness}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Closed cumulants and first moment jets}

Let \(B_r\) denote the Bernoulli numbers with \(B_1=-1/2\), and let
\[
 \QInteger{r}{q}=\frac{1-q^r}{1-q}
\]
be the \(q\)-integer.

\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli--\(q\)-integer cumulants]
\label{p12:thm:cumulants}
For \(r\ge2\), the centered cumulants of \(Z_q\) are
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_r(q)
 =\frac{B_r}{r}\frac{(1-q)^r}{1-q^r}
 =\frac{B_r}{r}\frac{(1-q)^{r-1}}{\QInteger{r}{q}}.
 \label{p12:eq:q-cumulant}
\end{equation}
At the Fabius point,
\begin{align}
 \kappa_r(1/2)&=\frac{B_r}{r(2^r-1)},
 \label{p12:eq:half-cumulant}\\
 \dot\kappa_r
 :=\left.\partial_q\kappa_r(q)\right|_{q=1/2}
 &=-2B_r\frac{2^r-2}{(2^r-1)^2}.
 \label{p12:eq:half-cumulant-derivative}
\end{align}
All odd values with \(r>1\) vanish.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The centered uniform digit has cumulant generating function
\[
 \log\frac{\sinh(z/2)}{z/2}
 =\sum_{r\ge2}\frac{B_r}{r}\frac{z^r}{r!}.
\]
Since \(Z_q=\GeoLawCentered q\), \eqref{p12:eq:q-cumulant} is \cref{p0:thm:cumulants} in
the letters of this part; the interchange of the sum over \(j\) with the cumulant expansion
is justified there.  Concretely, with \(\sinhc w=\sinh w/w\) one has
\(|\log\sinhc w|\le|w|^2\) for complex \(|w|\le1\), so
\(K_q(z)=\log\Expectation\EulerE^{zZ_q}=\sum_j\log\sinhc(c_j(q)z/2)\) converges uniformly on
\(|z|\le2/(1-q)\) and its Taylor coefficients at \(0\) are the sums of the termwise
coefficients; summing \(c_j(q)^r\) over \(j\) gives \eqref{p12:eq:q-cumulant}.  At
\(q=\tfrac12\), \((1-q)^r/(1-q^r)=1/(2^r-1)\), which is \eqref{p12:eq:half-cumulant}; and
\[
 \frac{\Differential}{\Differential q}\frac{(1-q)^r}{1-q^r}
 =\frac{-r(1-q)^{r-1}(1-q^r)+rq^{r-1}(1-q)^r}{(1-q^r)^2}
 \Big|_{q=1/2}
 =\frac{r\,2^{1-2r}\,(2-2^r)}{(2^r-1)^2/2^{2r}}
 =-\frac{2r\,(2^r-2)}{(2^r-1)^2},
\]
which multiplied by \(B_r/r\) is \eqref{p12:eq:half-cumulant-derivative}.
\end{proof}

Let \(\mu_n(q)=\Expectation Z_q^n\), \(\mu_n=\mu_n(1/2)\), and
\(\dot\mu_n=\partial_q\mu_n(q)|_{1/2}\).

\begin{corollary}[Bell moment response]
\label{p12:cor:moment-response}
For every \(n\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \dot\mu_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\binom nr\dot\kappa_r\mu_{n-r}.}
 \label{p12:eq:moment-response}
\end{equation}
In particular, for even orders,
\begin{equation}
 \dot\mu_{2n}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\binom{2n}{2m}
 \dot\kappa_{2m}\mu_{2n-2m}.
 \label{p12:eq:even-moment-response}
\end{equation}
The first values are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}c c c@{}}
\toprule
\(n\) & \(\mu_n\) & \(\dot\mu_n\)\\
\midrule
2 & \(1/36\) & \(-2/27\)\\
4 & \(19/10800\) & \(-83/10125\)\\
6 & \(583/3810240\) & \(-599/617400\)\\
8 & \(132809/8328096000\) & \(-57910967/464551605000\)\\
10 & \(46840699/24990950476800\) & \(-32576528018233/1901452086371376000\)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(M_q(z)=\Expectation\EulerE^{zZ_q}=\exp K_q(z)\).  Since \(|Z_q|\le\tfrac12\), one has
\(|\mu_n(q)|\le2^{-n}\), so \(M_q(z)=\sum_n\mu_n(q)z^n/n!\) is entire; and by the pathwise
derivative of \cref{p12:thm:pathwise-response},
\(\partial_q\mu_n(q)=n\,\Expectation[Z_q^{n-1}\partial_qZ_q]\) with
\(|\partial_q\mu_n(q)|\le n2^{1-n}\sum_j\sup_K|c_j'|\), so \(\partial_qM_q(z)\) is obtained by
differentiating the series termwise in \(q\).  On the disc \(|z|<2/(1-q)\) of the previous
proof, \(M_q\) has no zeros and \(K_q=\log M_q\) is analytic in \(z\) and \(C^1\) in \(q\), with
\(\partial_qK_q(z)=\partial_qM_q(z)/M_q(z)=\sum_r\partial_q\kappa_r(q)z^r/r!\), the last series
converging because \(|\partial_q\kappa_r(q)|\le C_K\,r\,|B_r|\,(1-\alpha)^{r-1}\) on
\(K=[\alpha,\beta]\) and \(|B_r|\le4\,r!/(2\pi)^r\).  Hence \(\partial_qM_q=M_q\,\partial_qK_q\)
is an identity between convergent power series in \(z\), and comparing the coefficients of
\(z^n/n!\) gives \eqref{p12:eq:moment-response}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[All parameter jets and complete Bell polynomials]
\label{p12:prop:all-qjets}
For \(s\ge1\), put
\(
 K_j(z)=\partial_q^j\log M_q(z).
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
 \partial_q^sM_q(z)
 =M_q(z)\,\mathcal B_s\bigl(K_1(z),\ldots,K_s(z)\bigr),
 \label{p12:eq:complete-bell-qjets}
\end{equation}
where \(\mathcal B_s\) is the complete exponential Bell polynomial.  At \(q=1/2\), every
coefficient is rational.  More precisely, the odd part of the denominator of
\(\partial_q^s\kappa_r(1/2)\) divides the odd part of
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{den}\!\left(\frac{B_r}{r}\right)(2^r-1)^{s+1}.
 \label{p12:eq:cyclotomic-denominator-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Equation \eqref{p12:eq:complete-bell-qjets} is the Fa\`a di Bruno formula for the exponential.
By induction on \(s\), \(\partial_q^s\kappa_r(q)=\frac{B_r}{r}\,P_{r,s}(q)/(1-q^r)^{s+1}\)
with \(P_{r,s}\in\IntegerNumbers[q]\): indeed \(P_{r,0}=(1-q)^r\), and
\(\partial_q\bigl[P/(1-q^r)^{s+1}\bigr]
 =\bigl[P'(1-q^r)+(s+1)rq^{r-1}P\bigr]/(1-q^r)^{s+2}\) keeps integer coefficients.  At
\(q=\tfrac12\), \(P_{r,s}(\tfrac12)\) is an integer divided by a power of two, and
\((1-2^{-r})^{s+1}=(2^r-1)^{s+1}2^{-r(s+1)}\); hence the odd part of the denominator of
\(\partial_q^s\kappa_r(\tfrac12)\) divides the odd part of \eqref{p12:eq:cyclotomic-denominator-bound}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact rational shifted-Legendre spectrum}

Let \(P_k\) be the ordinary Legendre polynomial and
\(P_k^*(x)=P_k(2x-1)\).  Orthogonality on \([0,1]\) gives
\[
 \int_0^1P_k^*(x)P_\ell^*(x)\Differential x=\frac{\delta_{k\ell}}{2k+1}.
\]
Since \(\rho\) is symmetric about \(1/2\), only even degrees occur.

\begin{theorem}[Legendre coefficients of the tangent density]
\label{p12:thm:legendre-response}
Write
\begin{equation}
 \rho(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_{2n}P_{2n}(2x-1).
 \label{p12:eq:rho-legendre}
\end{equation}
The expansion converges in \(C^m[0,1]\) for every \(m\), and the coefficients are rational.
If
\(
 P_{2n}(y)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}p_{n,j}y^{2j},
\)
then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 a_{2n}=(4n+1)\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{n,j}2^{2j}\dot\mu_{2j}.}
 \label{p12:eq:legendre-coeff-formula}
\end{equation}
The first coefficients are
\begin{align}
 a_2&=-\frac{20}{9},&
 a_4&=\frac{1088}{225},&
 a_6&=-\frac{37076}{11025},\notag\\
 a_8&=\frac{49280096}{75907125},&
 a_{10}&=-\frac{65166997444}{756561977325},&
 a_{12}&=\frac{10886281949792992}{31325448671141625}.
 \label{p12:eq:first-legendre-coeffs}
\end{align}
Moreover \(a_{2n}=\BigO_A(n^{-A})\) for every \(A>0\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Orthogonality gives
\[
 a_k=(2k+1)\int_0^1\rho(x)P_k(2x-1)\Differential x
 =(2k+1)\left.\partial_q\Expectation P_k(2Z_q)\right|_{q=1/2}.
\]
Expanding the polynomial proves \eqref{p12:eq:legendre-coeff-formula}.  Rationality follows from
\cref{p12:cor:moment-response}.  For the decay put \(u(y)=\rho((1+y)/2)\), a \(C^\infty\)
function on \([-1,1]\) (indeed on \(\RealNumbers\)), so that
\(a_k=\tfrac{2k+1}2\int_{-1}^1u(y)P_k(y)\Differential y\), and let
\(\mathcal Lv=((1-y^2)v')'\) be the Legendre operator, with \(\mathcal LP_k=-k(k+1)P_k\).  For
any \(v,w\in C^2[-1,1]\), two integrations by parts give
\(\int_{-1}^1v\,\mathcal Lw=\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal Lv)\,w\), the boundary terms
\([v(1-y^2)w']_{-1}^1\) and \([(1-y^2)v'w]_{-1}^1\) vanishing because the weight \(1-y^2\)
does --- no endpoint flatness of \(u\) is needed.  Iterating,
\[
 |a_k|=\frac{2k+1}{2\,(k(k+1))^m}\left|\int_{-1}^1(\mathcal L^mu)\,P_k\right|
 \le\frac{(2k+1)\,\|\mathcal L^mu\|_{L^1[-1,1]}}{2\,(k(k+1))^m}
 \qquad(m\ge0),
\]
which is \(a_k=\BigO_A(k^{-A})\) for every \(A\).  For the \(C^m\) convergence, the Markov
inequality \(\|p'\|_{L^\infty[-1,1]}\le(\deg p)^2\|p\|_{L^\infty[-1,1]}\), iterated \(m\) times
with \(\|P_k\|_\infty=1\), gives \(\|P_k^{(m)}\|_{L^\infty[-1,1]}\le k^{2m}\), so
\(\|\tfrac{\Differential^m}{\Differential x^m}P_{2n}(2x-1)\|_{L^\infty[0,1]}\le2^m(2n)^{2m}\)
and \(\sum_n|a_{2n}|\,2^m(2n)^{2m}<\infty\); the series \eqref{p12:eq:rho-legendre} therefore
converges in \(C^m[0,1]\) for every \(m\), and its limit is \(\rho\) because it is the
\(L^2\) limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A useful failed pattern]
The signs alternate through degrees \(2,4,\ldots,14\), which might suggest
\((-1)^na_{2n}>0\).  Exact arithmetic disproves this at degree \(16\):
\[
 a_{16}=
 -\frac{20997028161526723805395541511872}
 {64367687808725429829005095415625}
 \approx-0.3262044805.
\]
Thus any eventual sign theorem must involve a more subtle phase, and the low-degree pattern
should not be promoted to a conjecture without additional asymptotic analysis.
\end{remark}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/figures/tangent_legendre_coefficients.png}
\caption{Exact shifted-Legendre coefficients of the tangent density through degree \(20\),
shown in decimal form.  The same-sign pair at degrees \(14\) and \(16\) is visible.}
\label{p12:fig:legendre-coeffs}
\end{figure}

\section{A global smooth Schr\"oder coordinate for Fabius iteration}
\label{p12:sec:koenigs}

Let
\[
 p=\frac12,
 \qquad Q=F^{-1}:(0,1)\to(0,1).
\]
The primary exposition already supplies the smooth inverse, strict curvature, and the exact
midpoint defect.  After the dynamical preliminaries, the local linearization statement
\(\mathrm{(K)}\) is isolated and proved, and the global composition claims follow from it.

\subsection{The global basin of the midpoint}

\begin{lemma}[Diagonal inequalities and inverse attraction]
\label{p12:lem:diagonal}
For \(0<x<p\), \(F(x)<x\); for \(p<x<1\), \(F(x)>x\).  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 Q^n(x)\longrightarrow p
 \qquad(x\in(0,1)).
 \label{p12:eq:inverse-attraction}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
On \([0,p]\), strict convexity places the graph strictly below the chord joining
\((0,0)\) and \((p,p)\), which is the diagonal.  Reflection gives the right inequality.  If
\(x<p\), then \(Q(x)>x\) and \(Q(x)<p\); the increasing bounded orbit converges to a fixed
point.  The only fixed points in \((0,p]\) are \(p\), because the diagonal inequality excludes
all others.  The right half is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A flat local contraction}

Center the inverse at \(p\):
\begin{equation}
 g(y)=Q(p+y)-p,
 \qquad |y|<p.
 \label{p12:eq:g-def}
\end{equation}
The midpoint transfer \eqref{p12:eq:midpoint-transfer-input} implies, for \(\delta\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
 g(\delta)=\frac\delta2+\frac12F(g(\delta)).
 \label{p12:eq:g-fixed}
\end{equation}
Reflection makes \(g\) odd.

\begin{lemma}[Flat local normal form]
\label{p12:lem:flat-local-map}
There is a smooth flat function \(r\) at zero such that
\begin{equation}
 g(y)=\frac y2+r(y),
 \qquad
 r^{(k)}(0)=0\quad(k\ge0).
 \label{p12:eq:g-flat}
\end{equation}
The function \(r\) is odd and nonzero; for \(y>0\), \(r(y)>0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Equation \eqref{p12:eq:g-fixed} gives \(r(\delta)=F(g(\delta))/2\) for \(\delta\ge0\).  Endpoint
flatness says \(F(t)=\LittleO(t^N)\) as \(t\downarrow0\) for every \(N\), while
\(g(\delta)=\BigO(\delta)\).  Hence \(r\) is flat from the right, and oddness gives the full
statement.  Positivity follows from \(F(t)>0\) for \(t>0\).
\end{proof}

The local \(C^\infty\) linearization is the one analytic step that the absorbed report did
not complete: it isolated the statement as a hypothesis \(\mathrm{(K)}\), and the later results
were stated conditionally on it.  The statement is kept under its name, because the later
results refer to it, and is proved in \cref{p12:thm:flat-koenigs}.

\begin{definition}[Flat Koenigs statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\)]
\label{p12:hyp:flat-koenigs}
For the map \(g\) in \eqref{p12:eq:g-def}, statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\) is the assertion that on a
neighborhood of zero the limit
\begin{equation}
 \theta(y)=\lim_{n\to\infty}2^n g^n(y)
 \label{p12:eq:local-koenigs-limit}
\end{equation}
exists in \(C^\infty\), is a local increasing diffeomorphism, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \theta(g(y))=\frac12\theta(y),
 \qquad \theta'(0)=1,
 \qquad \theta(y)-y\text{ is flat at }0.
 \label{p12:eq:local-koenigs-properties}
\end{equation}
It also asserts uniqueness among local \(C^1\) solutions with derivative one at zero.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Flat Koenigs linearization]
\label{p12:thm:flat-koenigs}
Statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\) of \cref{p12:hyp:flat-koenigs} holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{A contracting interval.}  By \cref{p12:lem:flat-local-map}, \(g=\tfrac12\,\mathrm{id}+r\)
with \(r\) smooth and flat at \(0\); choose \(\delta_0\in(0,p)\) with \(|r'|\le\tfrac14\) on
\(J=[-\delta_0,\delta_0]\).  Then \(\tfrac14\le g'\le\tfrac34\) on \(J\), so \(g\) is increasing,
maps \(J\) into itself, and
\begin{equation}
 |g^k(y)|\le(3/4)^k|y|\qquad(y\in J,\ k\ge0).
 \label{p12:eq:iterate-contraction}
\end{equation}
Flatness means that for every \(j\ge0\) and \(N\ge0\) there is \(C_{j,N}\) with
\(|r^{(j)}(u)|\le C_{j,N}|u|^N\) on \(J\).

\emph{Derivatives of the iterates.}  We claim that for every \(m\ge1\) there is \(A_m\) with
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{y\in J}\bigl|(g^k)^{(m)}(y)\bigr|\le A_m(3/4)^k\qquad(k\ge0).
 \label{p12:eq:iterate-derivative-bound}
\end{equation}
For \(m=1\), \((g^k)'(y)=\prod_{i<k}g'(g^i(y))\le(3/4)^k\).  Let \(m\ge2\) and assume
\eqref{p12:eq:iterate-derivative-bound} for all orders below \(m\).  By the Fa\`a di Bruno
formula applied to \(g^k=g\circ g^{k-1}\),
\[
 (g^k)^{(m)}=g'(g^{k-1})\,(g^{k-1})^{(m)}
 +\sum_{j=2}^{m}g^{(j)}(g^{k-1})\,B_{m,j}\bigl((g^{k-1})',\ldots,(g^{k-1})^{(m-j+1)}\bigr),
\]
where \(B_{m,j}\) is the partial Bell polynomial.  For \(j\ge2\), \(g^{(j)}=r^{(j)}\), so by
flatness of order \(2\) and \eqref{p12:eq:iterate-contraction},
\(|g^{(j)}(g^{k-1}(y))|\le C_{j,2}\delta_0^2(3/4)^{2(k-1)}\); the arguments of \(B_{m,j}\) have
orders at most \(m-1\), hence are bounded by the induction hypothesis.  Writing
\(a_k=\sup_J|(g^k)^{(m)}|\) this gives \(a_k\le\tfrac34a_{k-1}+C(3/4)^{2k}\) with \(a_0=0\), and
unrolling, \(a_k\le C\sum_{i=1}^k(3/4)^{k-i}(3/4)^{2i}\le C(3/4)^k\sum_{i\ge1}(3/4)^i\), which
is \eqref{p12:eq:iterate-derivative-bound}.

\emph{The telescoped series.}  Since \(g(y)-\tfrac12y=r(y)\), induction on \(n\) gives the
telescoping identity
\begin{equation}
 2^ng^n(y)=y+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{k+1}r\bigl(g^k(y)\bigr),
 \qquad y\in J.
 \label{p12:eq:koenigs-telescope}
\end{equation}
Put \(T_k(y)=2^{k+1}r(g^k(y))\).  By \eqref{p12:eq:iterate-contraction} and flatness of order
\(3\), \(|T_k(y)|\le2^{k+1}C_{0,3}\delta_0^3(3/4)^{3k}=C(27/32)^k\).  For \(m\ge1\), the
Fa\`a di Bruno formula gives
\[
 T_k^{(m)}=2^{k+1}\sum_{j=1}^mr^{(j)}(g^k)\,B_{m,j}\bigl((g^k)',\ldots,(g^k)^{(m-j+1)}\bigr),
\]
in which \(|r^{(j)}(g^k(y))|\le C_{j,3}\delta_0^3(3/4)^{3k}\) and, by
\eqref{p12:eq:iterate-derivative-bound}, \(|B_{m,j}|\le C_m(3/4)^{jk}\le C_m(3/4)^k\); hence
\[
 \sup_J\bigl|T_k^{(m)}\bigr|\le C'_m\,2^{k+1}(3/4)^{4k}=2C'_m\,(81/128)^k .
\]
Every derivative series \(\sum_kT_k^{(m)}\), \(m\ge0\), therefore converges uniformly on
\(J\), so \(\theta(y)=\lim_n2^ng^n(y)=y+\sum_{k\ge0}T_k(y)\) exists, is \(C^\infty\) on \(J\), and
the convergence in \eqref{p12:eq:local-koenigs-limit} holds in every \(C^m(J)\).

\emph{The properties in \eqref{p12:eq:local-koenigs-properties}.}  Passing to the limit in
\(2^{n}g^{n}(g(y))=\tfrac12\cdot2^{n+1}g^{n+1}(y)\) gives \(\theta(g(y))=\tfrac12\theta(y)\).
Since \((g^n)'(0)=g'(0)^n=2^{-n}\), differentiating the limit termwise gives \(\theta'(0)=1\),
so \(\theta\) is an increasing diffeomorphism near \(0\).  Each \(T_k\) is flat at \(0\), because
\(g^k(0)=0\) and every derivative of \(r\circ g^k\) at \(0\) is a sum of products containing
some \(r^{(j)}(0)=0\); as \(\sum_kT_k^{(m)}\) converges uniformly, the \(m\)-th derivative of
\(\theta-\mathrm{id}=\sum_kT_k\) at \(0\) is \(\sum_kT_k^{(m)}(0)=0\), so \(\theta-\mathrm{id}\)
is flat.  Finally, if \(\psi\) is \(C^1\) near \(0\) with \(\psi(g(y))=\tfrac12\psi(y)\) and
\(\psi'(0)=1\), then for \(y\ne0\) in \(J\), \(g^n(y)\ne0\) and
\[
 \psi(y)=2^n\psi(g^n(y))
 =2^ng^n(y)\cdot\frac{\psi(g^n(y))}{g^n(y)}\longrightarrow\theta(y)\cdot\psi'(0)=\theta(y),
\]
which is the uniqueness assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{statusbox}{Status of \(\mathrm{(K)}\)}
The absorbed report assumed statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\) as a hypothesis and stated everything
involving \(\Theta\), its inverse-iterate expansion, its escape clock, and the periodic
quotient with \(B\) conditionally.  \cref{p12:thm:flat-koenigs} proves it, so those results
are unconditional in this volume; the phrase ``statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\)'' below is a pointer
to that theorem.  No current Lean theorem covers it.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Globalization and exact conjugacy}

\begin{theorem}[Global Fabius Schr\"oder coordinate]
\label{p12:thm:global-theta}
There is a unique
\(C^\infty\) increasing diffeomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \Theta:(0,1)\longrightarrow\RealNumbers
 \label{p12:eq:theta-domain}
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(p)=0,\qquad \Theta'(p)=1,
 \label{p12:eq:theta-normalization}
\end{equation}
that satisfies either, hence both, of the conjugacy equations
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \Theta(Q(x))=\frac12\Theta(x),
 \qquad
 \Theta(F(x))=2\Theta(x).}
 \label{p12:eq:theta-conjugacy}
\end{equation}
It is odd under reflection,
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(1-x)=-\Theta(x),
 \label{p12:eq:theta-odd}
\end{equation}
and has the global limit representation
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \Theta(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}2^n\left(Q^n(x)-\frac12\right).}
 \label{p12:eq:theta-global-limit}
\end{equation}
At the midpoint,
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(p+y)=y+\flatremainder(y),
 \qquad
 \Theta^{-1}(t)=p+t+\flatremainder(t),
 \label{p12:eq:theta-flat}
\end{equation}
where each displayed remainder is nonzero and flat.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\cref{p12:thm:flat-koenigs} supplies the local coordinate \(\theta\) of statement
\(\mathrm{(K)}\).  By
\cref{p12:lem:diagonal}, every interior point enters the local neighborhood under
some inverse iterate.  If \(m\) is large enough, define
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(x)=2^m\theta(Q^m(x)-p).
 \label{p12:eq:theta-globalize}
\end{equation}
Since \(Q^{m+1}(x)-p=g(Q^m(x)-p)\) by \eqref{p12:eq:g-def}, the local equation
\(\theta(g(y))=\theta(y)/2\) gives
\(2^{m+1}\theta(Q^{m+1}(x)-p)=2^m\theta(Q^m(x)-p)\), so the value is independent of the
admissible \(m\).  If \(Q^{m}(x_0)-p\) lies in the open interval on which \(\theta\) is
defined, then by continuity of \(Q^m\) so does \(Q^m(x)-p\) for all \(x\) in a neighborhood of
\(x_0\); on that neighborhood \(\Theta\) is given by \eqref{p12:eq:theta-globalize} with the
fixed \(m\), hence is \(C^\infty\).  Its derivative is positive because \(Q^m\) and \(\theta\)
are increasing.
The conjugacy and normalization are immediate, and the limit formula follows from the local
limit after a finite initial segment.

The image is an open interval containing zero.  It is invariant under multiplication by two
because \(\Theta(F(x))=2\Theta(x)\).  Since it contains both positive and negative values, it
must be all of \(\RealNumbers\).  Reflection and local uniqueness give oddness.  For global uniqueness, let
\(\widetilde\Theta\) be a \(C^1\) solution of \(\widetilde\Theta\circ Q=\tfrac12\widetilde\Theta\)
with \(\widetilde\Theta(p)=0\) and \(\widetilde\Theta'(p)=1\).  Iterating,
\(\widetilde\Theta(x)=2^n\widetilde\Theta(Q^n(x))\), and differentiability at \(p\) gives
\(\widetilde\Theta(Q^n(x))=(Q^n(x)-p)\bigl(1+\LittleO(1)\bigr)\) as \(n\to\infty\), because
\(Q^n(x)\to p\) by \cref{p12:lem:diagonal}.  Hence
\[
 \widetilde\Theta(x)
 =2^n(Q^n(x)-p)\bigl(1+\LittleO(1)\bigr)\longrightarrow\Theta(x)
\]
by \eqref{p12:eq:theta-global-limit}, the sequence \(2^n(Q^n(x)-p)\) being convergent and
therefore bounded; so \(\widetilde\Theta=\Theta\).
Flatness is part of statement \(\mathrm{(K)}\); flatness of the inverse follows
by composition.  The remainder is not identically zero because that would make \(F\) exactly
affine near \(p\), contradicting \eqref{p12:eq:midpoint-transfer-input} and \(F(h)>0\) for
\(h>0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Exact iterate formula and inverse asymptotic]
\label{p12:cor:iterate-formula}
For every \(x\in(0,1)\) and \(n\ge0\),
\begin{equation}
 F^n(x)=\Theta^{-1}(2^n\Theta(x)),
 \qquad
 Q^n(x)=\Theta^{-1}(2^{-n}\Theta(x)).
 \label{p12:eq:exact-iterates-theta}
\end{equation}
For every integer \(N\ge2\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 Q^n(x)=\frac12+2^{-n}\Theta(x)+\BigO_{x,N}(2^{-Nn})
 \qquad(n\to\infty).}
 \label{p12:eq:inverse-beyond-all-orders}
\end{equation}
Thus every algebraic correction between \(2^{-n}\) and \(2^{-Nn}\) vanishes: the first
correction is beyond all orders in the contraction scale.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Equation \eqref{p12:eq:exact-iterates-theta} is iteration of the conjugacy.  Since
\(\Theta^{-1}(t)-p-t\) is flat, it is \(\BigO(t^N)\) for every \(N\).  Substitute
\(t=2^{-n}\Theta(x)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Nonanalyticity of the linearizing coordinate]
\label{p12:cor:theta-nonanalytic}
Neither \(\Theta\) nor \(\Theta^{-1}\) is real analytic at the
midpoint.  Their Taylor series there are exactly \(x-p\) and \(p+t\), respectively.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If \(\Theta\) were analytic, its flat difference from \(x-p\) would vanish locally.  The
conjugacy would then force \(F(p+h)=p+2h\) locally, contradicting
\(F(p+h)=p+2h-F(h)\).  The inverse case is equivalent.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact escape clocks}

\begin{corollary}[Dyadic escape time]
\label{p12:cor:escape-clock}
Fix \(a\in(0,1/2)\).  For \(x\in(p,p+a)\), let
\[
 \tau_a(x)=\min\{n\ge0:F^n(x)\ge p+a\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \tau_a(x)=
 \Ceiling{\log_2\frac{\Theta(p+a)}{\Theta(x)}}.
 \label{p12:eq:escape-time}
\end{equation}
The left-half formula is obtained by absolute values.  As \(x\to p\),
\begin{equation}
 \log_2\frac{\Theta(p+a)}{|\Theta(x)|}
 =-\log_2|x-p|+\log_2\Theta(p+a)+\flatremainder(x-p).
 \label{p12:eq:escape-asymptotic}
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In the \(\Theta\)-coordinate, one forward iterate is multiplication by two.  Therefore the
first crossing of \(p+a\) is the first \(n\) with
\(2^n\Theta(x)\ge\Theta(p+a)\).  Flatness gives the final expansion.
\end{proof}

\section{A logarithmic B\"ottcher height at the endpoints}
\label{p12:sec:bottcher}

The coordinate \(\Theta\) solves the hyperbolic dynamics
globally, but its endpoint inverse \(\Theta^{-1}(t)\) as \(|t|\to\infty\) is highly
non-elementary.  Independently of the linearization, the leading endpoint law implies a
natural doubling height adapted to the endpoint logarithm.

Put
\begin{equation}
 L=\log2,
 \qquad a=\frac1{2L}.
 \label{p12:eq:a-endpoint}
\end{equation}
Equation \eqref{p12:eq:dyadic-leading-input} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
 -\log F(\EulerE^{-s})=a s^2(1+\LittleO(1))
 \qquad(s\to\infty).
 \label{p12:eq:endpoint-s-law}
\end{equation}
For \(0<x<p\), define
\begin{equation}
 z(x)=\log\bigl(a[-\log x]\bigr),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon(x)=z(F(x))-2z(x).
 \label{p12:eq:z-epsilon}
\end{equation}
Then \(\varepsilon(x)\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\): with \(s=-\log x\to\infty\),
\eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-s-law} gives
\(z(F(x))=\log\bigl(a\cdot as^2(1+\LittleO(1))\bigr)=2\log(as)+\LittleO(1)=2z(x)+\LittleO(1)\).
The function \(\varepsilon\) is continuous on \((0,p)\), being composed of continuous
functions.

\begin{theorem}[Endpoint dynamical height]
\label{p12:thm:endpoint-height}
For every \(x\in(0,p)\), the limit
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 B(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}2^{-n}
 \log\left(a[-\log F^n(x)]\right)}
 \label{p12:eq:B-limit}
\end{equation}
exists, is positive, and is continuous in \(x\).  It has the convergent cocycle series
\begin{equation}
 B(x)=z(x)+\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}2^{-k-1}\varepsilon(F^k(x))
 \label{p12:eq:B-series}
\end{equation}
and satisfies the exact B\"ottcher-type equation
\begin{equation}
 B(F(x))=2B(x).
 \label{p12:eq:B-doubling}
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every fixed \(x\in(0,p)\),
\begin{equation}
 -\log F^n(x)
 =2L\exp\bigl(2^nB(x)+\LittleO(1)\bigr),
 \label{p12:eq:double-exp-log}
\end{equation}
or equivalently
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 F^n(x)=
 \exp\left\{-2L\exp\bigl(2^nB(x)+\LittleO(1)\bigr)\right\}.}
 \label{p12:eq:double-exponential-orbit}
\end{equation}
For \(p<x<1\), define \(B_{\mathrm R}(x)=B(1-x)\).  Reflection gives the explicit
right-endpoint formula
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 1-F^n(x)=
 \exp\left\{-2L\exp\bigl(2^nB_{\mathrm R}(x)+\LittleO(1)\bigr)\right\}.}
 \label{p12:eq:double-exponential-right-orbit}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(x_n=F^n(x)\), \(s_n=-\log x_n\), and \(z_n=\log(as_n)\).  Since \(F(x)<x\) on the
left half, \(x_n\downarrow0\).  Equation \eqref{p12:eq:endpoint-s-law} gives
\begin{equation}
 z_{n+1}=2z_n+\varepsilon(x_n),
 \qquad \varepsilon(x_n)\to0.
 \label{p12:eq:z-recurrence}
\end{equation}
Thus
\[
 2^{-n}z_n=z_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{-k-1}\varepsilon(x_k),
\]
and the series converges absolutely because \(\varepsilon(x_k)\to0\), so that its terms are
eventually bounded by \(2^{-k-1}\).
This proves \eqref{p12:eq:B-limit} and \eqref{p12:eq:B-series}.  On a compact
\(K\Subset(0,p)\), the continuous functions \(F^k|_K\) decrease pointwise to the continuous
limit zero.  Dini's theorem makes this convergence uniform, i.e.\
\(\delta_k=\sup_KF^k\to0\).  Consequently
\(\sup_{x\in K}|\varepsilon(F^k(x))|\le\sup_{0<y\le\delta_k}|\varepsilon(y)|\to0\) by the limit
\(\varepsilon(y)\to0\) established above, and the geometrically weighted series in
\eqref{p12:eq:B-series} converges uniformly on \(K\).  This proves continuity of \(B\).  Shifting
the orbit proves \eqref{p12:eq:B-doubling}.

The tail identity
\[
 2^nB(x)-z_n
 =\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}2^{n-k-1}\varepsilon(x_k)
\]
tends to zero.  Therefore \(z_n=2^nB(x)+\LittleO(1)\), which gives
\eqref{p12:eq:double-exp-log} and \eqref{p12:eq:double-exponential-orbit}.  Also \(z_n\to+\infty\).
If \(B(x)<0\), the tail identity would force \(z_n\to-\infty\); if \(B(x)=0\), it would force
\(z_n\to0\).  Both alternatives are impossible, so \(B(x)>0\).

Finally, reflection iterates exactly:
\(
 1-F^n(x)=F^n(1-x)
\).
Applying \eqref{p12:eq:double-exponential-orbit} to \(1-x\in(0,p)\) proves
\eqref{p12:eq:double-exponential-right-orbit}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A periodic quotient of the two dynamical coordinates}

Let \(\Theta\) be the coordinate of \cref{p12:thm:global-theta}.  Both \(B\) and
\(-\Theta\) double under \(F\) on the left half.  Their quotient is invariant along each
orbit, and in the linear coordinate invariance becomes periodicity.

\begin{theorem}[Dynamical one-periodic factor]
\label{p12:thm:dynamical-periodic}
Define, for \(u\in\RealNumbers\),
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{dyn}}(u)
 =2^{-u}B\!\left(\Theta^{-1}(-2^u)\right).
 \label{p12:eq:Pdyn-def}
\end{equation}
Then \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{dyn}}\) is positive, continuous, and one-periodic.  For every
\(x\in(0,p)\),
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 B(x)=(-\Theta(x))\,
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{dyn}}\!\left(\log_2[-\Theta(x)]\right).}
 \label{p12:eq:B-theta-periodic}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If \(x_u=\Theta^{-1}(-2^u)\), then
\(
 x_{u+1}=F(x_u)
\)
by \cref{p12:thm:global-theta}.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{dyn}}(u+1)
 =2^{-u-1}B(F(x_u))
 =2^{-u}B(x_u).
\]
The representation \eqref{p12:eq:B-theta-periodic} is the definition with
\(u=\log_2[-\Theta(x)]\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The repository's sharp endpoint expansion contains a nonconstant periodic function
\(\Psi\) of a lower-Lambert phase.  The periodic factor
\(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{dyn}}\) is different in construction: it is extracted from composition
orbits and the global Schr\"oder coordinate.  Determining the transform between the two
periodic objects is one of the main open problems proposed below.
\end{remark}

\section{Numerical experiments and exact symbolic checks}
\label{p12:sec:numerics}

\begin{statusbox}{Role of computation}
All theorems above are proved independently of numerics.  The included Python program uses exact rational
arithmetic for cumulants, moments, and Legendre coefficients, and common-random-number Monte
Carlo only as a consistency check of the pathwise derivative formula.
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Reproducibility package}

This part's verification material is kept in the volume directory under
\path{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/}, which holds
\begin{itemize}
\item \path{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/code/fabius_q_response_experiments.py}, with detailed comments;
\item exact CSV tables under \path{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/data/};
\item Monte Carlo validation tables in the same \path{data/} directory;
\item the figures under \path{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/figures/}; and
\item \path{assets/q-fabius-parameter-deformations/Fabius_Flat_Parameter_Response_Dynamics/NUMERICAL_README.txt} with the run parameters.
\end{itemize}
The reported run used \(10^6\) pathwise samples, \(1.5\times10^6\) common-random-number CDF
samples, \(32\) geometric digits, and a central-difference step \(h=0.005\).  The omitted tail
weight near \(q=1/2\) is approximately \(2^{-32}\), far below the sampling resolution.

\subsection{Tangent CDF and antisymmetry}

A common set of digits was evaluated at \(q=1/2+h\) and \(q=1/2-h\), and the two empirical
CDFs were differenced.  The exact theory predicts \(G(1-x)=-G(x)\).  Across the displayed grid
the root-mean-square antisymmetry residual was approximately \(5.8\times10^{-3}\), compared
with a peak response magnitude of about \(0.43\) (the grid maximum of the estimate is
\(0.4337\)).
